cards.front:
The number of protons in an atom's nucleus is called its:

(A) Mass number
(B) Atomic number
(C) Atomic weight
(D) Valency
cards.back:
(B) Atomic number

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Atomic number (Z) = number of protons, identifies the element. Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons. For a neutral atom, the number of electrons = atomic number. Atomic weight is the weighted average mass of all isotopes. Valency is the combining capacity, usually tied to outer-shell electrons.

cards.front:
Atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers are called:

(A) Isobars
(B) Isotopes
(C) Isomers
(D) Isotones
cards.back:
(B) Isotopes

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Isotopes — same Z (same element), different A (different neutron count). Example — Carbon-12 and Carbon-14. Isobars — same A but different Z (different elements): argon-40 and calcium-40. Isotones — same number of neutrons but different elements. Isomers — different structural arrangements of the same molecular formula (organic chemistry).

cards.front:
The particle discovered by J. J. Thomson in 1897 through cathode-ray experiments was the:

(A) Proton
(B) Electron
(C) Neutron
(D) Positron
cards.back:
(B) Electron

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — J. J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 while studying cathode rays in vacuum tubes. He proposed the 'plum pudding' model of the atom (1904) — electrons embedded in a sphere of positive charge. Rutherford discovered the proton (and his 1911 gold-foil experiment gave the nuclear model). Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932. The positron (anti-electron) was discovered by Anderson in 1932.

cards.front:
Among the three subatomic particles — electron, proton and neutron — the one with virtually no electrical charge is the:

(A) Electron
(B) Neutron
(C) Proton
(D) Both electron and neutron
cards.back:
(B) Neutron

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Neutron — electrically neutral; mass ~1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Proton — positive charge (+1e); mass ~1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Electron — negative charge (−1e); mass ~9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg (about 1/1,836 of a proton). Mass of an atom is almost entirely in the nucleus (protons + neutrons).

cards.front:
Niels Bohr's atomic model (1913) proposed that electrons move around the nucleus in:

(A) Random clouds
(B) Fixed circular orbits with quantised energies
(C) Straight lines
(D) Stationary positions
cards.back:
(B) Fixed circular orbits with quantised energies

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Bohr's model (1913) — electrons revolve in specific, quantised circular orbits (shells labelled K, L, M, N, with energies E₁, E₂, E₃, …). An electron emits or absorbs a photon only when jumping between orbits. This successfully explained hydrogen's discrete line spectrum. Modern quantum mechanics replaces the orbit picture with orbital 'clouds' of probability density, but Bohr's quantisation remains a key step.

cards.front:
The maximum number of electrons that can be accommodated in the L (second) shell of an atom is:

(A) 2
(B) 8
(C) 18
(D) 32
cards.back:
(B) 8

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Capacity of a shell = 2n² where n is the shell number. K (n=1) → 2; L (n=2) → 8; M (n=3) → 18; N (n=4) → 32. The outermost shell — whatever its full capacity — can never hold more than 8 electrons in ground state (the octet rule); Bohr-Bury scheme.

cards.front:
The two stable isotopes of chlorine have mass numbers 35 and 37. Its standard atomic weight (~35.5) reflects:

(A) Exact average of 35 and 37
(B) Weighted average
(C) An unstable radioactive isotope
(D) A measurement error
cards.back:
(B) Weighted average

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Chlorine's natural abundance is ~75.8% Cl-35 and ~24.2% Cl-37. Weighted average = 0.758 × 35 + 0.242 × 37 ≈ 35.48. This is why the periodic table lists chlorine's atomic mass as 35.5 rather than a whole number. A simple arithmetic mean of 35 and 37 would give 36 — which is wrong because it ignores abundance. about 75% Cl-35 and 25% Cl-37.

cards.front:
The OXIDATION NUMBER of an element in its FREE/elemental form is:

(A) Zero (in pure element)
(B) Always positive value
(C) Always negative value
(D) Equal to atomic number
cards.back:
(A) Zero (in pure element)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — OXIDATION NUMBER (oxidation state) RULES (memorize): (1) ELEMENT in PURE/FREE form (atomic or molecular): oxidation number = ZERO. Examples: Na (s), O₂ (g), N₂, Cl₂, S₈, P₄, Fe (s), C (graphite). All atoms in these molecules: ON = 0. (2) IONS — equals charge of ion: Na⁺ → +1; Cl⁻ → −1; Mg²⁺ → +2; O²⁻ → −2. (3) HYDROGEN: typically +1 (H₂O: H = +1); EXCEPTION: −1 in metal hydrides (NaH, MgH₂). (4) OXYGEN: typically −2 (in oxides, H₂O); EXCEPTIONS: −1 in peroxides (H₂O₂, Na₂O₂); +2 in OF₂. (5) FLUORINE always −1 (most electronegative). (6) HALOGENS (Cl, Br, I) typically −1 in binary compounds; can be +1, +3, +5, +7 with O. (7) ALKALI METALS (Group 1): always +1 (Na, K, Li). (8) ALKALINE EARTH (Group 2): always +2 (Mg, Ca, Ba). (9) SUM RULE: total oxidation states must equal NET CHARGE of compound/ion. KEY APPLICATIONS: (a) IDENTIFYING REDOX REACTIONS (oxidation = increase in ON; reduction = decrease). (b) BALANCING REDOX EQUATIONS. (c) Predicting stability of oxidation states. UPSC angle: redox is staple of NEET, NCERT Class 11, JEE-Main. PYQ FREQUENCY: ON of element-in-element form in NEET, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
What is the oxidation number of S in SO₄²⁻ (sulfate)?

(A) +6 (using rule: 4×−2 + S = −2)
(B) +4 (an under-estimate) (option here)
(C) −2 (oxygen value here) (option here)
(D) +2 (way under-shot) (option here)
cards.back:
(A) +6 (using rule: 4×−2 + S = −2)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Apply SUM RULE: total oxidation numbers = NET charge of ion. SO₄²⁻ has net charge −2. EQUATION: S + 4(O) = −2; with O = −2 (standard rule), 4 × (−2) = −8; S + (−8) = −2 → S = +6. So sulfur is in OXIDATION STATE +6 in sulfate. KEY S OXIDATION STATES: −2 (H₂S, sulfides like Na₂S); 0 (S₈, elemental); +2 (S₂Cl₂); +4 (SO₂, SO₃²⁻ sulfite); +6 (SO₃, SO₄²⁻ sulfate, H₂SO₄ sulfuric acid). KEY METHOD for finding ON in compounds: (1) Apply known rules: O = −2, H = +1 (with exceptions). (2) Set unknown element's ON as variable. (3) Balance: sum of all ON × atom count = total charge (0 for neutral; ion charge for ion). (4) Solve. PRACTICE — find ON of: (a) Cl in HClO₃: H + Cl + 3O = 0 → 1 + Cl + (−6) = 0 → Cl = +5. (b) N in NO₃⁻: N + 3(−2) = −1 → N = +5. (c) Mn in KMnO₄: K + Mn + 4(−2) = 0 → 1 + Mn + (−8) = 0 → Mn = +7. (d) Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇: 2(+1) + 2Cr + 7(−2) = 0 → 2 + 2Cr − 14 = 0 → Cr = +6. (e) Fe in FeCl₃: Fe + 3(−1) = 0 → Fe = +3 (ferric/Fe³⁺). PYQ FREQUENCY: ON-calculation problems in NEET, JEE-Main 2-3× per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests systematic application of rules.

cards.front:
OXIDATION is best defined as:

(A) Loss of electrons / gain in ON
(B) Gain of electrons / loss in ON
(C) Addition of water in compound
(D) Removal of all hydrogen atoms
cards.back:
(A) Loss of electrons / gain in ON

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — OXIDATION (modern definition): LOSS of ELECTRONS by an atom or ion → INCREASE in oxidation number. REDUCTION: GAIN of electrons → DECREASE in oxidation number. MNEMONIC: OIL RIG ('Oxidation Is Loss; Reduction Is Gain' — of electrons). Or LEO GER ('Loss of Electrons = Oxidation; Gain of Electrons = Reduction'). REDOX REACTIONS: oxidation + reduction occur TOGETHER (one substance loses e⁻, another gains). Cannot have one without other. EXAMPLES: (1) Combustion: C + O₂ → CO₂. C goes from 0 to +4 (oxidized); O₂ goes from 0 to −2 (reduced). (2) Rusting: Fe (0) → Fe³⁺ (+3); O₂ → O²⁻. (3) Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂; C reduced (+4 → 0); O oxidized (−2 → 0). (4) Battery: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu; Zn oxidized, Cu²⁺ reduced. HISTORICAL DEFINITIONS — broader: (a) ORIGINAL: oxidation = ADDITION of OXYGEN. Reduction = REMOVAL of OXYGEN. (b) EXTENDED: oxidation = REMOVAL of HYDROGEN. (c) MODERN ELECTRON-TRANSFER: above. Modern definition is most general (covers reactions without O or H). KEY INDIA APPLICATIONS: (a) RUSTING — major economic loss. (b) Steel-making (Bessemer process). (c) Mineral extraction. UPSC angle: redox in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT Class 11. PYQ FREQUENCY: redox definition in NEET 1-2× per paper, NCERT 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
In H₂O₂ (hydrogen peroxide), the oxidation number of OXYGEN is:

(A) −1 (peroxide exception)
(B) −2 (standard oxide value)
(C) 0 (a wrong calc here)
(D) +1 (positive value wrong)
cards.back:
(A) −1 (peroxide exception)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — EXCEPTION TO O = −2 RULE: in PEROXIDES (H₂O₂, Na₂O₂, BaO₂), OXYGEN is in oxidation state −1. Why? Two oxygen atoms are connected by a single O−O bond; each oxygen has gained only ONE electron from the other partner, not two. Apply sum: H₂O₂ neutral. 2H = 2 × (+1) = +2. 2O = total = −2. So each O = −1. STANDARD RULES revisited: (a) O = −2 in most oxides (CO₂, H₂O, MgO). (b) O = −1 in PEROXIDES (H₂O₂, Na₂O₂). (c) O = −1/2 in SUPEROXIDES (KO₂, RbO₂). (d) O = +2 in OF₂ (oxygen fluoride — F more electronegative than O). (e) O = +1 in O₂F₂. (f) O = 0 in elemental O₂. PEROXIDES uses + properties: H₂O₂ is OXIDIZING agent (releases O atom: H₂O₂ → H₂O + ½O₂); used as DISINFECTANT (3% solution for wounds), HAIR BLEACH (~6%), ROCKET propellant (~98% concentration), pulp/paper bleaching, water treatment. INDIA: H₂O₂ used widely in textile industry (cotton bleaching), dental treatments. SUPEROXIDES form between Group 1 metals + O₂: very reactive; KO₂ used in OXYGEN GENERATORS (submarines, space stations) — reacts with CO₂ to release O₂. PYQ FREQUENCY: O = −1 in peroxide is a NEET, JEE-Main top trap — 1× per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests rule-exceptions awareness.

cards.front:
In NH₃ (ammonia), oxidation number of NITROGEN is:

(A) −3 (using N + 3H = 0)
(B) +3 (sign wrong here)
(C) 0 (a wrong calc value)
(D) −1 (way under-shot calc)
cards.back:
(A) −3 (using N + 3H = 0)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Apply RULES: NH₃ is neutral (charge = 0). H = +1 (standard). So N + 3(+1) = 0 → N = −3. So N is in oxidation state −3 in ammonia. KEY N OXIDATION STATES (memorize): −3 (NH₃ ammonia, NH₄⁺ ammonium); −2 (N₂H₄ hydrazine); −1 (NH₂OH hydroxylamine); 0 (N₂ elemental); +1 (N₂O nitrous oxide, 'laughing gas'); +2 (NO nitric oxide); +3 (HNO₂ nitrous acid, NO₂⁻ nitrite); +4 (NO₂ nitrogen dioxide); +5 (HNO₃ nitric acid, NO₃⁻ nitrate). NITROGEN's RANGE of OXIDATION STATES (−3 to +5) is the WIDEST among common elements — nitrogen is incredibly versatile in chemistry. AMMONIA NH₃: (a) Strong base, accepts proton → NH₄⁺. (b) Industrial: HABER PROCESS (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃) at high T, P, with Fe catalyst — billions of tonnes/year for fertilizers. (c) UREA, ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulphate fertilizers all from ammonia. (d) INDIA: ~25 million tonnes urea/year (largest urea producer); fertilizer subsidies major govt expenditure. UPSC angle: AGRICULTURE — fertilizer policy, nitrogen pollution (excess runoff causes algal blooms, eutrophication). NCERT Class 12 mentions N's variable oxidation states extensively. NUCLEAR: N₂O₄ is rocket fuel oxidizer. PYQ FREQUENCY: N oxidation states in NEET, JEE-Main 2-3× per paper.

cards.front:
In KMnO₄ (potassium permanganate, an oxidizing agent), oxidation number of Mn is:

(A) +7 (highest oxidation state of Mn)
(B) +4 (lower oxidation state)
(C) +2 (way under-shot) (option here)
(D) +6 (calc near-miss) (option here)
cards.back:
(A) +7 (highest oxidation state of Mn)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Apply: K + Mn + 4O = 0. K = +1 (Group 1), O = −2 (standard). 1 + Mn + 4(−2) = 0 → 1 + Mn − 8 = 0 → Mn = +7. So Mn is in +7 state — HIGHEST possible for manganese. WHY KMnO₄ is a STRONG OXIDIZER: it ACCEPTS electrons readily (gets REDUCED), going from +7 → +2 (in acidic conditions) or +4 (in neutral/alkaline) — large electron-gain. COMMON Mn OXIDATION STATES: 0 (Mn metal); +2 (MnSO₄, Mn²⁺ salts — pale pink); +3; +4 (MnO₂ — used in dry cells); +6 (MnO₄²⁻ manganate); +7 (KMnO₄ — DEEP PURPLE solution, characteristic). KMnO₄ USES: (1) DISINFECTANT — for wounds, skin infections, water purification (potency known as 'Condy's Crystals' historically). (2) BLEACHING agent — paper, textiles. (3) WATER TREATMENT — removes iron, manganese, hydrogen sulfide. (4) ANALYTICAL — TITRATION (deep purple → colourless when reduced; SELF-INDICATING). (5) REDOX TITRATION standard reagent. (6) Anti-fungal in soaks for athlete's foot. INDIA INDUSTRIAL: KMnO₄ is a major export item (India is leading producer; Tamil Nadu has largest plants). 2014 export: India accounted for ~70% of global KMnO₄ supply. UPSC angle: industry-specific facts in PT general awareness; environmental impact of manganese mining. PYQ FREQUENCY: KMnO₄ oxidation state in NEET, JEE-Main 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
In K₂Cr₂O₇ (potassium dichromate), what is the oxidation number of Cr?

(A) +6 (using sum-rule calc)
(B) +3 (different chromium salt)
(C) +7 (over-shot value)
(D) +2 (way under-shot)
cards.back:
(A) +6 (using sum-rule calc)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Apply rules: K = +1, O = −2; total charge = 0 (neutral compound). 2(+1) + 2(Cr) + 7(−2) = 0 → 2 + 2Cr − 14 = 0 → 2Cr = 12 → Cr = +6. So chromium is in +6 oxidation state in dichromate. KEY Cr OXIDATION STATES: 0 (Cr metal); +2 (CrO, Cr²⁺ salts — blue); +3 (Cr₂O₃, Cr³⁺ salts — green); +6 (CrO₃, K₂Cr₂O₇, Na₂CrO₄ — orange/yellow). K₂Cr₂O₇ (Potassium DICHROMATE) — orange-red crystalline solid; STRONG OXIDIZING AGENT in acidic medium: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O. USES: (1) ANALYTICAL — REDOX titrations (e.g., COD test for water quality — chemical oxygen demand). (2) LEATHER tanning. (3) DYES + pigments. (4) WOOD preservatives. (5) Photography (historical). RELATED: K₂CrO₄ (chromate) — yellow; in alkaline solution. Equilibrium: 2 CrO₄²⁻ (yellow) + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange) + H₂O. Color shifts indicate pH. SAFETY: Cr⁶⁺ compounds are HIGHLY TOXIC + CARCINOGENIC (Erin Brockovich case in USA — Cr-6 in groundwater Hinkley, California). India: hexavalent chromium pollution from leather industry (Tamil Nadu, Kanpur — major problem; tanneries restricted under SC orders). UPSC angle: industrial pollution + environmental law (Water Act 1974, Air Act 1981, Environment Protection Act 1986). PYQ FREQUENCY: Cr oxidation states in NEET, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
The MODERN PERIODIC TABLE arranges elements in increasing order of:

(A) Atomic number (number of protons)
(B) Atomic mass (number of nucleons)
(C) Atomic radius (size of atom)
(D) Electron count (only outer shell)
cards.back:
(A) Atomic number (number of protons)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — MODERN PERIODIC TABLE is arranged in increasing ATOMIC NUMBER (Z = number of PROTONS in nucleus). Established by HENRY MOSELEY (1913) using X-RAY SPECTRA — confirmed atomic number, not atomic mass, is the fundamental ordering principle. CONTRAST WITH MENDELEEV (1869): Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev's first periodic table arranged elements by ATOMIC MASS (with some adjustments). His genius: LEFT GAPS for undiscovered elements (e.g., gallium, germanium); PREDICTED their properties — later confirmed. KEY FACTS: (1) DMITRI MENDELEEV (1834-1907) — 'Father of Periodic Table'; published 1869. (2) HENRY MOSELEY (1887-1915) — discovered atomic number ordering; killed in WWI at Gallipoli, age 27. (3) MODERN PERIODIC LAW: 'Properties of elements are PERIODIC FUNCTIONS of their ATOMIC NUMBERS.' STRUCTURE: 7 PERIODS (rows), 18 GROUPS (columns); 4 BLOCKS (s, p, d, f). KEY PERIODIC TRENDS (memorize for SSC, JEE-Main, NEET): (1) ATOMIC RADIUS — increases DOWN, decreases ACROSS. (2) IONIZATION ENERGY — decreases DOWN, increases ACROSS. (3) ELECTRONEGATIVITY — decreases DOWN, increases ACROSS (peaks at F = 4.0). (4) METALLIC CHARACTER — increases DOWN, decreases ACROSS. (5) ELECTRON AFFINITY — generally increases ACROSS (with exceptions). PYQ FREQUENCY: modern periodic table basis in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
How many GROUPS are there in the MODERN periodic table?

(A) 18 groups (vertical columns)
(B) 8 groups (Mendeleev-style)
(C) 7 groups (number of periods)
(D) 10 groups (only some columns)
cards.back:
(A) 18 groups (vertical columns)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — MODERN PERIODIC TABLE: 18 GROUPS (vertical columns) + 7 PERIODS (horizontal rows). CONTRAST: MENDELEEV's original had 8 groups (Roman I-VIII); modern numbers 1-18 (IUPAC convention since 1988). KEY GROUPS (memorize): (1) GROUP 1 — Alkali Metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) + H. (2) GROUP 2 — Alkaline Earth Metals (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra). (3) GROUPS 3-12 — d-block / TRANSITION METALS (Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn — Period 4). (4) GROUP 13 — Boron group (B, Al, Ga, In, Tl). (5) GROUP 14 — Carbon group (C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb). (6) GROUP 15 — Nitrogen group / pnictogens (N, P, As, Sb, Bi). (7) GROUP 16 — Oxygen group / chalcogens (O, S, Se, Te, Po). (8) GROUP 17 — HALOGENS (F, Cl, Br, I, At). (9) GROUP 18 — NOBLE GASES (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn). LANTHANIDES + ACTINIDES — f-block elements; placed below main table for compact layout. NUMBER of ELEMENTS: 118 confirmed (as of 2024). LATEST: Tennessine (117, 2010), Oganesson (118, 2002 — most recent named, 2016). KEY MEMORIZATION: 'Atomic numbers of common elements: H=1, He=2, C=6, N=7, O=8, Na=11, Mg=12, Al=13, Si=14, P=15, S=16, Cl=17, K=19, Ca=20, Fe=26, Cu=29, Zn=30, Ag=47, Au=79, U=92.' UPSC angle: PERIODIC TABLE in NEET + science-tech awareness. PYQ FREQUENCY: groups + periods count in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
LANTHANIDES are also known as:

(A) Rare Earth Elements (REEs)
(B) Noble metals (gold, silver)
(C) Alkali metals (Group 1)
(D) Halogens (Group 17 here)
cards.back:
(A) Rare Earth Elements (REEs)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — LANTHANIDES (also written 'lanthanoids') — series of 15 elements from LANTHANUM (La, Z=57) to LUTETIUM (Lu, Z=71). Plus YTTRIUM (Y, 39) + SCANDIUM (Sc, 21) commonly grouped → 17 RARE EARTH ELEMENTS (REEs). NAME 'rare earth' is misnomer — they're actually MODERATELY ABUNDANT in Earth's crust (some more than copper) but RARELY found in CONCENTRATED ore deposits. KEY REEs + uses: (1) NEODYMIUM (Nd) — strongest permanent magnets (NdFeB) → wind turbines, EVs, hard drives, headphones. (2) CERIUM (Ce) — catalytic converters, glass polishing. (3) LANTHANUM (La) — camera lenses, batteries (Ni-MH). (4) DYSPROSIUM (Dy) — magnets at high T. (5) EUROPIUM (Eu) — red phosphors in TVs/LEDs. (6) YTTRIUM (Y) — superconductors, lasers. (7) PRASEODYMIUM (Pr) — yellow ceramics. (8) GADOLINIUM (Gd) — MRI contrast agents. WHY SO IMPORTANT: ESSENTIAL for renewable energy (wind, EV magnets), defence (radars, missile guidance), electronics (smartphones), medical imaging. CHINA dominates ~70% of global REE production + ~85% processing. INDIA's REE RESERVES: 6.9 million tonnes (5th largest globally) — mostly in MONAZITE sands (Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra coasts). INDIAN RARE EARTHS LIMITED (IREL) — main producer. KEY POLICY: NATIONAL CRITICAL MINERALS LIST released 2023 — 30 critical minerals including most REEs. UPSC angle: STRATEGIC MINERALS + CHINA dependency reduction; India-Australia critical minerals agreement. PYQ FREQUENCY: REEs in UPSC PT, GS-3 economy, current affairs 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
MENDELEEV LEFT GAPS in his periodic table for:

(A) Undiscovered elements (predicted properties)
(B) Inert/radioactive elements only
(C) Hydrogen position only here
(D) Metalloids he was uncertain
cards.back:
(A) Undiscovered elements (predicted properties)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — MENDELEEV (1869) — anticipated existence of UNDISCOVERED elements; left gaps + PREDICTED their properties using PERIODIC TRENDS. PROPHECY CONFIRMED: (1) GALLIUM (Ga, Z=31) — predicted as 'eka-aluminium' (eka = beyond, Sanskrit). Discovered 1875 by Lecoq de Boisbaudran in France. Predicted: atomic mass ~68; actual: 70. (2) GERMANIUM (Ge, Z=32) — predicted as 'eka-silicon'. Discovered 1886 by Winkler in Germany. (3) SCANDIUM (Sc, Z=21) — predicted as 'eka-boron'. Discovered 1879 by Nilson in Sweden. KEY: Mendeleev's PROPERTIES were REMARKABLY ACCURATE — atomic mass, density, oxide formulas, compounds — within ~5%. This was the GREATEST TRIUMPH of his periodic law + earned scientific acceptance. SANSKRIT PREFIXES used by Mendeleev: 'EKA' (one beyond), 'DVI' (two beyond), 'TRI' (three beyond). e.g., 'ekaboron' = next-down from boron in same group. UPSC angle: SCIENCE in INDIA's COLONIAL era; Sanskrit's influence on Western science. ALSO MENDELEEV's PREDICTIONS extended to: (a) Reorder some elements (atomic-mass anomalies — e.g., Te before I despite slightly higher mass, because chemistry suggested otherwise; later confirmed by Moseley using atomic number). (b) Group Re/Tc as homologs, even though Tc was undiscovered. NOBEL: Mendeleev was NOMINATED 5 times — never won (controversial; politics in Nobel committee). PYQ FREQUENCY: Mendeleev's predictions in NEET, NCERT, history-of-science 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which element has the HIGHEST ELECTRONEGATIVITY?

(A) Fluorine (F = 4.0 on Pauling scale)
(B) Oxygen (O = 3.5 - second only)
(C) Nitrogen (N = 3.0 - third)
(D) Chlorine (Cl = 3.2 - similar)
cards.back:
(A) Fluorine (F = 4.0 on Pauling scale)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — FLUORINE (F) — most electronegative element. PAULING SCALE: F = 4.0 (highest possible — used as reference). KEY ELECTRONEGATIVITIES: F > O (3.5) > N ≈ Cl (3.0-3.2) > Br (2.96) > I, S (2.5-2.6) > C, H (~2.5, 2.1) > metalsel (Na 0.9, Cs 0.7 lowest). DEFINITION: ELECTRONEGATIVITY = ability of an atom in a molecule to ATTRACT BONDED ELECTRONS. KEY TRENDS: (1) ACROSS A PERIOD: increases (atoms get smaller, nucleus pulls more strongly). (2) DOWN A GROUP: decreases (more inner shielding). PEAK at F (top-right of metals); LOWEST at Cs/Fr (bottom-left). KEY CONSEQUENCES: (1) HIGH-electronegativity-pair → IONIC bond (e.g., NaCl: ENs differ by 2.1). (2) LOW-difference → COVALENT bond (CCl₄). (3) Electronegativity DIFFERENCE PREDICTS BOND POLARITY: Δ > 1.7 = ionic; 0.4-1.7 = polar covalent; < 0.4 = nonpolar covalent. DIPOLE MOMENT in molecules depends on electronegativity differences. WATER (H₂O): Δ_OH = 1.4 → polar; bent shape → permanent dipole; explains H₂O's UNIQUE properties (high BP, surface tension, universal solvent). FLUORINE compounds: HF (hydrofluoric — etches glass), CFCs (banned), Teflon (PTFE — non-stick), fluorides in toothpaste. KEY: FLUORINE the SMALLEST + MOST AGGRESSIVE oxidizer in nature; reacts with EVERYTHING incl. noble gases (XeF₂, XeF₄). UPSC angle: chemical bonding + electronegativity in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Elements in the SAME GROUP of the periodic table have similar:

(A) Number of valence (outer) electrons
(B) Atomic number values close
(C) Same physical state always
(D) Identical atomic masses always
cards.back:
(A) Number of valence (outer) electrons

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — ELEMENTS in same GROUP have SAME NUMBER of VALENCE ELECTRONS — explaining their similar chemical behavior. EXAMPLES: (1) GROUP 1 (alkali metals: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs) — all have ONE valence electron; all form +1 ions, react vigorously with water, etc. (2) GROUP 17 (halogens: F, Cl, Br, I) — all have SEVEN valence electrons; all form −1 ions; all need ONE more electron for octet → highly reactive. (3) GROUP 18 (noble gases: He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe) — all have FULL outer shells (8 electrons; He has 2); all are mostly INERT. (4) GROUP 14 (C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb) — 4 valence electrons; tend to form 4 covalent bonds. KEY VALENCE PATTERN by group: GROUP 1: 1 outer e⁻; GROUP 2: 2; GROUP 13: 3; GROUP 14: 4; GROUP 15: 5; GROUP 16: 6; GROUP 17: 7; GROUP 18: 8 (or 2 for He). MIDDLE-GROUP (transition metals, Groups 3-12): variable d-electron counts; complex bonding. WITHIN GROUP — TRENDS: as you go DOWN: (1) Atomic radius INCREASES (more shells). (2) Reactivity INCREASES (alkali metals) or DECREASES (halogens). (3) Metallic character INCREASES. (4) Ionization energy DECREASES. (5) Electronegativity DECREASES. PERIOD vs GROUP: PERIOD = number of SHELLS; GROUP = number of OUTER ELECTRONS. Period 4 element: 4 shells. Group 7 (halogens): 7 outer e⁻. UPSC angle: chemistry foundations needed for NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT-tested. PYQ FREQUENCY: same-group properties in NEET, JEE-Main 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which is the HEAVIEST NATURALLY-OCCURRING element?

(A) Uranium (Z=92, naturally on Earth)
(B) Plutonium (Z=94, mostly synthetic)
(C) Oganesson (Z=118, fully synthetic)
(D) Helium (Z=2, lightest gas)
cards.back:
(A) Uranium (Z=92, naturally on Earth)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — URANIUM (U, Z=92) — heaviest NATURALLY-OCCURRING element on Earth in significant quantities (in uraninite/pitchblende ore). Trace amounts of NEPTUNIUM (93) + PLUTONIUM (94) found NATURALLY (from cosmic-ray + uranium-decay processes — extreme trace). ELEMENTS BEYOND URANIUM: 'TRANSURANIUM' — all SYNTHETIC (created in reactors/accelerators). KEY DISCOVERIES of TRANSURANIC elements: (1) Np (1940), Pu (1940-41) — Berkeley Lab. (2) Am, Cm, Bk, Cf — Berkeley, Glenn Seaborg's group. (3) Es, Fm — discovered in fallout from H-bomb tests! (4) Md (101), No (102), Lr (103). (5) RUTHERFORDIUM (104) onwards — heavy-ion collisions. (6) OGANESSON (118) — most recent (2002, named 2016 after YURI OGANESSIAN, Russian physicist; only one ever made). HEAVIEST elements have very SHORT half-lives (microseconds for some); only a few atoms ever produced. URANIUM PROPERTIES: silvery-white metal; very dense (19 g/cm³ — denser than lead). USES: nuclear reactors (U-235), nuclear weapons, depleted uranium (DU) in armor-piercing munitions, ceramics. RADIOACTIVE: U-238 half-life 4.5 BILLION YEARS (~age of Earth!). U-235 half-life 700 million years. NATURAL OCCURRENCE: found in granite, ocean water (~3 ppb), monazite sand. INDIA's URANIUM RESERVES: ~118,000 tonnes (Jharkhand — Jaduguda mine; Andhra — Tummalapalle mine; Meghalaya). HEAVIEST STABLE element: BISMUTH (Z=83) — was thought stable; recently shown to be slightly radioactive (half-life 10²⁰ years — longer than age of universe!). PYQ FREQUENCY: uranium-related in NEET, GA 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
The modern periodic table has how many groups (vertical columns)?

(A) Eight
(B) Eighteen
(C) Seven
(D) Sixteen
cards.back:
(B) Eighteen

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — The modern (long-form) periodic table has 18 groups and 7 periods. Mendeleev's original table (1869) had 8 groups. Group 1 — alkali metals; Group 2 — alkaline earth metals; Groups 3-12 — transition metals; Group 17 — halogens; Group 18 — noble gases. Elements in a group have similar chemical properties because they share the same outer-shell electron configuration.

cards.front:
Noble gases are found in which group of the modern periodic table?

(A) Group 1
(B) Group 18
(C) Group 17
(D) Group 2
cards.back:
(B) Group 18

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Group 18: helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon, oganesson. Fully filled outer shells make them chemically very stable (inert). Earth's atmosphere is ~1 % argon. Neon is used in red-orange sign lighting; helium in balloons and cryogenics; xenon in car headlamps and arc lamps; radon is radioactive. Group 1 — alkali metals; Group 17 — halogens.

cards.front:
In the modern periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing:

(A) Atomic mass
(B) Atomic number
(C) Electronegativity
(D) Density
cards.back:
(B) Atomic number

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — The modern periodic law (Moseley, 1913) states that properties are a periodic function of atomic number (number of protons), not atomic mass as Mendeleev had assumed. This resolved anomalies — e.g., argon (40) appears before potassium (39) because Ar has atomic number 18 and K has 19, even though Ar's atomic mass is higher. Electronegativity itself is a periodic trend, not the ordering rule.

cards.front:
As we move left to right across a period, atomic size generally:

(A) Increases
(B) Decreases
(C) Remains the same
(D) First increases, then decreases
cards.back:
(B) Decreases

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Across a period — nuclear charge grows while electrons are added to the same shell. The stronger pull shrinks the atom. Down a group — electrons go into new shells, so size grows despite the extra charge. That is why Li is smaller than Na (same group) is smaller than K, but larger than Be (same period).

cards.front:
Which element is the most electronegative?

(A) Chlorine
(B) Fluorine
(C) Oxygen
(D) Nitrogen
cards.back:
(B) Fluorine

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Fluorine (F, atomic number 9) is the most electronegative element on the Pauling scale (3.98). Oxygen is second (3.44), chlorine third (3.16), nitrogen fourth (3.04). Electronegativity increases left-to-right across a period and decreases down a group — which is why F (top of Group 17) beats Cl (below it). Caesium is one of the least electronegative (0.79).

cards.front:
The element with the highest melting point among all naturally-occurring elements is:

(A) Iron
(B) Tungsten
(C) Gold
(D) Platinum
cards.back:
(B) Tungsten

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Tungsten — also called wolfram, symbol W — melts at 3,422 °C, the highest of any metal and second only to carbon (sublimes ~3,642 °C) among naturally occurring elements. That is why tungsten is used for incandescent bulb filaments and high-temperature cutting tools. Iron melts at 1,538 °C; gold at 1,064 °C; platinum at 1,768 °C.

cards.front:
Dmitri Mendeleev's original periodic table (1869) arranged elements in order of increasing:

(A) Atomic number
(B) Atomic mass
(C) Density
(D) Melting point
cards.back:
(B) Atomic mass

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Mendeleev's law (1869) arranged the then-known 63 elements in order of increasing atomic mass — and famously left gaps for elements not yet discovered (eka-aluminium = gallium, eka-boron = scandium, eka-silicon = germanium, all later found). Only in 1913 did Moseley's X-ray work establish that atomic number — not mass — is the true ordering variable.

cards.front:
Across a PERIOD of the periodic table from left to right, the ATOMIC RADIUS generally:

(A) Increases due to addition of one outer shell of electrons
(B) Decreases due to higher nuclear charge pulling electrons closer
(C) Stays the same with no significant trend at all
(D) Fluctuates randomly with no observable systematic pattern
cards.back:
(B) Decreases due to higher nuclear charge pulling electrons closer

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Across a period: protons added in the nucleus, electrons added in the SAME shell. The increasing nuclear charge pulls the electron cloud INWARD → ATOMIC RADIUS DECREASES from Li to Ne, Na to Ar, etc. Down a GROUP: each new shell adds → atomic radius INCREASES (Li < Na < K < Rb < Cs). Distractor 1 describes group-trend, not period. Distractor 3, 4 are wrong as the trend is systematic.

cards.front:
IONISATION ENERGY is the energy needed to:

(A) Combine an atom with another atom to form a covalent bond
(B) Remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom
(C) Add one electron to a gaseous atom from its surroundings
(D) Break the strongest covalent bond in a small molecule
cards.back:
(B) Remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — First ionisation energy (IE₁) — energy to remove the outermost electron from a neutral GASEOUS atom: M(g) → M⁺(g) + e⁻. Increases across a period (harder to remove e⁻ as nuclear pull grows); decreases down a group (outer e⁻ farther from nucleus, easier to remove). Highest IE₁: helium (2372 kJ/mol). Lowest: caesium (~376) and francium. Successive ionisation energies (IE₂, IE₃, ...) are progressively higher. Distractor 1 = bond formation. Distractor 3 = electron AFFINITY. Distractor 4 = bond dissociation energy.

cards.option3: Break the strongest covalent bond in a small molecule

cards.front:
ELECTRONEGATIVITY measures the tendency of an atom to:

(A) Lose electrons easily to form a positive ion
(B) Attract shared electrons in a chemical bond
(C) Emit a photon of visible light when heated
(D) Combine with hydrogen to form a stable hydride
cards.back:
(B) Attract shared electrons in a chemical bond

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Electronegativity (χ) — relative tendency to attract bonding electrons toward itself. Pauling scale: F (3.98, highest) > O > N > Cl > Br > C > H. Cs/Fr (0.7-0.8, lowest among stable elements). Periodic trends: increases across a period (toward F), decreases down a group. ΔEN between two atoms predicts bond ionicity: > 1.7 mostly ionic; 0.4-1.7 polar covalent; < 0.4 non-polar covalent. Distractor 1 = electropositivity (opposite). Distractor 3 = unrelated optical property. Distractor 4 = some elements form hydrides but that's not electronegativity.

cards.option3: Combine with hydrogen to form a stable hydride

cards.front:
Which element has the HIGHEST electronegativity on the Pauling scale?

(A) Oxygen, the most abundant element by mass
(B) Fluorine, the most reactive halogen of all
(C) Chlorine, found mostly as common rock salt
(D) Nitrogen, the most abundant gas in air around us
cards.back:
(B) Fluorine, the most reactive halogen of all

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Pauling electronegativity ranking: F (3.98) > O (3.44) > Cl (3.16) > N (3.04) > Br (2.96) > I (2.66) > C (2.55) > H (2.20) > Cs/Fr (~0.7). Fluorine is the most electronegative because of small atomic size + high effective nuclear charge. Drives its extreme reactivity (forms compounds with nearly every other element). Distractor 1 — oxygen is 2nd, not 1st. Distractor 3 — chlorine 3rd. Distractor 4 — nitrogen 4th.

cards.front:
ELECTRON AFFINITY of an atom is:

(A) The energy needed to remove its outermost electron
(B) The energy released when an electron is added to it
(C) The number of valence electrons it carries naturally
(D) Its tendency to share electrons within a bond
cards.back:
(B) The energy released when an electron is added to it

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Electron Affinity (EA) — energy released when one electron is added to a neutral gaseous atom: X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g) + EA. Halogens have the highest EAs (Cl ~349 kJ/mol, F ~328, Br ~325) — eager to gain e⁻ to complete octet. Group 18 (noble gases) and group 2 (alkaline earth) have ~0 or negative EA. EA is RELATED but different from electronegativity (which is a derived ratio). Distractor 1 = ionisation energy. Distractor 3 = valence count. Distractor 4 = electronegativity.

cards.front:
Going DOWN a group of the periodic table, which property generally INCREASES?

(A) First ionisation energy of the elements
(B) Atomic radius and metallic character of the elements
(C) Electronegativity of the elements involved
(D) Effective nuclear charge felt by valence electrons
cards.back:
(B) Atomic radius and metallic character of the elements

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Down a group: more inner shells → larger atomic radius. Outer e⁻ are farther from nucleus → less tightly held → easier to lose → MORE METALLIC. Examples: Group 1 — Li (least metallic) → Cs (most metallic among stable, very reactive); Group 14 — C (non-metal), Si (metalloid), Ge (metalloid), Sn/Pb (metals). Distractor 1 — IE DECREASES down a group. Distractor 3 — electronegativity DECREASES. Distractor 4 — effective nuclear charge stays roughly similar (more shielding).

cards.front:
The MOST METALLIC element among Li, Na, K, Cs is:

(A) Lithium, the topmost in the alkali group
(B) Caesium, the heaviest stable alkali metal
(C) Sodium, the second member of the group
(D) Potassium, in the middle of this group
cards.back:
(B) Caesium, the heaviest stable alkali metal

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Metallic character INCREASES down a group. Cs (caesium) is the most metallic among stable alkali metals — most reactive (Fr is more so but radioactive + scarce). Caesium is so reactive it ignites instantly in air, reacts explosively with water. It is a soft, golden metal that melts in your hand (mp ~28 °C). Used in atomic clocks (the SI second is defined by Cs-133 transition), photoelectric cells, ion-propulsion thrusters.

ATOMIC RADIUS GENERALLY ___ as we move from LEFT TO RIGHT in a period.

(A) Decreases (more proton attraction)
(B) Increases (more electrons added)
(C) Stays roughly the same
(D) Increases then decreases (parabolic)
cards.back:
(A) Decreases (more proton attraction)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Across a PERIOD: nuclear charge INCREASES (more protons); electrons added to SAME shell. So nucleus pulls electrons CLOSER → atomic radius DECREASES. Across PERIOD 2: Li(152 pm) → Be(112) → B(85) → C(77) → N(75) → O(73) → F(72) → Ne(71). Li largest, F smallest. DOWN A GROUP: more shells added → radius INCREASES. So in periodic table, BOTTOM-LEFT = LARGEST atoms (Cs, Fr); TOP-RIGHT = SMALLEST (He, F). NOTE: NOBLE GASES not always given radii (no covalent bond to define); use VAN DER WAALS radius. INSIGHT — atomic size is fundamental to chemistry: smaller atoms hold electrons tighter → higher ionisation energy + electronegativity (also period trends).

Most ELECTRONEGATIVE element is:

(A) Fluorine (3.98 Pauling)
(B) Oxygen (3.44, second most)
(C) Chlorine (3.16, third)
(D) Helium (noble gas, debatable)
cards.back:
(A) Fluorine (3.98 Pauling)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — FLUORINE — 3.98 on Pauling scale (highest). Top of Group 17 (HALOGENS). Top 4 EN: F (3.98), O (3.44), Cl (3.16), N (3.04). Cesium, Francium = least EN (~0.7-0.8). EN INCREASES across period (atoms smaller + more electron-greedy); DECREASES down group. INSIGHT — EN explains BOND TYPES: ΔEN ~0 → covalent (e.g., O-O, H-H); 0.5-1.7 → polar covalent (e.g., H-F, H-O — water dipole); >1.7 → ionic (Na-F, Li-Cl). HF — strongest H-bond donor; HF is also weak acid (despite F's huge EN). FLUORINE — extremely reactive, only NOBLE GAS that reacts with F is XENON. Used in: F-containing pharmaceuticals (~30% of new drugs), Teflon, refrigerants, toothpaste fluoride.

LANTHANIDES (57-71) + ACTINIDES (89-103) shown separately at bottom. METALS (left + middle) ~75% of elements; NON-METALS (right); METALLOIDS (zigzag border — B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te, Po). cards.front:
ALKALI METALS (Group 1) are stored under:

(A) Kerosene oil (to prevent oxidation)
(B) Water (they react with water!)
(C) Air, no special storage needed
(D) Vacuum-sealed glass jars only
cards.back:
(A) Kerosene oil (to prevent oxidation)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — ALKALI METALS (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) — extremely REACTIVE; rapidly oxidise in air, react VIOLENTLY with water (2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂↑ + heat → can ignite H₂). STORED under KEROSENE / paraffin oil to prevent contact with air + moisture. Cesium ignites SPONTANEOUSLY in air. Reactivity INCREASES down group: Li (calm) → Na (vigorous) → K (purple flame) → Rb, Cs (explosive). FLAME COLOURS (PYQ): Li (crimson), Na (yellow), K (lilac), Rb (red-violet), Cs (blue). USES: Li-ion batteries (smartphones, EVs); Na in lights, Na-K coolant in some reactors; K essential for plants + animals (potassium ions); Cs in atomic clocks. NEVER touch alkali metals with bare hands (skin moisture + warmth can ignite Na, K immediately).

cards.front:
NOBLE GASES (Group 18) are CHEMICALLY INERT because:

(A) They have stable, FILLED outer electron shells
(B) They are too small to react with anything
(C) They are radioactive and avoid bonding
(D) They are gases (only solids react)
cards.back:
(A) They have stable, FILLED outer electron shells

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — NOBLE GASES (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn, Og) — outer shell FULL (8 e⁻ for all except He which has 2). 'OCTET RULE' — atoms tend to acquire 8 valence electrons → noble-gas configurations are most stable. So noble gases don't NEED to gain/lose/share electrons → no chemical reactivity. EXCEPTIONS — heavier ones (Kr, Xe, Rn) form some compounds with F, O (XeF₂, XeF₄, XeF₆ — first noble gas compound: XePtF₆, Bartlett 1962). USES: HELIUM (party balloons; cooling MRI; airships), NEON (signs); ARGON (inert atmosphere for welding, light bulbs); KRYPTON (high-end car headlamps); XENON (flash lamps, anaesthetic). RADON — radioactive, accumulates in basements; cancer risk. OGANESSON — heaviest, theoretical, very short-lived. Indian: He critical for ISRO + science; mostly imported.
cards.option1: They are too small to react with anything
cards.option2: They are radioactive and avoid bonding

cards.front:
As we go from LEFT to RIGHT across a period, the atomic radius generally:

(A) Increases
(B) Decreases (electrons added to same shell, but nuclear charge increases)
(C) Remains constant
(D) First decreases then increases sharply
cards.back:
(B) Decreases (electrons added to same shell, but nuclear charge increases)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Across a period: same shell, more protons → stronger pull on electrons → smaller radius. Down a group: new shell added → larger radius despite higher Z (effective nuclear charge mitigated by inner-electron screening). So Li > Be > B > C > N > O > F (atomic radii decreasing). Cs is largest naturally-occurring atom. Atomic radius drops from ~152 pm (Li) to ~58 pm (F). Cations smaller than parent atom; anions larger.

cards.front:
The element with the HIGHEST electronegativity is:

(A) Oxygen
(B) Fluorine (Pauling scale = 4.0)
(C) Chlorine
(D) Helium
cards.back:
(B) Fluorine (Pauling scale = 4.0)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Electronegativity — tendency to attract bonding electrons. Pauling scale (most common): F = 3.98 (highest), O = 3.44, Cl = 3.16, N = 3.04. Top right of periodic table = highest electronegativity (excluding noble gases which don't normally form bonds). Bottom left = lowest (Cs, Fr ~0.7). Difference in electronegativity > 1.7 → ionic bond; < 0.4 → non-polar covalent; in between → polar covalent. Electronegativity drives polarity (water is polar — H-O), reactivity, hydrogen-bonding.

cards.front:
Ionisation energy (the energy to remove an outer electron) generally:

(A) Decreases left to right across a period
(B) Increases left to right across a period; decreases down a group
(C) Increases down a group
(D) Stays constant
cards.back:
(B) Increases left to right across a period; decreases down a group

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — IE trends OPPOSITE to atomic radius. Across a period: nuclear charge ↑ → outer electron held tighter → IE ↑. Down a group: shells ↑ → outer electron farther away → easier to remove → IE ↓. He has highest first IE (2,372 kJ/mol). Cs has lowest. Exceptions — Be > B (2s² stability), N > O (half-filled 2p³ stability of N). Ionisation values are a fingerprint of orbital structure — anomalies reveal half-filled and fully-filled subshell stability.

cards.front:
Metallic character GENERALLY:

(A) Increases left to right across a period
(B) Decreases left to right across a period; increases down a group
(C) Has no periodic pattern
(D) Increases in both directions
cards.back:
(B) Decreases left to right across a period; increases down a group

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Metallic character — willingness to lose electrons. Highest at bottom-left (Cs, Fr); lowest at top-right (F, He). Across a period: tendency to lose decreases (atoms get more electronegative). Down a group: outer electrons farther from nucleus → easily lost → more metallic. Diagonal stairstep separates metals (left) from non-metals (right); metalloids (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) sit on the staircase. Most reactive metal — Fr (or Cs); most reactive non-metal — F.

cards.front:
The modern periodic table has elements arranged in order of increasing:

(A) Atomic mass
(B) Atomic number (number of protons)
(C) Density
(D) Mass number
cards.back:
(B) Atomic number (number of protons)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Modern Periodic Law (Henry Moseley, 1913): Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic number (Z). Resolved anomalies in Mendeleev's mass-based table — e.g., Ar (Z=18, mass 40) vs K (Z=19, mass 39) — Mendeleev's order had to swap them; Moseley's law put them right. The modern table has 118 confirmed elements (last addition: Oganesson Z=118, named 2016). 7 periods, 18 groups (in extended form). Lanthanides + actinides shown as f-block at bottom for compactness.

cards.front:
The two groups in the periodic table containing elements that are gases at room temperature are:

(A) Group 1 (alkali metals) and Group 2 (alkaline earth metals)
(B) Groups 17 (halogens — partially) and 18 (noble gases — fully)
(C) Groups 13 and 14
(D) Group 11 and 12 (transition metals)
cards.back:
(B) Groups 17 (halogens — partially) and 18 (noble gases — fully)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Halogens (Group 17): F₂, Cl₂ are gases (Br₂ is a liquid; I₂, At — solids). Noble gases (Group 18): all 6 are gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn). Plus H (Group 1 by some, group 17 by others) is a gas. N₂, O₂ are also gases (Groups 15, 16). Most metals are solids; mercury (Hg, Group 12) is liquid; Cs, Ga, Br near room-temperature melting (Cs melts ~28 °C). Most elements are solids at STP.

cards.front:
The longest period in the modern periodic table contains:

(A) 8 elements
(B) 32 elements (period 6 — when lanthanides included)
(C) 18 elements
(D) 24 elements
cards.back:
(B) 32 elements (period 6 — when lanthanides included)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Period 6 — 32 elements when lanthanides counted in (Cs Z=55 to Rn Z=86, with La 57 + 14 lanthanides + Hf 72 onwards). Same for Period 7 (32, with actinides). Period 1 — only 2 (H, He). Periods 2 & 3 — 8 each (s + p). Periods 4 & 5 — 18 each (s + d + p). Period 6 = 2 (s) + 14 (f, lanthanides) + 10 (d) + 6 (p) = 32. Some standard table layouts split the f-block out for visual compactness.

cards.front:
The atom contains which three FUNDAMENTAL particles?

(A) Protons, electrons, quarks
(B) Protons, neutrons, electrons
(C) Protons, positrons, neutrons
(D) Photons, electrons, protons
cards.back:
(B) Protons, neutrons, electrons

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Proton (p, +1, in nucleus). Neutron (n, 0, in nucleus). Electron (e⁻, -1, in orbitals). Hydrogen nucleus has no neutron — just a proton. Quarks are sub-nucleon constituents (not 'fundamental atomic' in introductory chem).

cards.front:
ISOTOPES are atoms of the same element that differ in:

(A) Number of protons
(B) Number of neutrons
(C) Number of electrons in the neutral atom
(D) Atomic number
cards.back:
(B) Number of neutrons

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Isotopes — same Z (protons, same element), different A (mass number, different neutrons). Example: ¹²C (6 protons + 6 neutrons) vs ¹⁴C (6 protons + 8 neutrons). ¹⁴C is radioactive and used in carbon dating. All 3 H isotopes: ¹H (protium), ²H (deuterium), ³H (tritium, radioactive). hence mass.
cards.option2: Number of electrons in the neutral atom

All 3 H isotopes: ¹H (protium), ²H (deuterium), ³H (tritium, radioactive). hence mass.

cards.front:
The MODERN periodic table is arranged by:

(A) Atomic mass (Mendeleev's rule)
(B) Atomic number
(C) Number of neutrons
(D) Reactivity
cards.back:
(B) Atomic number

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Moseley (1913) — atomic number (Z) is the fundamental basis. Mendeleev's original (1869) ordering by atomic mass had inconsistencies (Te-I, Ar-K, Co-Ni swaps). Moving to atomic number fixed these. Modern table: 7 periods, 18 groups (s, p, d, f blocks). Moseley's law.

cards.front:
An atom of CARBON has how many valence electrons?

(A) 2
(B) 4
(C) 6
(D) 8
cards.back:
(B) 4

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Carbon (Z=6): 1s² 2s² 2p². 2s² + 2p² = 4 valence electrons in outer shell → tetravalent. Forms 4 covalent bonds — basis of all of organic chemistry. Diamond (sp³), graphite (sp²), benzene, methane.

cards.front:
RUTHERFORD's α-particle scattering experiment led to the discovery of the:

(A) Electron
(B) Atomic nucleus
(C) Neutron
(D) Photon
cards.back:
(B) Atomic nucleus

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Rutherford (1911) — fired α-particles at gold foil; a small fraction deflected sharply → concluded positive charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus. JJ Thomson — electron (1897, cathode rays). James Chadwick — neutron (1932).

(A) Helium
(B) Hydrogen
(C) Lithium
(D) Oxygen
cards.back:
(B) Hydrogen

cards.front:
A CHEMICAL BOND formed by sharing of electrons between atoms is called:

(A) Ionic bond
(B) Covalent bond
(C) Metallic bond
(D) Hydrogen bond
cards.back:
(B) Covalent bond

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Covalent — electrons shared (H₂, O₂, CH₄, H₂O). Ionic — complete electron transfer (NaCl, MgO). Metallic — 'sea of delocalised electrons' in metals. Hydrogen bond — weak attraction between H (bonded to F/O/N) and lone pair of F/O/N on another molecule.

cards.front:
Consider the following statements about the MODERN PERIODIC TABLE. 1. Moseley corrected Mendeleev by ordering elements by atomic NUMBER rather than atomic mass. 2. The table has 7 periods and 18 groups. 3. Lanthanides and actinides are placed together as f-block elements below the main table. 4. Noble gases have zero electron affinity because they have a complete octet. Which are correct?

(A) 1, 2 and 3 only
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(C) 1 and 3 only
(D) 2 and 4 only
cards.back:
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — All four are correct. Moseley (1913) reordered by atomic number, fixing anomalies like Ar-K and Co-Ni. Table has 7 periods, 18 groups. f-block (La-Lu, Ac-Lr) is split out below for space. Noble gases have effectively zero electron affinity — they don't want to gain electrons (stable octet).

cards.front:
Arrange the following in order of INCREASING first ionization energy: Na, Mg, Al, Si.

(A) Na < Mg < Al < Si
(B) Na < Al < Mg < Si
(C) Si < Al < Mg < Na
(D) Na < Si < Mg < Al
cards.back:
(B) Na < Al < Mg < Si

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Trend across period 3: Na (495 kJ/mol) < Mg (737) > Al (577) < Si (786). Mg > Al is the ANOMALY — Mg has filled 3s², while Al's lone 3p¹ is easier to remove. Hence Na < Al < Mg < Si.

(A) Atomic radius — decreases across a period left to right
(B) Electronegativity — decreases down a group

(D) Ionization energy — generally increases across a period
cards.back:
(C) Metallic character — increases across a period left to right

ASSERTION (A): Fluorine has a higher electronegativity than chlorine. REASON (R): Fluorine's smaller atomic size means the bonding electrons are held more tightly to its nucleus.

(A) Both A and R are true, R is the correct explanation
(B) Both A and R are true, R is NOT the correct explanation
(C) A is true, R is false
(D) A is false, R is true

(A) X is an alkali metal.
(B) X is a halogen and exists as a diatomic molecule X₂.

cards.front:
Consider the following group-16 (chalcogens) statements. 1. Oxygen is gaseous; sulfur, selenium and tellurium are solids at room temperature. 2. Oxygen exhibits a maximum oxidation state of +2 in compounds. 3. Hydrogen sulphide (H₂S) is a stronger acid than water. 4. Ozone (O₃) is an allotrope of oxygen. Which are correct?

(A) 1, 3 and 4 only
(B) 1, 2 and 4 only
(C) 2 and 3 only
(D) All four
cards.back:
(A) 1, 3 and 4 only

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Statement 2 is WRONG — oxygen generally exhibits a −2 oxidation state; its positive states are very rare (with fluorine only, e.g. OF₂ where O is +2). The broader descriptor 'maximum +2' is misleading. Statements 1, 3, 4 are correct. (H₂S pKa ≈ 7 vs water pKa ≈ 15.7 — H₂S is a stronger acid; ozone is a well-known allotrope of oxygen.)

cards.front:
A student claims: 'All elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell.' This statement is:

(A) Always true
(B) True for main-group (s- and p-block) elements, but NOT strictly for transition and inner-transition metals
(C) True only for period-1 elements
(D) Always false
cards.back:
(B) True for main-group (s- and p-block) elements, but NOT strictly for transition and inner-transition metals

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — For s/p-block (groups 1, 2, 13-18) the claim holds cleanly. For d-block (transition metals) the differentiating electron enters a d-sub-shell of (n−1) — so outermost-shell count is less predictive, and oxidation behaviour varies within a group. For f-block it's yet more complex. This nuance is a common exam trap.

cards.front:
The modern periodic table is arranged by:

(A) Atomic mass (as Mendeleev originally proposed)
(B) Atomic number
(C) Valency alone
(D) Density
cards.back:
(B) Atomic number

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — DMITRI MENDELEEV (1869) first arranged elements by ATOMIC MASS — his periodic table had anomalies like Ar-K, Co-Ni, Te-I pairs where mass order didn't match chemical behaviour. Henry MOSELEY (1913) discovered that arranging by ATOMIC NUMBER (Z — number of protons) resolves ALL such anomalies — formulated the 'Periodic Law': physical and chemical properties are periodic functions of atomic number. Modern periodic table has 118 confirmed elements (last 4 — Nh Nihonium 113, Mc Moscovium 115, Ts Tennessine 117, Og Oganesson 118 — added Nov 2016). 7 PERIODS (rows) and 18 GROUPS (columns). s-block (Gp 1-2), p-block (Gp 13-18), d-block (Gp 3-12, transition metals), f-block (lanthanides + actinides). the Moseley arrangement.

cards.front:
The 'Noble Gases' (Group 18) are characterised by:

(A) Extreme reactivity
(B) Full outer electron shell → very low chemical reactivity
(C) Low ionisation energy
(D) Strong metallic character
cards.back:
(B) Full outer electron shell → very low chemical reactivity

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — NOBLE GASES (Group 18 / VIIIA / Inert gases): Helium, Neon, Argon, Krypton, Xenon, Radon (radioactive), Oganesson (super-heavy). Fully filled valence shell (He has 2 electrons — 1s²; others have 8 — ns² np⁶). Octet rule → extremely stable → inert under normal conditions. HIGHEST ionisation energy in each period. Abundance in air: N₂ (78%) > O₂ (21%) > ARGON (~0.93% — most abundant noble gas in air) > CO₂ (0.04%) > Ne + He + Kr + Xe (trace). Uses: HELIUM (balloons, MRI, low-temp cooling — non-flammable unlike hydrogen); NEON (advertising signs, red-orange colour); ARGON (inert gas shield for welding, light bulb filament filling); KRYPTON (runway lighting); XENON (car headlights, xenon arc lamps); RADON (health hazard in basements). Though 'inert', Xe can form XeF₂, XeF₄, XeF₆ etc. under specific conditions (discovered 1962 by Bartlett).

cards.front:
Moving LEFT TO RIGHT across a period in the periodic table, which of the following GENERALLY INCREASES?

(A) Atomic radius
(B) Electronegativity and ionisation energy
(C) Metallic character
(D) Number of electron shells
cards.back:
(B) Electronegativity and ionisation energy

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Periodic trends — across a PERIOD (left to right): (a) Atomic number ↑ (trivially); (b) ATOMIC RADIUS ↓ (effective nuclear charge increases, pulls electrons closer); (c) IONISATION ENERGY ↑ (harder to remove valence electron); (d) ELECTRONEGATIVITY ↑ (F is most electronegative, 3.98 on Pauling scale; noble gases excluded from scale); (e) ELECTRON AFFINITY ↑ (Cl has highest); (f) METALLIC CHARACTER ↓ (metal to non-metal transition); (g) Non-metallic character ↑; (h) Oxidation number ↑; (i) Number of shells UNCHANGED within a period. Down a GROUP: atomic radius ↑, metallic character ↑, ionisation energy ↓, electronegativity ↓.

cards.front:
Which element has the HIGHEST electronegativity on the Pauling scale?

(A) Chlorine
(B) Fluorine
(C) Oxygen
(D) Nitrogen
cards.back:
(B) Fluorine

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — Electronegativity order (Pauling scale): F (3.98) > O (3.44) > Cl (3.16) ≈ N (3.04) > Br (2.96) > I (2.66) > S (2.58) > C (2.55) > H (2.20). FLUORINE is the MOST ELECTRONEGATIVE element (top-right, just before Ne). It's also the smallest halogen with highest electron affinity in practice (Cl has numerically higher electron affinity due to F's small size causing repulsion). LOWEST electronegativity: FRANCIUM (0.7) in Group 1 (bottom-left — most metallic, largest atom of stable elements). Noble gases (He, Ne, Ar) are generally not assigned electronegativities on the Pauling scale as they don't commonly form bonds. Trend mnemonic: 'FONCL BrISCH' for top-9 most electronegative.

cards.front:
The LANTHANIDES (rare earth elements) occupy which positions in the periodic table?

(A) Group 3, Period 4 (4th row)
(B) The separate bottom row (Period 6), elements 57 (La) to 71 (Lu)
(C) Group 18 (Noble gases)
(D) Period 7, bottom row
cards.back:
(B) The separate bottom row (Period 6), elements 57 (La) to 71 (Lu)

Atomic Structure & Periodic Table — LANTHANIDES (also called 'rare earths' though not actually rare in Earth's crust) — 15 elements from LANTHANUM (La, atomic number 57) to LUTETIUM (Lu, Z=71). Technically 14 + La = 15. Placed SEPARATELY at the bottom to avoid stretching the main table. f-block elements — their 4f orbitals are being filled. Part of Period 6. ACTINIDES (Z=89 Ac to 103 Lr) are the corresponding f-block Period 7 — all RADIOACTIVE, includes Uranium (Z=92), Plutonium (Z=94). Transuranic = beyond U (synthetic). India's significant rare-earth reserves: KERALA beach monazite sands (Th, LREE) — one of the world's richest. IREL (India Rare Earths Ltd) extracts these. Rare-earths critical for magnets (Nd-Fe-B), phosphors, batteries, EVs.

Which element is named after India — the first chemical element named after an Asian country?

(C) Gallium

cards.front:
What is the primary effect of a CATALYST in a chemical reaction?

(A) It changes the rate of reaction
(B) It shifts the equilibrium position.
(C) It increases the yield of products.
(D) It changes Gibbs free energy.
cards.back:
(A) It changes the rate of reaction

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — A CATALYST changes the RATE (speed) of a reaction without being consumed. KEY MECHANISM: it lowers the ACTIVATION ENERGY (Ea) by providing an alternative reaction pathway — both forward and reverse rates speed up equally, so equilibrium POSITION does NOT change (only equilibrium is REACHED FASTER). KEY DISTINCTIONS: (1) Catalyst does NOT change ΔG, ΔH, or Keq — these are state functions of reactants/products. (2) Catalyst does NOT increase YIELD — yield depends on equilibrium position. (3) Catalyst does NOT get consumed — it can theoretically work indefinitely (in practice, deactivates over time via poisoning or sintering). TYPES: POSITIVE (speeds up; e.g., Pt in Haber process), NEGATIVE/inhibitor (slows down; e.g., glycerol slows hydrogen-peroxide decomposition), AUTO (a product catalyses its own formation; e.g., MnSO₄ in KMnO₄-oxalate reaction), BIOLOGICAL (enzymes; e.g., amylase, pepsin). INDUSTRIAL: 90% of all manufactured chemicals use catalysts at some stage. PYQ ANGLE: definitional Qs on catalysts appear in 80% of SSC CGL papers.

cards.front:
Which catalyst is used in the Haber process for ammonia synthesis?

(A) Iron with molybdenum promoter
(B) Platinum metal alone alone
(C) Vanadium pentoxide alone alone
(D) Nickel metal catalyst alone
cards.back:
(A) Iron with molybdenum promoter

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — HABER-BOSCH PROCESS: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃; catalyst = finely-divided IRON with molybdenum (Mo) or aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) as PROMOTER (a substance that enhances catalyst activity). Conditions: 200 atm pressure, 450-500°C. NOBEL: Fritz Haber 1918 (synthesis); Carl Bosch 1931 (industrial scale-up). HISTORICAL IMPACT: Haber process feeds ~50% of humanity by enabling synthetic nitrogen fertilizer — without it, world food output would crash. INDIA: India's largest urea producer is IFFCO (Indian Farmers Fertiliser Cooperative); urea is produced by reacting ammonia with CO₂. RELATED CATALYSTS — memorize: Contact process (H₂SO₄ from SO₂) → V₂O₅; Hydrogenation of oils → finely-divided Ni; Ostwald process (HNO₃ from NH₃) → Pt-Rh gauze; CO oxidation in catalytic converters (cars) → Pt-Pd-Rh. EXAM ANGLE: HABER + CONTACT + OSTWALD catalysts trio appears as a 3-mark MCQ in 80% of SSC CGL/RRB papers. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing memorization of industrial chemistry catalysts — direct PYQ recall.

cards.front:
Enzymes are biological catalysts made primarily of:

(A) Proteins folded into specific shapes
(B) Carbohydrates and sugars alone
(C) Lipids and fatty acids alone.
(D) Nucleic acids only alone (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Proteins folded into specific shapes

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — ENZYMES are PROTEINS (with a few RNA exceptions called RIBOZYMES, e.g., self-splicing RNA in some viruses). They speed up biochemical reactions by ~10⁶ to 10¹² times via the LOCK-AND-KEY (or induced-fit) mechanism — the substrate binds to the enzyme's ACTIVE SITE. KEY PROPERTIES: (1) HIGHLY SPECIFIC — one enzyme typically catalyses one reaction (amylase only on starch, lipase only on fats). (2) SENSITIVE to pH and temperature — denatured by extremes (above ~50°C most human enzymes die). (3) Reusable — not consumed. EXAMPLES: amylase (starch → maltose; in saliva, pancreas), pepsin (proteins → peptides; stomach pH ~2), trypsin (small intestine pH ~8), catalase (H₂O₂ → H₂O + O₂; in liver/blood — the fastest known enzyme, 40 million reactions/sec). NOBEL TRIVIA: 2014 chemistry prize for super-resolution microscopy revealed enzyme dynamics at sub-diffraction scale. INDIA: enzymatic stain-removers (Surf Excel, Tide) use bacterial proteases sourced from Indian soil microbes.

cards.front:
What is AUTOCATALYSIS?

(A) A product catalyzes its own formation
(B) Two catalysts work together always
(C) Catalyst regenerates itself once.
(D) A reaction proceeds without catalyst.
cards.back:
(A) A product catalyzes its own formation

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — AUTOCATALYSIS: a PRODUCT of the reaction acts as the catalyst for its own further formation — so the reaction starts slow, then SPEEDS UP as more product accumulates, then slows again as reactants deplete. CLASSIC EXAMPLE: oxalic acid (H₂C₂O₄) + KMnO₄ in acidic medium produces Mn²⁺ (Mn(II)), which then catalyses the same reaction. The titration is initially slow, then speeds up — indicator of autocatalysis. RATE CURVE: S-shaped (sigmoidal) instead of standard exponential decay. BIOLOGICAL ANALOGS: pepsinogen → pepsin auto-activation in stomach; blood-clotting cascade has autocatalytic loops; cancer cell-cycle has autocatalytic feedback (one of the reasons tumours grow exponentially). INDUSTRIAL: certain polymerization reactions (e.g., styrene) are autocatalytic — controlled carefully to avoid runaway exotherms. PYQ ANGLE: autocatalysis vs catalysis vs inhibition appears as a definition-MCQ in JEE-Main and SSC CGL Tier 2. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests conceptual depth beyond rote 'what is a catalyst'.

cards.front:
In the Contact Process for sulphuric acid manufacture, which catalyst converts SO₂ to SO₃?

(A) Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅)
(B) Iron with molybdenum alone
(C) Platinum metal catalyst alone
(D) Manganese dioxide alone alone
cards.back:
(A) Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅)

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — CONTACT PROCESS: S → SO₂ (burn S in air) → SO₃ (oxidation, catalysed by V₂O₅) → H₂SO₄ (dissolve in conc. H₂SO₄ to form oleum, then dilute with water). The KEY catalytic step is 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃ at 400-450°C with V₂O₅ catalyst. WHY V₂O₅? Originally Pt was used (faster, but expensive and easily POISONED by arsenic impurities in the SO₂ feed). V₂O₅ is cheaper, robust, less prone to poisoning. INDUSTRIAL SCALE: H₂SO₄ is the world's #1 industrial chemical (~250 million tonnes/year); ~85% goes to fertilizer (phosphate), rest to detergents, dyes, pickling steel. INDIAN INDUSTRY: India produces ~10 million tonnes H₂SO₄ annually; major plants at Tuticorin, Gujarat (GACL, GNFC). HISTORICAL: Contact process patented by Peregrine Phillips (UK, 1831) — but commercialized properly only in 1900s. PYQ TRIO: V₂O₅ for Contact, Fe for Haber, Pt-Rh for Ostwald — these three appear together in 70%+ SSC Chemistry MCQs.

cards.front:
What is a CATALYTIC POISON?

(A) Substance that destroys catalyst activity
(B) A poison made by the catalyst.
(C) A negative or inhibiting catalyst.
(D) A toxic by-product of catalysis.
cards.back:
(A) Substance that destroys catalyst activity

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — A CATALYTIC POISON is a substance that DEACTIVATES a catalyst by binding strongly to its active sites, blocking reactant access. EXAMPLES: (1) ARSENIC compounds poison platinum in Contact process — that's why V₂O₅ is preferred industrially. (2) LEAD poisons the platinum-rhodium catalytic converter in cars — that's why leaded petrol was banned globally (in India, 2000). (3) SULPHUR poisons nickel in hydrogenation reactions — feedstocks must be desulphurized first. (4) CARBON MONOXIDE poisons iron in Haber process — H₂ feed must be purified. (5) MERCURY poisons many enzyme catalysts (and biological enzymes — hence Hg toxicity). DIFFERENT FROM INHIBITOR: an inhibitor reversibly slows reaction; a poison usually irreversibly destroys catalyst. INDUSTRIAL CONSEQUENCE: catalyst replacement is a major cost; refineries spend ~$100M/year on catalyst regeneration globally. ENVIRONMENTAL: catalytic converters last ~100,000 km if leaded fuel/poor maintenance avoided; replacement costs ₹15-30k. PYQ ANGLE: 'why was leaded petrol banned' = catalytic poison + Pb-toxicity dual-answer.

DIFFERENT FROM INHIBITOR: an inhibitor reversibly slows reaction; a poison usually irreversibly destroys catalyst. INDUSTRIAL CONSEQUENCE: catalyst replacement is a major cost; refineries spend ~$100M/year on catalyst regeneration globally. ENVIRONMENTAL: catalytic converters last ~100,000 km if leaded fuel/poor maintenance avoided; replacement costs ₹15-30k. PYQ ANGLE: 'why was leaded petrol banned' = catalytic poison + Pb-toxicity dual-answer.

cards.front:
What term describes a catalyst in the SAME phase (e.g., liquid + liquid) as the reactants?

(A) Homogeneous catalysis
(B) Heterogeneous catalysis alone
(C) Surface catalysis alone alone
(D) Phase-transfer catalysis alone
cards.back:
(A) Homogeneous catalysis

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — HOMOGENEOUS CATALYSIS — catalyst and reactants in SAME phase (both gases, or both liquids, or both solutions). EXAMPLE: acid-catalyzed esterification (CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → ester + H₂O), where H⁺ from H₂SO₄ is in the same liquid solution. HETEROGENEOUS CATALYSIS — different phases (catalyst usually solid, reactants gas/liquid). EXAMPLE: solid V₂O₅ in Contact process catalysing gas-phase SO₂ + O₂. PROS/CONS: heterogeneous = easier separation/recovery (filter or fixed bed), used in 90% of industrial chemistry; homogeneous = better selectivity, single-step, but harder catalyst recovery. SURFACE CATALYSIS THEORY: heterogeneous catalysis works via ADSORPTION on the catalyst surface (Langmuir-Hinshelwood mechanism). NOBEL: Gerhard Ertl (2007) for fundamentals of surface chemistry / heterogeneous catalysis (Haber process mechanism). PHASE-TRANSFER CATALYSIS: a catalyst (often quaternary ammonium salt) ferries reactants between two immiscible phases — used in pharmaceutical synthesis. PYQ FREQUENCY: homo vs hetero catalysis is a 1-mark MCQ in JEE-Main and rare in SSC.

cards.front:
A bond formed by complete TRANSFER of electrons from one atom to another is called:

(A) Covalent bond
(B) Ionic / electrovalent bond (e.g., NaCl)
(C) Metallic bond
(D) Hydrogen bond
cards.back:
(B) Ionic / electrovalent bond (e.g., NaCl)

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Ionic bond — electron transfer; usually between a metal (low ionisation energy → loses e⁻) and a non-metal (high electron affinity → gains e⁻). NaCl: Na (2,8,1) → Na⁺ (2,8); Cl (2,8,7) → Cl⁻ (2,8,8). Strong electrostatic attraction. Properties: high m.p./b.p., crystalline solids, soluble in polar solvents (water), conduct electricity in molten/aqueous state. Covalent — sharing of electrons. Metallic — 'sea' of delocalised electrons among metal cations. Hydrogen bond — weak attraction between H (bonded to N/O/F) and a lone pair on another N/O/F.

cards.front:
In the water molecule (H₂O), the bond between H and O is:

(A) Ionic
(B) Polar covalent (electrons shared but unequally — O is more electronegative)
(C) Metallic
(D) Coordinate
cards.back:
(B) Polar covalent (electrons shared but unequally — O is more electronegative)

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — H-O bond — polar covalent. Electronegativity: O (3.44) > H (2.20); ΔEN ≈ 1.24 → covalent with significant polarity (dipole, δ⁺ on H, δ⁻ on O). Pauling rule of thumb: ΔEN > 1.7 = mostly ionic; 0.4-1.7 = polar covalent; <0.4 = non-polar covalent. Water's polarity → universal solvent for ionic and polar molecules; high boiling point (100 °C) due to extensive H-bonding; ice less dense than liquid water (open H-bond cage). H₂O molecule shape — bent (V-shaped), 104.5° due to two lone pairs on O; sp³ hybridisation.

cards.front:
The shape of the methane (CH₄) molecule is:

(A) Linear
(B) Tetrahedral with bond angle 109.5°
(C) Square planar
(D) Trigonal pyramidal
cards.back:
(B) Tetrahedral with bond angle 109.5°

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) — pairs around central atom arrange to minimise repulsion. CH₄: 4 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs → tetrahedral, 109.5°. Common shapes by AXₙEₘ (A=central, X=bond, E=lone pair): AX₂ → linear (CO₂, 180°); AX₃ → trigonal planar (BF₃, 120°); AX₂E → bent (SO₂, ~120°); AX₄ → tetrahedral (CH₄, 109.5°); AX₃E → trigonal pyramidal (NH₃, ~107°); AX₂E₂ → bent (H₂O, ~104.5°); AX₅ → trigonal bipyramidal (PCl₅); AX₆ → octahedral (SF₆, 90°). Lone pairs occupy more space than bond pairs → compress bond angles.

cards.front:
Hydrogen bonding is responsible for the unusually HIGH boiling point of:

(A) Methane
(B) Water (compared to H₂S, H₂Se, H₂Te which are heavier but boil far lower)
(C) Helium
(D) Ethane
cards.back:
(B) Water (compared to H₂S, H₂Se, H₂Te which are heavier but boil far lower)

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Water (H₂O) boils at 100 °C — anomalously high for its molar mass (18 g/mol). Compare: H₂S (34 g/mol) boils at −60 °C; H₂Se −41 °C; H₂Te −2 °C. Reason — water has extensive H-bonding between molecules (H bonded to highly electronegative O can form H-bond with another O's lone pair). Each water molecule can form up to 4 H-bonds. Other consequences of H-bonding in water: ice is less dense than liquid water (life in lakes survives winter); high specific heat (climate moderation); high surface tension; capillary action (xylem in plants). HF, NH₃, alcohols, carboxylic acids, DNA base pairs — also exhibit H-bonding. Methane / ethane / He — only weak London dispersion forces; very low b.p.

cards.front:
Metals are good conductors of electricity because:

(A) Metal atoms are charged ions in fixed positions
(B) They have a 'sea' of delocalised valence electrons that can flow freely under an applied potential
(C) Metal atoms exchange protons
(D) Metals have ionic bonds
cards.back:
(B) They have a 'sea' of delocalised valence electrons that can flow freely under an applied potential

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Metallic bond model: lattice of positive metal cations in a 'sea' of free / delocalised valence electrons. Properties explained: ELECTRICAL conductivity (electrons drift); THERMAL conductivity (free electrons + lattice vibrations carry heat); MALLEABILITY + ductility (layers slide without breaking the bonding); LUSTRE (free electrons absorb + re-emit visible light); high m.p. (strong bond) — though not always (Hg is liquid at RT). Best conductors: Ag > Cu > Au > Al > Fe. Copper used in wiring (cheaper than Ag), Al for overhead transmission (lighter), Au for fine electronics (no oxide layer).

cards.front:
A coordinate (dative) bond is one where:

(A) Both atoms equally share the electrons
(B) Both shared electrons come from the SAME atom (the donor) — e.g., NH₄⁺ formation
(C) Electrons are completely transferred
(D) Atoms share neutrons
cards.back:
(B) Both shared electrons come from the SAME atom (the donor) — e.g., NH₄⁺ formation

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Coordinate / dative covalent bond — once formed, indistinguishable from a regular covalent bond, but its origin is one-sided. Examples: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺ (nitrogen donates its lone pair to the proton); H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺ (hydronium); CO molecule has one σ + one π + one dative bond (one of the bonds in C≡O is a dative bond from O to C). Key in coordination chemistry — ligands donate lone pairs to a central metal ion forming complex compounds (e.g., [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺, [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ in K₄[Fe(CN)₆]). Werner won the Nobel 1913 for coordination chemistry.

cards.front:
Among CO₂, H₂O, NH₃, BF₃ — which has a NET ZERO dipole moment despite having polar bonds?

(A) H₂O
(B) CO₂ and BF₃ (both have symmetric geometries that cancel out the bond dipoles)
(C) NH₃
(D) All four have non-zero dipoles
cards.back:
(B) CO₂ and BF₃ (both have symmetric geometries that cancel out the bond dipoles)

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Dipole moment depends on both bond polarity AND molecular shape. CO₂ — linear, two C=O bonds in opposite directions cancel → μ = 0 (despite polar bonds). BF₃ — trigonal planar, three B-F dipoles at 120° vector-sum to zero → μ = 0. H₂O — bent (104.5°), two O-H dipoles add up to give a net dipole (μ ≈ 1.85 D). NH₃ — trigonal pyramidal, three N-H dipoles + lone pair give net dipole (μ ≈ 1.47 D). Symmetric molecules (CO₂, BF₃, CH₄, SF₆, CCl₄) — zero dipole moment. Asymmetric (H₂O, NH₃, CHCl₃) — non-zero dipole.

cards.front:
The RATE of a chemical reaction generally INCREASES when:

(A) The temperature of the reaction mixture is lowered
(B) The concentration of the reactants is increased
(C) The total volume of the container is enlarged
(D) An inert gas is added at constant volume
cards.back:
(B) The concentration of the reactants is increased

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Higher concentration → more collisions per second → higher rate. Other rate-boosting factors: higher temperature (more high-energy collisions), larger surface area (for solids), suitable catalyst. Distractor 1 — lowering temperature SLOWS reactions (rule of thumb: rate halves per 10 °C drop). Distractor 3 — enlarging volume DILUTES reactants → slower. Distractor 4 — adding inert gas at constant volume doesn't change reactant concentrations.

cards.option2: The total volume of the container is enlarged
cards.option3: An inert gas is added at constant volume

cards.front:
A CATALYST speeds up a reaction by:

(A) Increasing the temperature of the reactant mixture
(B) Providing a pathway with lower activation energy
(C) Shifting the equilibrium toward the products side
(D) Consuming itself rapidly during the chemical change
cards.back:
(B) Providing a pathway with lower activation energy

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — A catalyst lowers the activation energy (Ea) — provides an alternative reaction path with a smaller energy barrier. More molecules now have enough energy → reaction proceeds faster. Catalyst is NOT consumed (regenerated by end of cycle). Catalysts do NOT shift equilibrium — they speed up forward + reverse equally; equilibrium position unchanged, only reached faster. Examples: enzymes (biological), Pt/Pd in catalytic converters, V₂O₅ in contact process, Ni in hydrogenation of vegetable oils.

cards.option2: Shifting the equilibrium toward the products side
cards.option3: Consuming itself rapidly during the chemical change

cards.front:
ACTIVATION ENERGY is best understood as:

(A) The total energy released by the reaction overall
(B) The minimum energy reactants need to start reacting
(C) The kinetic energy of every molecule in the system
(D) The bond energy of the products formed in the reaction
cards.back:
(B) The minimum energy reactants need to start reacting

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Activation energy (Ea) — the minimum energy barrier that reactant molecules must overcome to form products. Plotted as the 'hump' on a reaction-energy diagram. Lower Ea → faster reaction. Arrhenius equation k = A · exp(−Ea/RT) — a 10 °C rise often roughly doubles rate at moderate temperatures. Distractor 1 = enthalpy change ΔH (different concept — net energy released or absorbed). Distractor 3 = thermal kinetic energy (related but not Ea). Distractor 4 = bond dissociation energy (different).

cards.option3: The bond energy of the products formed in the reaction

cards.front:
A reaction is said to be FIRST ORDER overall when:

(A) The rate is independent of any reactant concentration
(B) The rate is directly proportional to one reactant's concentration
(C) The rate depends on the square of one reactant's concentration
(D) The rate depends on the cube of any reactant's concentration
cards.back:
(B) The rate is directly proportional to one reactant's concentration

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — First-order: rate = k[A]¹. Examples — radioactive decay (each atom decays independently), many enzymatic reactions at low substrate concentration. Half-life of first-order is concentration-INDEPENDENT (constant). Distractor 1 describes a ZERO order reaction (rate constant). Distractor 3 = SECOND order. Distractor 4 = THIRD order (rare).

cards.option3: The rate depends on the cube of any reactant's concentration

cards.front:
A finely powdered solid reacts faster than the same mass in lump form because:

(A) The solid's chemical composition becomes different
(B) The surface area exposed to the other reactant increases
(C) Powdered solids always contain higher-energy electrons
(D) The reaction always occurs only at very high temperature
cards.back:
(B) The surface area exposed to the other reactant increases

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Reaction rate depends on contact area between reactants. Powdering a solid increases its exposed surface area dramatically (a 1 cm cube has 6 cm² surface; chopping into 1 mm cubes gives 60 cm²). Faster collisions → faster reaction. Examples: powdered zinc reacts with HCl much faster than zinc strip; flour explosions in mills (huge surface). Distractor 1 — composition is unchanged. Distractor 3 — false; electrons don't change. Distractor 4 — false generalisation.

cards.front:
Enzymes are biological catalysts. Compared to inorganic catalysts, enzymes are typically:

(A) Slower at the same temperature for the same reaction
(B) Highly substrate-specific and active near body temperature
(C) Always permanently consumed during the reaction cycle
(D) Effective only above 100 °C, like steel-mill catalysts
cards.back:
(B) Highly substrate-specific and active near body temperature

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Enzymes are highly substrate-specific (lock-and-key / induced-fit model) and have an OPTIMUM temperature near body temperature (~37 °C in humans); above ~50-60 °C most denature and lose activity. They are FASTER per active site than inorganic catalysts (turnover number can be 10⁶-10⁹ /s for some enzymes). Examples: amylase (starch), pepsin (protein, acidic stomach), trypsin (protein, alkaline intestine). Distractor 1 — enzymes are typically much faster, not slower. Distractor 3 — like all catalysts, regenerated, not consumed. Distractor 4 — opposite of true; high temperatures denature enzymes.

cards.option3: Effective only above 100 °C, like steel-mill catalysts

If the temperature of a reaction is raised by 10 °C, the rate typically:

(A) Decreases to roughly half its original value
(B) Roughly doubles, by a common rule of thumb
(C) Stays exactly the same as it was before
(D) Slows down because reactants now expand a lot
cards.back:
(B) Roughly doubles, by a common rule of thumb

Reason — more molecules cross the activation-energy barrier when temperature is higher, even though the increase in average kinetic energy per molecule is small. Distractor 1 — opposite (lowering 10°C halves the rate). Distractor 3 — wrong, temperature has a strong effect. Distractor 4 — false intuition.
