cards.front:
At chemical equilibrium, the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are:

(A) Both equal to zero, so the reaction stops completely
(B) Equal to each other, so concentrations stay constant
(C) Forward rate is faster than the reverse rate value
(D) Reverse rate is faster than the forward rate value
cards.back:
(B) Equal to each other, so concentrations stay constant

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — DYNAMIC equilibrium — molecular reactions continue in both directions, but rates are equal so net concentrations don't change. Equilibrium ≠ stopping. Distractor 1 — common misconception; reactions DO continue. Distractors 3 and 4 describe non-equilibrium states (where reaction proceeds in one net direction).

cards.front:
LE CHATELIER'S PRINCIPLE states that a system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance by:

(A) Speeding up both reactions until the disturbance is gone
(B) Shifting in a direction that opposes the change applied
(C) Reaching a new equilibrium with the same constant value
(D) Producing only the original reactants and no products
cards.back:
(B) Shifting in a direction that opposes the change applied

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Le Chatelier (1884): if a system in equilibrium is disturbed (change in concentration, temperature, or pressure), it shifts in the direction that opposes the disturbance, restoring a new equilibrium. Examples: increase reactant → forward shift; remove product → forward shift; increase pressure → shift to side with fewer moles of gas; raise temperature → shift in endothermic direction. Distractor 3 false because Kc CAN change with temperature.

cards.option3: Producing only the original reactants and no products

cards.front:
For the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (exothermic), increasing the TEMPERATURE will:

(A) Shift equilibrium toward more ammonia formation
(B) Shift equilibrium back toward N₂ and H₂ reactants
(C) Have no effect because Kc remains exactly constant
(D) Cause both reactions to halt completely at higher heat
cards.back:
(B) Shift equilibrium back toward N₂ and H₂ reactants

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Forward reaction is EXOTHERMIC (releases heat). Raising temperature ADDS heat → equilibrium shifts in the ENDOTHERMIC direction (consumes heat) → REVERSE direction → less ammonia, more N₂ and H₂. Industrial Haber-Bosch process compromises: moderate temperature (~450 °C — high enough for adequate rate but not so high that equilibrium goes backwards), high pressure (~200 atm — pushes forward by Le Chatelier since 4 mol gas → 2 mol). Iron catalyst speeds up both forward and reverse equally.

Adding a CATALYST to a reaction at equilibrium will:

(A) Shift equilibrium toward more products being formed
(B) Help equilibrium be reached faster without shifting position
(C) Increase the equilibrium constant for the forward step
(D) Decrease both forward and reverse reaction rates equally
cards.back:
(B) Help equilibrium be reached faster without shifting position

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — A catalyst speeds up FORWARD AND REVERSE reactions equally → equilibrium reached faster, but POSITION of equilibrium (Kc) is UNCHANGED. Catalyst does not appear in the equilibrium expression. Industrial significance: catalysts make commercial-scale reactions feasible by reducing the time to reach equilibrium, even though they can't change the maximum yield. Distractor 1 false. Distractor 3 — catalysts don't change Kc. Distractor 4 — they INCREASE rates, not decrease.

cards.front:
For the reaction A(g) + B(g) ⇌ 2C(g), if the volume of the container is HALVED (pressure doubled), equilibrium will:

(A) Shift toward the products since they have more atoms
(B) Stay in place since the moles of gas are equal on both sides
(C) Shift toward the reactants since they were given first
(D) The forward and reverse rates both fall to zero now
cards.back:
(B) Stay in place since the moles of gas are equal on both sides

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Le Chatelier and pressure: equilibrium shifts toward the side with FEWER moles of gas when pressure is increased. Here both sides have 2 moles of gas (1+1 reactants vs 2 products) → no shift. Example: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI is also pressure-insensitive. CONTRAST: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ has 4 → 2 moles → high pressure favours products (forward).

cards.front:
If the equilibrium constant Kc for a reaction is VERY LARGE (e.g., 10⁶), it means at equilibrium:

(A) Reactants are present in much larger amounts than products
(B) Products are formed almost completely from the reactants
(C) The reaction proceeds equally in both directions still
(D) The reaction has not started since rate is far too low
cards.back:
(B) Products are formed almost completely from the reactants

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Kc = [products]^stoich / [reactants]^stoich. Large Kc → numerator (products) >> denominator (reactants) → equilibrium lies far toward the products. Practical implication: reaction is essentially complete (e.g., combustion reactions have Kc ~10⁴⁰, considered to 'go to completion'). Small Kc (<<1) → equilibrium lies toward reactants; very little product forms. Kc ≈ 1 → comparable amounts of both. Note: Kc only describes the equilibrium position, NOT the rate.

cards.front:
If we DOUBLE the concentration of one of the reactants in a reversible reaction at equilibrium, the system will:

(A) Shift the equilibrium backward to undo the addition
(B) Shift forward to consume the added reactant gradually
(C) Halt all reaction since equilibrium is now disturbed
(D) Decompose into the original elements automatically
cards.back:
(B) Shift forward to consume the added reactant gradually

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Le Chatelier: adding more reactant → forward reaction speeds up (relative to reverse) until a NEW equilibrium is reached, with more products formed. Some of the added reactant gets consumed; final concentration of reactant is higher than original equilibrium but lower than the disturbed value. Industrial principle: removing product (or adding reactant) keeps reaction going; this is exploited in continuous processes. Distractor 1 reverses direction. Distractor 3 — equilibrium doesn't HALT. Distractor 4 — false.

cards.front:
Which of these factors does NOT generally affect the rate of a chemical reaction?

(A) Volume of empty container space
(B) Temperature of the reaction mix
(C) Concentration of the reactants here
(D) Presence of a suitable catalyst
cards.back:
(A) Volume of empty container space

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — FACTORS that AFFECT reaction rate: (1) CONCENTRATION of reactants — higher conc → more collisions → faster rate. (2) TEMPERATURE — higher T → more KE → more effective collisions → faster (rate roughly DOUBLES per 10°C rise). (3) SURFACE AREA — for solids, finer particles = more reactive surface = faster (powdered Mg burns faster than a Mg ribbon). (4) CATALYST — lowers activation energy, speeds up reaction without being consumed. (5) PRESSURE (for gases) — higher P = higher concentration, faster rate. (6) NATURE of reactants — ionic reactions in solution are very fast; covalent bond breaking is slower. (7) RADIATION/light — for photochemical reactions (e.g., chlorine + methane). FACTOR THAT DOESN'T MATTER (in most basic-chem contexts): EMPTY VOLUME of container — only reactant concentrations and contact matter; whether you have 1 L or 10 L of empty headspace (with same concentrations) doesn't change rate. EXCEPTION: in gas-phase, total volume affects pressure/concentration; but in solution, empty volume is irrelevant. PYQ FREQUENCY: factor-affecting Qs are 1-mark guarantees in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT-driven CGL.

cards.front:
Increasing the temperature by 10°C typically increases the reaction rate by approximately:

(A) 2-3 times (Arrhenius rule)
(B) 10 times exactly always
(C) 100 times always now
(D) It always halves the rate
cards.back:
(A) 2-3 times (Arrhenius rule)

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — GENERAL RULE OF THUMB (Van't Hoff's rule): for every 10°C rise in temperature, reaction rate roughly DOUBLES (sometimes triples for some reactions). MORE PRECISE: ARRHENIUS EQUATION: k = A·e^(−Ea/RT), where k = rate constant, A = pre-exponential factor, Ea = activation energy, R = gas constant, T = temperature in K. WHY does T affect rate so strongly? At higher T: (1) MORE molecules have kinetic energy ≥ Ea (Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution shifts right). (2) Effective collision frequency increases. (3) The exponential dependence on T means small T changes have big effects. PRACTICAL EXAMPLE — REFRIGERATION: food kept at 4°C lasts ~10× longer than at room temp (~25°C). The 21°C lower temperature slows microbial enzymes. EXAMPLE — PRESSURE COOKER: increases water boiling point from 100°C to 120°C → cooks food ~3-4× faster (by Van't Hoff's rule). ACTIVATION ENERGY: minimum energy required for reactants to convert into products. CATALYSTS work by REDUCING Ea — making rate increase even at the same T. PYQ FREQUENCY: T-effect on rate appears in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT MCQs ~1× per cycle.

cards.front:
ACTIVATION ENERGY of a reaction is:

(A) Minimum energy needed for reaction
(B) Heat released by the reaction here
(C) Energy to break only one bond
(D) Total energy in the reaction mix
cards.back:
(A) Minimum energy needed for reaction

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — ACTIVATION ENERGY (Ea) = the MINIMUM ENERGY threshold that REACTANT MOLECULES must possess for a successful reaction to occur. Unit: kJ/mol. INTUITION: imagine pushing a boulder over a hill — Ea is the hill's HEIGHT. Reactants 'climb' the energy hill to form an unstable TRANSITION STATE (or activated complex), then 'roll down' to form products. PROPERTIES: (1) Lower Ea → faster reaction. (2) Higher Ea → slower reaction. (3) Catalysts LOWER Ea (provide an alternative reaction pathway). (4) Ea is INDEPENDENT of concentration; only depends on the reaction itself + temperature. KEY CONTRASTS: (a) ENTHALPY (ΔH) = NET energy change between reactants and products (can be + or −). (b) Ea is the BARRIER height, regardless of overall ΔH. EXAMPLES: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O has high Ea (needs spark or flame to start) — but ΔH is highly EXOTHERMIC (releases lots of heat). At room temp, mixture sits stable; once initiated, it explodes. Ea concept is foundational to ENZYMES (biological catalysts), explosives, and combustion engines. PYQ FREQUENCY: Ea is a top-3 chemical-kinetics MCQ in NEET, JEE-Main.

cards.front:
What is the ORDER of a reaction whose rate equation is: rate = k[A]²[B]?

(A) Third order overall (2+1=3)
(B) Second order overall (just A)
(C) First order overall always
(D) Zero order (no concentration)
cards.back:
(A) Third order overall (2+1=3)

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — ORDER of a REACTION = SUM of the powers of concentrations in the rate law. rate = k[A]²[B] means: order w.r.t. A = 2; order w.r.t. B = 1; OVERALL ORDER = 2 + 1 = 3 (third-order reaction). KEY DEFINITIONS: (1) MOLECULARITY = number of MOLECULES involved in an ELEMENTARY step (always whole number, max 3 — termolecular). (2) ORDER = derived from EXPERIMENTAL rate law; can be FRACTIONAL or ZERO (e.g., catalytic reactions on surfaces are often zero-order). RATE LAW: experimentally determined, NOT directly read from balanced equation (except for elementary reactions). EXAMPLE — H₂ + I₂ → 2HI: rate = k[H₂][I₂] (second-order, despite balanced eqn having 2 mol gas). EXAMPLE — DECOMPOSITION of N₂O₅ → 2NO₂ + ½O₂: rate = k[N₂O₅] (first order). UNITS of k depend on order: zero-order: M/s; first-order: 1/s; second-order: M⁻¹·s⁻¹; third-order: M⁻²·s⁻¹. ZERO ORDER: rate INDEPENDENT of concentration (e.g., enzyme reactions at saturation). PYQ FREQUENCY: order/rate-law MCQ appears in NEET, JEE-Main 2-3× per paper.

cards.front:
Why does a powdered solid react FASTER than the same amount in a single lump?

(A) Greater surface area in powder
(B) Powder is at higher temperature
(C) Powder has more atoms per gram
(D) Powder has higher activation energy
cards.back:
(A) Greater surface area in powder

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — POWDERED solids have a much GREATER SURFACE AREA per unit mass than a single lump. Reactions occur AT THE SURFACE (or interface) — more surface = more reactive sites = faster reaction. NUMERICAL: a 1 cm cube has surface area 6 cm². If you cut it into 1000 small (1mm)³ cubes, total surface area becomes 60 cm² — TEN TIMES more. Smaller particles = even greater ratio. SAFETY EXAMPLES: (1) FLOUR DUST EXPLOSIONS — fine flour suspended in air ignites violently due to massive effective surface (Imperial Sugar refinery explosion 2008, USA). (2) COAL DUST EXPLOSIONS in mines — Senghenydd, Wales 1913 killed 439. (3) MAGNESIUM RIBBON burns in air; magnesium POWDER (turnings) explodes more violently. INDUSTRIAL: ground catalysts (e.g., platinum in catalytic converters) are deposited as nanoparticles to maximize surface. KEY INSIGHT: total amount of substance is unchanged; only ACCESSIBILITY of reactant atoms changes. EXAM FAVOURITE: 'why does iron filings rust faster than iron rod?' = surface area. PYQ FREQUENCY: surface-area-affects-rate is a Class 9-10 NCERT MCQ — appears in SSC, NEET, IBPS GA 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
A CATALYST changes the rate of reaction by:

(A) Lowering activation energy barrier
(B) Raising the activation energy
(C) Heating the reaction mixture
(D) Increasing reactant concentration
cards.back:
(A) Lowering activation energy barrier

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — CATALYST = substance that SPEEDS UP a reaction WITHOUT being consumed itself. MECHANISM: provides an ALTERNATIVE pathway with LOWER ACTIVATION ENERGY (Ea). It does NOT change ΔH (the overall energy difference between reactants and products) — it only lowers the BARRIER. PROPERTIES: (1) Used in small quantities. (2) Recovered chemically unchanged. (3) Specific to particular reactions. (4) Can be poisoned by certain impurities. (5) Doesn't affect equilibrium position — both forward and reverse rates equally. TYPES: (a) HOMOGENEOUS (same phase as reactants — e.g., acid catalyzing ester hydrolysis in solution). (b) HETEROGENEOUS (different phase — e.g., solid Pt catalyzing gas reactions in catalytic converters). (c) ENZYMES — biological protein catalysts; extraordinarily specific (lock-and-key), can speed reactions by 10¹⁷×. INDUSTRIAL EXAMPLES: (1) Iron catalyst in HABER PROCESS (NH₃ synthesis). (2) Vanadium oxide V₂O₅ in CONTACT PROCESS (H₂SO₄). (3) Nickel in HYDROGENATION of vegetable oils → vanaspati. (4) Pt-Pd in catalytic converters (CO + NOx removal). NOBEL: Ostwald (1909), Sabatier (1912), Haber (1918) — all catalysis-related. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-mark guarantee.

cards.front:
The HALF-LIFE (t½) of a FIRST-ORDER reaction depends on:

(A) Rate constant k only — t½ = 0.693/k
(B) Both k and initial concentration
(C) Initial concentration only here
(D) Volume of reaction container
cards.back:
(A) Rate constant k only — t½ = 0.693/k

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — FIRST-ORDER reaction half-life: t½ = 0.693/k, INDEPENDENT of initial concentration. This means: regardless of where you start, half the substance disappears in the same time interval. Then half AGAIN in another t½, etc. — exponential decay. MOST IMPORTANT EXAMPLE: RADIOACTIVE DECAY (a first-order process). Carbon-14 has t½ = 5,730 years; uranium-238 has t½ = 4.5 billion years. PHARMACOKINETICS: most drugs follow first-order elimination — dosage intervals are set as ~t½ to maintain therapeutic levels. ZERO-ORDER half-life: t½ = [A]₀/(2k) — DEPENDS on initial concentration (alcohol elimination is approximately zero-order). SECOND-ORDER half-life: t½ = 1/(k[A]₀) — also depends on initial conc. RECOGNITION: in first-order graphs, ln[A] vs t is LINEAR with slope = −k. EXAMPLES of first-order: (1) Decomposition of N₂O₅. (2) Hydrolysis of esters in dilute acid. (3) Most enzyme reactions at LOW substrate concentration. INSIGHT: the 0.693 = ln 2 ≈ 0.6931. After 10 half-lives, only 1/1024 (~0.1%) of original remains. PYQ FREQUENCY: half-life kinetics is top NEET, JEE-Main, JEE-Adv.

cards.front:
An EXOTHERMIC reaction is one in which:

(A) Heat is absorbed from the surroundings into the system
(B) Heat is released from the system into the surroundings
(C) Mass is created from energy stored in the chemical bonds
(D) Reactants are converted but no temperature change happens
cards.back:
(B) Heat is released from the system into the surroundings

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — EXOTHERMIC — releases heat (ΔH < 0). Surroundings warm up. Examples: combustion (CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + heat), neutralisation (acid + base), respiration (glucose + O₂), most precipitation. ENDOTHERMIC — absorbs heat (ΔH > 0). Surroundings cool down. Examples: photosynthesis, melting, evaporation, dissolving NH₄NO₃ in water (cold pack). Distractor 1 = endothermic. Distractor 3 — mass is conserved in chemical reactions; only energy form changes. Distractor 4 — there is always some thermal change.

cards.option2: Mass is created from energy stored in the chemical bonds
cards.option3: Reactants are converted but no temperature change happens

cards.front:
The FIRST LAW of thermodynamics states that:

(A) Heat always flows from cold bodies to hot bodies spontaneously
(B) Energy can be neither created nor destroyed, only transformed
(C) Entropy of an isolated system is always increasing over time
(D) Absolute zero of temperature can be reached in finite steps
cards.back:
(B) Energy can be neither created nor destroyed, only transformed

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — FIRST LAW — energy conservation, applied to thermodynamic systems. Mathematically: ΔU = q − w (or q + w, sign convention varies); change in internal energy = heat added minus work done by the system. Forbids perpetual-motion machines of the FIRST kind. Distractor 1 — opposite of true; heat flows from hot to cold (Second Law / Clausius). Distractor 3 = SECOND law (entropy increase). Distractor 4 = THIRD law violation (absolute zero is unreachable in finite steps).

cards.option3: Absolute zero of temperature can be reached in finite steps

cards.front:
ENTROPY (S) is best described as a measure of:

(A) The total internal energy stored in the system
(B) The disorder or number of microscopic arrangements
(C) The rate at which the chemical reaction proceeds
(D) The total mass of substances in the system
cards.back:
(B) The disorder or number of microscopic arrangements

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — ENTROPY — measure of disorder / number of microstates. Boltzmann formula: S = k ln W (W = number of accessible microstates; k = Boltzmann constant). Higher disorder → higher entropy. Examples — ice (low S) → water (medium S) → vapour (high S). Mixing two gases increases entropy. SECOND LAW: total entropy of universe always increases in any spontaneous process. Distractor 1 = internal energy U. Distractor 3 = rate constant. Distractor 4 = mass.
cards.option1: The total internal energy stored in the system

Higher disorder → higher entropy. Examples — ice (low S) → water (medium S) → vapour (high S). Mixing two gases increases entropy. cards.front:
Gibbs FREE ENERGY change (ΔG) determines spontaneity. A reaction is spontaneous at constant T, P when:

(A) ΔG is positive and grows larger over time
(B) ΔG is negative (free energy decreases)
(C) ΔG is exactly zero (system at equilibrium)
(D) ΔG is undefined under these conditions
cards.back:
(B) ΔG is negative (free energy decreases)

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Spontaneity criterion at constant T, P: ΔG < 0 (free energy decreases). ΔG = 0 → equilibrium (no net change). ΔG > 0 → non-spontaneous (reverse is spontaneous). EXOTHERMIC + entropy-increasing reactions are always spontaneous. ENDOTHERMIC + entropy-decreasing are always non-spontaneous. The other two combinations depend on temperature: high T favours entropy-driven processes, low T favours enthalpy-driven processes.

cards.front:
HESS'S LAW states that the total enthalpy change of a chemical reaction is:

(A) Always equal to twice the activation energy of the reaction
(B) Independent of the path taken to convert reactants to products
(C) Proportional to the temperature at which it is carried out
(D) Negligible compared to entropy of the system in question
cards.back:
(B) Independent of the path taken to convert reactants to products

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — HESS'S LAW — enthalpy is a STATE FUNCTION; total ΔH depends only on initial and final states, NOT on the route. Practical use: if a reaction can't be measured directly (e.g., burning C to CO is hard to control vs CO₂), we sum up other measurable steps to get the desired enthalpy. Born-Haber cycle uses Hess's law to compute lattice enthalpies. Distractor 1 — confuses ΔH with Ea. Distractor 3 — wrong proportionality. Distractor 4 — false generalisation.

cards.front:
The SECOND LAW of thermodynamics implies that:

(A) Heat always flows spontaneously from cold to hot bodies
(B) Total entropy of an isolated system never decreases over time
(C) Energy can be created from nothing in a closed system
(D) Absolute zero is reachable using any cooling method available
cards.back:
(B) Total entropy of an isolated system never decreases over time

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — SECOND LAW — entropy of an isolated system never decreases; it stays the same in reversible processes and increases in irreversible (real) processes. Equivalent statements: (a) Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never the reverse without external work — Clausius. (b) No engine working between two reservoirs can be 100% efficient at converting heat to work — Kelvin-Planck. (c) Forbids perpetual-motion machines of the SECOND kind. Distractor 1 — opposite of correct direction. Distractor 3 violates first law. Distractor 4 violates third law.

cards.front:
Burning a fuel to release stored chemical energy as heat is an example of:

(A) An endothermic reaction with positive ΔH
(B) An exothermic reaction with negative ΔH
(C) A reaction with zero enthalpy change overall
(D) A reaction that violates the first law of thermodynamics
cards.back:
(B) An exothermic reaction with negative ΔH

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Combustion = exothermic; energy of bonds in reactants > energy of bonds in products → difference released as heat. Standard enthalpies of combustion: methane −890 kJ/mol; ethanol −1367 kJ/mol; petrol/octane −5470 kJ/mol; hydrogen −286 kJ/mol (cleanest, no CO₂). Bond enthalpies determine ΔH. Distractor 1 — endothermic = absorbs heat (e.g., photosynthesis, melting). Distractor 3 — combustion has large negative ΔH. Distractor 4 — combustion conserves energy (heat output = bond energy difference); doesn't violate any law.

cards.front:
The rusting of iron (Fe) in moist air — 4Fe + 3O₂ + 6H₂O → 4Fe(OH)₃ — is an example of:

(A) Displacement reaction
(B) Neutralisation reaction
(C) OXIDATION / REDOX / CORROSION
(D) Photosynthesis (not a chemistry reaction)
cards.back:
(C) OXIDATION / REDOX / CORROSION

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — RUSTING — corrosion of IRON in MOIST AIR; an ELECTROCHEMICAL process that is a form of OXIDATION (iron loses electrons) and therefore a REDOX reaction. Required: (a) IRON (Fe); (b) OXYGEN (O₂); (c) WATER (H₂O). If either oxygen OR water is absent, iron won't rust — that's why we paint, oil, grease, galvanise (zinc coating), tin-plate, chrome-plate, or alloy iron (stainless steel with Cr) to prevent rust. Saline/acidic conditions ACCELERATE rusting. CHEMISTRY: Fe is oxidised to Fe²⁺, which further oxidises to Fe³⁺; combining with water gives hydrated iron(III) oxide Fe₂O₃·xH₂O — the reddish-brown flaky substance we call RUST. Unlike aluminium's Al₂O₃ oxide layer (which is dense + protective), rust FLAKES off exposing fresh Fe → continues corroding → structural failure over time. CORROSION varieties: (1) DRY oxidation (at high T, direct O-Fe); (2) WET / ELECTROCHEMICAL (normal rusting); (3) GALVANIC (dissimilar metals in contact + electrolyte); (4) PITTING, STRESS, INTERGRANULAR. METALS & THEIR CORROSION: (a) SILVER → tarnishes BLACK (Ag₂S) in sulfur-containing air; (b) COPPER → develops GREEN patina (basic copper carbonate Cu₂(OH)₂CO₃, ‘verdigris’ as on Statue of Liberty); (c) ALUMINIUM → thin tough Al₂O₃ layer (passivation); (d) BRASS → tarnishes greenish; (e) BRONZE → green patina. PREVENTION: GALVANISATION (Zn on Fe — sacrificial anode), TINNING (Sn on Fe — protects by barrier), CHROME-plating, PAINTING, OILING, ENAMELLING, ALLOYING (stainless steel: Fe + Cr 10-12% + Ni). REDOX mnemonic: OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss (of e⁻), Reduction Is Gain (of e⁻). In rusting: Fe is oxidised (LOSES electrons); O₂ is reduced (GAINS electrons). iron loses electrons to oxygen; hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O, reddish-brown) is rust.

cards.front:
The reaction ‘Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu’ is an example of:

(A) Combination reaction
(B) Decomposition reaction
(C) DISPLACEMENT reaction
(D) Combustion reaction
cards.back:
(C) DISPLACEMENT reaction

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — DISPLACEMENT REACTION — a single element displaces another from its compound. Driven by the ACTIVITY SERIES of metals. In this case, ZINC (more reactive) displaces COPPER (less reactive) from COPPER SULPHATE: Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s). Observations: blue CuSO₄ solution fades (Cu²⁺ ions consumed); reddish-brown Cu deposits on Zn strip; Zn dissolves. ACTIVITY SERIES of metals (most reactive to least): K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au > Pt. Any metal higher in the list will DISPLACE any metal below it from its aqueous salt solution. EXAMPLES: (1) Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu (used in classroom demos). (2) Cu + FeSO₄ → NO reaction (Cu less reactive than Fe). (3) Mg + HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂↑ (metal displacing hydrogen from acid). (4) Au, Pt do NOT react with most acids — hence ‘noble metals’ (only dissolve in AQUA REGIA = 3:1 conc HCl:HNO₃). 5 MAJOR TYPES OF REACTIONS: (I) COMBINATION (A+B→AB): 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO; (II) DECOMPOSITION (AB→A+B): 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ (electrolysis), CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (heating of limestone); (III) DISPLACEMENT (A+BC → AC+B) — single displacement; (IV) DOUBLE DISPLACEMENT / METATHESIS (AB + CD → AD + CB): AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl↓ (white precipitate) + NaNO₃; (V) REDOX — includes combustion, rusting, photosynthesis, cellular respiration. PRECIPITATION reactions are a subset of double-displacement where an insoluble product forms. NEUTRALISATION: acid + base → salt + water, e.g., HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O (exothermic). Zn, being more reactive than Cu, displaces Cu from CuSO₄; single displacement / metal displacement.

cards.front:
The thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate in a limekiln — CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ — produces which commercially valuable product?

(A) Plaster of Paris
(B) QUICK LIME
(C) Washing soda
(D) Bleaching powder
cards.back:
(B) QUICK LIME

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — LIME KILN REACTION: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) at ~900-1000°C; example of THERMAL DECOMPOSITION. PRODUCTS: (1) CaO = CALCIUM OXIDE = ‘QUICKLIME’ / ‘BURNT LIME’ — highly exothermic reaction with water: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (SLAKED LIME, ‘white-wash’) + heat. Used in cement (~60% of a bag), steel-making (flux), purification of sugar, leather tanning, water softening, desulphurisation of flue gas (flue gas + lime → gypsum), glass manufacturing. (2) CO₂ — greenhouse gas released; cement industry is ~8% of global CO₂ emissions (split between limestone decomp + fuel burning). Indian cement industry major CO₂ source. CHEMICAL ‘NICKNAMES’ (VERY common exam topic): Chemical → common name: (a) CaCO₃ = LIMESTONE / CALCITE / MARBLE / CHALK (all CaCO₃ in different crystal forms); (b) CaO = QUICKLIME; (c) Ca(OH)₂ = SLAKED LIME / MILK OF LIME; (d) CaSO₄·½H₂O = PLASTER OF PARIS (gypsum heated to 150°C drives off water: 2CaSO₄·2H₂O → 2CaSO₄·½H₂O + 3H₂O); (e) CaSO₄·2H₂O = GYPSUM; (f) CaOCl₂ = BLEACHING POWDER (chloride of lime); (g) NaHCO₃ = BAKING SODA; (h) Na₂CO₃·10H₂O = WASHING SODA (from solvay process); (i) NaOH = CAUSTIC SODA; (j) H₂SO₄ = OIL OF VITRIOL, ‘KING of CHEMICALS’; (k) HNO₃ = AQUA FORTIS; (l) HCl = MURIATIC ACID; (m) FeSO₄·7H₂O = GREEN VITRIOL; (n) CuSO₄·5H₂O = BLUE VITRIOL; (o) ZnSO₄·7H₂O = WHITE VITRIOL; (p) AgNO₃ = LUNAR CAUSTIC; (q) NH₄Cl = SAL AMMONIAC; (r) KNO₃ = NITER / INDIAN SALTPETRE; (s) NaNO₃ = CHILE SALTPETRE; (t) Mg(OH)₂ = MILK OF MAGNESIA. USES of PoP: casts for broken bones, moulds, statues, wall ceilings — rapid setting with water. used in cement, steel making, flue-gas desulphurisation, paper, water treatment; calcium oxide, CaO.

cards.front:
In an EXOTHERMIC reaction:

(A) Heat is absorbed from surroundings
(B) HEAT is RELEASED to surroundings
(C) No heat change occurs
(D) Catalysts must be used
cards.back:
(B) HEAT is RELEASED to surroundings

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — EXOTHERMIC vs ENDOTHERMIC — classification of reactions by HEAT flow: (1) EXOTHERMIC — reaction RELEASES heat to surroundings; products have LOWER enthalpy than reactants, so ΔH (enthalpy change) is NEGATIVE. Examples: (a) COMBUSTION — burning of wood, LPG, candle; CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + heat; (b) RUSTING (slow exothermic, heat barely noticed); (c) NEUTRALISATION — HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O + heat (test-tube warms); (d) CELLULAR RESPIRATION — C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (ATP); (e) SETTING of CEMENT / PLASTER OF PARIS; (f) DISSOLVING of NaOH or H₂SO₄ in water; (g) FORMATION of most IONIC compounds; (h) CONDENSATION of steam → water. (2) ENDOTHERMIC — reaction ABSORBS heat; ΔH > 0. Examples: (a) PHOTOSYNTHESIS — 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + hν → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (uses sunlight energy); (b) THERMAL DECOMPOSITION — CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (needs 900°C heat input); (c) ELECTROLYSIS of water — 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ (needs electric energy); (d) DISSOLVING of AMMONIUM NITRATE in water (used in cold packs — container gets cold); (e) MELTING of ice (absorbs 334 kJ/kg latent heat); (f) BOILING of water (2260 kJ/kg). The LAW of CONSERVATION of ENERGY: heat released by exothermic reaction = reduction in chemical bond energy (bonds formed stronger than bonds broken). First law of THERMODYNAMICS: ΔU = q + w (internal energy change = heat added + work done on system). Hess's law: net enthalpy change is independent of path. IMPORTANT EXAM fact: when sulphuric acid is diluted, always add ACID to WATER (not water to acid) — the reaction is HIGHLY exothermic, and if water is added to concentrated H₂SO₄, water boils on contact, spattering acid.

cards.front:
The HABER-BOSCH process is used industrially to produce:

(A) Sulphuric acid
(B) Hydrochloric acid
(C) AMMONIA (NH₃)
(D) Nitric acid
cards.back:
(C) AMMONIA (NH₃)

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — HABER-BOSCH PROCESS — industrial synthesis of AMMONIA (NH₃) from atmospheric NITROGEN (N₂) and HYDROGEN (H₂). Reaction: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) + heat (exothermic, ΔH = -92 kJ/mol, reversible). CONDITIONS: (a) high PRESSURE — 150-250 atm (forward rxn reduces moles, so high P favours product per Le Chatelier); (b) moderate-high TEMPERATURE — 400-500°C (high T favours reverse rxn but needed for kinetics — compromise T); (c) IRON (Fe) CATALYST with molybdenum/aluminium oxide promoters (Mittasch 1910); (d) yield per pass only ~15-20% — unreacted N₂ + H₂ recycled in loop. HISTORY: (1) FRITZ HABER (German chemist) developed the process in a lab 1908-09; WON NOBEL in CHEMISTRY 1918 (controversially — he also developed chemical weapons used in WWI — Zyklon A/B, chlorine gas; considered ‘father of chemical warfare’). (2) CARL BOSCH (BASF chemist/engineer) scaled it up industrially by 1913; WON NOBEL 1931 for high-pressure chemistry. TOGETHER: ‘Haber-Bosch Process’ — named Chemistry Landmark. IMPACT: dubbed one of the most IMPORTANT inventions of the 20th century. Before 1910, nitrogen fertilisers came from CHILEAN SALTPETRE (NaNO₃ deposits) and guano (bird droppings, Peru) — both finite. Haber-Bosch made NITROGEN fertiliser MANUFACTURE limitless. Currently: produces ~175 MT of ammonia annually → ~80% used for fertilisers (urea, ammonium nitrate, DAP, NPK) → feeds nearly HALF the world population. WITHOUT Haber-Bosch, world agriculture could not support >3-4 billion. ENVIRONMENTAL COST: process uses 1-2% of GLOBAL ENERGY; emits ~1-2% of global CO₂; runaway N-fertiliser use has caused massive eutrophication (algal blooms), groundwater nitrate pollution, GHG emissions (N₂O). INDIA: world's 2nd-largest urea producer and consumer; relies on imported natural gas (H₂ feedstock) + imported/subsidised urea. Recent push: NEEM-COATED UREA, NANO UREA (IFFCO, 2021 — nano nitrogen, 500 ml bottle replaces 45 kg bag), green ammonia (from green H₂, a key NGHM 2023 outcome). from N₂ + H₂ under high T (~450°C) + high P (~200 atm) + Fe catalyst; basis of nitrogenous fertilisers (urea, ammonium nitrate) that feed ~half the world.

Reaction: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) + heat (exothermic, ΔH = -92 kJ/mol, reversible). CONDITIONS: (a) high PRESSURE — 150-250 atm (forward rxn reduces moles, so high P favours product per Le Chatelier); (b) moderate-high TEMPERATURE — 400-500°C (high T favours reverse rxn but needed for kinetics — compromise T); (c) IRON (Fe) CATALYST with molybdenum/aluminium oxide promoters (Mittasch 1910); (d) yield per pass only ~15-20% — unreacted N₂ + H₂ recycled in loop. HISTORY: (1) FRITZ HABER (German chemist) developed the process in a lab 1908-09; WON NOBEL in CHEMISTRY 1918 (controversially — he also developed chemical weapons used in WWI — Zyklon A/B, chlorine gas; considered ‘father of chemical warfare’). (2) CARL BOSCH (BASF chemist/engineer) scaled it up industrially by 1913; WON NOBEL 1931 for high-pressure chemistry. TOGETHER: ‘Haber-Bosch Process’ — named Chemistry Landmark. IMPACT: dubbed one of the most IMPORTANT inventions of the 20th century. Before 1910, nitrogen fertilisers came from CHILEAN SALTPETRE (NaNO₃ deposits) and guano (bird droppings, Peru) — both finite. Haber-Bosch made NITROGEN fertiliser MANUFACTURE limitless. Currently: produces ~175 MT of ammonia annually → ~80% used for fertilisers (urea, ammonium nitrate, DAP, NPK) → feeds nearly HALF the world population. WITHOUT Haber-Bosch, world agriculture could not support >3-4 billion. ENVIRONMENTAL COST: process uses 1-2% of GLOBAL ENERGY; emits ~1-2% of global CO₂; runaway N-fertiliser use has caused massive eutrophication (algal blooms), groundwater nitrate pollution, GHG emissions (N₂O). INDIA: world's 2nd-largest urea producer and consumer; relies on imported natural gas (H₂ feedstock) + imported/subsidised urea. cards.front:
CATALYSTS affect a reaction by:

(A) Shifting the equilibrium toward products
(B) Increasing the yield of products
(C) LOWERING the ACTIVATION ENERGY (Ea)
(D) Converting reactants into different products
cards.back:
(C) LOWERING the ACTIVATION ENERGY (Ea)

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — CATALYST — substance that INCREASES the RATE of a chemical reaction without being consumed or permanently altered by it. Works by providing an ALTERNATIVE REACTION PATHWAY with LOWER ACTIVATION ENERGY (Ea). Since it affects FORWARD and REVERSE rates EQUALLY, it does NOT change the EQUILIBRIUM POSITION or ΔH (enthalpy change) — only helps equilibrium get there FASTER. TYPES of catalysts: (1) POSITIVE — increases rate (most common; ‘catalyst’ usually means this). (2) NEGATIVE / INHIBITOR — decreases rate. (3) AUTOCATALYST — a PRODUCT of the reaction that catalyses further reaction. (4) HOMOGENEOUS — same phase as reactants (e.g., conc. H₂SO₄ in esterification). (5) HETEROGENEOUS — different phase (e.g., solid Fe catalysing gaseous Haber-Bosch). (6) BIOCATALYSTS / ENZYMES — biological proteins (amylase, pepsin, lipase — act at mild body temp, highly specific). FAMOUS INDUSTRIAL CATALYSTS + processes: (a) HABER-BOSCH — Fe (Mo-promoted) for NH₃; (b) CONTACT PROCESS — V₂O₅ (vanadium pentoxide) for H₂SO₄ via 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃; (c) OSTWALD PROCESS — Pt/Rh gauze for HNO₃ via 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O; (d) HYDROGENATION of vegetable oils — Ni (Ni-catalysed hydrogenation of unsaturated oils to solid ‘vanaspati’ / margarine); (e) CATALYTIC CRACKING (petroleum) — zeolites, alumina; (f) CATALYTIC CONVERTERS in vehicles — Pt/Pd/Rh — convert CO → CO₂, NOx → N₂ + O₂, unburnt HC → CO₂ + H₂O; (g) ZIEGLER-NATTA catalysts — for polymerisation of alkenes (Ziegler + Natta, Nobel 1963, TiCl₄ + AlEt₃). CATALYST POISONING — certain impurities block active sites (e.g., Pb in petrol poisons catalytic converters — hence unleaded petrol is mandatory). ENZYMES: (a) AMYLASE — starch to maltose (saliva); (b) PEPSIN — protein in acidic stomach; (c) TRYPSIN — pancreas; (d) LIPASE — fats; (e) DNA POLYMERASE — DNA replication; (f) RNA POLYMERASE — transcription; (g) RIBOZYMES — RNA catalysts. Enzymes are extremely specific (lock-key / induced-fit); rate enhancement can be 10⁶-10²⁰ times. speeds up the forward AND reverse reaction equally; does not alter equilibrium position or ΔH; is itself NOT consumed.

cards.front:
BAKING SODA is sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃). When it's HEATED, it decomposes according to: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂. The CO₂ released causes:

(A) The flour to turn brown
(B) The BAKED ITEM (cake, bread) to RISE / become POROUS
(C) A bitter taste
(D) Protein denaturation
cards.back:
(B) The BAKED ITEM (cake, bread) to RISE / become POROUS

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — BAKING SODA (NaHCO₃, sodium bicarbonate/sodium hydrogen carbonate) — decomposes on heating: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂. The released CO₂ gas creates BUBBLES in the batter/dough that EXPAND during baking, making the cake/bread RISE and become FLUFFY / POROUS. DOWNSIDE: pure baking soda leaves behind sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) which has a BITTER / soapy taste → that’s why bakers use BAKING POWDER instead. BAKING POWDER = NaHCO₃ + a mild EDIBLE ACID (e.g., TARTARIC ACID / cream of tartar, or MONOCALCIUM PHOSPHATE) + cornstarch (anti-caking). When water/moisture added + heat, NaHCO₃ + tartaric acid → sodium tartrate (tasteless) + H₂O + CO₂. The tartaric acid neutralises the bitter Na₂CO₃, giving a CLEAN taste. DOUBLE-ACTING BAKING POWDER: contains two acids — one fast-acting (reacts on mixing with water), one slow-acting (only on heating). Yeast is another leavening agent (living yeast fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂ + energy) — used in bread, pizza, beer. Uses of BAKING SODA beyond baking: (1) FIRE EXTINGUISHERS — CO₂ smothers fire; (2) MEDICINE — antacid (neutralises HCl in stomach: NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂); (3) CLEANING — mild abrasive; (4) PERSONAL CARE — deodorant, toothpaste; (5) SODA-ACID fire extinguisher (old type) — NaHCO₃ sol + H₂SO₄ → CO₂ foam; (6) BUFFER in biological systems (blood pH regulation via HCO₃⁻/H₂CO₃). WASHING SODA (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) uses: (1) removing permanent hardness of water (precipitates Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺); (2) glass, soap, paper manufacture; (3) cleaning. trapped CO₂ bubbles expand during baking.

cards.front:
AQUA REGIA (‘royal water’), which can dissolve even gold and platinum, is a mixture of:

(A) Equal parts HCl and HNO₃
(B) 3 parts CONC. HCl + 1 part CONC. HNO₃ (by volume)
(C) HCl and H₂SO₄
(D) HNO₃ and H₂SO₄
cards.back:
(B) 3 parts CONC. HCl + 1 part CONC. HNO₃ (by volume)

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — AQUA REGIA (Latin: ‘royal water’ / ‘king's water’) — a mixture of 3 parts concentrated HYDROCHLORIC ACID (HCl) + 1 part concentrated NITRIC ACID (HNO₃) by volume. Known since medieval alchemy (~8th-century Islamic alchemist Jabir ibn Hayyan / Geber) as it could dissolve GOLD and PLATINUM — the ‘royal metals’ — which neither acid alone can dissolve. REACTION: HNO₃ (oxidising agent) oxidises Cl⁻ from HCl to give NASCENT CHLORINE (Cl) + NITROSYL CHLORIDE (NOCl), both of which are highly reactive species; gold is first oxidised to Au³⁺ by nitric acid, and then chloride ions form stable [AuCl₄]⁻ (tetrachloroaurate) complex, removing Au³⁺ from equilibrium and driving the reaction forward. Au + HNO₃ + 4HCl → H[AuCl₄] + NO + 2H₂O. Similarly Pt → [PtCl₆]²⁻. USES: dissolving GOLD in refining and electrochemistry; etching / cleaning of precious metal residues; historically, used to ESCAPE NAZI theft — Hungarian chemist GEORGE DE HEVESY dissolved Nobel gold medals of JAMES FRANCK + MAX VON LAUE in aqua regia, stored the solution in Copenhagen, recovered gold after WWII. NEITHER HCl nor HNO₃ alone dissolves gold. TITANIUM, IRIDIUM, RUTHENIUM, OSMIUM, RHODIUM do NOT dissolve in aqua regia either (truly ‘noble’ in that sense). OTHER ACID FACTS: (1) HF (hydrofluoric acid) is used to etch GLASS (SiO₂ + 4HF → SiF₄↑ + 2H₂O); stored in wax/plastic, not glass. (2) CONCENTRATED sulphuric acid is HIGHLY HYGROSCOPIC and DEHYDRATING — will char sugar/cotton/wood to black carbon. (3) PHOSPHORIC ACID (H₃PO₄) — in cola drinks (flavouring + preservative); fertiliser manufacture. (4) CITRIC ACID — in citrus fruits, lemon. (5) LACTIC ACID — curd/sour milk, sore muscles. (6) OXALIC ACID — spinach, rhubarb (can cause kidney stones in excess). (7) FORMIC ACID — ant stings, nettles. formed ~1:3 mix of nitric:hydrochloric; nascent Cl₂ + NOCl species attack noble metals.

cards.front:
PHOTOSYNTHESIS (6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂) is an example of:

(A) Decomposition reaction only
(B) Exothermic combustion
(C) An ENDOTHERMIC, PHOTOCHEMICAL, REDOX REACTION
(D) Neutralisation reaction
cards.back:
(C) An ENDOTHERMIC, PHOTOCHEMICAL, REDOX REACTION

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — PHOTOSYNTHESIS — the biological process by which GREEN PLANTS, algae, and cyanobacteria convert LIGHT energy into CHEMICAL energy, storing it in the bonds of glucose (and ultimately all carbohydrates, amino acids, lipids). The reaction: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + 6O₂. TAKES PLACE in: CHLOROPLASTS (in plant/algae cells) — contain CHLOROPHYLL (green pigment) which absorbs mainly RED + BLUE light (reflects green, hence plants look green). TWO STAGES: (1) LIGHT-DEPENDENT (or ‘photo’) reactions — in THYLAKOID membranes; photons split WATER (photolysis: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂), generating O₂ (released as waste), ATP, NADPH. (2) LIGHT-INDEPENDENT / CALVIN CYCLE (‘dark’ reactions, misnomer — still need products of light phase) — in STROMA; CO₂ is FIXED onto ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP) by enzyme RuBisCO (most abundant protein on Earth); then reduced using ATP+NADPH to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P) → glucose. CLASSIFICATION: (1) ENDOTHERMIC — absorbs energy (solar → chemical); ΔH > 0. (2) REDOX — CO₂ is REDUCED (gains electrons, to form C-H bonds of glucose); H₂O is OXIDISED (loses electrons, releases O₂). (3) PHOTOCHEMICAL — requires LIGHT. (4) COMBINATION + REARRANGEMENT on atomic scale. IMPORTANCE: (1) produces ~100% of atmospheric O₂ (with plants + marine phytoplankton both major); (2) foundation of ALL food chains (autotrophy); (3) removes ~100 GtC/year of CO₂ from atmosphere; (4) source of fossil fuels (ancient photosynthesis). C3, C4, CAM plants — different variants of carbon fixation; C4 (maize, sugarcane) more efficient at high temperatures; CAM (cactus, pineapple) fix CO₂ at night to reduce water loss. OPPOSITE of photosynthesis: CELLULAR RESPIRATION (in mitochondria) — C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP energy; exothermic redox; opposite arrow. Together: the CARBON CYCLE on biological scale. Chlorophyll-a (the main pigment, blue-green, absorbs ~430+660 nm), Chl-b (accessory, yellow-green); also carotenoids (β-carotene, xanthophylls — yellows/oranges seen in autumn leaves when chl breaks down). uses light energy; CO₂ is reduced (gains H to form glucose), water is oxidised (loses H, releases O₂); chlorophyll absorbs photons.

cards.front:
Mixing AgNO₃ (silver nitrate) with NaCl (sodium chloride) solution produces a WHITE PRECIPITATE of:

(A) NaNO₃ (sodium nitrate)
(B) AgCl (SILVER CHLORIDE) — a DOUBLE DISPLACEMENT + PRECIPITATION reaction; AgCl is insoluble in water, white, turns grey in light (photosensitive) — basis of traditional photography
(C) NaCl (salt)
(D) Ag (metallic silver)
cards.back:
(B) AgCl (SILVER CHLORIDE) — a DOUBLE DISPLACEMENT + PRECIPITATION reaction; AgCl is insoluble in water, white, turns grey in light (photosensitive) — basis of traditional photography

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s)↓ + NaNO₃(aq) — a DOUBLE DISPLACEMENT (metathesis) reaction that is ALSO a PRECIPITATION reaction. Drive: AgCl has VERY LOW solubility in water (Ksp ~ 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰), so it precipitates out as a WHITE curdy solid. In light, AgCl darkens to Ag (metallic) + Cl₂ — this PHOTOCHEMICAL reaction was the basis of traditional black-and-white PHOTOGRAPHY (silver halide photographic film). 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂ (in sunlight). Test in chemistry lab: adding dilute AgNO₃ to an unknown solution and getting a white curdy precipitate that dissolves in excess NH₃ → confirms Cl⁻ ion. Similarly: with Br⁻ → PALE YELLOW AgBr (slight solubility in dilute NH₃); with I⁻ → YELLOW AgI (insoluble even in concentrated NH₃). This is the systematic test for halide ions. OTHER FAMOUS PRECIPITATION TESTS: (1) Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2KI → PbI₂ (BRIGHT YELLOW) + 2KNO₃ — ‘GOLDEN RAIN’ experiment. (2) BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ (WHITE) + 2NaCl — barium sulphate precipitation test for SO₄²⁻ ion; also barium meal for X-rays. (3) CaCl₂ + Na₂CO₃ → CaCO₃ (WHITE) + 2NaCl — hard water softening. (4) CuSO₄ + NaOH → Cu(OH)₂ (LIGHT BLUE) + Na₂SO₄. (5) FeCl₃ + 3NaOH → Fe(OH)₃ (RUSTY BROWN) + 3NaCl — iron identification. (6) AgNO₃ + NH₄OH → grey/black Ag₂O precipitate initially, dissolves in excess NH₃ to form diamminesilver(I) [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ — basis of TOLLEN’s REAGENT (silver mirror test for aldehydes). (7) Mg²⁺ + OH⁻ → Mg(OH)₂ (WHITE GELATINOUS) — ‘milk of magnesia’ nearly insoluble. (8) NH₄Cl + AgNO₃ → AgCl (WHITE) + NH₄NO₃. Precipitation is a way to test for ions, and industrially to PURIFY (drop out) unwanted species, or to manufacture pigments.

Precipitation is a way to test for ions, and industrially to PURIFY (drop out) unwanted species, or to manufacture pigments.

cards.front:
A reaction in which HEAT is RELEASED is called:

(A) Endothermic
(B) Exothermic
(C) Adiabatic
(D) Isothermal
cards.back:
(B) Exothermic

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Exothermic — releases heat (ΔH < 0). Examples: combustion, respiration, many neutralisation reactions. Endothermic — absorbs heat (ΔH > 0). Examples: photosynthesis, evaporation, most dissolution. First law of thermodynamics applies.
cards.storedExplanation: Exothermic — releases heat (ΔH < 0). Examples: combustion, respiration, many neutralisation reactions. Endothermic — absorbs heat (ΔH > 0). Examples: photosynthesis, evaporation, most dissolution. First law of thermodynamics applies.

cards.front:
When iron reacts with copper sulphate solution, it DISPLACES copper. This is a:

(A) Combination reaction
(B) Single-displacement reaction
(C) Decomposition reaction
(D) Combustion reaction
cards.back:
(B) Single-displacement reaction

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu. Iron (more reactive) displaces copper (less reactive) from its salt solution. Blue → pale green colour change. Demonstrates reactivity series. Zinc also displaces copper (Zn > Cu). more reactive metal displaces less reactive.
cards.storedExplanation: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu. Iron (more reactive) displaces copper (less reactive) from its salt solution. Blue → pale green colour change. Demonstrates reactivity series. Zinc also displaces copper (Zn > Cu). more reactive metal displaces less reactive.

cards.front:
In a REDOX reaction:

(A) Only oxidation occurs
(B) Oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously
(C) Only reduction occurs
(D) No electron transfer happens
cards.back:
(B) Oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — REDOX — shortened 'reduction-oxidation'. Oxidation = loss of electrons (OIL — Oxidation Is Loss). Reduction = gain of electrons (RIG — Reduction Is Gain). They always occur together. OILRIG mnemonic. Example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (H oxidised, O reduced).

cards.front:
CaCO₃ (limestone) → CaO + CO₂. This is an example of:

(A) Combination
(B) Thermal decomposition
(C) Displacement
(D) Neutralisation
cards.back:
(B) Thermal decomposition

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Decomposition — one reactant splits into two or more products on heating. CaCO₃ → CaO (quicklime) + CO₂ at ~825°C is industrially important (basis of cement and lime production). Electrolysis of water — another common decomposition.
cards.storedExplanation: Decomposition — one reactant splits into two or more products on heating. CaCO₃ → CaO (quicklime) + CO₂ at ~825°C is industrially important (basis of cement and lime production). Electrolysis of water — another common decomposition.

cards.front:
A CATALYST is a substance that:

(A) Is consumed in the reaction
(B) Speeds up a reaction without being consumed
(C) Slows down a reaction
(D) Only inhibits combustion
cards.back:
(B) Speeds up a reaction without being consumed

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Catalyst — alters reaction rate (speeds up via a lower-activation-energy pathway) without being permanently consumed. Enzymes = biological catalysts (enzymatic). Example: Ni in hydrogenation of oils; platinum in catalytic converters of cars; Haber process uses Fe catalyst.

cards.front:
The HABER process produces:

(A) Oxygen from air
(B) Ammonia (NH₃) from N₂ and H₂
(C) Sulphuric acid
(D) Nitric acid
cards.back:
(B) Ammonia (NH₃) from N₂ and H₂

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Haber-Bosch process (Fritz Haber, 1909; scaled up by Bosch). N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, using Fe catalyst at ~450°C and ~200 atm. Revolutionised fertiliser production. Nobel Chemistry 1918 (Haber), 1931 (Bosch). Critical for feeding the world's growing population in the 20th century.

cards.front:
Acid + Base → ?

(A) Salt + more acid
(B) Salt + water
(C) Salt + oxygen
(D) Nothing happens
cards.back:
(B) Salt + water

Chemical Bonding & Reactions — Neutralisation: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Exothermic. Forms salt + water. Useful antacid chemistry — Mg(OH)₂ (milk of magnesia) neutralises excess stomach HCl.

cards.front:
According to the Arrhenius theory, an ACID is a substance that:

(A) Donates an electron pair
(B) Releases H⁺ (hydrogen ion / proton) in aqueous solution
(C) Tastes salty
(D) Is always a metal
cards.back:
(B) Releases H⁺ (hydrogen ion / proton) in aqueous solution

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Arrhenius (1884) — Acid releases H⁺; Base releases OH⁻ in water. HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻; NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻. Brønsted-Lowry (1923) generalised: acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor (works for non-aqueous). Lewis theory (1923) — most general: acid = electron-pair acceptor, base = electron-pair donor. Different theories explain different reactions but Arrhenius is the school-textbook level.

cards.front:
The pH scale ranges from:

(A) −1 to +1
(B) 0 to 14 (acidic < 7 < basic; 7 = neutral)
(C) 0 to 100
(D) −14 to +14
cards.back:
(B) 0 to 14 (acidic < 7 < basic; 7 = neutral)

Acids, Bases & Solutions — pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]. Theoretical scale 0-14 at room temperature (in water). pH 0 = strong acid (1 M HCl); pH 14 = strong base (1 M NaOH); pH 7 = neutral pure water. Each 1 unit = 10× change in [H⁺]. Acidic: pH 0-6 (lemon ~2, vinegar ~2.5, tomato ~4.5, coffee ~5). Neutral: pH 7. Basic: pH 8-14 (baking soda ~9, ammonia ~11, bleach ~12). Strong acids (concentrated battery acid) can go below 0; very alkaline solutions can go above 14.

cards.front:
Litmus paper turns RED in:

(A) A neutral solution
(B) An acidic solution
(C) A basic solution
(D) Distilled water
cards.back:
(B) An acidic solution

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Litmus — natural dye from lichen Roccella tinctoria. BLUE litmus → RED in acid. RED litmus → BLUE in base. Stays the same in neutral. Two-paper test confirms acidity / basicity. Other indicators: PHENOLPHTHALEIN — colourless in acid/neutral, PINK in base (transition pH 8.3-10). METHYL ORANGE — red in acid, yellow above pH 4.4 (transition 3.1-4.4). UNIVERSAL INDICATOR — multi-colour spectrum showing pH numerical estimate. pH meter (electronic) is most precise.

cards.front:
When an acid reacts with a base to form salt + water, the reaction is called:

(A) Polymerisation
(B) Neutralisation (an exothermic reaction)
(C) Sublimation
(D) Catalysis
cards.back:
(B) Neutralisation (an exothermic reaction)

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Neutralisation: HA + BOH → BA + H₂O (acid + base → salt + water). Standard enthalpy of neutralisation ≈ −57.3 kJ/mol for any strong-acid + strong-base reaction (since the reaction is essentially H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O). Real-world examples: antacids neutralising stomach acid (Mg(OH)₂ in milk of magnesia, NaHCO₃ in baking soda); using lime to neutralise acidic soil; toothpaste (slight base) neutralising acidic plaque. Strong acid + weak base (e.g., HCl + NH₄OH) gives slightly acidic salt; strong base + weak acid → slightly basic salt.

cards.front:
Among the following, the STRONGEST acid in aqueous solution is:

(A) Acetic acid (CH₃COOH)
(B) Hydrochloric acid (HCl) — fully dissociates in water
(C) Carbonic acid (H₂CO₃)
(D) Citric acid
cards.back:
(B) Hydrochloric acid (HCl) — fully dissociates in water

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Strong acids (~100% dissociation in water) — HCl, HBr, HI, H₂SO₄ (1st step), HNO₃, HClO₄. Weak acids partial — CH₃COOH (vinegar, Ka ~1.8×10⁻⁵, pKa 4.76), H₂CO₃ (very weak, pKa1 6.35), citric (~3.13), lactic, oxalic. Among given options, HCl is strongest. 'Stomach acid' is dilute HCl, pH ~1.5-2. 'Aqua regia' = 3:1 HCl:HNO₃ — dissolves gold/platinum.

cards.front:
Common 'baking soda' is chemically:

(A) Sodium chloride (NaCl)
(B) Sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃) — a weak base
(C) Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃)
(D) Sodium hydroxide (NaOH)
cards.back:
(B) Sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃) — a weak base

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Baking soda = NaHCO₃ (sodium bicarbonate). Mildly basic (pH ~8.3 in solution). On heating: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ (releases CO₂ → bread/cake rises). Also a mild antacid. Used in fire extinguishers (releases CO₂ smothering flames). 'Washing soda' is sodium CARBONATE — Na₂CO₃·10H₂O — strongly basic, removes hard-water Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ ions. NaCl = common salt. NaOH = caustic soda — very strong base, used in soap-making (saponification).

Also a mild antacid. Used in fire extinguishers (releases CO₂ smothering flames). 'Washing soda' is sodium CARBONATE — Na₂CO₃·10H₂O — strongly basic, removes hard-water Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ ions. cards.front:
If a solution has [H⁺] = 10⁻⁵ M, its pH is:

(A) 9
(B) 5 (slightly acidic)
(C) 10⁻⁵
(D) 1
cards.back:
(B) 5 (slightly acidic)

Acids, Bases & Solutions — pH = −log₁₀[H⁺] = −log(10⁻⁵) = 5. Slightly acidic. To find pOH: pH + pOH = 14 (at 25 °C) → pOH = 9. [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁹ M. Quick conversion table: [H⁺] 10⁻¹ → pH 1; 10⁻⁷ → pH 7 (neutral); 10⁻¹³ → pH 13. Each integer step in pH means a 10× change in [H⁺]. pH 4 vs pH 6 → 100× more acidic.

Quick conversion table: [H⁺] 10⁻¹ → pH 1; 10⁻⁷ → pH 7 (neutral); 10⁻¹³ → pH 13. Each integer step in pH means a 10× change in [H⁺]. pH 4 vs pH 6 → 100× more acidic.

cards.front:
The pH of pure water at 25 °C is exactly:

(A) 0
(B) 7
(C) 10
(D) 14
cards.back:
(B) 7

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Pure water at 25 °C is neutral: [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ mol/L, so pH = 7. Acidic solutions have pH < 7 (higher H⁺), basic solutions pH > 7. The scale runs 0-14. A change of one pH unit means a ten-fold change in H⁺ concentration.

cards.front:
Litmus paper turns red in the presence of:

(A) A base
(B) An acid
(C) A neutral salt
(D) Pure water
cards.back:
(B) An acid

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Blue litmus turns red in acids; red litmus turns blue in bases. Litmus is a mixture of dyes from lichens. Other indicators: phenolphthalein — colourless in acid, pink in base; methyl orange — red in acid, yellow in base; turmeric — yellow in acid/neutral, red in base.

cards.front:
Common salt used in cooking has the chemical formula:

(A) NaHCO₃
(B) NaCl
(C) Na₂CO₃
(D) NaOH
cards.back:
(B) NaCl

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Common (table) salt is sodium chloride, NaCl. The other options are: NaHCO₃ — baking soda; Na₂CO₃ — washing soda; NaOH — caustic soda (a strong base). Most table salt in India is fortified with potassium iodate to prevent iodine-deficiency goitre.

cards.front:
A neutralisation reaction between an acid and a base produces:

(A) Only a salt
(B) A salt and water
(C) A salt and hydrogen
(D) A salt and oxygen
cards.back:
(B) A salt and water

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Acid + Base → Salt + Water. Example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Acid + active metal gives salt + H₂; metal oxide (basic) + acid also gives salt + water. Neutralisation is exothermic — the mixture warms up slightly.

cards.front:
The acid secreted by the stomach during digestion is:

(A) Sulphuric acid
(B) Hydrochloric acid
(C) Citric acid
(D) Acetic acid
cards.back:
(B) Hydrochloric acid

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Parietal cells of the stomach lining secrete hydrochloric acid, giving gastric juice a pH of around 1.5-3.5. It kills microbes and activates pepsin from pepsinogen. Antacids (milk of magnesia = Mg(OH)₂, or baking soda) neutralise excess HCl. Citric acid is found in citrus fruits; acetic acid in vinegar; sulphuric acid in lead-acid car batteries.

cards.front:
Match the common name with the chemical formula. A. Baking soda. B. Washing soda. C. Caustic soda. D. Plaster of Paris. List-II: 1. NaOH, 2. Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, 3. NaHCO₃, 4. CaSO₄·½H₂O.

(A) A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4
(B) A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4
(C) A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4
(D) A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4
cards.back:
(A) A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Baking soda — sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃). Washing soda — hydrated sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O). Caustic soda — sodium hydroxide (NaOH), a strong base used in soap-making. Plaster of Paris — calcium sulphate hemihydrate (CaSO₄·½H₂O); made by heating gypsum to ~120 °C.

cards.front:
Which acid is naturally present in sour milk and curd?

(A) Citric acid
(B) Lactic acid
(C) Formic acid
(D) Tartaric acid
cards.back:
(B) Lactic acid

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Lactic acid is produced when Lactobacillus bacteria ferment lactose in milk; it curdles the milk and gives curd its sour taste. Citric acid is in lemons and oranges; formic acid in ant stings and nettles; tartaric acid in grapes and tamarind; acetic acid in vinegar; oxalic acid in spinach.

cards.front:
The size of the dispersed particles in a true SOLUTION is typically:

(A) Greater than 1000 nm (settles on standing)
(B) Less than 1 nm (single molecules or ions)
(C) Between 100 nm and 1000 nm (visible cloudiness)
(D) Between 1 nm and 100 nm (typical colloid size)
cards.back:
(B) Less than 1 nm (single molecules or ions)

Acids, Bases & Solutions — True solution — particle size < 1 nm (single molecules / ions). Colloid — 1-100 nm (intermediate). Suspension — > 100 nm (visible particles, settle on standing). Tyndall effect (light scattering) is shown by COLLOIDS, not by true solutions. Distractor 1 = clear suspension range. Distractor 3 = coarse suspension. Distractor 4 = colloid range.
cards.option3: Between 1 nm and 100 nm (typical colloid size)

Tyndall effect (light scattering) is shown by COLLOIDS, not by true solutions. Distractor 1 = clear suspension range. Distractor 3 = coarse suspension. Distractor 4 = colloid range.

cards.front:
The TYNDALL EFFECT — visible scattering of a beam of light — is shown by:

(A) True solutions of salt or sugar in water
(B) Colloidal systems such as milk and dilute starch
(C) Pure distilled water in a clean glass beaker
(D) Crystals of solid sodium chloride lying still
cards.back:
(B) Colloidal systems such as milk and dilute starch

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Tyndall effect — visible scattering of light by particles in colloidal range (1-100 nm), comparable to wavelength of visible light. Demonstrated when sunlight passes through fog, smoke, or a beam of light through milk diluted in water. True solutions: particles too small to scatter visible light, so the beam passes invisibly. Distractor 4 — solids do not show Tyndall (no dispersion medium).

cards.option2: Pure distilled water in a clean glass beaker
cards.option3: Crystals of solid sodium chloride lying still

cards.front:
MILK is best classified as which type of colloid?

(A) Solid in liquid (sol — like paint or muddy water)
(B) Liquid in liquid (emulsion of fat globules in water)
(C) Gas in liquid (foam — like beer head or whipped cream)
(D) Liquid in gas (aerosol — like fog or hairspray mist)
cards.back:
(B) Liquid in liquid (emulsion of fat globules in water)

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Milk = an EMULSION — liquid (fat globules) dispersed in another liquid (water). Stabilised by casein protein acting as the emulsifying agent. Distractor 1 (sol) — paint/mud. Distractor 3 (foam) — beer head, whipped cream. Distractor 4 (aerosol) — fog, perfume mist. Other emulsions: butter (water in fat — reverse), mayonnaise (oil in water).

cards.option2: Gas in liquid (foam — like beer head or whipped cream)
cards.option3: Liquid in gas (aerosol — like fog or hairspray mist)

cards.front:
FOG is a colloidal system. The dispersed phase is _____ and the dispersion medium is _____.

(A) Solid in gas (smoke-like behaviour)
(B) Liquid in gas (fine water droplets in air)
(C) Gas in liquid (bubbles within a fluid)
(D) Liquid in solid (gel-like trapped water)
cards.back:
(B) Liquid in gas (fine water droplets in air)

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Fog / mist / cloud — tiny LIQUID water droplets dispersed in GAS (air). This is called an AEROSOL. Smoke — solid particles in gas (different aerosol). Foam — gas in liquid. Gel — liquid in solid (e.g. jelly, agar). Smog (smoke + fog) — mixed solid + liquid in gas; characteristic of polluted urban areas in winter (Delhi smog).

Which of the following is a TRUE SOLUTION (NOT a colloid or suspension)?

(A) Muddy river water held in a glass jar
(B) Salt fully dissolved in clean tap water
(C) Whole milk standing on a kitchen table
(D) Smoke rising from a freshly extinguished candle
cards.back:
(B) Salt fully dissolved in clean tap water

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Salt-in-water — true solution (Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions dispersed at molecular level). Distractor 4 — aerosol colloid (solid particles in gas).

cards.front:
Brownian motion of colloidal particles can be observed under a microscope. The motion is caused by:

(A) Convection currents in the surrounding liquid
(B) Random collisions with surrounding solvent molecules
(C) Electrostatic repulsion between dispersed particles
(D) Gravity pulling the particles toward the bottom
cards.back:
(B) Random collisions with surrounding solvent molecules

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Brownian motion — irregular zig-zag motion of colloidal particles caused by unequal random collisions with surrounding solvent molecules at any moment. Discovered by Robert Brown (1827) watching pollen grains in water. Einstein's 1905 paper on Brownian motion provided the first quantitative evidence for the existence of atoms — won him recognition. Distractor 1 — convection is bulk flow, not the random microscopic motion. Distractor 3 — repulsion would not produce random zig-zag. Distractor 4 — gravity gives a one-way drift, not zig-zag.

cards.option3: Gravity pulling the particles toward the bottom

cards.front:
An EMULSIFYING agent like soap added to oil + water mixture works by:

(A) Dissolving the oil completely into the water phase
(B) Coating each droplet so they cannot rejoin one another
(C) Heating the mixture so that the oil layer evaporates
(D) Filtering out the oil through extremely fine pores
cards.back:
(B) Coating each droplet so they cannot rejoin one another

Acids, Bases & Solutions — An emulsifier (soap, lecithin in egg yolk, casein in milk) has both hydrophilic and hydrophobic parts. The hydrophobic tail embeds in the oil droplet; the hydrophilic head faces water → forms a stable shell around each oil droplet, preventing coalescence. This is how soap cleans grease: surrounds + emulsifies the grease so water can wash it away. Distractor 1 — oil does not actually dissolve in water; it is dispersed. Distractor 3 — heating doesn't emulsify. Distractor 4 — filtering doesn't apply to liquid-liquid mixtures.

cards.front:
The pH scale ranges from:

(A) 0 to 14 (most aqueous solutions)
(B) 1 to 10 (limited basic range)
(C) −7 to +7 (around neutrality)
(D) 0 to 100 (percentage scale)
cards.back:
(A) 0 to 14 (most aqueous solutions)

Acids, Bases & Solutions — pH SCALE typically ranges from 0 to 14 for AQUEOUS solutions at 25°C. KEY VALUES: pH < 7 = ACIDIC. pH = 7 = NEUTRAL (pure water). pH > 7 = BASIC/ALKALINE. DEFINITION: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺] (negative log of hydrogen-ion concentration in mol/L). EACH UNIT change in pH = 10× change in [H⁺]: pH 3 has 10× more H⁺ than pH 4. EXAMPLES — pH of common things: (1) Battery acid: 0. (2) Stomach acid (HCl): 1-2. (3) Lemon juice: 2. (4) Vinegar: 2.4. (5) Coffee: 5. (6) Milk: 6.5. (7) Pure water: 7. (8) Blood: 7.4 (tightly regulated). (9) Sea water: 8.1. (10) Baking soda: 9. (11) Soap: 10. (12) Bleach: 12-13. (13) Drain cleaner (NaOH): 14. EXTREMES: super-acidic 'magic acid' has pH < 0; super-basic NaOH solutions can have pH > 14 (rare). HISTORY: pH invented by SØREN SØRENSEN (Danish, 1909) — the 'p' stands for 'potens' (power) or 'potentia hydrogenii'. TEMPERATURE EFFECT: pH of pure water is 7 only at 25°C; at higher T, pure water has lower pH (still neutral). PYQ FREQUENCY: pH range is a NEET, NCERT-driven SSC 1-mark guarantee.

cards.front:
RED LITMUS turns BLUE in:

(A) Basic (alkaline) solutions
(B) Acidic solutions specifically
(C) Neutral solutions like water
(D) Strongly oxidizing solutions only
cards.back:
(A) Basic (alkaline) solutions

Acids, Bases & Solutions — LITMUS — natural pH indicator extracted from LICHENS (e.g., Roccella tinctoria). PROPERTY: RED LITMUS turns BLUE in BASIC solutions (pH > 7); BLUE LITMUS turns RED in ACIDIC solutions (pH < 7). NEUTRAL (pH = 7) — both colours stay unchanged. MNEMONIC: 'Acid Reds, Base Blues' (or 'BB-AR' = base-blue, acid-red). LIMITATION: litmus is APPROXIMATE — only indicates above/below pH 7 (transition is gradual). MORE PRECISE INDICATORS: (1) METHYL ORANGE — RED in acid (pH < 3.1), YELLOW in base (pH > 4.4); transition pH ~3.7 (good for STRONG-acid titrations). (2) PHENOLPHTHALEIN — COLOURLESS in acid (pH < 8.2), PINK/MAGENTA in base (pH > 10); good for STRONG-base titrations. (3) UNIVERSAL INDICATOR — mixture of multiple dyes, gives a SPECTRUM of colours: RED (pH 1-3), ORANGE (4), YELLOW (5-6), GREEN (7), BLUE (8-9), VIOLET (10-14). NATURAL pH INDICATORS: red cabbage juice, turmeric, rose petals, hibiscus. PYQ FREQUENCY: litmus colour change is a NCERT Class 7-10 staple, tested in CGL, RRB GA 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
PHENOLPHTHALEIN indicator turns PINK in solutions with pH approximately:

(A) Above 10 (basic solutions)
(B) Below 4 (acidic solutions)
(C) Around 7 (neutral solutions)
(D) Above 14 (super-strong base)
cards.back:
(A) Above 10 (basic solutions)

Acids, Bases & Solutions — PHENOLPHTHALEIN — colourless in acid/neutral, PINK/MAGENTA in BASIC solutions. TRANSITION RANGE: colourless below pH 8.2, fully pink above pH 10.0; in between (8.2-10.0), pale pink. CHEMISTRY: phenolphthalein is a WEAK ACID; in basic solution, it ionizes and the conjugate base form is pink (extended π-conjugation absorbs in green spectrum, looks pink). USES: (1) ACID-BASE TITRATION — common indicator for STRONG BASE + WEAK ACID titrations. (2) MASONRY/CONCRETE testing — used to detect carbonation depth in concrete (pink = uncarbonated, alkaline; colourless = carbonated, neutral). (3) Forensic — historically used in laxatives (until banned in many countries due to potential carcinogenicity, ~1990s). (4) FORENSIC chemistry — Kastle-Meyer test for blood (phenolphthalein-based). KEY POINT: phenolphthalein is a 'one-way' indicator for BASIC range; doesn't show transitions in acidic range. LIMITATIONS: doesn't show concentration of acid/base; only above/below threshold. PYQ FREQUENCY: phenolphthalein in Class 10 NCERT — CGL, NEET, IBPS GA tested 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests indicator-pH-colour mapping memorization.

cards.front:
Pure water at 25°C has [H⁺] = 10⁻⁷ M. Its pH is:

(A) 7 (definition of neutral)
(B) 0 (a totally wrong calc)
(C) 14 (the basic-end value)
(D) 1 (a strongly acidic value)
cards.back:
(A) 7 (definition of neutral)

Acids, Bases & Solutions — pH = −log₁₀[H⁺] = −log₁₀(10⁻⁷) = −(−7) = 7. So pH 7 = NEUTRAL. KEY INSIGHTS: (1) PURE WATER autoionizes: 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻. Equilibrium constant Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C. (2) For NEUTRAL water: [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ M. (3) pH + pOH = 14 (always at 25°C). (4) ACIDIC: [H⁺] > 10⁻⁷ → pH < 7. BASIC: [H⁺] < 10⁻⁷ → pH > 7. PRACTICE PROBLEMS: (a) [H⁺] = 0.001 M → pH = 3 (acidic). (b) [H⁺] = 10⁻¹⁰ M → pH = 10 (basic). (c) pH = 5 → [H⁺] = 10⁻⁵ M; [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁹ M (10,000× less than [H⁺]). RAINWATER: pH ~5.6 due to dissolved CO₂ forming carbonic acid (NORMAL acid rain). 'ACID RAIN' (pollution-driven) has pH < 5.0 due to SO₂ + NOx → H₂SO₄ + HNO₃. ACID RAIN damage: corrodes Taj Mahal (Yamuna pollution) — landmark 1990s issue. PYQ FREQUENCY: pH calculations are NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT-driven SSC top MCQ — 1-2× per paper.

cards.front:
The NORMAL pH of HUMAN BLOOD is approximately:

(A) 7.4 (slightly basic, tightly regulated)
(B) 5.5 (acidic, like stomach acid)
(C) 9.0 (strongly basic always now)
(D) 6.5 (slightly acidic everyday)
cards.back:
(A) 7.4 (slightly basic, tightly regulated)

Acids, Bases & Solutions — BLOOD pH is tightly regulated at 7.35 to 7.45 (slightly BASIC). Deviations are LIFE-THREATENING: pH < 7.35 = ACIDOSIS (can cause coma, death); pH > 7.45 = ALKALOSIS (muscle spasms, seizures). REGULATION via THREE BUFFER SYSTEMS: (1) BICARBONATE BUFFER (most important): H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ — handles ~75% of pH regulation. (2) PHOSPHATE BUFFER. (3) PROTEIN BUFFER (hemoglobin, plasma proteins). FAST RESPONSE: lungs adjust CO₂ exhalation rate (acid = more CO₂ exhaled). SLOW RESPONSE: kidneys adjust HCO₃⁻ retention/excretion. KEY pH VALUES IN HUMAN BODY: (a) Stomach acid (HCl): 1.5-3.5. (b) Saliva: 6.5-7.5. (c) Blood: 7.35-7.45. (d) Pancreatic juice: 8.0-8.5. (e) Bile: 7.6-8.6. (f) Urine: 5.0-8.0 (variable). DISEASES: DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS — pH drops below 7.35 due to ketone body production; medical emergency. RESPIRATORY ACIDOSIS — CO₂ retention in COPD/asthma. RESPIRATORY ALKALOSIS — hyperventilation (panic attacks). PYQ FREQUENCY: blood pH appears in NEET, NCERT Class 11 biology, CGL biology section.

cards.front:
Antacid tablets (e.g., milk of magnesia) work by:

(A) Neutralizing excess stomach acid
(B) Increasing acid in the stomach
(C) Producing protective gas layer
(D) Coating the food undigested
cards.back:
(A) Neutralizing excess stomach acid

Acids, Bases & Solutions — ANTACIDS contain BASIC compounds that NEUTRALIZE excess HCl in the stomach, raising pH (relieving heartburn/acidity). COMMON ACTIVE INGREDIENTS: (1) MAGNESIUM HYDROXIDE — Mg(OH)₂ — milk of magnesia. (2) ALUMINIUM HYDROXIDE — Al(OH)₃ (often combined with Mg). (3) CALCIUM CARBONATE — CaCO₃ (Tums). (4) SODIUM BICARBONATE — NaHCO₃ (Eno, Alka-Seltzer). REACTIONS: (a) Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O. (b) NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂↑ (the 'fizz'). NORMAL STOMACH pH: 1.5-3.5 (very acidic, kills bacteria, denatures proteins for digestion). HYPERACIDITY: too much HCl → heartburn, GERD, ulcers. CHRONIC TREATMENT: PROTON PUMP INHIBITORS (PPIs) like omeprazole REDUCE acid production at source — more effective for chronic conditions. INDIA — POPULAR ANTACID BRANDS: Eno, Digene, Pudin Hara, Gelusil. SAFETY: long-term antacid use can cause magnesium imbalance (diarrhea), aluminum accumulation (rare). NCERT CLASS 10: antacid mechanism is a chapter staple. PYQ FREQUENCY: NEET, NCERT-driven SSC chemistry MCQ — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
If a solution has [H⁺] = 10⁻³ M, the [OH⁻] concentration in the same solution at 25°C is:

(A) 10⁻¹¹ M (using Kw = 10⁻¹⁴)
(B) 10⁻³ M (matching H+ value)
(C) 10⁻⁷ M (the neutral value)
(D) 10⁻¹⁴ M (a wrong product)
cards.back:
(A) 10⁻¹¹ M (using Kw = 10⁻¹⁴)

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Apply WATER ION-PRODUCT: Kw = [H⁺] × [OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C. Given [H⁺] = 10⁻³, so [OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ / 10⁻³ = 10⁻¹¹ M. INTERPRETATION: the solution is ACIDIC (pH = 3); H⁺ ions outnumber OH⁻ by 10⁸ (hundred million times). KEY RELATIONSHIPS at 25°C: (1) Kw = 10⁻¹⁴. (2) pH + pOH = 14. (3) Pure water: [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷; pH = pOH = 7. PRACTICE PROBLEMS: [H⁺] = 0.01 M (pH 2) → [OH⁻] = 10⁻¹² M (pOH 12); [H⁺] = 10⁻⁹ M (pH 9) → [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁵ M (pOH 5). TEMPERATURE EFFECT: Kw increases with temperature — at 100°C, Kw ≈ 10⁻¹². So pure water at 100°C has pH ≈ 6 — STILL neutral, just lower pH due to higher autoionization. RECONCILE: 'neutral' means [H⁺] = [OH⁻], not [H⁺] = 10⁻⁷. INDUSTRIAL: pH control in waste-water treatment, chemical reactors, brewing — all rely on Kw relationships. PYQ FREQUENCY: pH-pOH-Kw calculations in JEE-Main, NEET 2-3× per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests log-arithmetic discipline.

cards.front:
To separate a mixture of sand and common salt dissolved in water, one would use in sequence:

(A) Distillation, then filtration
(B) Filtration, then evaporation
(C) Sublimation, then crystallisation
(D) Chromatography, then filtration
cards.back:
(B) Filtration, then evaporation

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Sand is insoluble, salt is soluble. Step 1 — filtration separates the sand (on the filter paper) from the salt solution (the filtrate). Step 2 — evaporation of the filtrate leaves behind salt crystals. Distillation would also work for step 2 if you wanted to recover the water as well.

Step 2 — evaporation of the filtrate leaves behind salt crystals. Distillation would also work for step 2 if you wanted to recover the water as well.

cards.front:
Which separation technique would best suit separating iodine from common salt?

(A) Filtration
(B) Sublimation
(C) Magnetic separation
(D) Centrifugation
cards.back:
(B) Sublimation

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Iodine sublimes (directly turns from solid to vapour on heating), salt does not. On gentle heating, iodine vapour can be collected and re-deposited; salt stays behind. Other sublimable solids — ammonium chloride, naphthalene, camphor, dry ice. Magnetic separation works for iron filings. Centrifugation — for suspensions (e.g., blood plasma from cells).

cards.front:
'Fractional distillation' is used to separate:

(A) Two immiscible liquids
(B) Two miscible liquids with different boiling points
(C) A solid from a solid
(D) Charged ions
cards.back:
(B) Two miscible liquids with different boiling points

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Fractional distillation — for miscible liquids with different boiling points: crude oil into petrol, diesel, kerosene; liquid air into N₂ and O₂; ethanol-water (azeotropic limit 95.6 %). A fractionating column helps repeated vaporisation-condensation cycles to improve separation. Two immiscible liquids (oil + water) are separated with a separating funnel.

cards.front:
Which technique is used to separate colour pigments in ink or the constituents of chlorophyll?

(A) Distillation
(B) Chromatography
(C) Crystallisation
(D) Sedimentation
cards.back:
(B) Chromatography

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Chromatography — different components of a mixture travel at different speeds through a stationary phase carried by a moving solvent (mobile phase). Types — paper, thin-layer, column, gas-liquid, HPLC. Widely used for analysis in biology, chemistry, forensics, drug testing. Crystallisation — purifying a solid from solution by controlled cooling / evaporation.

Crystallisation — purifying a solid from solution by controlled cooling / evaporation.

cards.front:
Iron filings mixed with sulphur powder can be separated by using:

(A) Filtration
(B) A magnet
(C) Chromatography
(D) Distillation
cards.back:
(B) A magnet

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Iron is ferromagnetic; sulphur is not. Running a magnet through the mixture picks up the iron filings and leaves sulphur behind. If the mixture is HEATED first, iron and sulphur combine to form iron(II) sulphide (FeS) — a chemical change — and the mixture can no longer be separated by a magnet. A classic demonstration of 'physical vs chemical change'.

If the mixture is HEATED first, iron and sulphur combine to form iron(II) sulphide (FeS) — a chemical change — and the mixture can no longer be separated by a magnet. cards.front:
To obtain pure water from sea water, the most suitable technique is:

(A) Filtration
(B) Simple distillation
(C) Evaporation only
(D) Sedimentation
cards.back:
(B) Simple distillation

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Sea water contains dissolved salts that filtration can't remove. Simple distillation boils water → collects pure condensate. Reverse osmosis (RO) — pushes water through a semi-permeable membrane that blocks salt ions. Large-scale desalination plants use RO (e.g., Minjur, Nemmeli in Chennai; big ones in the Gulf). Evaporation alone gives water vapour but without condensation you have no liquid pure water to collect. or reverse osmosis.

cards.front:
A centrifuge separates a mixture based on difference in:

(A) Colour
(B) Density
(C) Melting point
(D) Electrical charge
cards.back:
(B) Density

Acids, Bases & Solutions — A centrifuge spins samples at high speed; denser components migrate to the outer edge (bottom of the tube), lighter components stay near the axis. Uses — separating blood plasma from cells, cream from milk, dust from industrial gases (cyclone separators), uranium isotope enrichment (gas centrifuges). Ultracentrifuges run at > 100,000 rpm for protein and DNA studies.

cards.front:
In a solution of SUGAR in WATER, sugar is the:

(A) Solute (substance dissolved)
(B) Solvent (the liquid medium)
(C) Solution itself overall
(D) Reactant of a chemical reaction
cards.back:
(A) Solute (substance dissolved)

Acids, Bases & Solutions — SOLUTION = SOLUTE + SOLVENT. SOLUTE — substance DISSOLVED (less amount, smaller component). SOLVENT — substance that DOES the dissolving (more amount, the medium). EXAMPLES: SUGAR (solute) in water (solvent); SALT (solute) in water (solvent); ALCOHOL (solute or solvent depending on which is more); GASES dissolved in water (CO₂ in cola, O₂ in seawater for fish). UNIVERSAL SOLVENT = water (dissolves more substances than any other solvent — due to its polarity + hydrogen bonding ability). TYPES OF SOLUTIONS: solid in liquid (sugar-water); liquid in liquid (alcohol-water); gas in liquid (CO₂-water); solid in solid (alloys: brass = Cu+Zn); etc.

cards.front:
MOLARITY (M) is defined as:

(A) Moles of solute per LITRE of solution
(B) Moles of solute per kg of solvent (molality)
(C) Mass of solute per litre of solution
(D) Volume of solute per litre of solvent
cards.back:
(A) Moles of solute per LITRE of solution

Acids, Bases & Solutions — MOLARITY (M) = moles of solute / VOLUME of solution (in litres). UNIT: mol/L or M. Most common concentration measure. KEY: based on volume of WHOLE SOLUTION (not just solvent). Temperature-DEPENDENT (volume changes with T). MOLALITY (m) = moles of solute / mass of solvent (in kg) — temperature-INDEPENDENT (mass doesn't change with T). NORMALITY (N) = gram-equivalents of solute per litre of solution (used in acid-base, redox titrations). MOLE FRACTION (x) = moles of one component / total moles. PPM = parts per million (10⁻⁶ — used for trace amounts; e.g., water hardness, air pollution). PPB = parts per billion (10⁻⁹ — even more dilute). %w/w, %v/v, %w/v — common percent forms.
