cards.front:
A SATURATED solution is one where:

(A) No more solute can dissolve at given temp
(B) Lots more solute can still dissolve
(C) Solute reacts with solvent chemically
(D) Solution is colourless and clear
cards.back:
(A) No more solute can dissolve at given temp

Acids, Bases & Solutions — SATURATED — solution containing maximum solute that can dissolve at given TEMPERATURE; any more added → undissolved. UNSATURATED — less than max → can dissolve more. SUPERSATURATED — temporarily holding MORE than max (unstable; tiny disturbance → crystallises out). SOLUBILITY = max solute that can dissolve in given solvent at given T. TEMPERATURE EFFECT: most solids' solubility INCREASES with T (sugar dissolves more in hot tea); GAS solubility DECREASES with T (warm cola loses fizz; that's why tropical seas have less dissolved O₂, fewer fish per area than cold waters — counter-intuitive but true). PRESSURE EFFECT: gases — Henry's law (solubility ∝ pressure; that's why opening soda bottle releases CO₂).

cards.front:
BRINE solution is essentially:

(A) Salt water (NaCl in H₂O)
(B) Sugar water (sucrose dissolved)
(C) Acid water (mild acid solution)
(D) Alcohol water (ethanol in water)
cards.back:
(A) Salt water (NaCl in H₂O)

Acids, Bases & Solutions — BRINE = concentrated salt water (NaCl solution; typically 3.5%+ — sea water is brine). USES: PRESERVATION (pickling fish, vegetables — high salt prevents bacteria growth, due to osmotic stress on microbes), brining meats (Thanksgiving turkey), DE-ICING roads (salt lowers freezing point of water). INDUSTRIAL: source of sodium + chlorine (electrolysis = chlor-alkali process → NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂). Salt also kept on Indian wedding plates as 'shagun' for some ceremonies; in Goa, salt pans (sea-water evaporation) yield commercial salt. SEA WATER: ~3.5% salt; DEAD SEA: 33%+; SAMBHAR LAKE: ~22%. INSIGHT — salt's role in HISTORY: Roman soldiers' 'salarium' (= salary, paid in salt); Gandhi's 1930 Salt March (Dandi) protested British salt tax.

cards.front:
TYNDALL EFFECT (scattering of light in colloidal solution) is shown by:

(A) Milk + fog + smoke (colloidal suspensions)
(B) Pure salt solution (a true solution)
(C) Pure distilled water (no particles)
(D) Strong sugar solution (transparent)
cards.back:
(A) Milk + fog + smoke (colloidal suspensions)

Acids, Bases & Solutions — TYNDALL EFFECT — light beam SCATTERS visibly when passing through COLLOIDAL solution (1-1000 nm particle size); not in TRUE solutions. EXAMPLES of colloids showing it: MILK (fat droplets in water — emulsion), FOG (water droplets in air), SMOKE (carbon particles in air), JELLY, BUTTER, BLOOD, MIST, AEROSOL, FOAM. WHY: particles BIG ENOUGH to scatter visible light (~400-700 nm), but small enough to stay suspended (don't settle). VISIBLE RAY OF SUNLIGHT through DUSTY ROOM (light beam visible) = same effect. NIGHT SKY appears blue from atmospheric scattering (Rayleigh scattering for molecules < 1 nm; Tyndall for larger particles 1-1000 nm). True solutions (salt, sugar) — particles ~0.1 nm — too small to scatter; light passes through unaffected.

cards.front:
Solubility of a GAS in liquid INCREASES with:

(A) Higher pressure (Henry's law) + lower temperature
(B) Higher temperature (solubility rises)
(C) Lower pressure (more gas dissolves) too
(D) Pure water without solutes only (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Higher pressure (Henry's law) + lower temperature

Acids, Bases & Solutions — GAS SOLUBILITY in liquid: (1) DIRECTLY proportional to PRESSURE (HENRY's LAW: P = k·x, where x = mole fraction). Open soda bottle → pressure drops → CO₂ comes out (fizz!). (2) INVERSELY proportional to TEMPERATURE (warm coke = flat). EXAMPLES: SCUBA divers must surface SLOWLY — 'BENDS' (decompression sickness): N₂ dissolved in blood at high pressure (deep) comes out as bubbles when returning to surface (lower pressure). Treated in HYPERBARIC chamber. WHY ICE WATER for fish tank? COOL water holds MORE dissolved O₂. ALSO: BOILED water = removes dissolved gases (taste 'flat'); explains why high-altitude tea + coffee taste different (lower pressure).

cards.front:
DISTILLATION is used to separate:

(A) Liquid mixtures by boiling-point difference
(B) Solid suspensions in water (filtration)
(C) Insoluble solid from liquid (decanting)
(D) Magnetic from non-magnetic solids
cards.back:
(A) Liquid mixtures by boiling-point difference

Acids, Bases & Solutions — DISTILLATION — separates LIQUIDS based on different BOILING POINTS. Heat mixture; lower-bp liquid evaporates first, condense vapour back (cool tube), collect. SIMPLE distillation: liquids with bp difference > 25°C. FRACTIONAL distillation: closer bps (used in petroleum refining — separates crude oil into petrol/kerosene/diesel/lubricants). DISTILLED WATER — pure water, gases removed, used in batteries, lab. DESALINATION (Saudi Arabia, Israel, UAE) — distill seawater for fresh water. ALCOHOL distillation — Indian liquor industry. PYQ FAVOURITE — separation methods: FILTRATION (insoluble solid from liquid), CHROMATOGRAPHY (mixture of dyes/inks), CRYSTALLISATION (purify solids), MAGNETIC SEPARATION (iron from sand), CENTRIFUGATION (cream from milk), SUBLIMATION (camphor from sand).

cards.front:
In a solution of common salt in water, the salt is the:

(A) Solvent
(B) Solute
(C) Mixture
(D) Catalyst
cards.back:
(B) Solute

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Solute = the substance dissolved (smaller quantity). Solvent = the medium that dissolves (larger quantity). Solute + solvent = solution. In salt water, salt = solute, water = solvent. Air is a solution where N₂ is the solvent (78%); O₂, Ar, CO₂ are solutes. Brass is a solid solution of Zn in Cu. The thumb rule — 'more abundant component is the solvent'.

cards.front:
Molarity (M) of a solution is defined as the number of moles of solute per:

(A) Litre of solvent
(B) Litre of solution
(C) Kilogram of solvent
(D) Mole of solvent
cards.back:
(B) Litre of solution

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Molarity (M) = moles of solute / litres of SOLUTION (NOT solvent). Easy to prepare in volumetric flask. Drawback: temperature-dependent (volume expands with heat). Compare: Molality (m) = moles of solute / kg of SOLVENT — temperature-independent. Normality (N) = gram-equivalents per litre of solution. Mole fraction = moles of component / total moles. Test trap: 'litre of solvent' is wrong.

cards.front:
20 g of NaOH (molar mass 40) dissolved in water to make 500 mL of solution gives a molarity of:

(A) 0.5 M
(B) 1.0 M
(C) 2.0 M
(D) 0.25 M
cards.back:
(B) 1.0 M

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Moles of NaOH = mass / molar mass = 20 / 40 = 0.5 mol. Volume of solution = 500 mL = 0.5 L. Molarity = moles / volume = 0.5 / 0.5 = 1.0 M. Standard formula: M = (w × 1000) / (M.W. × V_mL) = (20 × 1000) / (40 × 500) = 20000/20000 = 1.0.

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT a colligative property?

(A) Boiling-point elevation
(B) Freezing-point depression
(C) Osmotic pressure
(D) Density
cards.back:
(D) Density

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Colligative properties depend ONLY on the NUMBER of solute particles, not their identity. The four classical ones — Relative lowering of vapour pressure (Raoult's Law), Boiling-point elevation, Freezing-point depression, Osmotic pressure. Density depends on the chemical identity / mass of the species — NOT colligative. Real-world uses: salt on icy roads (depresses freezing point); pickle preservation by osmosis; antifreeze in radiators.

cards.front:
A solution that contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given solvent at a particular temperature is called:

(A) Dilute solution
(B) Saturated solution
(C) Concentrated solution
(D) Supersaturated solution
cards.back:
(B) Saturated solution

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Saturated — exactly at the solubility limit; any more solute will not dissolve. Unsaturated — below the limit (more can dissolve). Supersaturated — beyond the limit; metastable (can suddenly crystallise on disturbance). 'Concentrated' / 'dilute' are non-quantitative everyday terms — not the same as saturated. Solubility usually rises with temperature for solids, falls for gases — why warm beer goes flat fast.

cards.front:
If 25 g of glucose is dissolved in 75 g of water, the percentage strength (w/w) of the solution is:

(A) 20%
(B) 25%
(C) 33.3%
(D) 75%
cards.back:
(B) 25%

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Mass percentage (w/w) = (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 100 = 25 / (25 + 75) × 100 = 25 / 100 × 100 = 25%. Trap 33.3% would come from dividing by mass of SOLVENT (25/75 × 100), which is wrong. Volume percentage (v/v) is used for liquid solutions of liquids (e.g. ethanol in water).

cards.front:
Why does a saline IV drip use 0.9% NaCl solution rather than pure water?

(A) Pure water is too cold
(B) 0.9% saline is isotonic with blood — pure water would burst RBCs by osmosis
(C) Salt is needed to kill bacteria
(D) Salt sterilises the needle
cards.back:
(B) 0.9% saline is isotonic with blood — pure water would burst RBCs by osmosis

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Blood plasma osmolarity ≈ 0.9% NaCl by mass (also called 'normal saline' or 'physiological saline'). If pure water (hypotonic) entered the bloodstream, water would rush INTO red blood cells by osmosis, causing them to swell and burst (haemolysis). Hypertonic solutions would shrivel cells (crenation). Other isotonic IV fluids — Ringer's lactate, dextrose-saline. Real-life application of colligative property — osmotic pressure equality keeps cells stable.

cards.front:
'Hard water' owes its hardness primarily to the dissolved salts of:

(A) Sodium and potassium
(B) Calcium and magnesium
(C) Iron and lead
(D) Zinc and aluminium
cards.back:
(B) Calcium and magnesium

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Hardness of water is caused by dissolved calcium and magnesium ions, usually as bicarbonates (temporary hardness — removed by boiling) or chlorides and sulphates (permanent hardness — removed by ion-exchange resin or washing soda). Hard water lathers poorly with soap (forms scum) and leaves scale deposits in boilers and pipes. Soft water has sodium / potassium salts instead.

cards.front:
Pure water conducts electricity:

(A) Very well
(B) Very poorly
(C) Better than copper
(D) Not at all
cards.back:
(B) Very poorly

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Pure (distilled) water is a very poor conductor because it has very few ions (it self-ionises only slightly: H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻). Tap water, sea water and sweaty skin are good conductors because of dissolved salts that release ions. 'Not at all' is too strong — pure water has some conductivity but extremely low. Even so, never use water on an electric fire — the impurities in real water conduct.

cards.front:
Temporary hardness of water can be removed by:

(A) Filtration
(B) Boiling
(C) Freezing
(D) Adding salt
cards.back:
(B) Boiling

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Temporary hardness is due to calcium and magnesium BI-carbonates that on boiling break down into insoluble carbonates that settle out — Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃ ↓ + H₂O + CO₂. This is why an old kettle has scale deposits. Permanent hardness (due to chlorides/sulphates) cannot be removed by boiling; you need washing soda, zeolite, or ion-exchange resins.

cards.front:
A water molecule is bent (not linear) because of:

(A) Strong O=O bonds
(B) The two lone pairs on oxygen
(C) Equal sharing of electrons
(D) Hydrogen bonding with neighbours
cards.back:
(B) The two lone pairs on oxygen

Acids, Bases & Solutions — The oxygen atom in H₂O has two bond pairs (O-H) and two lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bond pairs, pushing the O-H bonds together. The resulting H-O-H angle is ~104.5° instead of the straight 180°. This bent shape gives water its polarity, and the polarity gives rise to hydrogen bonding — which explains water's many anomalous properties (high boiling point, ice floats, high specific heat).

cards.front:
Heavy water, used in some nuclear reactors, is chemically:

(A) Water contaminated with heavy metals
(B) D₂O, water with deuterium instead of ordinary hydrogen
(C) Sea water with high salt content
(D) H₂O at very high pressure
cards.back:
(B) D₂O, water with deuterium instead of ordinary hydrogen

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Heavy water — D₂O — has deuterium (²H), hydrogen's heavier stable isotope, in place of normal ¹H. It is used in pressurised heavy-water reactors (like India's CANDU-type PHWRs at Rawatbhata, Kakrapar) as a neutron moderator — it slows neutrons without absorbing them, so the reactor can use natural (unenriched) uranium. Density ~11 % higher than ordinary water; tastes indistinguishable but toxic in large amounts.

cards.front:
Water is called a 'universal solvent' because:

(A) It is abundant on Earth
(B) Its polarity lets it dissolve many substances
(C) It is colourless and tasteless
(D) It has a high boiling point
cards.back:
(B) Its polarity lets it dissolve many substances

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Water is a strongly polar molecule — the O end carries partial negative charge, the H ends partial positive. Ionic compounds (NaCl) and polar molecules (sugar) get surrounded by water molecules, are pulled apart, and dissolve. Non-polar substances (oils, petrol) do not. So the 'universal' label is a bit of an exaggeration — it is a universal solvent only for polar and ionic compounds.

cards.front:
The pH value of normal rainwater (saturated with atmospheric CO₂) is approximately:

(A) 7.0
(B) 5.6
(C) 4.0
(D) 8.5
cards.back:
(B) 5.6

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Normal rainwater has pH ~5.6 — slightly acidic because atmospheric CO₂ dissolves in it to form carbonic acid. Rain below pH 5.0 is called 'acid rain' — driven by SO₂ (from burning coal, smelters) and NOₓ (from vehicles and power plants) forming sulphuric and nitric acids. Acid rain damages forests, fish populations and heritage monuments (the Taj Mahal being a famous example).

cards.front:
The pH scale ranges from 0 to 14. A solution with pH = 7 is:

(A) Strongly acidic
(B) Neutral
(C) Strongly basic
(D) Weakly acidic
cards.back:
(B) Neutral

Acids, Bases & Solutions — At 25°C, pure water has pH = 7 — exactly neutral. pH < 7 is acidic (lower = more acidic); pH > 7 is basic (higher = more basic). The pH scale is LOGARITHMIC (base 10): a pH 4 solution has 10x more H⁺ ions than pH 5. Each unit change = 10-fold change in [H⁺]. Strong acids like HCl have pH ~0-1; strong bases like NaOH have pH ~13-14. Lemon juice pH ~2; stomach acid ~1.5; blood ~7.4. neither acidic nor basic.

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT a property of acids?

(A) Sour taste
(B) Turn blue litmus red
(C) React with metals to release hydrogen gas
(D) Turn red litmus blue
cards.back:
(D) Turn red litmus blue

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Turning RED litmus BLUE is a property of BASES, not acids. Acid properties: (1) sour taste (lemon, vinegar); (2) turn BLUE litmus RED; (3) react with active metals (Zn, Mg) to release H₂ gas; (4) react with bases to form salt + water (neutralization); (5) react with carbonates to release CO₂. Bases: bitter taste, slippery, turn red litmus blue, feel soapy.

cards.front:
According to the Arrhenius definition, an acid is a substance that:

(A) Accepts a proton (H⁺)
(B) Produces H⁺ ions in aqueous solution
(C) Accepts a pair of electrons
(D) Donates a pair of electrons
cards.back:
(B) Produces H⁺ ions in aqueous solution

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Three definitions of acid/base: (1) ARRHENIUS (1884): acid produces H⁺ in water, base produces OH⁻. (2) BRØNSTED-LOWRY (1923): acid donates H⁺ (proton); base accepts H⁺. (3) LEWIS (1923): acid accepts electron pair; base donates electron pair. Arrhenius is the narrowest (restricted to aqueous solutions); Lewis is the most general (covers non-proton reactions). Answer is B per Arrhenius. Option A describes a Brønsted base. Option C describes a Lewis acid.

(3) LEWIS (1923): acid accepts electron pair; base donates electron pair. Arrhenius is the narrowest (restricted to aqueous solutions); Lewis is the most general (covers non-proton reactions). cards.front:
If the pH of a solution is 3, its hydrogen ion concentration [H⁺] is:

(A) 3 M
(B) 10⁻³ M
(C) 10³ M
(D) 3 × 10⁻¹ M
cards.back:
(B) 10⁻³ M

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Definition: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]. So [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ. For pH = 3: [H⁺] = 10⁻³ M = 0.001 M. Common error: pH 3 DOES NOT mean [H⁺] = 3 M; the pH is a logarithmic measure. Similarly, pOH = −log[OH⁻], and at 25°C: pH + pOH = 14. So a pH-3 solution has [OH⁻] = 10⁻¹¹ M — highly acidic.

cards.front:
Which of the following salts would give a basic aqueous solution?

(A) Sodium chloride (NaCl)
(B) Ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl)
(C) Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃)
(D) Sodium sulphate (Na₂SO₄)
cards.back:
(C) Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃)

Acids, Bases & Solutions — Salt hydrolysis rules: (1) strong acid + strong base salt → NEUTRAL (e.g., NaCl from HCl+NaOH, Na₂SO₄ from H₂SO₄+NaOH); (2) strong base + weak acid salt → BASIC (e.g., Na₂CO₃ from NaOH+H₂CO₃ weak); (3) strong acid + weak base salt → ACIDIC (e.g., NH₄Cl from HCl+NH₃ weak). Sodium carbonate (washing soda) solution is basic (pH ~11-12) — used historically as a cleaning agent for this reason.

cards.front:
Acid rain is caused primarily by the presence of which gases in the atmosphere?

(A) CO₂ and CH₄
(B) SO₂ and NO₂
(C) O₃ and N₂O
(D) CFC and H₂O
cards.back:
(B) SO₂ and NO₂

Acids, Bases & Solutions — ACID RAIN forms when SO₂ (sulphur dioxide, from coal burning) and NO_x (nitrogen oxides, from vehicle exhaust) react with atmospheric water: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃; further oxidised to H₂SO₄ (sulphuric acid). NO₂ + H₂O → HNO₃ (nitric acid). These acids return to Earth as rain with pH ~4-5 (normal rain is pH ~5.6 due to dissolved CO₂ — not classified as acid rain unless <5). Effects: damage to aquatic ecosystems, forests, monuments (e.g., Taj Mahal).

cards.back:

Formic acid's Latin name 'acidum formicum' comes from 'formica' (Latin for ant).

cards.front:

(A) Hydrogen gas and water
(B) Salt and water
(C) Carbon dioxide and water
(D) Only salt
cards.back:
(B) Salt and water

Acids, Bases & Solutions — NEUTRALIZATION: Acid + Base → Salt + Water. Example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. The reaction is EXOTHERMIC (releases heat). In terms of ions, it reduces to H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O. (D) Sodium thiosulphate

cards.front:
Consider the following about ACID RAIN. 1. It is caused mainly by sulphur dioxide (SO₂) and oxides of nitrogen (NOₓ) emitted from fossil-fuel burning. 2. The typical pH range of acid rain is 4.2–5.0. 3. It damages marble monuments like the Taj Mahal because calcium carbonate reacts with acids. 4. Liming of lakes is one mitigation measure. (A) 1, 2 and 3 only
(B) 1, 3 and 4 only
(C) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(D) 2 and 4 only
cards.back:
(C) 1, 2, 3 and 4

cards.front:
In a GALVANIC (voltaic) CELL, chemical energy is converted to:

(A) Heat energy released as heat
(B) Electrical energy flowing as current
(C) Light energy emitted in cell
(D) Mechanical energy as motion
cards.back:
(B) Electrical energy flowing as current

Gases & Electrochemistry — GALVANIC / VOLTAIC CELL — chemical → electrical energy via SPONTANEOUS redox reaction. Two half-cells with different electrodes (e.g., Zn + Cu); SALT BRIDGE (or porous separator) carries ions; external wire carries electrons. EMF = electrochemical-cell voltage. ELECTROLYTIC CELL — opposite: ELECTRICAL energy drives a NON-SPONTANEOUS reaction (electrolysis). DANIELL CELL (Zn/Cu) = classic galvanic cell; ~1.1 V. PRIMARY cells = single-use (dry cells, alkaline). SECONDARY cells = rechargeable (lead-acid, Li-ion).

cards.front:
In any electrochemical cell, OXIDATION takes place at:

(A) Cathode (positive terminal)
(B) Anode (negative in galvanic cell)
(C) Salt bridge inside the cell
(D) External wire of the circuit
cards.back:
(B) Anode (negative in galvanic cell)

Gases & Electrochemistry — Mnemonic: 'AN OX' (Anode = OXidation), 'RED CAT' (REDuction = CAThode). ALWAYS, regardless of cell type. POLARITY differs: in GALVANIC cells, anode is NEGATIVE (gives up electrons); cathode POSITIVE. In ELECTROLYTIC cells, anode is POSITIVE (connected to + terminal of external power source); cathode NEGATIVE. Confuses students! Memory aid: anode = oxidation (always); polarity depends on cell type.

cards.front:
ELECTROPLATING (e.g., gold-plating jewellery, chrome-plating bumpers) uses:

(A) Galvanic cell with spontaneous reaction
(B) Electrolytic cell driven by external power
(C) Spontaneous chemical etching only
(D) Mechanical pressure to fuse layers
cards.back:
(B) Electrolytic cell driven by external power

Gases & Electrochemistry — ELECTROPLATING — coats one metal with thin layer of another. Object to be plated = CATHODE; plating metal = ANODE (or in solution as ions). External battery drives the redox: anode dissolves → ions → reduce + deposit on cathode. Examples: silver plating cutlery; gold plating jewellery; chrome plating bumpers; nickel plating tools; tin plating cans. Used to: improve appearance, corrosion-resistance, electrical contact. COMMERCIAL use: huge industry. Distractor 1 — galvanic (spontaneous) doesn't drive plating reliably.

cards.front:
A common LEAD-ACID battery (used in cars) consists of plates of:

(A) Lead (anode) + zinc (cathode), in saline
(B) Lead (anode) + lead dioxide (cathode), in H₂SO₄
(C) Carbon (anode) + zinc (cathode), in NH₄Cl
(D) Lithium (anode) + cobalt oxide (cathode), in lithium salt
cards.back:
(B) Lead (anode) + lead dioxide (cathode), in H₂SO₄

Gases & Electrochemistry — LEAD-ACID battery (Plante, 1859): Pb anode + PbO₂ cathode, dilute H₂SO₄ (~38%) as electrolyte. Reaction (discharge): Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O. Each cell ~2.1 V; car battery has 6 cells in series = ~12 V. RECHARGEABLE — reverses reaction during charging. Heavy + bulky but cheap + reliable. Used in: cars (starter battery), UPS, solar storage. Distractor 3 = LECLANCHE (dry) cell = Zn anode + carbon/MnO₂ cathode, NH₄Cl paste (~1.5 V; non-rechargeable). Distractor 4 = LITHIUM-ION battery (modern, high energy density, smartphones, laptops, EVs).

(D) Mercury cell (small button cell)

cards.front:
FUEL CELLS are a special type of electrochemical cell that:

(A) Store fuel internally and discharge slowly over time
(B) Generate electricity continuously from supplied fuel + oxidant
(C) Store electrical charge inside chemical bonds for later use
(D) Burn fuel in air to release heat energy + light only
cards.back:
(B) Generate electricity continuously from supplied fuel + oxidant

Gases & Electrochemistry — FUEL CELL — like a battery but FUEL + OXIDANT are continuously SUPPLIED (don't run out unless supply stops). Most common: HYDROGEN-OXYGEN fuel cell. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O + electricity. Output: ~70% efficiency (vs 30-40% for combustion engines). Clean: only WATER as exhaust. USED IN: spacecraft (Apollo, Space Shuttle), some buses + cars (Toyota Mirai, Hyundai Nexo), backup power. India's Hydrogen Mission (2021). Limitations: needs pure H₂ (currently mostly from natural gas); H₂ storage difficult.

(B) Hall-Héroult electrolytic process
(C) Roasting + magnetic separation
(D) Distillation in vacuum chamber
cards.back:
(B) Hall-Héroult electrolytic process

Gases & Electrochemistry — HALL-HÉROULT process (1886, independently by Charles Hall + Paul Héroult): Al₂O₃ (alumina, refined from bauxite by Bayer process) dissolved in molten CRYOLITE (Na₃AlF₆) at ~950°C; ELECTROLYSED with carbon electrodes. Cathode reaction: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al (collected as molten Al at bottom). Anode: O²⁻ → O₂; reacts with carbon → CO₂ (anodes consumed, replaced periodically). Why not smelting with C like iron? Al has very high affinity for O₂ — needs much higher temperature than Fe → impractical with reduction. Energy-intensive: ~13-15 kWh per kg Al → 'frozen electricity'. Recycling Al saves ~95% of energy vs new production.

cards.front:
In electrolysis, positively charged ions (cations) move towards the:

(A) Anode
(B) Cathode
(C) Electrolyte surface
(D) Battery's positive terminal
cards.back:
(B) Cathode

Gases & Electrochemistry — In electrolysis — cations (+) move to the cathode (negative electrode, hence 'cat' to 'cat-hode'). Anions (−) move to the anode (positive electrode). Opposite charges attract. Mnemonic — 'CATions go to the CAThode'. At the cathode, ions are reduced (gain electrons); at the anode, ions are oxidised (lose electrons).

cards.front:
A common dry-cell (torch) battery uses zinc as the:

(A) Cathode
(B) Anode (negative terminal)
(C) Electrolyte
(D) Separator
cards.back:
(B) Anode (negative terminal)

Gases & Electrochemistry — Leclanché dry cell — the zinc CASE serves as the anode (gets oxidised: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻). A carbon rod in the centre is the cathode (where MnO₂ is reduced). The electrolyte is a moist paste of ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl) + zinc chloride (ZnCl₂). As current is drawn, the zinc case slowly erodes from inside. EMF ~1.5 V. Modern alkaline cells (1.5 V) have a similar Zn/MnO₂ chemistry but a KOH electrolyte.

cards.front:
A lead-acid battery, used in most cars, has an electrolyte of:

(A) Hydrochloric acid
(B) Sulphuric acid (dilute)
(C) Nitric acid
(D) Phosphoric acid
cards.back:
(B) Sulphuric acid (dilute)

Gases & Electrochemistry — Lead-acid battery — Pb (anode) / PbO₂ (cathode) / ~30-40 % H₂SO₄ (electrolyte). On discharge both electrodes convert to PbSO₄; concentration of H₂SO₄ drops. Charging reverses the reaction — which is why car batteries can last many years with the engine's alternator recharging them. EMF 2 V per cell; 6 cells in series give the 12 V car battery.

cards.front:
Electroplating a metal object with silver involves making the object the:

(A) Anode in a silver-salt bath
(B) Cathode in a silver-salt bath
(C) Electrolyte itself
(D) A separator layer
cards.back:
(B) Cathode in a silver-salt bath

Gases & Electrochemistry — The object to be plated is the CATHODE (attracts Ag⁺ cations from the silver-nitrate / silver-cyanide electrolyte; they get reduced to Ag and deposit on the surface). The anode is typically a slab of PURE silver — it gets oxidised, replenishing the Ag⁺ in the bath. Used in jewellery, decorative cutlery, printed circuit boards (gold plating).

cards.front:
Which battery technology is dominant in modern smartphones and electric vehicles?

(A) Nickel-Cadmium
(B) Lithium-ion
(C) Lead-acid
(D) Zinc-carbon
cards.back:
(B) Lithium-ion

Gases & Electrochemistry — Lithium-ion (Li-ion) — high energy density, light, rechargeable thousands of times. Cathode typically LiCoO₂ or LFP (lithium-iron phosphate); anode graphite; electrolyte a non-aqueous lithium-salt solution. EMF ~3.6-3.7 V per cell. Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2019 went to Whittingham, Goodenough, Yoshino for Li-ion development. Ni-Cd is older technology (has toxic cadmium; being phased out). Lead-acid is still dominant in ICE cars. Zn-C is a non-rechargeable dry cell.

cards.front:
Galvanisation — to prevent iron from rusting — involves coating it with:

(A) Tin
(B) Zinc
(C) Gold
(D) Lead
cards.back:
(B) Zinc

Gases & Electrochemistry — Galvanisation = coating iron or steel with zinc — either by hot-dipping or electroplating. Zinc protects iron by 'sacrificial' oxidation: even when the coating is scratched, the zinc corrodes before the iron. Tinning (tin coating — used on food cans) is different; tin merely blocks oxygen but does not give sacrificial protection. Applications — roofing sheets, wire buckets, pipes, rebar.

cards.front:
Faraday's first law of electrolysis states that the mass of a substance deposited at an electrode is directly proportional to:

(A) The resistance of the circuit
(B) The quantity of charge passed
(C) The time the current is applied squared
(D) The temperature of the electrolyte
cards.back:
(B) The quantity of charge passed

Gases & Electrochemistry — Faraday's 1st law — m = Z × Q = Z × I × t, where Z is the electrochemical equivalent, I current, t time. Q = charge passed = I × t. Faraday's 2nd law — when the same Q is passed through different electrolytes, masses deposited are in proportion to the equivalent masses. 1 Faraday (96,485 C) will deposit 1 mole-equivalent of any species. These laws are exam-favourite application questions.

cards.front:
The most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere (by volume) is:

(A) Oxygen
(B) Nitrogen
(C) Carbon dioxide
(D) Argon
cards.back:
(B) Nitrogen

Gases & Electrochemistry — Dry air by volume — Nitrogen 78.09 %, Oxygen 20.95 %, Argon 0.93 %, CO₂ ~0.04 %. Trace gases — Ne, He, Kr, Xe. Water vapour varies from near zero to ~4 %. Plants get nitrogen from the soil (fixed by rhizobium bacteria in legumes, lightning, industrial Haber process), not directly from the air.

cards.front:
The lightest gas, used in weather balloons because it is not flammable (unlike the next-lightest), is:

(A) Hydrogen
(B) Helium
(C) Neon
(D) Methane
cards.back:
(B) Helium

Gases & Electrochemistry — Hydrogen is the lightest element but flammable — the Hindenburg disaster (1937). Helium (second-lightest, inert and non-flammable) is therefore preferred for weather balloons, airships and children's party balloons. Produced on Earth from natural-gas wells rich in radioactive decay helium. Neon is used in signs (red-orange glow); methane (CH₄) is the main component of natural gas and is highly flammable.

cards.front:
The gas produced as a by-product of photosynthesis in plants is:

(A) Carbon dioxide
(B) Oxygen
(C) Nitrogen
(D) Ozone
cards.back:
(B) Oxygen

Gases & Electrochemistry — Photosynthesis: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + sunlight → C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + 6 O₂. Plants take CO₂ in and give O₂ out during the day. At night they also respire, which consumes O₂ and releases CO₂ — but the daytime oxygen output is larger. Cellular respiration (in all aerobic organisms, including plants) is the reverse reaction.

cards.front:
'Laughing gas' — an anaesthetic used in dentistry — is chemically:

(A) Nitrogen monoxide (NO)
(B) Nitrous oxide (N₂O)
(C) Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)
(D) Ammonia (NH₃)
cards.back:
(B) Nitrous oxide (N₂O)

Gases & Electrochemistry — Nitrous oxide (N₂O) — 'laughing gas' — used as a mild anaesthetic and sedative, especially in dentistry, since the 19th century. It produces euphoria (hence the name) followed by analgesia. A potent greenhouse gas (~300 times stronger than CO₂ per kg). NO and NO₂ are 'NOₓ' — pollutants from vehicles; NH₃ is ammonia.

cards.front:
The gas that gives a rotten-egg smell is:

(A) Sulphur dioxide
(B) Hydrogen sulphide (H₂S)
(C) Chlorine
(D) Methane
cards.back:
(B) Hydrogen sulphide (H₂S)

Gases & Electrochemistry — H₂S has the characteristic rotten-egg smell; toxic at even small concentrations, potentially fatal at higher ones; detectable by the human nose at just 0.0005 ppm. Found around decaying organic matter, volcanoes, hot springs, rotten eggs. SO₂ has a sharp, acrid smell (burning matches). Chlorine has a pungent, bleach-like smell. Methane is odourless — LPG suppliers add ethyl mercaptan (ethanethiol) to give it a warning smell.

cards.front:
At standard temperature and pressure (STP: 0 °C and 1 atm), one mole of any gas occupies approximately:

(A) 11.2 L
(B) 22.4 L
(C) 24.0 L
(D) 44.8 L
cards.back:
(B) 22.4 L

Gases & Electrochemistry — Avogadro's law + ideal gas law — at STP (0 °C, 1 atm), 1 mole (6.022 × 10²³ molecules) of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 L. At 25 °C and 1 atm ('NTP' / 'ambient conditions' in the newer IUPAC definition of STP at 100 kPa) the molar volume is slightly different (~24.5 L). 11.2 L is half a mole at STP; 44.8 L is 2 moles.

cards.front:
Which of the following gases is a major contributor to acid rain?

(A) Methane
(B) Sulphur dioxide (SO₂)
(C) Argon
(D) Helium
cards.back:
(B) Sulphur dioxide (SO₂)

Gases & Electrochemistry — SO₂ (from burning sulphur-rich coal and oil, from smelters) combines with water and oxygen in the atmosphere to form sulphuric acid — the dominant component of acid rain. NOₓ from vehicle exhaust also forms nitric acid and adds to acid rain. Acid rain damages forests, fish populations and historical stonework (the Taj Mahal being a famous victim). Methane is a greenhouse gas; noble gases are essentially inert.

cards.front:
Boyle's Law states that at constant TEMPERATURE, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is:

(A) Inversely proportional to its pressure
(B) Directly proportional to pressure.
(C) Equal to absolute temperature alone
(D) Independent of pressure changes.
cards.back:
(A) Inversely proportional to its pressure

Gases & Electrochemistry — BOYLE'S LAW (Robert Boyle, 1662): at constant TEMPERATURE for a fixed mass of gas, P × V = constant, i.e., V ∝ 1/P. EXAMPLE: double the pressure → halve the volume; halve the pressure → double the volume. KEY GRAPH: P vs V is a hyperbola; PV vs P is a horizontal line; P vs 1/V is a straight line through origin. INTUITION: pushing gas molecules into smaller volume increases their wall-collision frequency → higher pressure. APPLICATIONS: (1) DEEP-SEA DIVING — at 30 m depth (4 atm pressure), lung gas volumes shrink to 1/4. (2) BICYCLE PUMP — compressing air heats it (the heat is from pressure work, not from Boyle alone). (3) HIGH-ALTITUDE BREATHING — at Mt Everest summit (~33% sea-level pressure), each breath carries only 1/3 the O₂ molecules. PYQ FREQUENCY: top-3 chemistry MCQ in NEET, JEE-Main, SSC; appears as a 1-mark guarantee. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests P-V relationship core fundamental.

cards.front:
Charles's Law states that at constant PRESSURE, the volume of a gas is:

(A) Directly proportional to absolute temperature
(B) Inversely proportional to temperature
(C) Independent of temperature change. (option here)
(D) Inversely proportional to pressure.
cards.back:
(A) Directly proportional to absolute temperature

Gases & Electrochemistry — CHARLES'S LAW (Jacques Charles, 1787): at constant PRESSURE, V ∝ T (T in KELVIN). So V/T = constant; V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂. CRITICAL: T must be in KELVIN, NOT Celsius. K = °C + 273. EXAMPLE: gas at 27°C (300 K) → heated to 327°C (600 K) at constant P → volume DOUBLES. ABSOLUTE ZERO — graphical extrapolation: V vs T graph hits zero volume at −273.15°C — this defines absolute zero (0 K). HOT-AIR BALLOONS: warm air expands → less dense than surrounding cold air → BUOYANT lift. Above ~120°C the fabric softens; pilots vary altitude by adjusting burner heat. RUNNING SHOES: the air pockets in your soles compress in cold weather (Charles's law in reverse) — feel firmer. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-2 Charles-law numericals per JEE-Main, NEET. EXAM TRAP: students forget to convert °C to K and get wrong answers. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests T-V proportion + Kelvin discipline.

cards.front:
What is the IDEAL GAS EQUATION?

(A) PV = nRT (universal gas constant R)
(B) PV = mRT/M alone alone alone
(C) P + V = nRT alone alone (option here)
(D) P/V = nR/T alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) PV = nRT (universal gas constant R)

Gases & Electrochemistry — IDEAL GAS EQUATION: PV = nRT, where P = pressure, V = volume, n = moles, R = universal gas constant = 8.314 J/(mol·K) = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K), T = temperature in Kelvin. ALTERNATE FORMS: PV = (m/M)RT (m = mass, M = molar mass); PV = NkT (N = molecules, k = Boltzmann constant 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K). COMBINATION OF GAS LAWS: ideal gas equation REPLACES Boyle's, Charles's, and Avogadro's laws — they're special cases when the other variables are held constant. AT STP (Standard Temp & Pressure: 0°C / 273.15 K, 1 atm): 1 mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 LITRES. NTP (Normal Temp & Pressure, 20°C, 1 atm): 1 mole = ~24.0 L. ASSUMPTIONS — IDEAL GAS: (1) Gas particles are point masses (no volume). (2) No intermolecular forces. (3) Collisions are perfectly elastic. REAL GASES deviate at HIGH P and LOW T — corrections via VAN DER WAALS equation. PYQ ANGLE: ideal gas is a top JEE-Main, NEET MCQ — 2-3 per paper.

cards.front:
Avogadro's Law states that equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain:

(A) Equal numbers of molecules always
(B) Equal masses of gas alone
(C) Different mole numbers always.
(D) Same density values always.
cards.back:
(A) Equal numbers of molecules always

Gases & Electrochemistry — AVOGADRO'S LAW (Amedeo Avogadro, 1811): equal volumes of gases at same T and P contain EQUAL numbers of MOLECULES (NOT equal mass — molecular weights differ). MATHEMATICALLY: V ∝ n (at constant T, P). AVOGADRO'S NUMBER: N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mole — defines the mole, the SI unit of substance. AT STP: 1 mole = 22.4 L = 6.022 × 10²³ molecules. APPLICATION: this law IS what allows chemical equations to be balanced in terms of MOLAR ratios → VOLUME ratios for gases. EXAMPLE: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O — 2 volumes hydrogen + 1 volume oxygen → 2 volumes water vapour. NOBEL: Avogadro's hypothesis was ignored for ~50 years; Cannizzaro revived it (1860). MOLE CONCEPT in NCERT Class 11 Ch. 1 — foundational. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'mole/Avogadro' is a 1-mark guarantee in JEE-Main, NEET, SSC; appears 1-2× per CGL Tier 1 paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests molecular-vs-mass distinction, often a student-confusion source.

cards.front:
At STP (0°C, 1 atm), what volume does 1 mole of any ideal gas occupy?

(A) 22.4 litres of any ideal gas
(B) 24 litres always alone alone
(C) 11.2 litres always alone alone
(D) 1 litre at STP alone alone
cards.back:
(A) 22.4 litres of any ideal gas

Gases & Electrochemistry — AT STP (Standard Temperature & Pressure: 273.15 K and 1 atm = 101.325 kPa): 1 mole of any ideal gas = 22.4 L = 22,400 cm³ = 22,400 mL. DERIVATION: V = nRT/P = 1 × 0.0821 × 273.15 / 1 ≈ 22.4 L. NOTE: IUPAC redefined STP in 1982 to 0°C and 100 kPa (~24 L for 1 mole) — but the CLASSIC 22.4 L is still the textbook standard for SSC, NEET, JEE-Main. APPLICATION — molar mass via gas density: M = (mass)(22.4) / (volume in L at STP). EXAMPLE: 22 g of CO₂ occupies (22/44) × 22.4 = 11.2 L at STP. PRACTICE — 11.2 L of any gas at STP = 0.5 mole = ~3 × 10²³ molecules. NTP variant: 20°C, 1 atm → 1 mole ~24.0 L. PYQ FREQUENCY: '22.4 L at STP' is a 1-mark MCQ in 90% of JEE-Main, NEET papers. SSC and CGL include this in the chemistry segment 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests STP molar volume — a fundamental gas-stoichiometry skill.

PRACTICE — 11.2 L of any gas at STP = 0.5 mole = ~3 × 10²³ molecules. NTP variant: 20°C, 1 atm → 1 mole ~24.0 L. PYQ FREQUENCY: '22.4 L at STP' is a 1-mark MCQ in 90% of JEE-Main, NEET papers. SSC and CGL include this in the chemistry segment 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests STP molar volume — a fundamental gas-stoichiometry skill.

cards.front:
A gas at 27°C is heated to 127°C at constant pressure. What is the ratio of final to initial volume?

(A) 4:3 (using Kelvin temperatures)
(B) 127:27 alone alone alone
(C) 1:1 (constant pressure) alone
(D) 100:300 alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) 4:3 (using Kelvin temperatures)

Gases & Electrochemistry — Apply CHARLES'S LAW: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂. CONVERT to KELVIN: T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K; T₂ = 127 + 273 = 400 K. So V₂/V₁ = T₂/T₁ = 400/300 = 4/3. INSIGHT: even though Celsius temperature changed by 100° (a big-feeling jump), in Kelvin the change is only from 300 to 400 K — a 33% increase. EXAM TRAP: students wrongly compute V₂/V₁ = 127/27 ≈ 4.7 (using °C directly) — gives a totally wrong answer. ALWAYS USE KELVIN for gas-law calculations. WHY KELVIN? Because Kelvin is an ABSOLUTE scale (0 K = no molecular motion), while Celsius has an arbitrary zero (water's freezing point). Gas-law ratios only make sense at absolute zero reference. PYQ FREQUENCY: this exact 27°C/127°C pair appears in JEE-Main, NEET 2-3× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests °C-to-K conversion + Charles's law application + ratio simplification.

cards.front:
Real gases deviate from ideal-gas behaviour MOST under conditions of:

(A) Low temperature and high pressure
(B) High temperature and low pressure
(C) Low temperature and low pressure
(D) High temperature and high pressure
cards.back:
(A) Low temperature and high pressure

Gases & Electrochemistry — Real gases deviate from PV = nRT MOST at LOW T and HIGH P. WHY? At LOW T: kinetic energy is low → INTERMOLECULAR ATTRACTIONS become significant (attractive forces ignored in ideal-gas model). At HIGH P: gas molecules are pushed close together → MOLECULAR VOLUME becomes significant compared to container volume (ideal-gas model assumes point particles). Both deviations correct via VAN DER WAALS EQUATION: (P + a·n²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT — where 'a' corrects for attraction, 'b' for molecular volume. CRITICAL POINT: above the critical temperature, a gas can't be liquefied no matter the pressure; below, it can be. EXAMPLES — gases LIQUEFY at low T, high P: O₂, N₂, CO₂, He (extreme). REAL-WORLD: liquid nitrogen (storage of biological samples, MRI cooling) — produced via Linde process (compression-expansion cycles). PYQ ANGLE: deviation conditions appear in JEE-Main 1× per year, NEET 1× per year. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests grasp of WHY ideal-gas model breaks down — concept beyond rote.

cards.front:
RUST formed on iron is chemically:

(A) Iron sulphate (FeSO₄), formed in air
(B) Hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O)
(C) Iron carbonate (FeCO₃) in moist air
(D) Iron chloride (FeCl₃) in salty air
cards.back:
(B) Hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O)

Gases & Electrochemistry — RUST — hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O. Formed when iron is exposed to BOTH water (or moisture) AND oxygen — neither alone is enough. Reddish-brown, flaky. Doesn't protect underlying metal (unlike aluminium oxide which forms a dense protective layer). Prevention: galvanising (zinc coating), painting, oiling, alloying (stainless steel — adds Cr, Ni). Distractors 1, 3, 4 are different iron compounds.

cards.front:
AMPHOTERIC OXIDES are those that react with both acids and bases. An example is:

(A) Sodium oxide (Na₂O), only basic in water
(B) Aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃), reacts with acids and bases
(C) Carbon dioxide (CO₂), only acidic anhydride
(D) Sulphur trioxide (SO₃), only acidic anhydride
cards.back:
(B) Aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃), reacts with acids and bases

Gases & Electrochemistry — AMPHOTERIC = reacts with both acids and bases. Examples: Al₂O₃, ZnO, BeO, SnO, PbO. Al₂O₃ + HCl → AlCl₃ + H₂O (acts basic). Al₂O₃ + NaOH → NaAlO₂ (sodium aluminate, acts acidic). BASIC oxides = metal oxides (Na₂O, CaO, MgO) — react with acids; form bases in water. ACIDIC oxides = non-metal oxides (CO₂, SO₃, NO₂) — react with bases; form acids in water (CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ carbonic acid).

cards.front:
OXIDATION in modern definition means:

(A) Loss of oxygen by a substance only
(B) Loss of electrons by a substance
(C) Gain of hydrogen by a substance
(D) Decrease in temperature of a system
cards.back:
(B) Loss of electrons by a substance

Gases & Electrochemistry — Modern definition (electron-transfer): OXIDATION = LOSS of electrons. REDUCTION = GAIN of electrons. Mnemonic: OIL RIG (Oxidation Is Loss; Reduction Is Gain). Older oxygen-hydrogen definitions: oxidation = gain of oxygen / loss of hydrogen; reduction = opposite. The electron-transfer definition is broader and includes reactions without oxygen (e.g., Mg + Cl₂ → MgCl₂; Mg loses electrons → oxidised; Cl gains → reduced). REDOX reaction = paired oxidation + reduction.

cards.option3: Decrease in temperature of a system

cards.front:
When iron reacts with chlorine to form ferric chloride (FeCl₃), the OXIDATION STATE of iron changes from:

(A) 0 to +2 in the product compound
(B) 0 to +3 in the product compound
(C) +2 to +3 in the product compound
(D) +3 to +2 in the product compound
cards.back:
(B) 0 to +3 in the product compound

Gases & Electrochemistry — Fe (elemental, oxidation state 0) → FeCl₃ (Fe is +3, Cl is −1 each). So Fe lost 3 electrons → oxidised from 0 to +3. Equation: 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃. Iron has two common oxidation states: +2 (ferrous, FeCl₂) and +3 (ferric, FeCl₃). With excess Cl₂, FeCl₃ forms preferentially. Distractor 1 = +2 (FeCl₂, different product). Distractor 3, 4 are between non-zero states.

cards.front:
GALVANISATION involves coating iron with which metal to prevent rust?

(A) Copper, the orange-red conductor metal
(B) Zinc, a more reactive sacrificial metal
(C) Tin, used inside food cans for protection
(D) Aluminium, a light silvery metal commonly
cards.back:
(B) Zinc, a more reactive sacrificial metal

Gases & Electrochemistry — GALVANISATION = coating iron with ZINC. Zinc is MORE REACTIVE than iron → preferentially oxidises (sacrifices itself) → protects iron underneath, even if scratched. Used for fences, roofing sheets, water-supply pipes, car bodies. Methods: hot-dip galvanising, electrogalvanising. TINNING — coating with TIN (used inside food cans; tin is LESS reactive, gives barrier protection only — fails if scratched). Galvanising is more robust. Distractor 1 — copper; not used for iron protection. Distractor 4 — Al used as alloy (aluminised steel for some applications).
cards.option2: Tin, used inside food cans for protection
cards.option3: Aluminium, a light silvery metal commonly

cards.front:
Which of these gases is responsible for ACID RAIN?

(A) Oxygen (O₂) and Nitrogen (N₂) in air
(B) SO₂ and NOₓ from fossil-fuel combustion
(C) CO₂ and CH₄ greenhouse gases mainly
(D) O₃ (ozone) and CFCs in stratosphere
cards.back:
(B) SO₂ and NOₓ from fossil-fuel combustion

Gases & Electrochemistry — Acid Rain — caused mainly by SO₂ (sulphur dioxide) + NOₓ (nitrogen oxides) released from fossil fuels (coal-fired power plants, vehicle exhaust). React with atmospheric water to form sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) and nitric acid (HNO₃). pH < 5.6 (normal rain ~5.6 due to CO₂). Damages forests (Black Forest, Germany), lakes (kills fish), buildings + monuments (Taj Mahal — discoloured by SO₂ from Mathura refinery, prompting court orders), human health (respiratory). Mitigated by FGD (flue-gas desulphurisation) scrubbers, EU Directive cuts. Distractor 3 — greenhouse warming, separate issue. Distractor 4 — ozone depletion, also separate.

cards.front:
When carbon dioxide is dissolved in water, the resulting solution is mildly:

(A) Basic, because metals neutralise CO₂
(B) Acidic, due to formation of carbonic acid
(C) Neutral, with no reaction occurring
(D) Highly alkaline, like soap water
cards.back:
(B) Acidic, due to formation of carbonic acid

Gases & Electrochemistry — CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid, weak). H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. Result: mildly acidic, pH ~5.6 (compared to neutral 7). This is why rainwater is naturally slightly acidic (NOT acid rain — that's pH < 5.6). Same chemistry: ocean acidification (rising CO₂ → ocean pH dropping ~0.1 since pre-industrial → coral bleaching, shellfish stress). Soda-water + soft drinks rely on CO₂ dissolved → pleasant fizz + tang.

cards.front:
OXIDATION is defined as:

(A) Loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen)
(B) Gain of electrons (loss of oxygen)
(C) Addition of hydrogen to compound
(D) Decrease in oxidation state count
cards.back:
(A) Loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen)

Gases & Electrochemistry — OXIDATION = LOSS OF ELECTRONS (or addition of oxygen / loss of hydrogen / increase in oxidation state). REDUCTION = GAIN OF ELECTRONS (or loss of oxygen / gain of hydrogen / decrease in oxidation state). MNEMONIC: 'OIL RIG' — Oxidation Is Loss; Reduction Is Gain (of electrons). Or 'LEO the lion says GER' — Loss of Electrons = Oxidation; Gain of Electrons = Reduction. REDOX = simultaneous oxidation + reduction (always paired — electrons must go somewhere). EXAMPLES: rusting (Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃, Fe oxidised); photosynthesis (CO₂ reduced to glucose); respiration (glucose oxidised to CO₂); combustion (fuel oxidised to CO₂ + H₂O); batteries; metallurgy (ores reduced to metals).

cards.front:
OXIDISING AGENT in a redox reaction is the:

(A) Substance that gets reduced (gains electrons)
(B) Substance that gets oxidised (loses electrons)
(C) Catalyst speeding up reaction without changing
(D) Solvent in which reaction takes place
cards.back:
(A) Substance that gets reduced (gains electrons)

Gases & Electrochemistry — OXIDISING AGENT (oxidant) = the species that GETS REDUCED (it gains electrons; in doing so, it OXIDISES the other species). REDUCING AGENT (reductant) = the species that GETS OXIDISED (loses electrons). Counter-intuitive at first, but logical: an oxidising agent CAUSES oxidation in something else. STRONG OXIDANTS: F₂ (most), O₂, Cl₂, KMnO₄ (purple), K₂Cr₂O₇ (orange), HNO₃, conc. H₂SO₄, O₃, H₂O₂, Fe³⁺. STRONG REDUCTANTS: alkali metals (Na, K, Cs — readily lose electron), Mg, Al, Zn, H₂, NaBH₄, LiAlH₄, sulfites. INSIGHT — strong oxidants are dangerous (corrosive, can ignite); SODIUM bursts in water due to redox + H₂ evolved.
cards.option2: Catalyst speeding up reaction without changing
cards.option3: Solvent in which reaction takes place

cards.front:
RUSTING of iron is essentially a:

(A) Slow oxidation reaction in moist air
(B) Reduction reaction with oxygen alone
(C) Pure physical process not chemical
(D) Acid-base reaction in metal here
cards.back:
(A) Slow oxidation reaction in moist air

Gases & Electrochemistry — RUSTING = slow OXIDATION of iron in presence of OXYGEN + WATER → forms hydrated iron(III) oxide Fe₂O₃·xH₂O (red-brown rust). Fe → Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ (oxidation). O₂ + H₂O get reduced. Both moisture + O₂ needed (rust doesn't form in dry air or pure water alone). ACCELERATING factors: salt (electrolyte; coastal cars rust faster), acidic air, mechanical stress. PREVENTION: GALVANIZATION (Zn coating — Zn corrodes preferentially), PAINTING / OILING (barrier), GREASE, ALLOYING (stainless steel — Fe + Cr + Ni; Cr oxide layer is invisible + protective + self-healing), CATHODIC PROTECTION (sacrificial anode of Mg or Zn — used on ship hulls, pipelines). India loses ~3-5% of GDP annually to corrosion.

O₂ + H₂O get reduced. Both moisture + O₂ needed (rust doesn't form in dry air or pure water alone). ACCELERATING factors: salt (electrolyte; coastal cars rust faster), acidic air, mechanical stress. cards.front:
PHOTOSYNTHESIS by plants is essentially a:

(A) Reduction of CO₂ to glucose (using H₂O as electron source)
(B) Oxidation of glucose to CO₂ + water (option here)
(C) Combustion of CO₂ + water to oxygen (option here)
(D) Acid-base neutralisation of carbonic acid (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Reduction of CO₂ to glucose (using H₂O as electron source)

Gases & Electrochemistry — PHOTOSYNTHESIS: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. CO₂ (carbon at +4) is REDUCED to glucose (carbon at 0); H₂O OXIDISED to O₂ (electrons from water reduce CO₂). LIGHT energy drives this uphill reaction (CO₂ + H₂O are stable; glucose is high-energy). RESPIRATION = REVERSE: glucose + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + ATP (energy). Glucose oxidised → CO₂ (back to +4); O₂ reduced. INSIGHT — life on Earth is essentially a vast REDOX cycle: photosynthesis (plants store sun energy by reducing CO₂); respiration (animals release energy by oxidising glucose). NET CYCLE: solar energy → biomass → metabolic energy. Roughly 10% of solar light hitting earth's plants gets converted to biomass.

cards.front:
Which of the following is a strong OXIDISING AGENT?

(A) Potassium permanganate (KMnO₄, deep purple)
(B) Sodium chloride (NaCl, table salt)
(C) Carbon (used in steel-making) too
(D) Hydrogen gas (used in fuel cells)
cards.back:
(A) Potassium permanganate (KMnO₄, deep purple)

Gases & Electrochemistry — KMnO₄ (POTASSIUM PERMANGANATE) — strong oxidant. Mn is in +7 state (highest possible). Bright purple → reduced products are colourless / brown. USES: water purification, antiseptic, organic chemistry titrations, decoloriser. K₂Cr₂O₇ (POTASSIUM DICHROMATE) — orange; Cr +6 → +3 (green). HNO₃ — strong oxidant, esp. concentrated. ATOMIC OXYGEN, FLUORINE, OZONE — extreme oxidants. Distractor 4: H₂ is a strong REDUCING agent (often used to reduce metal oxides → metal in metallurgy). REDUCING agents: alkali metals, Mg, H₂, C (in steel-making, carbon reduces iron ore Fe₂O₃ + C → Fe + CO₂).

cards.front:
When zinc is added to copper sulphate solution, the change is:

(A) Blue colour fades; Zn is oxidised, Cu deposits
(B) No reaction occurs at all (option here)
(C) Solution turns greenish-yellow (option here)
(D) Zinc absorbs water from solution (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Blue colour fades; Zn is oxidised, Cu deposits

Gases & Electrochemistry — Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Zinc DISPLACES copper (since Zn is HIGHER in REACTIVITY SERIES than Cu). Zn oxidised (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻); Cu²⁺ reduced (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu). Blue (Cu²⁺) colour FADES → colourless (Zn²⁺). Cu deposits as reddish-brown layer on Zn surface. Solution becomes ZnSO₄ + Cu solid. REACTIVITY SERIES (most reactive → least): K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Ag, Au. ANY metal HIGHER displaces ANY metal LOWER from its salt. APPLICATIONS: extraction of metals (e.g., Cu from CuSO₄ using scrap iron), galvanic cells (Daniel cell uses Zn-Cu redox to generate current). PYQ STAPLE.

cards.option3: Zinc absorbs water from solution (option here)

cards.front:
BLEACHING by chlorine works by:

(A) Oxidation of coloured organic compounds
(B) Reduction of stains via electron gain
(C) Dissolving stains in water mainly
(D) Mechanical scrubbing of fabric here
cards.back:
(A) Oxidation of coloured organic compounds

Gases & Electrochemistry — BLEACHING = oxidation of coloured compounds → colourless (chromophores destroyed). CHLORINE + water → HCl + HOCl (hypochlorous acid, the active oxidant). HOCl breaks down stain molecules. CHLORINE BLEACH (sodium hypochlorite NaOCl) — most common household bleach. OXYGEN BLEACH (H₂O₂, sodium percarbonate) — gentler, used for colour-safe bleaching, eco-friendly (decomposes to water + oxygen). BLEACHING POWDER = Ca(OCl)Cl. INDUSTRIAL: pulp/paper, textile, water treatment. CAUTION — never mix bleach with ammonia (forms toxic chloramine vapours) or with acids (releases Cl₂ gas). REDUCING bleaches also exist (SO₂ for wool/silk — gentler).

cards.front:
In a chemical reaction, OXIDATION is best defined as:

(A) Loss of hydrogen
(B) Loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen)
(C) Gain of electrons
(D) Decrease in oxidation number
cards.back:
(B) Loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen)

Gases & Electrochemistry — Modern definition: oxidation = loss of electrons; reduction = gain of electrons (mnemonic OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain). Older definitions: oxidation = gain of oxygen / loss of hydrogen / increase in oxidation number. Reduction = loss of oxygen / gain of hydrogen / decrease in oxidation number. The two always occur together = REDOX. Example: Mg + ½O₂ → MgO; Mg loses 2e⁻ (oxidised), O₂ gains 2e⁻ (reduced).

cards.front:
In the reaction Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu, the oxidising agent is:

(A) Zn
(B) Cu²⁺ (in CuSO₄)
(C) SO₄²⁻
(D) Both Zn and Cu²⁺
cards.back:
(B) Cu²⁺ (in CuSO₄)

Gases & Electrochemistry — Oxidising agent = species that ITSELF gets reduced (i.e. it OXIDISES the other). Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction; Cu²⁺ is oxidised — wait, reduced) — so Cu²⁺ is the OXIDISING AGENT. Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation; Zn loses electrons) — so Zn is the REDUCING AGENT. SO₄²⁻ is just a spectator ion (unchanged). Trick: 'oxidising agent' is read 'agent that causes oxidation' = it accepts electrons.

cards.front:
The 'rusting' of iron is essentially an example of:

(A) Pure reduction
(B) Slow electrochemical oxidation in presence of moisture and oxygen
(C) Combustion
(D) Polymerisation
cards.back:
(B) Slow electrochemical oxidation in presence of moisture and oxygen

Gases & Electrochemistry — Rust = hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃ · xH₂O), reddish-brown. Mechanism — galvanic micro-cells form on the iron surface; Fe loses electrons (anode: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻); oxygen + water consume them (cathode: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻); Fe²⁺ then oxidises further to Fe³⁺ and combines with hydroxide and water → rust. Prevention: galvanising (zinc coating, sacrificial anode), painting, alloying (stainless steel = Fe + Cr + Ni). Salt water accelerates rusting (electrolyte improves the cell).

cards.front:
The oxidation number of sulphur in H₂SO₄ is:

(A) +2
(B) +6
(C) +4
(D) −2
cards.back:
(B) +6

Gases & Electrochemistry — Sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral compound = 0. H₂SO₄ has 2 H (+1 each = +2), 4 O (−2 each = −8), and S = x. Equation: 2 + x − 8 = 0 → x = +6. So S is in +6 oxidation state in H₂SO₄. Other common S states: −2 (H₂S), 0 (S₈ elemental), +2 (S₂Cl₂), +4 (SO₂, H₂SO₃), +6 (SO₃, H₂SO₄). The +6 state is the highest oxidation number S can show.

cards.front:
Which of the following is a strong REDUCING agent?

(A) F₂
(B) Hydrogen gas (H₂) at high temperature
(C) Oxygen
(D) Cl₂
cards.back:
(B) Hydrogen gas (H₂) at high temperature

Gases & Electrochemistry — Reducing agent = donates electrons → gets oxidised. H₂ readily donates: H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ (used in metal extraction: WO₃ + 3H₂ → W + 3H₂O). F₂ is the strongest OXIDISING agent (most electronegative). Cl₂ and O₂ are also oxidising agents. Other reducing agents: alkali metals (Na, K), CO, H₂S, SO₂, hydrogen sulphite, ascorbic acid, NaBH₄ (mild). In organic chemistry: LiAlH₄ (very strong), DIBAL-H, Zn-Hg/HCl (Clemmensen), Zn/HOAc.

cards.front:
In a galvanic (voltaic) cell, oxidation occurs at the:

(A) Cathode (positive electrode)
(B) Anode (negative electrode in galvanic cells)
(C) Both electrodes equally
(D) Electrolyte
cards.back:
(B) Anode (negative electrode in galvanic cells)

Gases & Electrochemistry — Galvanic / voltaic cell — converts chemical energy → electrical energy spontaneously. Anode = oxidation site (loses electrons, called negative terminal because electrons leave). Cathode = reduction site (gains electrons, positive terminal). Mnemonic 'AN OX, RED CAT' — Anode Oxidation, Reduction Cathode. NOTE: in ELECTROLYTIC cells, signs reverse — anode is positive (electrons forced out by external supply) and cathode is negative. Daniell cell — Zn/Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺/Cu, EMF = +1.10 V.

cards.front:
The browning of cut apples is best classified as a:

(A) Combustion reaction
(B) Enzymatic oxidation (polyphenol oxidase + atmospheric O₂)
(C) Reduction reaction
(D) Hydrolysis
cards.back:
(B) Enzymatic oxidation (polyphenol oxidase + atmospheric O₂)

Gases & Electrochemistry — When an apple is cut, polyphenol oxidase (PPO) enzymes inside cells contact atmospheric O₂; they catalyse oxidation of phenolic compounds to brown quinones — hence the browning. Slowed by: refrigeration, dipping in lemon juice (vitamin C is a reducing agent — competes for O₂), salt water, blanching (heat denatures enzyme). Same mechanism: browning of bananas, potatoes, mushrooms. Genetically engineered 'Arctic apple' has the PPO gene silenced — does not brown when cut.

cards.front:
The MOST ABUNDANT gas in Earth's ATMOSPHERE is:

(A) Oxygen (21%)
(B) NITROGEN (N₂)
(C) Carbon dioxide
(D) Argon
cards.back:
(B) NITROGEN (N₂)

Gases & Electrochemistry — EARTH's ATMOSPHERE — COMPOSITION by VOLUME (dry air): (1) NITROGEN (N₂) — 78.08% — MOST ABUNDANT. (2) OXYGEN (O₂) — 20.95%. (3) ARGON (Ar) — 0.93%. (4) CARBON DIOXIDE (CO₂) — 0.042% (420 ppm, April 2025 — rising from 280 ppm pre-industrial; Mauna Loa record since 1958). (5) NEON (Ne) — 18 ppm. (6) HELIUM (He) — 5 ppm. (7) METHANE (CH₄) — 2 ppm + rising. (8) KRYPTON (Kr) — 1 ppm. (9) HYDROGEN (H₂) — 0.55 ppm. (10) NITROUS OXIDE (N₂O), OZONE (O₃), carbon monoxide (CO), xenon, chlorofluorocarbons — trace. PLUS WATER VAPOUR (variable, 0-4%). NITROGEN (N₂): (1) COLOURLESS, ODOURLESS, TASTELESS gas. (2) MW 28; density slightly less than air. (3) NON-REACTIVE at room temp (strong triple bond N≡N, bond energy 945 kJ/mol — hardest bond to break). (4) LIQUID NITROGEN — -196°C (77 K); cryogenic uses: food freezing, medical (cryosurgery, fertility storage), metal hardening, preserving biological samples, dermatology (wart removal). (5) NITROGEN FIXATION — crucial for life; N₂ → NH₃ / nitrates (plants can't use N₂ directly): (a) BIOLOGICAL — Rhizobium bacteria in LEGUME root nodules (peas, beans, alfalfa, clover, chickpea, lentil); Azotobacter + cyanobacteria free-living; ~200 million tonnes N/year. (b) LIGHTNING — atmospheric N + O combine into NOx, washed down as nitric acid; ~10 million tonnes/year. (c) INDUSTRIAL — HABER-BOSCH PROCESS (Fritz Haber 1909, Carl Bosch industrialised 1913, BASF Germany): N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ at 400-500°C + 200-300 atm with iron catalyst; basis of SYNTHETIC FERTILISERS — revolutionised agriculture; feeds half of world's 8 billion people; ~175 million tonnes/year. Haber Nobel Chemistry 1918; Bosch + Bergius 1931. NORMAN BORLAUG's Green Revolution depended on N-fertiliser. (6) NITROGEN CYCLE — fixation → assimilation → ammonification → nitrification → denitrification (back to N₂). (7) USES of N₂: (a) inert atmosphere in electronics manufacturing; (b) food packaging (crisps, chips — prevents oxidation); (c) fire prevention (nitrogen-filled aircraft fuel tanks); (d) refrigeration; (e) dry-cleaning; (f) making ammonia + nitric acid + fertilisers + explosives (TNT, ammonium nitrate, dynamite) + dyes + drugs. ATMOSPHERE LAYERS: (1) TROPOSPHERE (0-12 km, weather; 75% mass; temp drops with altitude). (2) STRATOSPHERE (12-50 km; ozone layer at 20-35 km; temp rises due to ozone UV absorption). (3) MESOSPHERE (50-85 km; coldest ~-90°C; meteors burn up). (4) THERMOSPHERE (85-600 km; very hot but thin; aurora; ISS orbits here 400 km). (5) EXOSPHERE (600-10,000 km). KÁRMÁN LINE (100 km) = space boundary (FAI). PAYNE-SHULTZ + KEELING CURVE (Mauna Loa CO₂ since 1958) is key climate-change evidence. 78.08%; inert diatomic; fixed biologically by legumes' Rhizobium bacteria + lightning + Haber-Bosch process.

cards.front:
Which GAS is used to FILL BALLOONS + airships, being LIGHTER than air + non-flammable?

(A) Hydrogen
(B) HELIUM (He)
(C) Methane
(D) Carbon dioxide
cards.back:
(B) HELIUM (He)

Gases & Electrochemistry — HELIUM (He) — Group 18 NOBLE GAS; atomic number 2; 2nd most abundant element in UNIVERSE (23% after H 76%) but very RARE on Earth (0.00052% of atmosphere). Named after Greek HELIOS (sun) — discovered 1868 in SOLAR spectrum (sun) during eclipse by Pierre Janssen + Norman Lockyer — FIRST element found in SPACE before on Earth. Isolated on Earth 1895 by William Ramsay (from uranium ore cleveite). PROPERTIES: (1) Lightest NOBLE gas; 2nd lightest element (after H). (2) COLOURLESS, odourless, tasteless. (3) INERT — doesn't react with anything; no compounds known at normal conditions. (4) LOW boiling point = -268.9°C (4.2 K) — LOWEST of any element; CANNOT be solidified at normal pressure (only at 2.5 MPa + 0.95 K). (5) EXCEPTIONAL thermal conductivity. (6) LOW density ~0.178 g/L (air 1.29 g/L) — makes balloons float; inert = safer than hydrogen (infamous Hindenburg 1937 fire killed 36 — used H₂). USES: (1) BALLOONS — party balloons; meteorological weather balloons; airships (NON-flammable alternative to H₂). (2) MRI MACHINES — superconducting magnets need LIQUID HELIUM cooling to near absolute zero (4.2 K) to maintain superconductivity; one MRI uses 1,700 litres liquid He; He shortages threaten MRI industry. (3) DEEP-SEA DIVING — HELIOX (helium + oxygen mix) replaces nitrogen in breathing gas for depths >30m; prevents 'nitrogen narcosis' + 'the bends'. Trimix (He + O + N) even deeper. (4) SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH — cryogenics, superconductivity, superfluidity (He-II below 2.17 K has zero viscosity — Kapitsa, Nobel 1978). (5) Welding (TIG inert atmosphere). (6) Rocket propulsion (pressurising fuel tanks; NASA/ISRO use). (7) LEAK DETECTION (small molecule escapes easily). (8) Anti-aging research (recently). (9) Nuclear reactors (coolant in HTGRs). (10) Semiconductor manufacture. SOURCES: RADIOACTIVE DECAY of URANIUM + THORIUM; alpha particles = He-4 nuclei. Trapped in natural gas reservoirs (particularly USA Texas/Kansas fields — 75% world production). Separated by fractional distillation of natural gas. FACE: HELIUM is FINITE + IRREPLACEABLE — once released to atmosphere, escapes Earth's gravity to space; cannot be recovered. World faces HELIUM SHORTAGE; critical for science + medicine. Price hikes have been frequent. India: small quantities from Kutch Rajasthan natural gas; mostly imported (US, Qatar, Algeria, Russia). Project ONGC exploring indigenous helium. VOICE CHANGE effect — inhaling helium makes voice high-pitched because sound travels faster in less dense gas (~3× air), shifting resonance frequencies of vocal tract up. Dangerous if inhaled too much — asphyxiation (no O₂). OTHER NOBLE GASES (Group 18): (1) He. (2) Neon (Ne) — signs + discharge tubes; glows RED-ORANGE. (3) Argon (Ar) — ~1% of atmosphere; filament lamps + welding. (4) Krypton (Kr) — high-brightness lamps (headlights), lasers. (5) Xenon (Xe) — car HID headlights, anesthetics, nuclear reactors as detectors. (6) Radon (Rn) — RADIOACTIVE; lurks in basements; major lung cancer risk. NOBLE GASES historically called 'INERT GASES' but xenon + krypton + radon form some compounds (XeF₂ 1962 Neil Bartlett, XeO₃, etc.) — no longer wholly inert. 2nd lightest element; NOBLE gas (inert, non-flammable); boiling point -269°C; used in MRI magnets + deep-sea diving + party balloons.

cards.front:
LAUGHING GAS used in dentistry + as a whipped-cream propellant is:

(A) Carbon monoxide
(B) NITROUS OXIDE (N₂O)
(C) Oxygen
(D) Helium
cards.back:
(B) NITROUS OXIDE (N₂O)

Gases & Electrochemistry — NITROUS OXIDE (N₂O) — 'LAUGHING GAS'. COLOURLESS, sweet-smelling gas; dinitrogen monoxide or nitrous oxide. Discovered 1772 by Joseph PRIESTLEY. Humphry DAVY noted analgesic effects 1799 ('gas of paradise'). Used as party drug in late 1700s-1800s ('laughing parties'). PROPERTIES: stable at room temperature; less dense than air; supports combustion (auto racing cars use N₂O for boost!); non-toxic in small doses. BREAKS down at ~800°C releasing O₂. USES: (1) DENTAL + MEDICAL ANAESTHESIA — mild anaesthetic + analgesic; 'ENTONOX' (50% N₂O + 50% O₂) given during CHILDBIRTH pain relief + paramedic emergencies. NO loss of consciousness at normal doses; mild euphoria; hence 'laughing gas'. (2) FOOD — aerating propellant for WHIPPED CREAM (commercial whipped cream canisters). (3) AUTO RACING — 'NOS' injection; boosts engine oxygen supply; more combustion → more power. (4) AEROSPACE — rocket oxidiser (cheap alternative to LOX). (5) Semiconductor processing. RECREATIONAL ABUSE: 'nangs' / 'whippets' — people inhale from small whipped-cream chargers; pleasant but DANGEROUS (B12 deficiency + neuropathy with repeated use; hypoxia death); rising concern in UK banned recently; India mostly unregulated. GREENHOUSE GAS role: (a) N₂O is 3RD MOST IMPORTANT GHG after CO₂ + CH₄. (b) GWP (Global Warming Potential) = 300× CO₂ on 100-year timescale — VERY POTENT. (c) Atmospheric lifetime 114 years. (d) Atmospheric concentration rose from 270 ppb (pre-industrial) to 336 ppb (2024). (e) Sources: SYNTHETIC FERTILISERS (major — ~30% total; especially excess urea); agricultural soils (livestock manure + soil bacteria); fossil fuel combustion (esp. diesel), industrial processes (nylon, nitric acid production), biomass burning, wastewater. (f) Also an OZONE-DEPLETING substance — currently the largest ODS being emitted (replacing CFCs after Montreal Protocol phasing them out). (g) Contributes ~6% of global warming attribution. MITIGATION: reduce fertiliser use, 4R nutrient stewardship, nitrification inhibitors, precision agriculture, livestock manure management, denitrification + destruction in industries. OTHER KEY ENV GASES: (1) METHANE (CH₄) — 28-34× GWP (100-yr), 80×+ on 20-yr; ~16% of global warming; sources: cattle burps (enteric fermentation), paddy fields, fossil fuels, landfills, wetlands, permafrost. Rising fast. India is MAJOR methane source (cattle 30 CR + paddy; 3rd largest emitter). (2) CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) — POISONOUS, odourless, colourless; from incomplete combustion (cars, coal, gas geysers, smoking). Binds haemoglobin 240× tighter than O₂ → tissue hypoxia. Cause of DEATH in closed rooms with faulty water heaters; carbon monoxide alarms mandatory in many countries. (3) SULPHUR DIOXIDE (SO₂) — ACID RAIN + respiratory irritant. cards.front:
Which GAS is known as 'DRY ICE' in its SOLID form?

(A) Oxygen
(B) CARBON DIOXIDE (CO₂)
(C) Nitrogen
(D) Ammonia
cards.back:
(B) CARBON DIOXIDE (CO₂)

Gases & Electrochemistry — DRY ICE — SOLID FORM of CARBON DIOXIDE (CO₂). SUBLIMES (goes directly from SOLID to GAS without melting to liquid) at -78.5°C (-109°F) at normal atmospheric pressure. No liquid phase unless pressure raised above ~5.1 atm (triple point). NAMED 'dry' because leaves NO LIQUID residue. DENSITY: 1.5 g/cm³ (denser than ice). PRODUCTION: compress CO₂, cool + expand rapidly (Joule-Thomson cooling) → solidifies into SNOW → compressed into blocks/pellets. USES: (1) FOOD-GRADE REFRIGERATION — transport of ice cream, frozen foods, perishables, vaccines (cold chain); effective (-78°C cooling); hotter dry ice advantages (no melt, leaves no liquid, sterile; no water damage). (2) SPECIAL EFFECTS — 'FOG' or 'SMOKE' machines in theatres, concerts, Halloween events, horror films; dry ice in warm water → dense cold CO₂ fog (heavier than air, rolls downward). (3) Industrial cleaning (dry ice BLASTING — replaces sandblasting; no abrasive residue). (4) MEDICAL — transporting biological samples, organs. (5) Scientific — cooling experiments, removing wasps' nests. HAZARDS: (1) VERY COLD — frostbite on skin contact; handle with gloves. (2) SUFFOCATION — when sublimating in closed rooms, CO₂ (heavier than air) displaces oxygen; 6-8% CO₂ causes suffocation. NEVER transport dry ice in CAR with closed windows. (3) EXPLOSION — never seal dry ice in airtight container — pressure builds up from sublimation. CO₂ PROPERTIES: (1) COLOURLESS, odourless, slightly acidic taste (dissolves to form carbonic acid). (2) MW 44. Denser than air (1.52× air). (3) Not flammable; doesn't support combustion. (4) Forms CARBONIC ACID (H₂CO₃) with water; soda water/carbonated drinks. Weakly acidic, pH ~4. (5) CRITICAL point: 31°C + 73 atm; SUPERCRITICAL CO₂ used as green solvent (decaffeination of coffee, dry cleaning, extracts). USES of CO₂: (1) FIRE EXTINGUISHERS — CO₂ fires + electrical + flammable liquid fires (non-conductive; leaves no residue; suffocates flame by displacing O₂). (2) CARBONATED DRINKS — soda, cola, beer (dissolves at high pressure; fizzy when pressure released). (3) PLANT GROWTH in greenhouses — 'CO₂ fertilisation' boosts photosynthesis (1000+ ppm). (4) Welding shielding gas. (5) WATER TREATMENT — pH adjustment. (6) Enhanced Oil Recovery (EOR) — pumped into old oil wells. ATMOSPHERIC CO₂: 420 ppm (April 2025, NOAA Mauna Loa). Up from 280 ppm pre-industrial. Annual increase ~2-3 ppm. PRIMARY driver of GLOBAL WARMING — traps heat via greenhouse effect. Sources: FOSSIL FUEL COMBUSTION (oil, coal, gas — 90%+), cement production, deforestation, land-use change. CARBON CYCLE — CO₂ ↔ photosynthesis ↔ respiration ↔ decomposition ↔ ocean dissolution ↔ carbonate rocks. PHOTOSYNTHESIS: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂. Plants + oceans absorb ~55% of human CO₂ emissions (carbon sinks); ~45% remains in atmosphere. NET-ZERO emissions goal: reduce emissions + absorb rest via forests, oceans, carbon capture tech. INDIA committed to Net Zero by 2070; G20 Bali (2022) declaration aimed at 2050 global. CARBON CAPTURE + STORAGE (CCS) + Direct Air Capture (DAC) — emerging tech. Ocean acidification = CO₂ dissolving in oceans → H₂CO₃ → lower pH (8.2 → 8.1 in 150 yrs) → harms marine calcifiers (corals, oysters, plankton). SOLID CO₂ sublimes directly to gas at -78.5°C (no liquid state at atm pressure); used for cooling + fog effects + shipping perishables.

cards.front:
The VERY TOXIC gas that binds HAEMOGLOBIN 240x more strongly than OXYGEN + is produced by INCOMPLETE combustion is:

(A) Carbon dioxide
(B) CARBON MONOXIDE (CO)
(C) Chlorine
(D) Hydrogen sulphide
cards.back:
(B) CARBON MONOXIDE (CO)

Gases & Electrochemistry — CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) — 'SILENT KILLER'. Colourless, odourless, tasteless, highly toxic gas. Discovered 1776 by French chemist De Lassone. PRODUCTION: INCOMPLETE COMBUSTION of carbon-containing fuels (not enough oxygen) — (1) car EXHAUST (petrol/diesel engines); (2) faulty gas GEYSERS / water heaters; (3) burning CHARCOAL in closed rooms (sigri, barbecue indoors); (4) cigarette smoke; (5) industrial fires; (6) poorly-ventilated stoves; (7) generators in enclosed spaces; (8) volcanic activity (trace). TOXICITY: (1) CO binds HAEMOGLOBIN (to form CARBOXYHEMOGLOBIN, COHb) with ~240× AFFINITY vs O₂. Blocks O₂ transport. (2) Binds tightly — doesn't release for many hours. (3) Shift O₂ dissociation curve to LEFT → less O₂ delivered to tissues even if bound. (4) Effects at exposure levels (%COHb in blood): (a) 10% (heavy smoker) — mild dyspnea. (b) 20% — headache, fatigue, confusion. (c) 30% — severe headache, vomiting, chest pain. (d) 40-60% — unconsciousness, convulsions, cardiac failure. (e) >60% = LETHAL. DEATHS: accidental CO poisoning causes thousands of deaths globally each year (USA ~500/yr; India often unrecorded/attributed). Common in winter (closed windows + gas heaters) + bathrooms with gas geysers (poorly vented). SYMPTOMS: cherry-red lips (classic sign), headache, dizziness, nausea — often mistaken for flu. Chronic low exposure → brain damage. DETECTION: CO DETECTORS / ALARMS (mandatory in buildings in many countries; not in India yet). Detect CO via electrochemical or semiconductor sensors. ~5-10,000 ₹ domestic unit. TREATMENT: (1) REMOVE from source. (2) 100% OXYGEN (high-flow mask) — reduces COHb half-life from 4-6 hrs in air to ~80 min. (3) HYPERBARIC OXYGEN — 100% O₂ at 2-3 atm pressure in chamber; for severe cases; reduces COHb half-life to 20 min; also flushes CO from tissues. CHEMISTRY: CO molecule is LINEAR; C≡O triple bond (despite C's valence). WEAK partial charge. REACTIVE — can form metal carbonyls (Ni(CO)₄, Fe(CO)₅ — very toxic). USES (industrial): (1) FUEL — producer gas, water gas, syngas (CO + H₂); (2) METALLURGY — reducing agent to smelt iron ore (C + O₂ → CO₂; CO₂ + C → 2CO; 3CO + Fe₂O₃ → 2Fe + 3CO₂ — blast furnace). (3) CHEMICAL SYNTHESIS — Monsanto process (methanol production from syngas); Fischer-Tropsch process (hydrocarbons from syngas). (4) Flame atomic absorption spectroscopy. HINDENBURG DISASTER 1937 — not CO; hydrogen airship explosion. DEADLY HISTORIC CO EVENTS: (a) 1939-45 Nazis used CO in extermination camps (Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka — diesel engines) before switching to Zyklon B (hydrogen cyanide). (b) Cardiff coal pits + mining disasters. (c) Many Indian bathroom deaths from geyser. BHOPAL GAS TRAGEDY (2-3 DEC 1984, Madhya Pradesh) — NOT CO — MIC (Methyl Isocyanate) leak from Union Carbide pesticide plant; 3,787+ deaths (official, actual 15,000-25,000 over years); 558,000+ injured; WORST industrial disaster in history. Anderson (CEO) never extradited. Settlement $470M (1989; inadequate). 2 DEC = NATIONAL POLLUTION CONTROL DAY in INDIA. 'silent killer' — odourless + colourless + tasteless; from gas geysers, car exhausts, stoves; cause of accidental deaths.

cards.front:
The GAS responsible for BLEACHING + DISINFECTION of drinking water is:

(A) Oxygen
(B) CHLORINE (Cl₂)
(C) Nitrogen
(D) Argon
cards.back:
(B) CHLORINE (Cl₂)

Gases & Electrochemistry — CHLORINE (Cl₂) — Group 17 halogen; GREENISH-YELLOW gas with PUNGENT irritating odour. Discovered 1774 by Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele; named 1810 by Humphry Davy (Greek 'chloros' = green). DENSER than air (2.49×). HIGHLY TOXIC — lethal at 1000 ppm for 1 min; 100 ppm dangerous. USED as CHEMICAL WEAPON in WWI (first at Ypres, 22 April 1915 by Germans; Fritz Haber ironically the architect — same who synthesised ammonia to feed world). PROPERTIES: (1) Strong OXIDISER. (2) Reacts with WATER: Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl (HYPOCHLOROUS acid — the actual bleaching + disinfecting agent). (3) Reacts with ALKALIS: Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaOCl + H₂O (sodium hypochlorite = HOUSEHOLD BLEACH). (4) Reacts with DRY SLAKED LIME: Cl₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaOCl₂ + H₂O (BLEACHING POWDER). (5) Reacts with METALS to form chlorides. MANUFACTURE: CHLOR-ALKALI PROCESS — electrolysis of brine (NaCl solution); products: Cl₂ + NaOH + H₂; world's largest chemical industry. USES: (1) WATER DISINFECTION — MUNICIPAL water treatment to kill bacteria + protozoa + viruses; 1-5 ppm residual chlorine maintained in pipes. JOHN SNOW's 1854 London cholera map + later chlorination transformed public health; stopped waterborne disease epidemics. Swimming POOLS chlorinated. India: CPWD + Municipal water; BIS IS 10500-2012 standards. (2) BLEACH — textiles, paper, pulp, sewage treatment. (3) PVC (POLYVINYL CHLORIDE) PLASTIC — pipes, flooring, cable insulation; chlorine industry. (4) Solvents (tetrachloroethylene = PERC, for dry cleaning — though being phased out). (5) Hydrochloric Acid (HCl) — pickling steel, food industry. (6) REFRIGERANTS historically (CFCs, HCFCs — now phased out per Montreal Protocol). (7) Pharmaceuticals, pesticides, dyes, rubber, photography. (8) WATER PURIFICATION TABLETS (chloramine). CHLORINE-BASED PRODUCTS: (a) HOUSEHOLD BLEACH (NaOCl, 5% solution) — Clorox, Vim, Harpic; disinfectant + stain remover; caution: don't mix with ammonia (produces toxic chloramine vapours + potentially chlorine gas), don't mix with vinegar (produces chlorine gas). (b) POOL CHLORINE (Ca(OCl)₂ — calcium hypochlorite, stronger). (c) TABLE SALT (NaCl; sodium chloride — not toxic as salt). (d) STOMACH ACID — HCl; essential for digestion (pH 1-2). SIDE EFFECTS + CONCERNS: (1) CHLORINATION BY-PRODUCTS — TRIHALOMETHANES (THMs), haloacetic acids (HAAs) formed when Cl reacts with organic matter in water; mildly carcinogenic; limits (WHO + BIS <80 µg/L THMs). (2) Chloramines (when chlorine + amines/ammonia react) — irritate eyes + lungs; alternative disinfectant chlorine dioxide (ClO₂, Europe). (3) OZONE (O₃) + UV — alternative water disinfection (no taste issues, but expensive; don't persist in pipes). HALOGENS — Group 17: (1) FLUORINE (F₂) — most reactive; pale yellow; even more toxic than Cl₂; tooth paste (as fluoride). (2) CHLORINE (Cl₂). (3) BROMINE (Br₂) — reddish-brown LIQUID (only liquid non-metal at rt); red-light-like flame retardants. (4) IODINE (I₂) — lustrous purple-black SOLID; antiseptic (tincture of iodine); thyroid hormone. (5) ASTATINE (At) — extremely rare, radioactive. ACID + HALOGENS cause many chem accidents. greenish-yellow toxic gas; kills pathogens in water + forms bleach NaOCl; used in paper + textile bleaching + PVC + HCl.
