cards.front:
The LIGHTEST GAS known is:

(A) Helium
(B) HYDROGEN (H₂)
(C) Oxygen
(D) Nitrogen
cards.back:
(B) HYDROGEN (H₂)

Gases & Electrochemistry — HYDROGEN (H₂) — LIGHTEST element (atomic number 1, atomic mass 1.008; molecular mass of H₂ = 2.016); LIGHTEST gas at normal conditions (density 0.0899 g/L at STP vs air 1.29 g/L — 14.3× lighter). Most abundant element in UNIVERSE (75% by mass, 92% by atoms). Makes up stars (including Sun, where fusion creates helium). DISCOVERED 1766 by HENRY CAVENDISH; name 'hydrogen' by Antoine Lavoisier (Greek 'water-former'). ISOTOPES: (1) PROTIUM (¹H) — 99.98%, 0 neutrons, most common. (2) DEUTERIUM (²H or D) — 0.015%, 1 neutron, 'heavy hydrogen'; D₂O = 'heavy water' used as moderator in NUCLEAR REACTORS. (3) TRITIUM (³H or T) — trace, radioactive (β decay, 12.3-yr half-life), 2 neutrons; used in H-BOMBS + tritium-glow-in-dark watch dials + fusion reactors. PROPERTIES: (1) COLOURLESS, odourless, tasteless. (2) HIGHLY FLAMMABLE — burns in air with pale blue flame. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (produces WATER, no pollution). EXPLOSIVE mix 4-75% H₂ in air. (3) Boiling point -253°C (20 K); LIQUID H₂ used as ROCKET FUEL (high specific impulse; Space Shuttle, SLS, Ariane, GSLV-Mk III). (4) Low density + escapes Earth gravity + earth atmosphere has very little. (5) Forms H-BONDS giving WATER unique properties. USES: (1) AMMONIA SYNTHESIS — Haber-Bosch process (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃) — consumes ~55% of world H₂ production; foundational for fertilisers. (2) PETROLEUM REFINING — hydrogenation (crude oil into fuels + removing sulfur 'hydrodesulfurisation'); ~25%. (3) HYDROGENATION of vegetable OILS — to make VANASPATI / margarine; saturates fats. Though trans-fat concerns. (4) METHANOL (CO + 2H₂ → CH₃OH) — fuel, chemical feedstock. (5) METALLURGY — reducing agent. (6) Electronics manufacture. (7) FUEL for ROCKETS — SpaceX + NASA + ISRO CE-20 + CE-7.5 cryogenic engines. (8) FUEL CELLS — chemical energy → electrical via H₂ + O₂ → H₂O electrochemistry; ZERO EMISSIONS tailpipe; used in Toyota Mirai, Hyundai Nexo, hydrogen-powered buses, forklifts, BackUp power. Lower cost + better batteries favour EVs for cars; fuel cells for heavy transport + aviation + shipping. (9) WELDING (oxy-hydrogen torch). FUTURE — 'GREEN HYDROGEN': H₂ produced by ELECTROLYSIS of water using RENEWABLE electricity (solar, wind) — ZERO CARBON. Seen as decarbonisation pathway for industries + heavy transport + seasonal energy storage. INDIA's NATIONAL GREEN HYDROGEN MISSION (Jan 2023, ₹19,744 crore): target 5 MILLION TONNES p.a. GREEN H₂ production by 2030 + 125 GW renewables; aim to make India global H₂ hub. Reliance + Adani + NTPC + Indian Oil + GAIL + tatas major investors; GW-scale electrolyser factories being built. cards.front:
Which GAS is responsible for the ROTTEN EGG SMELL + is highly POISONOUS?

(A) Ammonia
(B) HYDROGEN SULFIDE (H₂S)
(C) Chlorine
(D) Sulphur dioxide
cards.back:
(B) HYDROGEN SULFIDE (H₂S)

Gases & Electrochemistry — HYDROGEN SULFIDE (H₂S) — distinctive ROTTEN EGG SMELL at low concentrations. COLOURLESS, FLAMMABLE, HIGHLY POISONOUS gas. MW 34; slightly denser than air (1.19×); accumulates in LOW-LYING areas (trenches, sewers, basements). SOURCES: (1) BIOLOGICAL — decaying organic matter (anaerobic bacterial reduction of sulfates); sewers, septic tanks, manure pits, swamps, stagnant waters, rotten eggs. (2) GEOLOGICAL — VOLCANOES + hot springs + natural gas wells ('sour gas'). (3) INDUSTRIAL — petroleum refining, natural gas processing, paper pulp (kraft process), rayon, leather tanning, coal mines. TOXICITY — VERY DANGEROUS: (1) At LOW conc (0.01-1 ppm) — strong rotten-egg smell. (2) 10-20 ppm — eye irritation, headache, nausea. (3) 100-200 ppm — OLFACTORY FATIGUE (paralyses smell receptors!; you can no longer smell it → FALSE sense of safety → MAJOR KILLER). (4) 500-1000 ppm — rapid unconsciousness, death in minutes (inhibits cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondria — similar to cyanide). HISTORICALLY killed many sewer workers, oil refinery + drilling workers; MUMBAI sewer worker deaths (2014, 2019 — collapsed into manholes from H₂S). SEWER GAS primarily H₂S + methane. PROTECTION: (a) gas detectors (portable electronic H₂S monitors mandatory for workers); (b) forced ventilation; (c) self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA); (d) AT LEAST 2-person 'buddy system' for confined-space entry. MANUAL SCAVENGING BAN: India banned manual scavenging (PROHIBITION Act 1993 + more stringent 2013 Act); SEWER WORKER DEATHS still 100+/year due to H₂S + methane; mechanisation pushed (RobotS + machines). 'SAFAI KARAMCHARI ANDOLAN' (Bezwada Wilson, Ramon Magsaysay 2016). PROPERTIES: (1) SOLUBLE in water; forms HYDROSULPHURIC ACID (weak acid, pH ~3). (2) FLAMMABLE — burns in air to SO₂ + H₂O. (3) REDUCING agent. (4) Reacts with metals → sulfides (tarnish on silver = Ag₂S black). (5) Tarnishes copper → black CuS; 'Blacken' silverware. USES (limited due to toxicity): (1) Sulfide production for minerals + chemicals. (2) Sulfuric acid manufacture (Claus process — H₂S → S → H₂SO₄). (3) Heavy water (D₂O) production. (4) SOME DRUGS. OTHER PUNGENT / TOXIC GASES: (1) AMMONIA (NH₃) — sharp pungent smell; toilet cleaners, fertilisers; toxic at high conc (respiratory failure, chemical burns). (2) SULFUR DIOXIDE (SO₂) — irritating; acid rain + asthma trigger; volcanic + coal burning + metal smelting. (3) CHLORINE (Cl₂) — greenish-yellow, pungent; WWI weapon. (4) METHANE (CH₄) — actually ODOURLESS (natural gas smell is added mercaptan for detection). (5) PROPANE (C₃H₈) — LPG cooking gas; odourless (ethyl mercaptan added). (6) ETHYLENE (C₂H₄) — ripens fruit. (7) METHYL ISOCYANATE (MIC) — killed thousands in Bhopal 1984. (8) CYANIDE (HCN) — almond-bitter smell; inhibits cellular respiration. MONITORING in INDIA: (a) BIS Standards for industrial gases; (b) DGFASLI (Directorate General Factory Advice Service + Labour Institutes) oversees factory safety; (c) PCB monitors emissions. Safety training for workers + public is important. toxic; paralyses smell receptors at high conc (insidious); from sewers, volcanoes, oil refining, decaying organic matter.

cards.front:
The COMPONENT of NATURAL GAS (used for cooking + heating) that has the molecular formula CH₄ is:

(A) Propane
(B) METHANE
(C) Butane
(D) Ethane
cards.back:
(B) METHANE

Gases & Electrochemistry — METHANE (CH₄) — simplest hydrocarbon; SATURATED alkane; TETRAHEDRAL molecule (carbon at center, 4 H at corners; sp³ hybridisation). MW 16.04; COLOURLESS + ODOURLESS (stenched with MERCAPTAN for leak detection in domestic supply); flammable. PRINCIPAL component of NATURAL GAS (70-90%); rest is ethane + propane + butane + N + CO₂ + H₂O. SOURCES: (1) FOSSIL — natural gas reservoirs (often with oil; 'associated gas') or alone ('non-associated'). Origin: organic matter buried + subjected to heat + pressure over millions of years. World reserves: ~200 trillion m³; ~45-50 years at current use. TOP producers: USA (shale gas boom since 2000s), Russia, Iran, Qatar, China, Saudi, Canada. (2) BIOGENIC — anaerobic DECOMPOSITION of organic matter by METHANOGENIC ARCHAEA (not bacteria; archaea domain). Sources: LANDFILLS, wetlands, paddy fields (~10% global anthropogenic methane), livestock (cattle belches — ENTERIC FERMENTATION; 30% global anthropogenic; 3 crore+ Indian cattle biggest emitter country), manure, sewage treatment. Cows + buffalo burp ~100-250 kg methane/year each! (3) THERMOGENIC — natural gas wells. (4) BIOGAS — from anaerobic digesters (cow dung in rural India; scaling with GOBAR-Dhan). USES: (1) COOKING / HEATING FUEL — PIPED NATURAL GAS (PNG) in homes; CNG (Compressed Natural Gas) for vehicles (India's ~5 million CNG vehicles, esp auto-rickshaws + buses in major cities post-Delhi 2002 Supreme Court order). LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas — propane + butane, NOT methane) different — used in Indian household cylinders (mostly 14.2 kg + 19 kg). (2) ELECTRICITY — combined-cycle gas turbines (CCGT); 40%+ efficiency, cleanest fossil fuel. (3) INDUSTRIAL — fertiliser manufacture (H₂ for ammonia), chemicals, steel. (4) TRANSPORT — CNG vehicles; LNG ships emerging. (5) FEEDSTOCK for methanol, acetylene, ethylene, ammonia. COMBUSTION: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + energy (890 kJ/mol). Cleaner than coal or oil (less CO₂ per unit energy; no particulates; less SO₂, NOx). METHANE as GHG: (1) 28-34× GWP of CO₂ on 100-yr; 80+× on 20-yr. (2) ATMOSPHERIC lifetime 12 years (shorter than CO₂). (3) Concentrations rising fast — 720 ppb (pre-ind) → 1910 ppb (2023) — 2.5× increase. Accelerating since 2007. (4) Human sources: 60% of total; natural gas/oil leaks, landfills, livestock, paddy fields, biomass burning, coal mines. (5) GLOBAL METHANE PLEDGE (COP-26 Glasgow 2021) — 150+ countries pledged to REDUCE methane emissions 30% by 2030 vs 2020. INDIA did NOT sign initially (cattle + paddy concerns); still considering + partial participation. Major sectoral effort needed. LIQUEFIED NATURAL GAS (LNG) — cooling methane to -162°C → liquid at 1/600 volume; transported via TANKER SHIPS. Qatar + USA + Australia top exporters. India LNG imports: Qatar, USA, UAE, Nigeria, Oman. INDIA's gas pipeline: GAIL owns ~17,000 km network. HBJ pipeline (Hazira-Bijaipur-Jagdishpur, gas from ONGC's Bombay High). CGD (City Gas Distribution) — massive rollout 2014+; ~450+ cities covered. NATURAL GAS accounts for only 6% of India's energy mix (vs global 23%); govt target 15% by 2030 (One Nation One Grid). PM-GATI SHAKTI coordinates. 70-90% of natural gas; world's LARGEST hydrocarbon reserves; pipelines + LNG tankers transport globally; 2nd most impactful GHG.

cards.front:
The IDEAL GAS LAW relates pressure, volume, temperature for an ideal gas. It is:

(A) PV = nRT
(B) P = mV/T
(C) V = PRT
(D) T = P/V
cards.back:
(A) PV = nRT

Gases & Electrochemistry — IDEAL GAS LAW: PV = nRT. (1) P = PRESSURE (Pa, atm, etc.); (2) V = VOLUME (m³, litres); (3) n = number of MOLES; (4) R = UNIVERSAL GAS CONSTANT = 8.314 J/(mol·K) = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) = 1.987 cal/(mol·K); (5) T = TEMPERATURE in KELVIN. Derived by combining GAS LAWS: (1) BOYLE's LAW (Robert Boyle 1662) — at CONSTANT T + n, P ∝ 1/V (PV = constant). Squeeze bike pump → warmer gas has higher pressure. (2) CHARLES's LAW (Jacques Charles 1787) — at constant P + n, V ∝ T (V/T = constant). Hot-air balloons rise. (3) GAY-LUSSAC's LAW (1802) — at constant V + n, P ∝ T (P/T = constant). Tire pressure rises in summer. (4) AVOGADRO's LAW (Amedeo Avogadro 1811) — at constant P + T, V ∝ n. Equal volumes of gas at same T + P have same number of molecules. (5) COMBINED GAS LAW: PV/T = nR constant. STP = Standard Temperature + Pressure: (a) OLD (pre-1982, still common): 0°C (273.15 K) + 1 atm (101.325 kPa); 1 mole gas = 22.4 L. (b) NEW IUPAC: 0°C + 100 kPa; 1 mole gas = 22.7 L. NTP = Normal Temperature + Pressure: 20°C + 1 atm (not universally defined). APPLICATIONS + EXAMPLES: (1) BREATHING — lungs expand (V↑) decreasing P below atmospheric → air flows IN (inhale); diaphragm relaxes V↓, P↑ → air flows out (exhale). (2) BALLOONS — hot air rises because heated gas expands (V↑) for given P, so density drops below surrounding air. Montgolfier brothers 1783 first hot-air balloon. (3) CAR TYRES — check pressure when cold (driven tyres heat up, pressure rises). Over-inflation danger. (4) COOKING at altitude — lower atm pressure → water boils at lower temp → food undercooked; pressure cooker helps. (5) SODA bottle — CO₂ dissolved at high pressure; opening releases P → CO₂ bubbles out (Henry's Law). (6) DIVING — as depth increases, pressure increases (every 10 m = 1 atm). Divers' breath-holds shrink at depth (Boyle); rising too fast → expanding gas → embolism. (7) Aeroplane CABIN pressurised to ~0.75 atm (8000 ft equivalent) at cruise. (8) Climbing EVEREST — 0.33 atm at top; needs oxygen supplementation. DEVIATIONS from IDEAL: Real gases deviate at HIGH pressure (molecules close enough for attraction) + LOW temperature (molecules slow, attractions matter). VAN DER WAALS EQUATION corrects: (P + a(n/V)²)(V - nb) = nRT; a = attractive forces, b = molecular volume. REAL-GAS calculations use compressibility factor Z. KINETIC MOLECULAR THEORY explains gas laws: (a) Gas = large number of tiny point-like molecules in CONSTANT RANDOM MOTION. (b) Collisions perfectly ELASTIC. (c) Molecules exert no inter-molecular force (ideal). (d) Average kinetic energy ∝ TEMPERATURE (KE = 3/2 kT per molecule; or 3/2 RT per mole). (e) Pressure = collisions with container walls. DIFFUSION (Graham's Law): rate ∝ 1/√(MW); lighter gases diffuse faster. EFFUSION: escape through small hole. BROWNIAN MOTION (Einstein 1905) — random motion of pollen/particles in gas/liquid proves molecular reality. Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mole — reverse-engineered from many phenomena.

(5) SODA bottle — CO₂ dissolved at high pressure; opening releases P → CO₂ bubbles out (Henry's Law). (6) DIVING — as depth increases, pressure increases (every 10 m = 1 atm). Divers' breath-holds shrink at depth (Boyle); rising too fast → expanding gas → embolism. (7) Aeroplane CABIN pressurised to ~0.75 atm (8000 ft equivalent) at cruise. (8) Climbing EVEREST — 0.33 atm at top; needs oxygen supplementation. DEVIATIONS from IDEAL: Real gases deviate at HIGH pressure (molecules close enough for attraction) + LOW temperature (molecules slow, attractions matter). VAN DER WAALS EQUATION corrects: (P + a(n/V)²)(V - nb) = nRT; a = attractive forces, b = molecular volume. REAL-GAS calculations use compressibility factor Z. KINETIC MOLECULAR THEORY explains gas laws: (a) Gas = large number of tiny point-like molecules in CONSTANT RANDOM MOTION. (b) Collisions perfectly ELASTIC. (c) Molecules exert no inter-molecular force (ideal). (d) Average kinetic energy ∝ TEMPERATURE (KE = 3/2 kT per molecule; or 3/2 RT per mole). (e) Pressure = collisions with container walls. DIFFUSION (Graham's Law): rate ∝ 1/√(MW); lighter gases diffuse faster. EFFUSION: escape through small hole. BROWNIAN MOTION (Einstein 1905) — random motion of pollen/particles in gas/liquid proves molecular reality. Avogadro's number = 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mole — reverse-engineered from many phenomena.

The gas that makes up approximately 78% of the Earth's atmosphere is:

(A) Oxygen
(B) Nitrogen
(C) Carbon dioxide
(D) Argon
cards.back:
(B) Nitrogen

Gases & Electrochemistry — Dry atmosphere composition: N₂ ~78%, O₂ ~21%, Ar ~0.93%, CO₂ ~0.04%. Water vapour varies. Biological N-fixation and industrial Haber-Bosch process both transform this abundant but inert N₂ into usable forms.

A gas used to preserve food by INHIBITING OXIDATION in packaged snacks is:

(A) Oxygen

cards.front:
BOYLE'S LAW states that at constant temperature, for a fixed mass of gas, pressure and volume are:

(A) Directly proportional
(B) Inversely proportional
(C) Equal
(D) Unrelated
cards.back:
(B) Inversely proportional

Gases & Electrochemistry — Boyle's law: P ∝ 1/V → PV = constant (at constant T, n). Squeeze a syringe → volume halves, pressure doubles. Charles's law: V ∝ T at constant P. Combined: PV/T = constant → PV = nRT (ideal gas law).

cards.front:
Which of the following is the LIGHTEST gas known?

(A) Hydrogen
(B) Helium
(C) Nitrogen
(D) Methane
cards.back:
(A) Hydrogen

Gases & Electrochemistry — Hydrogen (molar mass ≈ 2 g/mol) is the lightest gas. Helium ≈ 4 g/mol is the lightest noble gas and is used in airships and balloons instead of H₂ because He is non-flammable (Hindenburg disaster made H₂ unsafe for passenger airships).

cards.front:
At STP (Standard Temperature and Pressure: 0 °C, 1 atm), one mole of ANY ideal gas occupies a volume of:

(A) 11.2 L
(B) 22.4 L
(C) 24.0 L
(D) 30.0 L
cards.back:
(B) 22.4 L

Gases & Electrochemistry — Avogadro's law → molar volume at STP = 22.4 litres. From PV = nRT with P = 1 atm, T = 273.15 K, n = 1, V = RT/P = (0.0821 × 273.15) ≈ 22.4 L. (Under the newer IUPAC STP with P = 100 kPa instead of 101.325 kPa, molar volume is 22.7 L — exam usually expects 22.4 L.)

The gas responsible for the DISTINCT SMELL OF ROTTEN EGGS and given off when hydrogen and sulphur combine is:

(A) SO₂
(B) H₂S
(C) NH₃
(D) CO
cards.back:
(B) H₂S

Gases & Electrochemistry — Hydrogen sulphide (H₂S) — characteristic smell of rotten eggs. Toxic in higher concentrations (deadens olfactory nerves, so high doses are undetectable by smell). SO₂ has a choking sulphurous smell; NH₃ is pungent ammonia; CO is odourless and lethal.

The NOBLE GASES (Group 18) are generally unreactive because:

(A) They have an incomplete outer shell
(B) They have a complete outer electron shell

The ALKALI METALS belong to which group of the periodic table?

(A) Group 2, the alkaline earth metals like Mg, Ca
(B) Group 1 (excluding hydrogen), Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr
(C) Group 17, the halogens like F, Cl, Br, I
(D) Group 18, the noble gases like He, Ne, Ar

(B) Group 1 (excluding hydrogen), Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — ALKALI METALS — Group 1 (formerly IA): Lithium, Sodium, Potassium, Rubidium, Caesium, Francium. (Hydrogen sits in Group 1 by electron configuration but is NOT classified as an alkali metal.) Single valence electron → eager to lose it → form +1 cations. Highly reactive — must be stored under oil to prevent reaction with air/moisture. Distractor 1 = Group 2 alkaline earth metals (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra). Distractor 3 = halogens. cards.front:
Alkali metals are stored under KEROSENE OIL because they:

(A) Float on top of kerosene for easy retrieval
(B) React vigorously with both air and moisture
(C) Smell pleasant when sealed under kerosene
(D) Become much harder if stored long under it
cards.back:
(B) React vigorously with both air and moisture

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Alkali metals are EXTREMELY REACTIVE — react with O₂ in air (forming oxides), water vapour (forming hydroxides + H₂ which can ignite). Storing under kerosene (water-free, hydrophobic, non-reactive) excludes both. Lithium can also be stored under petroleum jelly. Sodium and potassium especially dangerous — react explosively with water. Distractor 1 — sodium is denser than kerosene, sinks. Distractors 3, 4 — irrelevant.

cards.front:
Down the alkali metal group from Li to Cs, REACTIVITY toward water:

(A) Decreases gradually as we move downward
(B) Increases dramatically (Cs reacts explosively)
(C) Stays exactly the same for every alkali metal
(D) Has no clear pattern from element to element
cards.back:
(B) Increases dramatically (Cs reacts explosively)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Alkali metals + water → alkali hydroxide + H₂. Reactivity: Li (slow fizz) < Na (vigorous, may catch fire) < K (ignites instantly) < Rb (explodes) < Cs (explodes more violently). Reason: ionisation energy DECREASES down the group → outer e⁻ more easily lost → more reactive. Compare halogens — opposite trend (reactivity decreases down).

cards.option2: Stays exactly the same for every alkali metal

cards.front:
When sodium reacts with chlorine gas, the product is:

(A) Sodium hydroxide, a strong base solution
(B) Sodium chloride, common salt with ionic structure
(C) Sodium chlorate, used in matches industry
(D) Sodium hypochlorite, used in bleach products
cards.back:
(B) Sodium chloride, common salt with ionic structure

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — 2 Na + Cl₂ → 2 NaCl. Vigorous reaction with bright yellow flame. Sodium loses 1 e⁻ (Na → Na⁺); chlorine gains 1 e⁻ (Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻). Forms ionic NaCl crystal lattice. Distractor 1 = NaOH (Na + H₂O reaction). Distractor 3 = NaClO₃ (made by electrolysis of NaCl). Distractor 4 = NaClO (active ingredient in liquid bleach).

cards.front:
Sodium and potassium are essential for human physiology because they:

(A) Form bones and teeth structurally
(B) Maintain electrolyte balance and nerve signals
(C) Are major components of haemoglobin in blood
(D) Form digestive enzymes inside the stomach lining
cards.back:

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Na⁺ and K⁺ — major electrolytes. Na/K-ATPase pump in cell membranes maintains the gradient (high K inside, high Na outside). This gradient drives nerve impulses (action potentials), muscle contraction, kidney function. Daily intake: Na ~1.5-2.3 g; K ~3.5-4.7 g. Imbalance → arrhythmias, weakness, cramps. Distractor 1 — Ca + P. Distractor 3 — Iron in haem. Distractor 4 — proteins / acids, not Na/K specifically.

cards.front:
Which is the most REACTIVE halogen?

(A) Fluorine (smallest, most electronegative)
(B) Iodine (least reactive of group)
(C) Bromine (mid-group reactivity)
(D) Astatine (radioactive, rare)
cards.back:
(A) Fluorine (smallest, most electronegative)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — FLUORINE (F, atomic no. 9) — the MOST REACTIVE halogen and most electronegative element on the periodic table. WHY: smallest atomic radius → strongest pull on bonding electrons. REACTIVITY ORDER (decreasing): F > Cl > Br > I > At. STATES: F₂ — pale yellow gas; Cl₂ — yellow-green gas; Br₂ — red-brown LIQUID; I₂ — purple-black SOLID. EXTREME REACTIVITY of F₂: (a) Reacts with NEARLY ALL elements (including noble gases like Xe — to form XeF₂, XeF₄, XeF₆!). (b) Reacts EXPLOSIVELY with H₂ even in dark/cold. (c) Reacts with WATER → HF + O₂ (vigorous). (d) Reacts with GLASS (SiO₂) — must be stored in nickel/Teflon containers. KEY F COMPOUNDS: (1) HF (hydrofluoric acid) — etches glass; weak acid (only partially dissociated) but extremely corrosive to skin. (2) NaF — added to drinking water (~1 ppm) to prevent dental caries. (3) Teflon (PTFE) — non-stick polymer. (4) UF₆ — uranium-235 enrichment for nuclear fuel. (5) HFCs — refrigerants. ELECTRONEGATIVITY (Pauling scale): F = 4.0 (highest), O = 3.5, N = 3.0, Cl = 3.2. PYQ FREQUENCY: halogen reactivity-order in NEET, JEE-Main 1× per paper.

cards.front:
Common table salt (NaCl) is a compound of which two elements?

(A) Sodium and Chlorine
(B) Sodium and Hydrogen here
(C) Sulfur and Chlorine alone
(D) Calcium and Carbon together
cards.back:
(A) Sodium and Chlorine

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — TABLE SALT (NaCl, sodium chloride) — IONIC compound formed by Na⁺ + Cl⁻. SOURCES: (1) SEA SALT — evaporated from sea water (3.5% salinity). (2) ROCK SALT (HALITE) — mined from underground deposits (e.g., Khewra Salt Mine, Pakistan — world's 2nd largest). (3) BRINE WELLS. STRUCTURE: face-centered cubic crystal lattice; melting point 801°C. USES: (1) FOOD — preservation (osmotic pressure inhibits microbes), flavor, mineral. (2) INDUSTRIAL — chlor-alkali process (electrolysis of NaCl solution → NaOH + Cl₂ + H₂; both major industrial chemicals). (3) DE-ICING ROADS — lowers freezing point of water (winter use in temperate regions). (4) WATER SOFTENING — ion exchange with calcium. INDIA: GANDHI's DANDI MARCH (1930) — protested British SALT TAX; non-violent civil disobedience; iconic moment in independence movement. SODIUM CONTENT: human body needs ~1.5 g salt/day (~600 mg sodium); excess linked to hypertension. WHO recommends < 5 g/day. RICH-SALT FOODS: pickles, papads, snacks, cured meats. IODIZED SALT (with KI or KIO₃) — added since 1960s to prevent iodine deficiency (goiter); mandatory in India. PYQ FREQUENCY: chlorine compounds in NEET, NCERT-driven SSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
BLEACHING POWDER (chloride of lime) is chemically:

(A) Calcium oxychloride Ca(OCl)Cl
(B) Sodium chloride (table salt)
(C) Calcium chloride salt only
(D) Hydrogen chloride gas
cards.back:
(A) Calcium oxychloride Ca(OCl)Cl

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — BLEACHING POWDER — chemical formula: Ca(OCl)Cl or Ca(OCl)₂·CaCl₂·Ca(OH)₂ (a complex mix), commonly written CaOCl₂. The active species is the HYPOCHLORITE ion (OCl⁻) which oxidizes pigments → bleaching action. PREPARATION: Cl₂ + Ca(OH)₂ (slaked lime) → CaOCl₂ + H₂O. USES: (1) BLEACHING textiles (cotton, linen, paper). (2) WATER DISINFECTION — kills bacteria (~1-3 ppm chlorine in drinking water). (3) Disinfecting swimming pools, hospital floors, drains. (4) Chemical industry — producing other chlorine compounds. (5) Removing stains from clothes. ACTIVE CHLORINE CONTENT: ~30-35% available chlorine. WHY EFFECTIVE: when bleaching powder dissolves in water, it releases HOCl (hypochlorous acid) which is a powerful oxidizing agent. SAFETY: emits toxic Cl₂ gas if mixed with acids (NEVER mix bleach with toilet cleaners — risk of poisoning). HISTORICAL: developed by Charles Tennant (1799, Scotland) — sparked the textile bleaching revolution. ALSO see SODIUM HYPOCHLORITE (NaClO, household bleach 'Clorox') — solution form. INDIA — 'Chlorination' of municipal water is standard public-health practice. PYQ FREQUENCY: NCERT Class 10 staple — SSC, NEET 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which halogen is essential in our diet to prevent GOITER (thyroid swelling)?

(A) Iodine (for thyroid hormones)
(B) Fluorine (helps dental health)
(C) Chlorine (for hydrochloric acid)
(D) Bromine (with no nutrition role)
cards.back:
(A) Iodine (for thyroid hormones)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — IODINE — essential micronutrient required for synthesis of THYROID HORMONES (T3 thyroxine, T4 triiodothyronine). DEFICIENCY: causes GOITER (enlarged thyroid gland), CRETINISM (severe in fetal development), hypothyroidism, learning disabilities. RDA: 150 µg/day for adults. SOURCES: iodized salt, sea-foods (fish, shrimp, seaweed), milk, eggs, dairy. INDIA — IODINE DEFICIENCY DISORDERS PROGRAMME (1962, renamed 1992): mandatory IODIZATION of all edible salt. India was among the first countries to mandate; sometimes briefly relaxed (2000-05) and then re-mandated. RESULT: goiter prevalence reduced from ~50% (1980s) to <5% in many areas. SALT-IODIZATION: KI (potassium iodide) or KIO₃ (potassium iodate) added at ~30 ppm. CHEMICAL FORMS of iodine: I₂ (purple-black solid), I⁻ (iodide ion in salts), IO₃⁻ (iodate), HI (hydroiodic acid). USES: (1) MEDICAL — Lugol's solution (iodine + KI in water) for wound disinfection; tincture of iodine. (2) DAVAVAN ('iodised salt') marketed widely in India. (3) RADIOLABEL — iodine-131 in thyroid imaging/treatment. EVENTS: WORLD IODINE DEFICIENCY DAY — 21 October. CHERNOBYL: I-131 release caused thyroid cancers; KI tablets distributed. PYQ FREQUENCY: iodine-thyroid in NEET, NCERT-driven SSC 1× per cycle.

(3) RADIOLABEL — iodine-131 in thyroid imaging/treatment. EVENTS: WORLD IODINE DEFICIENCY DAY — 21 October. CHERNOBYL: I-131 release caused thyroid cancers; KI tablets distributed. cards.front:
When chlorine gas is bubbled through KBr solution, the reaction is:

(A) Cl₂ displaces Br (KBr → KCl + Br₂)
(B) No reaction occurs at room temp
(C) Cl forms KClO₃ as the product
(D) Br displaces Cl from KBr there
cards.back:
(A) Cl₂ displaces Br (KBr → KCl + Br₂)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — DISPLACEMENT REACTION: a MORE REACTIVE halogen DISPLACES a LESS REACTIVE halogen from its salt. Reactivity: F > Cl > Br > I. So Cl₂ (more reactive) DISPLACES Br⁻ from KBr solution: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂. VISUAL: solution turns BROWNISH-RED (Br₂ liquid color); can be confirmed by adding hexane — Br₂ partitions into hexane (orange layer). SIMILAR: Cl₂ + KI → 2KCl + I₂ (forms purple iodine; hexane layer turns violet). ALSO: Br₂ + KI → 2KBr + I₂ (Br can displace I). REVERSE NOT POSSIBLE: I₂ + KCl ↛ no reaction (I is less reactive than Cl). CHEMISTRY PRINCIPLE: this is an OXIDATION-REDUCTION reaction. Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ (Cl reduced); 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ (Br oxidized). The HIGHER STANDARD ELECTRODE POTENTIAL species takes the electrons. KEY APPLICATION: extraction of bromine from sea water (Br⁻ in sea bittern is oxidized by Cl₂ to liberate Br₂); similarly iodine from sea-weed or brine. PYQ FREQUENCY: halogen displacement reactions in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT Class 10 — 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
FLUORIDE in toothpaste helps prevent cavities by:

(A) Forming hard fluoroapatite enamel
(B) Killing bacteria in mouth here
(C) Whitening the teeth surface
(D) Removing tartar from gums
cards.back:
(A) Forming hard fluoroapatite enamel

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — FLUORIDE replaces hydroxyl ions in tooth enamel: HYDROXYAPATITE [Ca₅(PO₄)₃OH] → FLUOROAPATITE [Ca₅(PO₄)₃F]. Fluoroapatite is HARDER and MORE RESISTANT to ACID DECAY (caused by mouth bacteria fermenting sugars). DELIVERY: (1) FLUORIDATED WATER — ~0.7-1.0 ppm in many countries; widely debated due to skeletal fluorosis at higher doses. (2) FLUORIDE TOOTHPASTE — 1000-1500 ppm typical for adults. (3) Topical fluoride applications (dental clinics). (4) Fluoride mouth rinses. INDIA: water fluoridation NOT mandatory; some districts have natural fluoride > 1.5 mg/L causing FLUOROSIS — Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Rajasthan, Punjab particularly affected. FLUOROSIS — types: DENTAL FLUOROSIS (white/brown staining of teeth, irreversible cosmetic effect — not painful); SKELETAL FLUOROSIS (bone deformities, joint pain — long-term high exposure). MITIGATION: National Programme for Prevention and Control of Fluorosis (NPPCF, since 2008). FLUORIDE LIMIT: WHO permissible ≤ 1.5 mg/L. KEY CHEMISTRY: F⁻ small ion easily fits into apatite lattice; HF reactions with bone create stronger crystal structure. NOBEL: no specific Nobel; pioneered by H. T. Dean (USA, 1930s). PYQ FREQUENCY: fluoride health-effects in NEET, SSC GA, UPSC environment 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
AT ROOM TEMPERATURE, which halogen exists as a SOLID?

(A) Iodine (purple-black crystals)
(B) Chlorine (yellow-green gas)
(C) Bromine (red-brown liquid)
(D) Fluorine (pale yellow gas)
cards.back:
(A) Iodine (purple-black crystals)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — STATES OF HALOGENS at room temperature (25°C, 1 atm): (1) FLUORINE (F₂) — pale yellow GAS, BP −188°C. (2) CHLORINE (Cl₂) — yellow-green GAS, BP −34°C. (3) BROMINE (Br₂) — red-brown LIQUID, BP 59°C; ONLY non-metal liquid at RT besides mercury. (4) IODINE (I₂) — purple-black SOLID, MP 114°C, BP 184°C. (5) ASTATINE (At) — radioactive, ultra-rare, predicted solid (though never isolated in bulk to confirm). TREND: as we go DOWN the group (F → I), MELTING and BOILING POINTS INCREASE. WHY: bigger molecules → stronger LONDON DISPERSION FORCES (van der Waals) holding them together. SUBLIMATION of IODINE: I₂ readily SUBLIMES (solid → gas without going through liquid) at slightly above room T — used to demonstrate sublimation in classroom; iodine vapor is purple-violet. USE: SUBLIMATION TEST is a way to PURIFY iodine (heat impure iodine, condense pure crystals on cold surface). DISCOVERY: chlorine by Scheele (1774); iodine by Courtois (1811, France) — discovered in seaweed ash; bromine by Balard (1826, France); fluorine by Moissan (1886, Nobel 1906). PYQ FREQUENCY: physical states of halogens in NEET, JEE-Main, SSC chemistry — 1× per cycle.

(A) Group 1, the alkali metals on the leftmost edge
(B) Group 17, just before the noble gases on the right
(C) Group 18, the rightmost group of noble gases
(D) Group 14, the carbon family of elements

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Halogens — Group 17 (formerly VII A): Fluorine (F), Chlorine (Cl), Bromine (Br), Iodine (I), Astatine (At), Tennessine (Ts, synthetic). 7 valence electrons → eager to gain 1 to complete octet → form ⁻1 ions readily. Distractor 1 = alkali metals (Li, Na, K). Distractor 3 = noble gases (He, Ne, Ar). Distractor 4 = carbon family (C, Si, Ge).

cards.front:
Going DOWN the halogen group from F to I, the reactivity:

(A) Increases gradually as atomic radius grows down the group
(B) Decreases as atoms grow larger and bind electrons loosely
(C) Stays approximately constant for every halogen species
(D) Has no clear systematic pattern across the halogen group
cards.back:
(B) Decreases as atoms grow larger and bind electrons loosely

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Halogen reactivity DECREASES down the group (F > Cl > Br > I). Reason: as atomic radius grows, the outer shell is farther from the nucleus → less attraction to gain an electron → less reactive. Fluorine is the most reactive non-metal known; reacts explosively with H₂ in dark; can corrode glass. Iodine is comparatively mild. Distractor 1 — opposite (atomic radius increases yes, but reactivity decreases). Distractors 3, 4 — false; trend is consistent.

cards.option2: Stays approximately constant for every halogen species
cards.option3: Has no clear systematic pattern across the halogen group

cards.front:
IODINE deficiency in the diet causes:

(A) Beri-beri due to nutritional thiamine loss
(B) Goitre, an enlargement of the thyroid gland
(C) Scurvy, with bleeding gums and skin spots
(D) Rickets, with softened bones in growing children
cards.back:
(B) Goitre, an enlargement of the thyroid gland

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Iodine — required for thyroid hormones T3 (triiodothyronine) and T4 (thyroxine). Deficiency → thyroid enlarges (goitre) trying to compensate; can cause cretinism in children, hypothyroidism in adults. India had high goitre belt in Sub-Himalayan zones; Universal Salt Iodisation (UPS) program since 1990s — iodised salt mandatory under Food Safety law. Distractor 1 = thiamine deficiency. Distractor 3 = vitamin C deficiency. Distractor 4 = vitamin D deficiency.

cards.front:
Halogens generally exist as DIATOMIC molecules (X₂). This is because:

(A) They are too small to remain alone as single atoms
(B) Each atom completes its octet by sharing one electron pair
(C) They are always stable as monatomic species at room temperature
(D) Pairing makes them gases at very high temperatures
cards.back:
(B) Each atom completes its octet by sharing one electron pair

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Each halogen atom has 7 valence electrons; needs 1 more for octet. Two atoms share one electron pair → single covalent bond → diatomic molecule X₂ (F-F, Cl-Cl, Br-Br, I-I). Same applies to other diatomic gases: H₂, N₂, O₂. Bond strength: F-F ≈ 158 kJ/mol (weakest among Cl, Br); Cl-Cl ≈ 243; Br-Br ≈ 193; I-I ≈ 151. Fluorine's anomalously low bond energy is due to electron repulsion in its small atom.

cards.option3: Pairing makes them gases at very high temperatures

(A) Protium, the lightest H isotope of all
(B) Tritium, the radioactive H isotope
(C) Deuterium, the heavy H isotope
(D) Helium, a different element entirely
cards.back:

(B) Water (H₂O) plus a lot of energy released
(C) Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is the only product

Distractor 4 — H₂ is currently expensive.

cards.front:
Hydrogen does NOT have a fixed position in the periodic table because:

(A) It is too rare on Earth to be classified well
(B) It shares some properties with both Group 1 and Group 17
(C) It is the most reactive element on Earth
(D) It does not form chemical compounds in nature
cards.back:
(B) It shares some properties with both Group 1 and Group 17

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Hydrogen ANOMALY: 1 valence electron — like ALKALI METALS (Group 1) — can lose to form H⁺. BUT also needs 1 more to fill its shell — like HALOGENS (Group 17) — can gain to form H⁻ (hydride). Different periodic tables place H in Group 1, Group 17, or floating alone. NOT a metal at room temp + pressure (gas, non-metallic), unlike alkali metals. Forms diatomic molecule (H₂) like halogens. Sometimes called 'rogue' element.

cards.option2: It is the most reactive element on Earth
cards.option3: It does not form chemical compounds in nature

cards.front:
When dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with zinc metal, the gas evolved is:

(A) Oxygen, supporting combustion strongly
(B) Hydrogen, with characteristic 'pop' sound test
(C) Chlorine, a yellow-green choking gas
(D) Carbon dioxide, turning lime water milky
cards.back:
(B) Hydrogen, with characteristic 'pop' sound test

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂↑. Hydrogen gas. Test: bring a lit splint near the gas → makes a CHARACTERISTIC 'POP' SOUND (mini-explosion as H₂ + O₂ in air ignites). Reactivity series — metals more reactive than H (Zn, Mg, Al, Fe) displace H from acids. Cu, Ag, Au don't react with dilute HCl. Distractor 1 = decomposition of H₂O₂ produces O₂. Distractor 3 = reaction with strong oxidisers. Distractor 4 = carbonate + acid reactions.
cards.option3: Carbon dioxide, turning lime water milky

cards.front:
ALUMINIUM is extracted from BAUXITE ore by:

(A) Hall-Héroult electrolytic process
(B) Smelting in a blast furnace
(C) Roasting in air with carbon
(D) Direct reduction with hydrogen
cards.back:
(A) Hall-Héroult electrolytic process

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — ALUMINIUM EXTRACTION — Hall-Héroult Process (1886, independently invented by Charles Hall in USA + Paul Héroult in France). STEPS: (1) BAUXITE (Al₂O₃·xH₂O) is purified to ALUMINA (Al₂O₃) via BAYER PROCESS (treat with NaOH, dissolve as Na[Al(OH)₄], precipitate as Al(OH)₃, calcine to Al₂O₃). (2) ALUMINA is dissolved in MOLTEN CRYOLITE (Na₃AlF₆) — lowers melting point from ~2050°C to ~960°C. (3) ELECTROLYSIS in CARBON-LINED steel cell: cathode = molten Al collects at bottom; anode = carbon blocks consumed (oxidized to CO₂). REACTIONS: at cathode Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al; at anode 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ (then C + O₂ → CO₂). HUGE ELECTRICITY needed: ~13-15 kWh per kg of Al. INDIA: aluminium plants located NEAR HYDROELECTRIC plants (cheap power) — Hirakud (Odisha-NALCO), Korba (Chhattisgarh-BALCO), Renukoot (UP-HINDALCO). MAJOR INDIAN PRODUCERS: Vedanta, HINDALCO, NALCO, BALCO. USES OF Al: (1) Aircraft, automobile bodies (light + corrosion-resistant). (2) Electrical cables (cheaper than copper, less density). (3) Cookware, foil. (4) Doors, windows, packaging. (5) Beverage cans. RECYCLING: Al is HIGHLY RECYCLABLE — only 5% of original energy needed for re-melting. PYQ FREQUENCY: Hall-Héroult in NEET, NCERT, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
IRON is extracted from HEMATITE ore in a:

(A) Blast furnace (with coke + limestone)
(B) Reverberatory furnace (Cu only)
(C) Electrolysis cell (for Al, Mg)
(D) Open-hearth furnace (steel-making)
cards.back:
(A) Blast furnace (with coke + limestone)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — IRON EXTRACTION — BLAST FURNACE process: HEMATITE (Fe₂O₃) + COKE (Carbon) + LIMESTONE (CaCO₃) added at top; HOT AIR blasted from bottom. KEY REACTIONS: (1) C + O₂ → CO₂ (combustion). (2) CO₂ + C → 2CO (CO is the actual reducer). (3) Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (REDUCTION at top). (4) CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (decomposes). (5) CaO + SiO₂ (silica impurity) → CaSiO₃ (SLAG, removes impurities; SLAG floats on molten iron, drained separately). PRODUCT: PIG IRON (~93% iron, 4% C, plus Si, Mn, P, S impurities) — collected at bottom. CONVERSION TO STEEL: pig iron processed in BASIC OXYGEN FURNACE (BOF) or ELECTRIC ARC FURNACE (EAF) — reduces carbon to ~0.1-2%. INDIAN STEEL: SAIL (Steel Authority of India), Tata Steel, JSW are major producers. KEY PLANTS: Bhilai (Chhattisgarh), Bokaro (Jharkhand), Rourkela (Odisha) — built post-Independence with USSR, UK, Germany cooperation respectively. INDIA is 2ND LARGEST CRUDE STEEL PRODUCER (after China; ~135 million tonnes/yr 2024). UPSC angle: steel sector is core to industrial growth — covered in GS-3 (economy/infrastructure). KEY CHALLENGES: pollution (steel sector ~7-8% global CO₂ emissions), competition from China. PYQ FREQUENCY: blast furnace in NEET, NCERT, SSC chemistry 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which metal is the MOST REACTIVE in the metal reactivity series?

(A) Potassium (top of series)
(B) Iron (mid-series moderate)
(C) Copper (low reactivity)
(D) Gold (least reactive)
cards.back:
(A) Potassium (top of series)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — REACTIVITY SERIES (memorize for SSC, NEET, JEE-Main): K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > (H) > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au > Pt. POTASSIUM is the MOST reactive shown (above K is a few even more reactive like Cs, Rb, Fr — but K is what's typically referenced in school chemistry). MNEMONIC: 'PSC Mg Aluminium Zinc Iron Pb (Hydrogen) Cu Hg Ag Au Pt' or 'Please Send Cute Monkeys And Zebras In Lions' Pen Hesitating Cause Hippo's Stink Awfully Past'. KEY OBSERVATIONS: (1) MOST REACTIVE (K, Na) — react VIOLENTLY with water, even cold; produce H₂ + heat (sometimes igniting); stored in KEROSENE/oil. (2) MODERATELY REACTIVE (Mg, Al) — react with hot water/steam; oxide layer protects (Al passivates). (3) Mid (Zn, Fe) — react slowly with steam, dilute acids. (4) BELOW HYDROGEN (Cu, Hg, Ag, Au, Pt) — DO NOT react with dilute acids; only with concentrated oxidizing acids. (5) GOLD, PLATINUM — extremely inert (jewelry). DISPLACEMENT REACTION: more reactive metal displaces less reactive from its salt: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu (Fe more reactive, displaces Cu). UPSC GS angle: rare-earth metals + critical minerals strategy (lithium, cobalt, copper imports) is a contemporary policy issue. PYQ FREQUENCY: reactivity series order in NEET, NCERT, JEE-Main 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
BRASS is an alloy of:

(A) Copper and zinc (Cu+Zn)
(B) Copper and tin (Cu+Sn = bronze)
(C) Iron and carbon (Fe+C = steel)
(D) Aluminium and copper (Cu+Al)
cards.back:
(A) Copper and zinc (Cu+Zn)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — BRASS — alloy of COPPER (~70%) + ZINC (~30%); proportions vary by use. PROPERTIES: golden-yellow color, more workable than pure copper, corrosion-resistant. USES: musical instruments (trumpets, trombones, saxophones — 'brass band'), screws, locks, plumbing fittings, decorative items, ammunition cartridges (brass casings), idols (especially in India — kanchi/madurai brass idols). KEY ALLOYS to memorize: (1) BRASS — Cu + Zn. (2) BRONZE — Cu + Sn (the 'Bronze Age', ~3000 BCE; tools, statues, bells). (3) STEEL — Fe + C (~0.1-2% C); MILD steel ~0.2%, HIGH-CARBON steel ~0.7-1%. (4) STAINLESS STEEL — Fe + Cr (10-30%) + Ni; rust-resistant. (5) DURALUMIN — Al + Cu + Mg + Mn; light + strong; aircraft. (6) GERMAN SILVER — Cu + Zn + Ni (no actual silver, despite name). (7) SOLDER — Pb + Sn (lead-tin); used for joining wires. (8) PEWTER — Sn + Sb + Cu; tableware. (9) MAGNALIUM — Al + Mg; light-weight aircraft parts. (10) AMALGAM — Hg + other metals (dental fillings, gold extraction). HISTORICAL: Brass cymbals popular in many percussion sets; bronze coinage in ancient Rome, Greece, Mauryan India. PYQ FREQUENCY: alloy compositions in NEET, NCERT, SSC GA 1-2× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests memory of alloy compositions.

cards.front:
ELECTROLYTIC REFINING is used to PURIFY which metal?

(A) Copper (impure → 99.99% pure)
(B) Sodium (electrolysis of NaCl is for extraction)
(C) Iron (purified by other methods)
(D) Carbon (not a metal here)
cards.back:
(A) Copper (impure → 99.99% pure)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — ELECTROLYTIC REFINING of COPPER (most common application): impure copper as ANODE; pure copper as CATHODE; electrolyte is dilute CuSO₄ solution. PROCESS: (1) Apply DC current. (2) Anode oxidation: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ (impure copper dissolves). (3) Cathode reduction: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (pure copper deposits on cathode). (4) IMPURITIES separate: noble metals (Ag, Au, Pt) form 'ANODE MUD' (settles below); reactive impurities (Zn, Fe) stay in solution. RESULT: 99.99%+ pure copper — needed for electrical wiring (impurities reduce conductivity). ECONOMIC: ANODE MUD is rich in precious metals — selling it offsets refining costs! KEY: this works for any metal more LESS noble than the impurities you want to leave behind. OTHER ELECTROLYTIC REFINING: Zinc, Nickel, Lead, Silver, Gold (gold from copper anode mud is further refined). EXTRACTION (different from refining): (a) Aluminium — Hall-Héroult (extraction from molten Al₂O₃ in cryolite). (b) Sodium, potassium, magnesium — extracted from molten chlorides via electrolysis (Castner-Kellner / Down's process). (c) Iron — blast furnace (no electrolysis). DIFFERENCE — EXTRACTION (from ore) vs REFINING (purification of crude metal). UPSC angle: electricity-intensive metallurgy concerns (energy security, Net-Zero pathway). PYQ FREQUENCY: electrolytic refining in NEET, NCERT, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
RUSTING of iron requires:

(A) Both oxygen and water (moisture)
(B) Only oxygen (pure dry air)
(C) Only water (no oxygen ever)
(D) Only sunlight (UV radiation)
cards.back:
(A) Both oxygen and water (moisture)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — RUSTING — slow oxidation of iron in presence of OXYGEN + WATER (moisture in air). RESULT: HYDRATED IRON OXIDE (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O) — flaky, reddish-brown, weakens metal. CHEMISTRY: 4Fe + 3O₂ + 6H₂O → 2Fe₂O₃·3H₂O (simplified). FACTORS that ACCELERATE rusting: (1) HUMID AIR (high water vapour). (2) SALT WATER (sea air corrosion fastest — chlorides accelerate). (3) ACID RAIN (low pH). (4) SCRATCHED metal (exposes iron beneath any protective layer). PREVENTION methods: (1) PAINTING — barrier between iron and air/water. (2) GREASING/OILING — moving parts. (3) GALVANIZING — coating with zinc; zinc is more reactive, corrodes preferentially (sacrificial protection). (4) CHROME PLATING — decorative + protective. (5) STAINLESS STEEL — alloy with Cr (>10.5%); chromium oxide layer protects. (6) BLUEING (gun metal) — controlled oxidation creating protective Fe₃O₄ layer. INDIA: ~$ billions lost annually to rust/corrosion (railway tracks, bridges, ships, infrastructure). KEY: dry oxygen alone DOES NOT rust iron quickly — needs MOISTURE. Boiled distilled water + iron in airless container also doesn't rust. EXPERIMENT: 3 test tubes — (a) iron + distilled water, no air → no rust. (b) iron + dry air → no rust. (c) iron + air + water → rust. UPSC angle: corrosion engineering, infrastructure life-cycle costs. PYQ FREQUENCY: rusting in NEET, NCERT, SSC GA 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which method is used to extract HIGHLY REACTIVE metals (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al)?

(A) Electrolysis of molten salts
(B) Roasting in air with oxygen
(C) Reduction with carbon (coke)
(D) Direct heating in vacuum (no)
cards.back:
(A) Electrolysis of molten salts

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — EXTRACTION method depends on REACTIVITY of the metal: (1) HIGHLY REACTIVE METALS (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) — at top of reactivity series; their oxides are TOO STABLE to be reduced by ordinary reducers (C, CO). EXTRACT via ELECTROLYSIS of MOLTEN SALTS (chlorides, hydroxides, oxides). Examples: NaCl(molten) — sodium at cathode (Castner-Kellner / Down's process); MgCl₂(molten) — Mg at cathode; Al₂O₃ in cryolite — Hall-Héroult. (2) MODERATELY REACTIVE (Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu) — REDUCED with CARBON (coke) in BLAST FURNACE or similar. (3) LEAST REACTIVE (Ag, Au, Pt) — found NATIVE (uncombined) in nature; mined directly + purified. KEY: discovery of HIGHLY REACTIVE metals was DELAYED until ELECTRICITY was harnessed (early 1800s): (a) HUMPHRY DAVY (UK, 1807) — discovered POTASSIUM, SODIUM via electrolysis of molten potash, soda. (b) Davy also discovered Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba (1808). EARLIER metals (Cu, Au, Ag, Pb, Sn) — known since antiquity (Bronze Age). HALL-HÉROULT (1886) for Al — before this, Al was MORE EXPENSIVE than gold; Napoleon III had aluminium cutlery for top guests (silver for lesser). UPSC angle: metallurgy energy intensity vs sustainability — green hydrogen-based reduction (replacing carbon) being researched (e.g., Tata Steel's HYBRIT-style projects). PYQ FREQUENCY: extraction-method-by-reactivity in NEET, NCERT, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
The most abundant metal in the Earth's crust is:

(A) Iron
(B) Aluminium
(C) Copper
(D) Silver
cards.back:
(B) Aluminium

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Earth's crust composition by mass (order): Oxygen (46%), Silicon (28%), Aluminium (8.2%), Iron (5.6%), Calcium, Sodium, Potassium, Magnesium. Aluminium is the most abundant metal and 3rd most abundant element overall. Its chief ore is bauxite (Al₂O₃·2H₂O); extracted by Hall-Héroult electrolysis (1886). Very reactive — does NOT occur in free state, only as oxide.

cards.front:
The process of heating a sulphide ore strongly in presence of excess air — below its melting point — to convert it into an oxide is called:

(A) Calcination
(B) Roasting
(C) Smelting
(D) Leaching
cards.back:
(B) Roasting

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Roasting — sulphide ore + O₂ → metal oxide + SO₂. Example: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂. Applied to sulphide ores (galena PbS, zinc blende ZnS, copper pyrites CuFeS₂). Calcination — heat a carbonate / hydrated oxide in absence of air (limestone CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂). Smelting = reduction in a blast furnace. Leaching = dissolving the ore in a suitable solvent.

cards.front:
In the extraction of iron from haematite in a blast furnace, the reducing agent that actually reduces iron(III) oxide is:

(A) Coke directly
(B) Carbon monoxide
(C) Limestone
(D) Molten slag
cards.back:
(B) Carbon monoxide

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Though coke is the fuel, the actual reducing agent in most reactions is CO (not C). Blast furnace reactions (top to bottom): Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (main reduction, 500-900 °C); C + CO₂ → 2CO (Boudouard reaction regenerates CO); C + O₂ → CO₂ at the tuyeres. Limestone decomposes — CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ — then CaO + SiO₂ (silica gangue) → CaSiO₃ slag, separates from molten iron.

cards.front:
'Froth flotation' is a concentration technique used primarily for:

(A) Oxide ores
(B) Sulphide ores
(C) Carbonate ores
(D) Silicate ores
cards.back:
(B) Sulphide ores

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Froth flotation separates sulphide ores (CuFeS₂, ZnS, PbS) from gangue. Ore is ground, mixed with water, pine oil (frothing agent) and xanthate (collector). Compressed air creates froth; sulphide particles — being hydrophobic — attach to the oil-coated bubbles and float. Hydrophilic gangue sinks. Basis — difference in wettability. Widely used in India's Kolar gold mines and Hindustan Zinc operations.

cards.front:
Aluminium is commercially extracted from bauxite by:

(A) Reduction with coke in blast furnace
(B) Electrolysis of molten alumina dissolved in cryolite
(C) Displacement by zinc
(D) Thermal decomposition
cards.back:
(B) Electrolysis of molten alumina dissolved in cryolite

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Hall-Héroult process (1886): pure Al₂O₃ (from Bayer process) is dissolved in molten cryolite Na₃AlF₆ at ~950 °C (cryolite lowers alumina's melting point from 2050 °C). Electrolysis — carbon anodes, steel cathode. Cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al. Anode: O²⁻ ions oxidise, gradually consuming the carbon anodes (2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻; C + O₂ → CO₂). Very energy-intensive — major users are near hydro power.

cards.front:
The substance added to an ore during smelting to remove siliceous (SiO₂) impurities is a:

(A) Reducing agent
(B) Basic flux (e.g. limestone)
(C) Acidic flux (e.g. silica)
(D) Depressant
cards.back:
(B) Basic flux (e.g. limestone)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Flux — an added substance that reacts with impurities to form fusible 'slag' separable from molten metal. Rule: pair acid-base opposites. Silica (SiO₂) is acidic → use basic flux (limestone CaCO₃ / CaO) → CaSiO₃ slag. If ore's gangue is basic (CaO, FeO) → use acidic flux (SiO₂) → silicate slag. Slag is less dense, floats on molten metal, easy to tap off separately.

cards.front:
Match the ore with its metal — which pairing is INCORRECT?

(A) Haematite — Iron
(B) Bauxite — Copper
(C) Cinnabar — Mercury
(D) Galena — Lead
cards.back:
(B) Bauxite — Copper

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Bauxite is an ore of ALUMINIUM, not copper. Chief copper ore is chalcopyrite (CuFeS₂). Common ore-metal pairs: haematite Fe₂O₃ — Fe; magnetite Fe₃O₄ — Fe; bauxite Al₂O₃·2H₂O — Al; galena PbS — Pb; cinnabar HgS — Hg; zinc blende ZnS — Zn; malachite Cu₂(OH)₂CO₃ — Cu. Approximately what percentage of Earth's atmosphere is NITROGEN gas?

(A) 21% of the atmospheric mixture
(B) 78% of the atmospheric mixture
(C) 0.93% of atmospheric mixture
(D) 0.04% of atmospheric mixture
cards.back:
(B) 78% of the atmospheric mixture

cards.front:
Atmospheric NITROGEN is converted to ammonia industrially by which process?

(A) Ostwald process for making nitric acid
(B) Haber-Bosch process for ammonia synthesis
(C) Contact process for sulphuric acid mainly
(D) Solvay process for soda ash output
cards.back:
(B) Haber-Bosch process for ammonia synthesis

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — HABER-BOSCH process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (at ~450°C, 200 atm, with iron catalyst). Fritz HABER (Nobel 1918) + Carl BOSCH (Nobel 1931). One of most consequential reactions of 20th c. — fertilizers from this feed ~50% of world population. Distractor 1 = Ostwald (NH₃ → HNO₃). Distractor 3 = Contact (S → SO₃ → H₂SO₄). Distractor 4 = Solvay (Na₂CO₃).

cards.front:
PHOSPHORUS exists in several allotropes. WHITE phosphorus is:

(A) Stable, can be stored in air
(B) Highly reactive, stored under water
(C) Used as graphite electrode in cells
(D) A heavy metal at room temperature
cards.back:
(B) Highly reactive, stored under water

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — WHITE PHOSPHORUS (P₄ tetrahedra) — waxy, soft, ignites in air at ~30°C, glows in dark (chemiluminescence — gives the name). Stored under WATER to prevent contact with air. Highly toxic. RED phosphorus — polymeric, stable, used in safety match strikers. BLACK phosphorus — most stable allotrope. cards.front:
AMMONIA gas turns moist red litmus paper:

(A) Red, no colour change at all
(B) Blue, indicating basic / alkaline gas
(C) Black, due to a redox reaction
(D) Yellow, with phenolphthalein indicator
cards.back:
(B) Blue, indicating basic / alkaline gas

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Ammonia (NH₃) is a BASE (alkaline gas) — turns moist RED litmus BLUE. NH₃ dissolves readily in water → NH₄OH (ammonium hydroxide), pH > 7. Distinct test: pungent smell + blue litmus. NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl (white fumes, used to detect). Used in: refrigeration (anhydrous), fertilizers, household cleaners. Phenolphthalein turns PINK (not yellow) in NH₃ solution — distractor 4 wrong.

NITRIC ACID (HNO₃) is industrially produced from ammonia by the:

(A) Haber process for ammonia making
(B) Ostwald process for HNO₃ production
(C) Contact process for sulphuric acid
(D) Castner-Kellner process for caustic
cards.back:
(B) Ostwald process for HNO₃ production

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — OSTWALD process: NH₃ + O₂ (Pt catalyst, 800°C) → NO; 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂; 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃. Inputs: NH₃ from Haber + O₂ from air. Wilhelm OSTWALD (Nobel 1909). HNO₃ uses: fertilizers (ammonium nitrate), explosives (TNT, dynamite, RDX), metal etching, dyes. Aqua regia = 3 HCl : 1 HNO₃ (dissolves Au, Pt). Brown ring test for nitrate ion.

UREA, the most widely-used nitrogenous fertilizer in India, has the chemical formula:

(A) NH₄NO₃, the ammonium nitrate
(B) (NH₂)₂CO, with 46% N content
(C) Ca(NO₃)₂, of calcium nitrate
(D) (NH₄)₂SO₄, ammonium sulphate
cards.back:
(B) (NH₂)₂CO, with 46% N content

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — UREA — (NH₂)₂CO or CO(NH₂)₂. ~46% nitrogen by mass — HIGHEST among solid nitrogenous fertilizers. India is world's 2nd largest urea producer (~25 MT/year). (A) NO, the brown nitric oxide gas
(B) N₂O, the nitrous oxide gas
(C) NO₂, dark brown toxic pollutant
(D) N₂O₅, the white solid form
cards.back:
(B) N₂O, the nitrous oxide gas

cards.front:
Noble gases are also called INERT gases because they:

(A) Have stable filled outer electron shells
(B) React only with the alkali metals
(C) Are radioactive in their natural state
(D) Exist as solid metals at room temp
cards.back:
(A) Have stable filled outer electron shells

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — NOBLE GASES (Group 18 / Group 0): He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn. CHEMICALLY INERT (mostly) because they have FULL OUTER ELECTRON SHELLS — electron configuration ends in ns² np⁶ (except He = 1s²). Full octet means MAXIMUM STABILITY; no tendency to gain or lose electrons → no chemical reactions in normal conditions. EXCEPTIONS: starting in 1962, Neil Bartlett showed XENON forms compounds with very electronegative elements (XePtF₆); since then dozens of Xe and Kr compounds synthesized (XeF₂, XeF₄, XeF₆, XeO₃, XeO₄). Helium, Neon, Argon STILL essentially unreactive. PROPERTIES: (1) Colorless, odorless, tasteless gases. (2) Monatomic (single atoms, not molecules). (3) Low boiling points: He = 4.2 K (lowest of any element); Ne = 27 K; Ar = 87 K; Kr = 120 K; Xe = 165 K; Rn = 211 K. (4) Increasing density down the group (He lighter than air; Rn ~7× denser than air). DISCOVERY: ARGON (1894, Lord Rayleigh + William Ramsay — Nobel 1904); HELIUM detected in sun's spectrum (1868) before being isolated on Earth; Ne, Kr, Xe (1898 by Ramsay). RADON (1900) — radioactive. PYQ FREQUENCY: noble gas inertness in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which noble gas is used to fill BALLOONS and AIRSHIPS?

(A) Helium (lighter than air, non-flammable)
(B) Argon (heavier, in light bulbs)
(C) Krypton (used in flash lamps) (option here)
(D) Xenon (used in arc lamps) (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Helium (lighter than air, non-flammable)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — HELIUM (He, atomic no. 2) — used to fill balloons because it's: (1) LIGHTER THAN AIR (density 0.18 g/L vs air's 1.29 g/L; ~7× less dense). (2) NON-FLAMMABLE (unlike hydrogen which is even lighter but explodes — Hindenburg disaster, 1937 — 36 deaths; ended commercial hydrogen-airship era). (3) COLORLESS, ODORLESS, NON-TOXIC. APPLICATIONS: (1) BALLOONS — party balloons, weather balloons, rescue balloons. (2) BLIMPS / AIRSHIPS — Goodyear blimp etc. use He. (3) MRI MACHINES — liquid helium (4.2 K) cools superconducting magnets. (4) DEEP-SEA DIVING — He-O₂ 'heliox' breathing mix avoids nitrogen narcosis. (5) WELDING shielding gas (with Ar). (6) SEMICONDUCTOR manufacturing. (7) LEAK DETECTION (small atom, escapes through tiny holes). HELIUM SHORTAGE: He is FINITE on Earth — collected from natural gas wells (where helium accumulates from radioactive decay). U.S. Federal Helium Reserve was main source. Modern shortage threatens MRI/research. SOLUTIONS: capture during natural gas processing; some new producers in Qatar, Russia. INDIA imports almost all helium. ON THE SUN: helium is the SECOND most abundant element (after hydrogen), ~24% of stellar mass. NAME: from 'helios' (Greek for sun). PYQ FREQUENCY: helium uses in NEET, NCERT, SSC chemistry 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which noble gas is commonly used in NEON SIGN BOARDS, glowing red?

(A) Neon (Ne — bright orange-red glow)
(B) Helium (a yellowish-pink glow)
(C) Argon (light blue or violet)
(D) Xenon (white-blue glow only)
cards.back:
(A) Neon (Ne — bright orange-red glow)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — NEON (Ne) — when an electric current passes through low-pressure neon gas in a sealed glass tube, it emits a CHARACTERISTIC ORANGE-RED GLOW. Used in NEON SIGNS (Las Vegas, Tokyo, etc.) — the term 'neon sign' is now generic, but ORIGINAL neon glows red. OTHER COLORS in 'neon' signs use different gases: (1) ARGON — pale BLUE/VIOLET. (2) HELIUM — pale yellowish-pink. (3) KRYPTON — yellow-greenish white. (4) XENON — bluish-white. (5) MERCURY VAPOR — bright blue (in fluorescent tubes; UV exciting phosphor coating gives white light). (6) NEON + MERCURY + Phosphor combinations — full color range. INDIA NEON SIGNS: bustling around Mumbai, Bengaluru tech hubs, Connaught Place Delhi. NAME: 'NEON' from 'neos' (Greek for 'new'). DISCOVERED 1898 by William Ramsay + Morris Travers in London. CURRENT TRENDS: traditional neon being replaced by LED-based 'neon-flex' for energy efficiency, longevity, lower maintenance. NEON's CHEMISTRY: most inert of the noble gases — even Bartlett-style xenon compounds don't readily form for neon. INDUSTRIAL USES: (1) Helium-Neon (HeNe) lasers — common red laser pointers (633 nm). (2) Neon vacuum tubes for indicators in electronic equipment. PYQ FREQUENCY: neon-orange glow is a SSC GA, NEET classic 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which noble gas is filled in INCANDESCENT bulbs to extend filament life?

(A) Argon (often with traces of N₂)
(B) Neon (would glow not white)
(C) Helium (escape too fast)
(D) Xenon (very expensive choice)
cards.back:
(A) Argon (often with traces of N₂)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — ARGON (Ar) — most common gas filled in INCANDESCENT BULBS. WHY: (1) INERT — won't react with hot tungsten filament (which would oxidize/burn out in air). (2) Heavier than helium/neon → BETTER at suppressing tungsten evaporation from filament (extends life). (3) Cheap — Argon is ~1% of Earth's atmosphere; obtained by FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION of LIQUID AIR. (4) Doesn't conduct heat well → keeps filament hot. TYPICAL FILL: 90% Argon + 10% Nitrogen. HALOGEN BULBS use halogens (iodine, bromine) + Ar — halogen gas reacts with evaporated tungsten and redeposits it on filament (HALOGEN CYCLE) — much longer life, brighter. KRYPTON (Kr) — used in some HIGH-PERFORMANCE bulbs (better filament protection but more expensive). USE in OTHER APPLICATIONS: (1) WELDING — argon shielding gas (prevents oxidation of weld). (2) DOUBLE-PANE WINDOWS — Ar between panes for insulation. (3) FOOD PACKAGING — flushing oxygen out (extends shelf life). (4) WINE PRESERVATION (replaces oxygen above wine in opened bottle). (5) Lab inert atmosphere for sensitive chemistry. ABUNDANCE: Ar is the THIRD most abundant gas in atmosphere (~0.93%, after N₂ and O₂); produced industrially as byproduct of liquid-air distillation (millions of tonnes/year). PYQ FREQUENCY: argon uses in NEET, NCERT, SSC GA 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
RADON (Rn), a noble gas, is significant because it is:

(A) Radioactive (causes lung cancer)
(B) Non-flammable and very stable
(C) The lightest known noble gas
(D) Common in atmosphere abundantly
cards.back:
(A) Radioactive (causes lung cancer)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — RADON (Rn, atomic no. 86) — the only RADIOACTIVE noble gas. Half-life ~3.8 days (Rn-222, the most stable isotope). Comes from URANIUM-238 decay chain in soil/rock; seeps into homes through cracks, well water. HEALTH HAZARD: SECOND LEADING CAUSE OF LUNG CANCER (after smoking). Inhaled radon decays in lungs; alpha particles damage tissue. Globally ~3-14% of lung cancers attributed to radon. INDIA — not as severe as USA/Europe (less granitic geology in residential areas). USA has comprehensive radon-mitigation programs (vent fans under basements). DISCOVERY: 1900 by Friedrich Ernst Dorn (Germany). ALL RADON ISOTOPES are radioactive — no stable form. ABUNDANCE: in air ~10⁻¹⁹% (extremely rare). USES: (1) RADIATION THERAPY (some old cancer treatments — now mostly replaced). (2) GEOLOGICAL — radon levels predict earthquakes, locate uranium deposits. RADON DAUGHTERS: decays into Polonium-218, Lead-214, etc. — the alpha-emitters that lodge in lungs and cause damage. SAFETY MEASURES: radon detection kits available; ventilation; sealing basement cracks. ANALOG: PURE NOBLE GASES are mostly safe; only HEAVIEST (Rn) is hazardous due to radioactivity. PYQ FREQUENCY: radon-radioactivity in NEET, NCERT, UPSC environment 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which noble gas is used in HIGH-INTENSITY arc lamps (like in cinema projectors and car headlamps)?

(A) Xenon (bright white-blue arc)
(B) Helium (only used in MRI)
(C) Neon (orange-red color glow)
(D) Argon (used in light bulbs)
cards.back:
(A) Xenon (bright white-blue arc)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — XENON (Xe, atomic no. 54) — used in HIGH-INTENSITY DISCHARGE (HID) arc lamps because: (1) Produces VERY BRIGHT WHITE-BLUE LIGHT (close to natural daylight). (2) HIGH efficacy + good color rendering. (3) Stable arc, long life. APPLICATIONS: (1) CINEMA PROJECTORS — XENON SHORT-ARC LAMPS — power 1-15 kW; produce immense brightness needed for huge screens. (2) CAR HEADLAMPS (HID 'XENON' headlights) — much brighter than halogen, longer-life. (3) STROBE LIGHTS / FLASH LAMPS for photography (xenon flash tubes — short bursts, ~1/1000 sec). (4) IMAX projectors (high-power xenon). (5) SEARCHLIGHTS / lighthouse lamps. (6) UV light therapy (some skin treatments). KEY ADVANTAGES: (a) DIMMABLE, can be cycled. (b) Doesn't contain mercury (unlike fluorescent lamps). (c) Extremely high luminous output. CHEMISTRY MILESTONE: in 1962, Neil Bartlett synthesized XePtF₆ — FIRST stable noble gas COMPOUND, shattering the 'inert' label. Now Xe and Kr are known to form many compounds: XeF₂, XeF₄, XeF₆, XeO₃, XeOF₄, XeO₄, even XeCl₂ (transient). DISCOVERED: 1898 by Ramsay + Travers. RECENT: xenon is also studied as a future ANESTHETIC gas (very potent + safe but expensive). PYQ FREQUENCY: xenon uses in NEET, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
ELECTRON CONFIGURATION ending in ns²np⁶ is characteristic of which group?

(A) Group 18 (noble gases)
(B) Group 1 (alkali metals)
(C) Group 17 (halogens)
(D) Group 14 (carbon family)
cards.back:
(A) Group 18 (noble gases)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — GROUP 18 (NOBLE GASES) have FULL OUTER SHELLS: ns² np⁶ (8 outer electrons, octet). EXCEPTION: HELIUM has only 1s² (2 electrons; n=1 only has s subshell, no p subshell). FULL CONFIGURATIONS (memorize): (1) HELIUM: 1s². (2) NEON: [He] 2s² 2p⁶. (3) ARGON: [Ne] 3s² 3p⁶. (4) KRYPTON: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁶. (5) XENON: [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s² 5p⁶. (6) RADON: [Xe] 4f¹⁴ 5d¹⁰ 6s² 6p⁶. RELATED CONFIGURATIONS by group: GROUP 1 (alkali metals, Li, Na, K): ns¹ — one outer electron; very reactive (lose e⁻ to form +1 ion). GROUP 2 (alkaline earth, Be, Mg, Ca): ns². GROUP 17 (halogens, F, Cl, Br): ns² np⁵ — one less than octet, very reactive (gain e⁻ to form −1 ion). GROUP 16 (chalcogens, O, S, Se): ns² np⁴. KEY: noble gases are TARGETS — when other elements REACT, they often try to ACHIEVE noble-gas configuration by gaining/losing electrons (OCTET RULE). PERIODIC TRENDS in NOBLE GASES: (1) ATOMIC SIZE increases down (more shells). (2) Ionization energy DECREASES down. (3) Boiling/melting points INCREASE down (more London dispersion). PYQ FREQUENCY: noble gas e-config in NEET, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
NOBLE GASES are characterised by being chemically:

(A) Highly reactive with most metals usually
(B) Largely inert due to a complete outer shell
(C) Acidic in water at room temperature only
(D) Toxic to humans and to plants in air
cards.back:
(B) Largely inert due to a complete outer shell

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Noble gases (Group 18) — He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn (+ synthetic Og). All have COMPLETE outer electron shell (He has 2; rest have 8). Hence chemically inert — don't readily form compounds. He never forms compounds. Other noble gases (Xe, Kr, Rn) form a few compounds with strong oxidisers (XeF₂, XeF₄, XeO₃) — discovered by Neil Bartlett 1962, breaking the assumption of total inertness. Distractor 1 — opposite. Distractor 3 — false. Distractor 4 — generally non-toxic, though radon is radioactive.

cards.option2: Acidic in water at room temperature only

cards.front:
HELIUM is widely used in airships and weather balloons because it is:

(A) The lightest gas, hydrogen, easily combustible
(B) Less dense than air but non-flammable, unlike H₂
(C) Heavier than air and gives stable downward lift
(D) Coloured pink and gives an attractive appearance
cards.back:
(B) Less dense than air but non-flammable, unlike H₂

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Helium — second-lightest gas (after H₂). Density ~0.18 g/L (vs air 1.2 g/L). NON-FLAMMABLE, unlike hydrogen (which caused the Hindenburg disaster, 1937). Used in airships, blimps, weather balloons, party balloons. Other uses: cryogenic cooling (LHe at 4K, for MRI superconducting magnets), purging rocket-fuel tanks, deep-sea breathing mix (heliox — replaces nitrogen to avoid bends). Distractor 1 — He is gas #2, lighter than only H₂. Distractor 3 — He is much LESS dense than air. Distractor 4 — colourless.

cards.front:
The reddish-orange glow of NEON SIGNS is produced by:

(A) Burning the neon gas with oxygen in tubes
(B) Electric current exciting neon atoms to emit light
(C) Reflecting external red light off coloured glass
(D) Neon gas heated until it gets red-hot
cards.back:
(B) Electric current exciting neon atoms to emit light

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Neon sign — high-voltage electrical discharge through low-pressure neon gas excites atoms; on returning to ground state, they emit characteristic reddish-orange light (~640 nm). Different colours in 'neon' signs come from different gases or coated glass — argon (blue/lavender), krypton (greenish white), xenon (blue-violet), helium (pink), Hg + phosphor (white, blue, green). Genuine neon-only signs are red-orange. Distractor 1 — noble gases don't burn. Distractor 3 — they self-emit. Distractor 4 — incandescence not the mechanism.

cards.front:
ARGON is used to fill ELECTRIC LIGHT BULBS because it:

(A) Reacts with the tungsten filament to extend life
(B) Is inert, preventing oxidation of the hot filament
(C) Lights up itself, giving extra brightness inside
(D) Cools the filament rapidly during operation
cards.back:
(B) Is inert, preventing oxidation of the hot filament

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Tungsten filament gets hot (~2500-3000°C). In air, it would oxidise + burn quickly. Filling the bulb with INERT GAS (Ar, sometimes Kr/Xe for premium bulbs) prevents oxidation, extends bulb life. Argon is the cheapest noble gas (~1% of atmosphere). Some bulbs add nitrogen (also unreactive at these conditions). LED bulbs don't need this — solid-state, no hot filament. Distractor 1 — opposite. Distractor 3 — argon doesn't self-light. Distractor 4 — gases conduct some heat but cooling isn't the main reason.

cards.front:
RADON, the heaviest naturally-occurring noble gas, is a health concern because it is:

(A) Highly explosive in confined spaces near homes
(B) Radioactive and a major cause of lung cancer indoors
(C) Toxic by direct contact with the human skin
(D) Acidic when dissolved in indoor air moisture
cards.back:
(B) Radioactive and a major cause of lung cancer indoors

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Radon (Rn-222, half-life 3.8 days) — radioactive decay product of uranium in soil + rock. Seeps into homes through foundations, accumulates in poorly-ventilated basements + ground floors. Inhaled radon decays into radioactive progeny that lodge in lungs → SECOND LEADING CAUSE OF LUNG CANCER after smoking (in many developed countries). Mitigation: sealing cracks, sub-slab ventilation. Common in granite-rich areas. Health limit: < 4 pCi/L typical. Distractor 1 — not explosive (inert). Distractor 3 — chemically inert; danger is radioactivity, not chemical contact. Distractor 4 — not acidic.

cards.front:
Helium-Neon (HeNe) lasers and Argon-ion lasers are examples of:

(A) Solid-state lasers built from doped crystals
(B) Gas lasers, with a noble gas as the lasing medium
(C) Liquid lasers using dye solutions inside cells
(D) Semiconductor lasers used in CD and DVD readers
cards.back:
(B) Gas lasers, with a noble gas as the lasing medium

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — GAS LASERS — population inversion in gaseous medium under electric discharge. HeNe (632.8 nm red, classroom + barcode-scanner) — first continuous-wave laser, 1960. Distractor 1 = ruby, Nd:YAG, Ti:sapphire (solid-state). Distractor 3 = dye lasers (tunable, used in research). Distractor 4 = laser diodes (small, efficient, ubiquitous in consumer electronics).

cards.front:
OZONE (O₃) in the upper atmosphere is important because it:

(A) Adds to atmospheric oxygen (O₂)
(B) Absorbs harmful UV radiation from Sun
(C) Causes the rain on planet Earth
(D) Makes the sky appear blue colour
cards.back:
(B) Absorbs harmful UV radiation from Sun

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — OZONE LAYER (stratosphere, 15-35 km altitude): absorbs ~97-99% of Sun's UV-B + UV-C radiation → protects life from skin cancer, cataracts, plant damage. Discovered to have a 'hole' over Antarctica (1985, Farman et al.), caused by CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons in refrigerants, aerosols). MONTREAL PROTOCOL (1987) — international treaty to phase out CFCs; ozone layer recovering. World Ozone Day = 16 September. Distractor 1 — adds, but its function isn't supplemental O₂. Distractor 4 = Rayleigh scattering.

cards.front:
SULPHURIC ACID (H₂SO₄, 'King of Chemicals') is industrially produced by:

(A) Haber process for ammonia making
(B) Contact process for sulphuric acid
(C) Solvay process for sodium carbonate
(D) Ostwald process for nitric acid output
cards.back:
(B) Contact process for sulphuric acid

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — CONTACT PROCESS: S + O₂ → SO₂; 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (V₂O₅ catalyst, 450°C); SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇ (oleum); oleum + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄. (Direct SO₃ + H₂O is too vigorous — uses oleum.) H₂SO₄ called 'KING OF CHEMICALS' — produced/consumed in vast quantities; an indicator of industrialisation. Uses: fertilizers (~60% — single super phosphate, ammonium sulphate), batteries (lead-acid), petroleum refining, dyes, drugs, detergents. India: Hazira, IFFCO produce it.

(B) Rhombic (S8), the yellow crystals

(D) Hot liquid sulphur, S_n chains form
cards.back:
(B) Rhombic (S8), the yellow crystals

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — RHOMBIC SULPHUR (α-sulphur) — stable at < 96°C; yellow octahedral crystals; S₈ rings (puckered crown shape). Most common allotrope. MONOCLINIC SULPHUR (β-sulphur) — stable 96-119°C; long needle-like crystals. PLASTIC SULPHUR — formed when molten S is cooled rapidly; rubbery, S∞ chains; unstable, reverts to rhombic. S has many S-atom oligomers: S₂, S₃, S₆, S₇... S₁₂. Sulphur sublimes at ~445°C with characteristic blue flame. Found native in volcanic regions, oil/gas (recovered as Claus process by-product).

cards.front:
Which gas, released by burning sulphur-containing fuel, is the main contributor to ACID RAIN?

(A) Carbon dioxide (CO₂), greenhouse gas
(B) Sulphur dioxide (SO₂), then forms H₂SO₄
(C) Methane (CH₄), the greenhouse gas
(D) Nitrogen (N₂), the main air gas
cards.back:
(B) Sulphur dioxide (SO₂), then forms H₂SO₄

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — ACID RAIN: SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ (sulphurous acid); 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ (sulphuric acid). Also NOx (from vehicles, lightning) → HNO₃. pH of acid rain < 5.6 (normal rain pH ~5.6 due to CO₂). Damages: forests, lakes (kills fish), buildings (corrodes marble — Taj Mahal yellowing), soils. Sources: coal-burning power plants (high-S coal), smelters, vehicles. Solutions: scrubbers (FGD), low-S fuels, catalytic converters. Distractor 1 — CO₂ is a greenhouse gas, makes mildly acidic rain (carbonic acid) but not the major acid-rain culprit.

cards.front:
OXYGEN was discovered (officially credited) by:

(A) Lavoisier, who named it 'oxygen' but didn't discover
(B) Joseph Priestley, in 1774, by heating HgO
(C) Cavendish, who studied hydrogen mainly
(D) Dalton, who proposed the atomic theory
cards.back:
(B) Joseph Priestley, in 1774, by heating HgO

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Joseph PRIESTLEY (Britain) — isolated O₂ on 1 Aug 1774 by heating mercuric oxide (HgO) with sunlight focused by a lens. Earlier, Carl SCHEELE (Sweden) had isolated it (1772-73) but published later. Antoine LAVOISIER (France) — named it 'OXYGENE' (Greek = 'acid maker', wrongly thought all acids contain it), recognised its role in combustion + respiration → overthrew the phlogiston theory. Distractor 3 = Cavendish discovered hydrogen (1766). Distractor 4 = Dalton's atomic theory (1808).

cards.front:
Hydrogen sulphide (H₂S) gas has the characteristic smell of:

(A) Almonds, somewhat sweetish smell
(B) Rotten eggs (very pungent smell)
(C) Mint, fresh and cooling smell
(D) Garlic, like fresh garlic cloves
cards.back:
(B) Rotten eggs (very pungent smell)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — H₂S — colourless gas, smells like ROTTEN EGGS. Highly toxic (more than HCN at high concentrations), but human nose is very sensitive (detects from <0.5 ppb). Olfactory FATIGUE — at high concentrations, sense of smell is paralysed (dangerous!) — can't detect anymore. Sources: anaerobic decay (sewers, marshes), volcanic gases, oil/gas wells (sour gas). Used in lab: Lassaigne's test for sulphur in organic compounds; sulphide precipitation in qualitative analysis. Distractor 1 = HCN (cyanide). Distractor 4 = phosphine PH₃ partly.

cards.front:
s-BLOCK consists of which periodic groups?

(A) Groups 13 to 18 (the p-block region)
(B) Groups 1 and 2 (alkali + alkaline earth)
(C) Groups 3 to 12 (transition metals only)
(D) Lanthanides + actinides (f-block series)
cards.back:
(B) Groups 1 and 2 (alkali + alkaline earth)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — s-BLOCK = elements where the LAST valence electron enters s-orbital. GROUP 1 = ALKALI METALS (H, Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr); 1 valence electron, +1 oxidation state. GROUP 2 = ALKALINE EARTH METALS (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra); 2 valence electrons, +2 oxidation state. H is technically Group 1 by configuration but behaves differently (covalent, gaseous, etc.). REACTIVITY INCREASES down the group (atomic radius increases, ionization energy decreases).

cards.front:
Why are SODIUM (Na) and POTASSIUM (K) stored under KEROSENE OIL?

(A) To preserve their metallic shine
(B) To prevent reaction with air + moisture
(C) To make them magnetic in nature here
(D) To slow down their natural radioactivity
cards.back:
(B) To prevent reaction with air + moisture

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Alkali metals (Na, K, Cs, Rb) — extremely REACTIVE: react with air's oxygen + moisture. Reaction with water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂↑ (exothermic; can ignite the H₂; K reaction even more violent — purple flame; Cs nearly explosive). Stored under kerosene (or paraffin oil) — these are non-polar, don't react with metals. Distractor 4 — Na, K not radioactive (Fr is, but rare).

(A) Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃)
(B) Sodium chloride (NaCl)
(C) Sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃)
(D) Sodium sulphate (Na₂SO₄)
cards.back:
(B) Sodium chloride (NaCl)

cards.front:
GYPSUM (used in plaster of paris) chemically is:

(A) Calcium oxide (CaO, quicklime)
(B) Calcium sulphate dihydrate (CaSO₄·2H₂O)
(C) Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃, marble)
(D) Calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)₂, lime)
cards.back:
(B) Calcium sulphate dihydrate (CaSO₄·2H₂O)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — GYPSUM = CaSO₄·2H₂O. PLASTER OF PARIS (POP) = CaSO₄·½H₂O — formed by heating gypsum to ~150°C (loses 1.5 of 2 H₂O). When mixed with water, sets back to gypsum + hardens — used in casts, ceiling, sculpture. Other Ca compounds: LIMESTONE / MARBLE / CHALK = CaCO₃; QUICKLIME = CaO; SLAKED LIME = Ca(OH)₂; BLEACHING POWDER = Ca(OCl)Cl. India: Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat are major gypsum producers.

cards.front:
Which alkaline earth metal is MOST important for HUMAN BONES + TEETH?

(A) Magnesium (Mg) is most important
(B) Calcium (Ca) is most important
(C) Beryllium (Be) is most important
(D) Barium (Ba) is most important
cards.back:
(B) Calcium (Ca) is most important

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — CALCIUM (Ca) — major mineral in BONES (~99% of body's Ca) + TEETH (as hydroxyapatite — Ca₅(PO₄)₃(OH)). Also crucial for: muscle contraction (including heart), nerve signaling, blood clotting. RDA ~1000 mg/day adult. Sources: milk, yogurt, cheese, leafy greens, fish bones (sardines), tofu, ragi. DEFICIENCY → osteoporosis (esp. post-menopausal women), rickets in children, muscle cramps. MAGNESIUM (Mg) also in bones (~25 g body Mg) but less. CHLOROPHYLL has Mg at center (like Fe in haemoglobin). Distractor 4 — Barium is TOXIC; used in BaSO₄ for X-ray contrast (insoluble = safe).

FLAME TEST: which alkali metal gives a CRIMSON RED flame?

(A) Sodium (Na) gives yellow flame
(B) Lithium (Li) gives crimson red
(C) Potassium (K) gives lilac flame
(D) Calcium (Ca) gives brick red
cards.back:
(B) Lithium (Li) gives crimson red

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — FLAME TESTS — characteristic colours from electronic transitions when metal salts heated: LITHIUM (Li) = crimson/red; SODIUM (Na) = bright yellow (most common, very intense); POTASSIUM (K) = lilac/purple; RUBIDIUM (Rb) = red-violet; CESIUM (Cs) = blue. Group 2: CALCIUM (Ca) = brick red; STRONTIUM (Sr) = crimson; BARIUM (Ba) = pale green; COPPER (Cu) = blue-green. Used in classroom QUALITATIVE analysis. Fireworks COLOURS use this principle: Sr salts → red, Cu → green/blue, Na → yellow, K → purple, Ba → green.
