cards.front:
WASHING SODA (used in cleaning) is chemically:

(A) NaHCO₃ (the common baking soda)
(B) Na₂CO₃·10H₂O (Na carbonate decahydrate)
(C) NaCl (the common table salt)
(D) NaOH (the strong caustic soda)
cards.back:
(B) Na₂CO₃·10H₂O (Na carbonate decahydrate)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — WASHING SODA = sodium carbonate decahydrate (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O). Mildly basic (pH ~11) → softens hard water (binds Ca²⁺ + Mg²⁺), removes greasy stains. Made by SOLVAY process (NH₃ + CO₂ + NaCl + H₂O → NaHCO₃ + NH₄Cl; heat NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂). BAKING SODA (NaHCO₃) — milder; used in cooking + as antacid + fire extinguishers. CAUSTIC SODA (NaOH) — very strong base; soap-making (saponification), paper, drain cleaners. CHLOR-ALKALI process (electrolysis of brine) produces NaOH, Cl₂, H₂.

d-BLOCK elements (transition metals) occupy which groups in the periodic table?

(A) Groups 1 and 2 (alkali + alkaline earth)
(B) Groups 3 to 12 in the middle
(C) Groups 13 to 18 in p-block region
(D) Lanthanide and actinide series only
cards.back:
(B) Groups 3 to 12 in the middle

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — D-BLOCK = transition metals; Groups 3-12; have partially filled d-orbital. 4 SERIES: 3d (Sc → Zn — Period 4), 4d (Y → Cd — Period 5), 5d (Lu → Hg — Period 6), 6d (Lr → Cn — Period 7). Common ones in daily life: Fe (iron), Cu (copper), Zn (zinc), Au (gold), Ag (silver), Pt (platinum), Cr (chromium), Mn (manganese), Ni (nickel), Ti (titanium). Distractor 1 = s-block. Distractor 3 = p-block. Distractor 4 = f-block.

cards.front:
Transition metals are characterised by which property NOT typical of s/p-block metals?

(A) High electrical conductivity (also Cu in s-block)
(B) Variable oxidation states + coloured compounds
(C) Low boiling points common to most metals
(D) Soft cuttable like the alkali metals
cards.back:
(B) Variable oxidation states + coloured compounds

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Distinct properties of transition metals: (1) VARIABLE OXIDATION STATES — Fe (+2, +3), Cr (+2, +3, +6), Mn (+2, +3, +4, +6, +7); s-block metals have one valence (Na = +1; Ca = +2). (2) COLOURED ions/compounds — due to d-d electronic transitions: Cu²⁺ blue, Fe³⁺ yellow, Cr³⁺ green, Mn²⁺ pink. (3) form COMPLEX ions / coordination compounds (with ligands like NH₃, CN⁻, H₂O). (4) MAGNETIC properties (Fe, Co, Ni — ferromagnetic). (5) act as catalysts. (6) HARD + high m.p./b.p. (Distractor 3, 4 wrong.)

cards.front:
Which of the following is the MOST DUCTILE metal (drawn into the thinnest wire)?

(A) Iron, the workhorse industrial metal
(B) Gold, the most ductile of all
(C) Aluminium, lightweight versatile metal
(D) Silver, second most ductile only
cards.back:
(B) Gold, the most ductile of all

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — GOLD (Au) — most DUCTILE + most MALLEABLE metal. 1 g of gold can be drawn into a wire 1.6 km long, or beaten into ~1 sq m of gold leaf (only ~100-150 atoms thick!). Used in jewellery, electronics (corrosion-free contacts), dentistry, gilding. Why so ductile: FCC crystal structure + weak metal bonds. Other very ductile: silver (2nd), copper, aluminium, iron. India is world's 2nd largest gold consumer. Most malleable: gold ≈ silver > aluminium > copper. Most thermally conductive: silver (=most conductive, then Cu, then Au).

cards.front:
Which transition metal is the BEST conductor of electricity (highest σ)?

(A) Copper, second-best conductor here
(B) Silver, the highest conductivity metal
(C) Gold, expensive standard for contacts
(D) Aluminium, used in transmission lines
cards.back:
(B) Silver, the highest conductivity metal

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — SILVER (Ag) — highest electrical AND thermal conductivity of all elements. Conductivity ranking (decreasing): Ag > Cu > Au > Al > Fe. But silver is too expensive for general use. COPPER is the standard for everyday wiring (still excellent conductivity, much cheaper). ALUMINIUM used for long-distance high-voltage transmission lines (lighter than Cu, cheaper, less sag). GOLD used in critical contacts where corrosion resistance > pure conductivity. Aluminium is not a transition metal (p-block), but wide industrial use.

cards.front:
STAINLESS STEEL is mainly an alloy of:

(A) Iron + carbon only (plain steel)
(B) Iron + chromium (~10-30% Cr) + nickel
(C) Iron + aluminium + zinc lining
(D) Pure iron with no other added
cards.back:
(B) Iron + chromium (~10-30% Cr) + nickel

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — STAINLESS STEEL = Fe + Cr (10-30%) + Ni (3-12%) + small C. Cr forms a thin, invisible, self-healing oxide layer (Cr₂O₃) on the surface → resists corrosion. Common types: 304 (18% Cr, 8% Ni — household, food); 316 (with Mo for chemical/marine resistance); 410, 430 (cheaper, magnetic, with less Ni). Other STEELS: PLAIN CARBON STEEL (just Fe + C); HSLA (high-strength low-alloy); TOOL steel (W, V, Cr); STAINLESS variants. India: SAIL, JSPL, JSW, Tata Steel are major producers.

Which metal is liquid at room temperature?

(A) Sodium (Na), a soft metal
(B) Mercury (Hg), the only one
(C) Potassium (K), reactive alkali
(D) Aluminium (Al), light metal
cards.back:
(B) Mercury (Hg), the only one

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — MERCURY (Hg) — ONLY METAL liquid at standard room temperature (m.p. = −38.83°C). Group 12, d-block. Latin name 'hydrargyrum' (Hg) = 'liquid silver'. Uses: thermometers (now banned), barometers, fluorescent lamps, dental amalgams (decreasing), gold extraction. TOXIC (especially organic Hg, e.g., methyl-Hg) — Minamata disaster (Japan, 1950s, mercury poisoning). MINAMATA CONVENTION (2013) — phasing out mercury globally. Other metals close to liquid at RT: Cs (m.p. 28.5°C — melts in hand); Ga (m.p. 29.8°C — melts on warm day); Fr, Br (Br is the only liquid non-metal at RT).

cards.front:
BRONZE, a famous historic alloy used for tools, statues, and bells, is mainly:

(A) Iron + carbon (a hardened steel)
(B) Copper + tin (Cu base, ~10-12% Sn)
(C) Copper + zinc (which is brass alloy)
(D) Iron + chromium (stainless lining)
cards.back:
(B) Copper + tin (Cu base, ~10-12% Sn)

(A) Groups 1 and 2 (alkali + alkaline earth)
(B) Groups 13 to 18 (boron to noble gases)
(C) Groups 3 to 12 (transition metals)
(D) Lanthanide and actinide series only
cards.back:
(B) Groups 13 to 18 (boron to noble gases)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — p-BLOCK = elements where the LAST valence electron enters a p-orbital. Includes GROUPS 13-18: 13 (Boron family — B, Al, Ga, In, Tl); 14 (Carbon family — C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb); 15 (Nitrogen family — N, P, As, Sb, Bi); 16 (Oxygen family — O, S, Se, Te, Po); 17 (Halogens — F, Cl, Br, I, At); 18 (Noble gases — He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn). Distractor 1 = s-block. Distractor 3 = d-block. Distractor 4 = f-block.

cards.front:
ALUMINIUM (Al, Group 13) is the most abundant METAL in:

(A) Earth's atmosphere by volume share
(B) Earth's CRUST by mass percentage
(C) Earth's mantle (silicate layer)
(D) Earth's outer core (liquid iron)
cards.back:
(B) Earth's CRUST by mass percentage

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Earth's CRUST composition by mass: O (46%), Si (28%), Al (8.1%), Fe (5%), Ca, Na, K, Mg... ALUMINIUM = MOST ABUNDANT METAL in crust (3rd most abundant element overall). Main ore: BAUXITE (Al₂O₃·xH₂O). India's bauxite: Odisha, Andhra, Jharkhand, Maharashtra. NALCO (Odisha), HINDALCO (UP/Odisha) — major producers. Aluminium uses: aircraft, vehicles, foil, cans, electrical wires, frames. Iron is the most abundant metal in the WHOLE Earth (concentrated in core).

cards.front:
DIAMOND and GRAPHITE are both forms (allotropes) of:

(A) Silicon (Si), Group 14 element
(B) Carbon (C), Group 14 element
(C) Sulphur (S), Group 16 element
(D) Boron (B), Group 13 element
cards.back:
(B) Carbon (C), Group 14 element

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — DIAMOND + GRAPHITE = both pure CARBON, but different structures. DIAMOND: tetrahedral, sp³ hybridised, 3D network → very hard, insulator, refracts light (sparkle). GRAPHITE: layered planar, sp² hybridised, hexagonal sheets → soft, slippery, conducts electricity (free electrons in delocalised π bonds). Other carbon allotropes: FULLERENE (C₆₀ buckyball), GRAPHENE (single layer of graphite — Nobel 2010, Geim + Novoselov), CARBON NANOTUBES, AMORPHOUS (charcoal, soot, coal). DIAMOND + GRAPHITE under STP — graphite slightly more stable.

cards.front:
The most ELECTRONEGATIVE element of the periodic table is:

(A) Oxygen (O), 3.44 on Pauling scale
(B) Fluorine (F), 3.98 on Pauling scale
(C) Chlorine (Cl), 3.16 on the scale
(D) Nitrogen (N), 3.04 on the scale
cards.back:
(B) Fluorine (F), 3.98 on Pauling scale

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — FLUORINE (F) — most electronegative element (Pauling scale = 3.98). Top of HALOGENS (Group 17). Strongest oxidiser; readily forms F⁻. EN trend: increases LEFT → RIGHT (across period); DECREASES TOP → BOTTOM (down a group). Top 4 EN: F (3.98), O (3.44), Cl (3.16), N (3.04). Cesium / Francium least EN. F is so reactive it reacts with most things (water, glass) — special handling needed. Used in fluorides (toothpaste), Teflon (PTFE), refrigerants (Freons banned), uranium enrichment (UF₆).

cards.front:
TIN (Sn) and LEAD (Pb), both Group 14 elements, were used historically for making:

(A) Currency coins, only of gold or silver
(B) Solder + plumbing pipes (Sn/Pb alloys)
(C) Steel reinforcement bars used in concrete
(D) Fertilizer for agriculture in India
cards.back:
(B) Solder + plumbing pipes (Sn/Pb alloys)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Tin (Sn) + Lead (Pb) — both relatively soft, low-melting metals. Used together: SOLDER (60% Sn / 40% Pb traditional; Pb-free now standard for environment + health) — joins electronic components. PLUMBING — Romans used lead pipes (Latin 'plumbum' = lead, hence symbol Pb + 'plumber'). Lead is TOXIC (neurotoxin); banned from petrol (lead-tetra-ethyl octane booster), paint, pipes. Pb still used in: car batteries, X-ray shields, fishing weights, ammunition. Tin uses: tin cans (steel coated with thin Sn layer), bronze (Cu+Sn), pewter.

cards.front:
INERT pair effect (s-electrons of valence shell unwilling to bond) is most pronounced in which p-block elements?

(A) Top elements of each group only
(B) Heavier ones (Tl, Pb, Bi) at the bottom
(C) Middle elements like Si, As, Se
(D) Noble gases (Group 18) primarily
cards.back:
(B) Heavier ones (Tl, Pb, Bi) at the bottom

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — INERT PAIR EFFECT — outermost s-electrons (ns² pair) of HEAVIER p-block elements are reluctant to participate in bonding, behaving as 'inert'. Caused by poor shielding by inner d/f electrons → s-electrons held more tightly + farther from valence frontier. Most pronounced for: Tl (Group 13), Pb (Group 14), Bi (Group 15). Result: heavier elements show LOWER OXIDATION STATE more readily than expected. E.g., Pb⁺² (more stable than Pb⁺⁴); Tl⁺ (more stable than Tl⁺³); Bi⁺³ (more stable than Bi⁺⁵). Lighter members (B, C, N) show their group oxidation state more readily.

cards.front:
GLASS (used in windows, bottles) is mainly:

(A) Pure aluminium oxide layer cast
(B) Amorphous silica (SiO₂) with additives
(C) Crystalline carbon nano-structure
(D) Polymer of plastic with glass colour
cards.back:
(B) Amorphous silica (SiO₂) with additives

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — GLASS = AMORPHOUS (non-crystalline) form of SILICA (SiO₂). Made by melting sand (~73% SiO₂), soda ash (Na₂CO₃ ~14%), limestone (CaCO₃ ~9%) at ~1500°C → cools to amorphous solid. Common 'soda-lime glass' for windows, bottles. PYREX = borosilicate (added B₂O₃) — heat-resistant for lab + cookware. CRYSTAL glass = lead glass (PbO added, higher refractive index, 'sparkle'). FIBRE-OPTIC glass = ultra-pure silica with controlled refractive index profile. Glass is technically a SUPERCOOLED LIQUID — flows extremely slowly over long periods.

cards.front:
Which is the ONLY liquid metal at room temperature (25°C)?

(A) Gallium
(B) Mercury (Hg)
(C) Cesium
(D) Rubidium
cards.back:
(B) Mercury (Hg)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — MERCURY (Hg, atomic number 80) is the ONLY metal liquid at standard room temperature (~25°C). Melting point: −38.83°C. Also called 'quicksilver'. Used in thermometers, barometers, fluorescent lamps — but toxic, so being phased out (Minamata Convention 2013). GALLIUM (Ga, mp 29.76°C) — melts in your warm hand but SOLID at 25°C. CESIUM (mp 28.44°C) and RUBIDIUM (mp 39.31°C) also melt just above room temp but are SOLID at 25°C — and they're highly reactive alkali metals. FRANCIUM (mp ~27°C estimated; highly radioactive). Among NON-METALS, BROMINE is the only element liquid at room temp (mp −7°C). So the other LIQUID element at RT is BROMINE (non-metal).

cards.front:
Brass is an alloy of:

(A) Copper and tin
(B) Copper and zinc
(C) Iron and carbon
(D) Aluminium and magnesium
cards.back:
(B) Copper and zinc

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Key alloys with compositions: BRASS = Cu (~70%) + Zn (~30%). BRONZE = Cu + Sn (tin) — the oldest alloy (Bronze Age ~3300 BCE). STEEL = Fe + C (< 2%). STAINLESS STEEL = Fe + Cr (11%+) + Ni. CAST IRON = Fe + C (2-4%). WROUGHT IRON = Fe + C (<0.2%). SOLDER = Pb + Sn (historically). PEWTER = Sn + Sb + Cu. DURALUMIN = Al + Cu + Mg + Mn (aircraft). MAGNALIUM = Al + Mg (light). NICHROME = Ni + Cr + Fe (heating elements). GERMAN SILVER (despite name, no silver) = Cu + Ni + Zn. MONEL = Ni + Cu. AMALGAM = any metal + Hg (dental fillings: Hg + Ag + Sn + Cu). WHITE GOLD = Au + Pd or Au + Ni. ROSE GOLD = Au + Cu.

Which metal is extracted from the ore BAUXITE?

(A) Copper
(B) Aluminium
(C) Zinc
(D) Iron
cards.back:
(B) Aluminium

MAGNESIUM from DOLOMITE (MgCO₃·CaCO₃), MAGNESITE, seawater. URANIUM from PITCHBLENDE / URANINITE (UO₂), MONAZITE (also Th).

cards.front:
Galvanisation is a process in which iron is coated with which metal to prevent rusting?

(A) Copper
(B) Zinc
(C) Tin
(D) Nickel
cards.back:
(B) Zinc

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — GALVANISATION = coating iron with ZINC to prevent rusting. Zinc is more reactive than iron — acts as SACRIFICIAL PROTECTION (even if the zinc layer scratches, Zn corrodes preferentially). Hot-dip (most common) or electroplating. Used for GI sheets, pipes, nails, water tanks. TINNING = iron coated with TIN (less reactive, forms barrier; used for food cans — tin doesn't react with most foods). Comparison corrosion protection methods: (1) GALVANISATION (Zn coat); (2) TINNING (Sn coat); (3) PAINTING / ENAMELLING; (4) ELECTROPLATING (Cu, Cr, Ni); (5) ALLOYING (stainless steel = Fe + Cr); (6) CATHODIC PROTECTION with a more reactive sacrificial anode (Mg bars on ship hulls).

cards.front:
Which metal has the HIGHEST electrical conductivity at room temperature?

(A) Copper
(B) Silver
(C) Gold
(D) Aluminium
cards.back:
(B) Silver

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Electrical conductivity (highest to lower among common metals): SILVER (Ag — highest), COPPER (Cu — 2nd, widely used due to lower cost), GOLD (Au — 3rd, used in fine electronics for corrosion resistance), ALUMINIUM (Al — lighter, used in overhead power lines), TUNGSTEN, ZINC, NICKEL. Heat conductivity has a similar order (Wiedemann-Franz law). Diamond (non-metal) actually has the highest THERMAL conductivity, but is an electrical INSULATOR. Among metals, silver is also the most REFLECTIVE (mirrors historically used silver backing). Superconductors (like Hg below 4.2K, YBa2Cu3O7 above 77K 'high-Tc') have ZERO electrical resistance below critical temp.

cards.front:
Stainless steel is primarily an alloy of iron with which two other metals?

(A) Copper and zinc
(B) Chromium and nickel
(C) Aluminium and magnesium
(D) Tin and lead
cards.back:
(B) Chromium and nickel

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — STAINLESS STEEL = Fe + Chromium (≥ 10.5%) + Nickel (often 8%+) + small C. The chromium forms a passive Cr₂O₃ layer that prevents rusting — this is the 'stainless' property. Discovered 1913 by Harry Brearley (Sheffield, UK). Grades: 304 (18-8 — most common, 18% Cr 8% Ni), 316 (adds Mo for marine corrosion), 410 (cutlery). Mo is sometimes added for acid resistance. Nichrome = Ni + Cr + Fe (heating coils). Invar = Fe + Ni (36% Ni — low thermal expansion, used in precision instruments). Kovar = Fe + Ni + Co (matches borosilicate glass expansion).

cards.front:
The process of heating an ore in the presence of EXCESS AIR to convert it into an oxide is called:

(A) Calcination
(B) Roasting
(C) Smelting
(D) Refining
cards.back:
(B) Roasting

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Metallurgy steps: (1) CRUSHING & GRINDING; (2) CONCENTRATION (froth flotation for sulphides, gravity separation, magnetic separation, leaching); (3) CONVERSION TO OXIDE: • ROASTING = heat in presence of EXCESS AIR (sulphide ores → oxides; e.g., 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂); • CALCINATION = heat in LIMITED / absence of air (carbonate/hydrate ores → oxides; e.g., ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂ or CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ or Al₂O₃·xH₂O → Al₂O₃ + H₂O); (4) REDUCTION: • SMELTING (carbon reduction in blast furnace — for Fe, Cu, Zn, Pb); • ALUMINOTHERMIC (for Mn, Cr); • ELECTROLYSIS (for reactive metals — Al, Mg, Na); (5) REFINING (liquation, poling, electrolytic — Cu, Zn, Al, Ag, Au).

The MOST reactive metal in the reactivity series (from those commonly tested) is:

(A) Iron
(B) Potassium
(C) Copper
(D) Zinc
cards.back:
(B) Potassium

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — Reactivity series (most → least reactive): K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Ag > Au > Pt. Potassium reacts violently with water. Gold and platinum are the least reactive (noble metals).

cards.front:
The ONLY non-metal that is LIQUID at room temperature is:

(A) Mercury
(B) Bromine
(C) Iodine
(D) Sulphur
cards.back:

cards.front:
The most ABUNDANT gas in the Earth's atmosphere by volume is:

(A) Oxygen (~21%)
(B) Carbon dioxide (~0.04%)
(C) NITROGEN (N₂) — ~78.09% by volume; inert diatomic molecule with a very strong triple bond (bond energy 946 kJ/mol)
(D) Argon (~0.93%)
cards.back:
(C) NITROGEN (N₂) — ~78.09% by volume; inert diatomic molecule with a very strong triple bond (bond energy 946 kJ/mol)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — EARTH'S ATMOSPHERE composition (by volume, in dry air): (1) NITROGEN N₂ — 78.09%; (2) OXYGEN O₂ — 20.95%; (3) ARGON Ar — 0.93%; (4) CARBON DIOXIDE CO₂ — 0.042% (420+ ppm, 2024); (5) TRACES of Neon, Helium, Methane CH₄, Krypton, Hydrogen, Xenon, Nitrous oxide N₂O, Ozone O₃. WATER VAPOUR is variable (0-4%). NITROGEN — diatomic molecule N≡N with very STRONG triple bond (946 kJ/mol), making it EXTREMELY UNREACTIVE at ordinary temperatures. Despite abundance, N₂ is unusable directly by most organisms. Must be ‘FIXED’ (converted to NH₃ or nitrates) by: (a) BIOLOGICAL FIXATION — symbiotic Rhizobium bacteria in leguminous root nodules; cyanobacteria (BGA — blue-green algae) like Anabaena, Nostoc; free-living soil bacteria Azotobacter, Clostridium; (b) LIGHTNING FIXATION — atmospheric N₂ + O₂ under lightning discharge → NO → NO₂ → HNO₃ (rain → soil nitrates); minor but historically important (few kg N/hectare/year); (c) INDUSTRIAL — HABER-BOSCH PROCESS (1908-13): N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ at high T + P over Fe catalyst; produces ammonia → fertilisers; feeds ~half the world. USES OF NITROGEN: (1) in fertilisers — urea (CO(NH₂)₂, 46% N, world's most used fertiliser), ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulphate, DAP, NPK; (2) PACKAGING — inert atmosphere for food packaging (chips, snacks) to prevent oxidation + rancidity; (3) LIQUID NITROGEN (boiling point -196°C) — cryogenic cooling (superconducting magnets in MRI, semiconductor industry, biological preservation of sperm/ova/tissue), food freezing, cryotherapy for warts; (4) TYRE INFLATION — more stable pressure under temperature variation than air; used in F1 + aviation; (5) FLUSHING INDUSTRIAL PIPELINES; (6) EXPLOSIVES — TNT (trinitrotoluene), RDX (cyclotrimethylenetrinitramine), PETN, dynamite. NITROGEN COMPOUNDS of EXAM interest: (a) NH₃ (ammonia) — pungent gas, key industrial chemical; (b) HNO₃ (nitric acid) — strong oxidising acid, manufactured by OSTWALD process (4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O → 2NO₂ → HNO₃ via Pt catalyst); used in fertilisers + explosives; (c) N₂O (nitrous oxide / LAUGHING GAS) — anaesthetic, whipped cream propellant, GHG (298x CO₂); (d) NO (nitric oxide) — signalling molecule in biology (1998 Medicine Nobel to Furchgott+Ignarro+Murad); (e) NO₂ (nitrogen dioxide) — brown toxic gas, vehicle exhaust + power plant, contributes to photochemical smog + acid rain; (f) NH₄NO₃ (ammonium nitrate) — fertiliser + explosive (Oklahoma City 1995, Beirut 2020); (g) DYNAMITE — nitroglycerin absorbed on diatomaceous earth (Nobel, 1867); (h) AZIDE NaN₃ — airbag propellant. NITROGEN CYCLE — see Environment book: fixation → nitrification (Nitrosomonas: NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻; Nitrobacter: NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻) → assimilation by plants → ammonification (decay) → denitrification (Pseudomonas: NO₃⁻ → N₂ back to atmosphere).

cards.front:
The only NON-METAL that is LIQUID at room temperature is:

(A) Mercury (liquid, but METAL)
(B) Iodine (solid, sublimes)
(C) BROMINE (Br₂) — reddish-brown, fuming, toxic liquid; melts at -7.2°C, boils at 58.8°C; one of only 2 LIQUID ELEMENTS at room temperature (the other is MERCURY, a metal)
(D) Sulphur (solid, yellow)
cards.back:
(C) BROMINE (Br₂) — reddish-brown, fuming, toxic liquid; melts at -7.2°C, boils at 58.8°C; one of only 2 LIQUID ELEMENTS at room temperature (the other is MERCURY, a metal)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — BROMINE (Br₂, atomic number 35) — a HALOGEN (group 17); at room temperature, it is a DEEP REDDISH-BROWN LIQUID that FUMES (evaporates easily). ONLY NON-METAL ELEMENT LIQUID at room temperature (25°C). Other LIQUID ELEMENTS at room temperature: MERCURY (Hg) — only liquid METAL; and close-to-liquid are CAESIUM (Cs, m.p. 28.4°C, liquid in tropical summer), GALLIUM (Ga, m.p. 29.8°C, melts in warm hand), RUBIDIUM (Rb, m.p. 39.3°C), FRANCIUM (m.p. ~27°C, but radioactive + extremely rare). DISCOVERY of BROMINE: 1826 by ANTOINE JÉRÔME BALARD (French chemist, age 24, working in Montpellier; obtained it from seaweed ash + later from bittern of sea salt brines). Independently by CARL JACOB LÖWIG in Germany. NAMED from Greek ‘bromos’ = ‘stench’ (intensely pungent smell). OCCURRENCE: mainly as BROMIDE SALTS in seawater (65 ppm); in brines of DEAD SEA (Israel-Jordan, 0.8% Br), Mediterranean, Arkansas (USA); some in Indian salt production at GUJARAT+TN coasts. Commercially extracted by oxidation of Br⁻ with Cl₂: 2NaBr + Cl₂ → 2NaCl + Br₂. HAZARDS: highly TOXIC + CORROSIVE; causes burns, respiratory damage; vapour 3.1× denser than air, settles in low areas. USES: (1) Fire retardants — brominated compounds in plastics, textiles (but some banned — PBDEs persistent pollutants). (2) Photography — SILVER BROMIDE (AgBr) in traditional B&W film emulsions (along with AgCl, AgI); this use declined with digital. (3) Pharmaceuticals — potassium bromide (KBr) was historically used as anti-epileptic / sedative (hence Victorian ‘take a bromide’); still veterinary use. (4) Drilling fluids — dense bromide brines (ZnBr₂, CaBr₂). (5) Water treatment — as BrO⁻ or BCDMH for swimming pools, hot tubs (less harsh than chlorine). (6) Agrochemicals — methyl bromide fumigant (largely banned under Montreal Protocol as ozone-depleting). (7) Gasoline additive — ethylene dibromide was scavenger in leaded gasoline (phased out). HALOGEN group (Group 17): FLUORINE (F₂, pale yellow gas, MOST ELECTRONEGATIVE element; MOST REACTIVE of all non-metals; found in fluorite CaF₂ + fluorapatite; added to water + toothpaste as fluoride for teeth; HF etches glass; Teflon PTFE non-stick); CHLORINE (Cl₂, pale green pungent gas; used to kill bacteria in drinking water + swimming pools; making PVC; bleaching powder CaOCl₂; HCl in gastric juice; mustard gas C4H8Cl2S is WWI chemical weapon); BROMINE (as above); IODINE (I₂, purple-black solid, sublimes to violet vapour; in seaweed, potassium iodide added to TABLE SALT to prevent goitre from iodine deficiency; tincture of iodine antiseptic; radioactive I-131 for thyroid imaging/treatment; I-127 is stable isotope). ASTATINE (At, extremely rare, radioactive). TENNESSINE (Ts, synthetic, 2010). All halogens form HALIDE SALTS with alkali metals (NaCl, KBr, etc.) and HALOGEN ACIDS with hydrogen (HF, HCl, HBr, HI).

cards.front:
Of the following, which NON-METAL has the HIGHEST MELTING POINT and is the HARDEST natural substance?

(A) Sulphur (m.p. 115°C)
(B) Phosphorus (white, m.p. 44°C)
(C) DIAMOND (allotrope of CARBON) — m.p. ~3,550°C; HARDEST natural substance (10 on Mohs scale); tetrahedral sp³ covalent network; high refractive index (2.42); UNIQUE non-metal exception to the rule that non-metals are soft + low-melting
(D) Iodine (m.p. 114°C, sublimes)
cards.back:
(C) DIAMOND (allotrope of CARBON) — m.p. ~3,550°C; HARDEST natural substance (10 on Mohs scale); tetrahedral sp³ covalent network; high refractive index (2.42); UNIQUE non-metal exception to the rule that non-metals are soft + low-melting

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — DIAMOND — one of the ALLOTROPES of CARBON (the others: graphite, fullerenes, graphene, amorphous carbon, carbon nanotubes, carbyne, lonsdaleite). Diamond's UNIQUE properties make it an EXCEPTION to the general rule that non-metals are soft + low-melting: (1) HARDEST known NATURAL material (10 on Mohs scale); (2) HIGHEST MELTING POINT among non-metals (m.p. ~3,550°C, even higher under high pressure); (3) BEST NATURAL THERMAL CONDUCTOR (5× better than copper at room T); (4) high REFRACTIVE INDEX (2.42) — causes the characteristic SPARKLE / ‘fire’ from TOTAL INTERNAL REFLECTION + dispersion of white light into rainbow colours; (5) densest form of carbon (3.52 g/cm³); (6) transparent to UV + visible; (7) ELECTRICAL INSULATOR (despite being carbon); (8) CHEMICALLY INERT — resistant to acids; burns in O₂ only at >700°C. STRUCTURE of DIAMOND: each carbon atom forms FOUR sp³ COVALENT BONDS with 4 neighbouring carbons in a TETRAHEDRAL arrangement; extends in all 3 dimensions creating a RIGID CRYSTAL lattice with NO WEAK DIRECTIONS — hence hardness + hardness anisotropy. NATURAL DIAMONDS formed in the Earth's MANTLE under extreme pressure (>45 kbar) + heat (>900°C) at depths of 140-190 km, over millions of years. Brought to surface by deep-volcanic KIMBERLITE PIPES (named after Kimberley, South Africa — major source). MAJOR PRODUCERS today: Russia (largest, Alrosa), Botswana (Debswana, GEM quality), Canada, DR Congo, Australia (Argyle — famous for pink diamonds, closed 2020), South Africa. INDIA's DIAMOND HISTORY: (a) KIMBERLEY/GOLCONDA diamonds of AP-Telangana (Raichur doab) were the world's only source for ~1,800 years till Brazilian + African discoveries; (b) FAMOUS Indian diamonds: KOH-I-NOOR (‘Mountain of Light’, 105.6 carats now, taken by British 1849 from Lahore after Sikh war; mounted in Queen Mother's Crown, at Tower of London), HOPE DIAMOND (45.5 ct blue, now at Smithsonian — allegedly cursed), REGENT (140 ct), NASSAK, ORLOFF, DARYA-I-NOOR (‘Sea of Light’, Iran), PITT; (c) Indian DIAMOND CUTTING industry — SURAT, GUJARAT — cuts 90% of world's small diamonds; turnover $25B+. OTHER CARBON ALLOTROPES: (1) GRAPHITE — hexagonal sheets, weak inter-layer forces → soft, slippery, good lubricant (+conducts electricity — electrodes, pencils). (2) FULLERENES (C₆₀ ‘buckminsterfullerene’ — 1985 Nobel Kroto, Curl, Smalley; shaped like soccer ball; superconductors, drug delivery). (3) CARBON NANOTUBES (1991 Iijima) — cylindrical rolled graphene; ultra-strong, conductive, 100x steel strength. (4) GRAPHENE (2004 Geim + Novoselov, Nobel 2010) — single atomic layer of graphite; strongest material ever measured, transparent, highly conductive, 200× stronger than steel; huge future potential. (5) AMORPHOUS CARBON — charcoal, soot, lampblack. SYNTHETIC DIAMONDS: produced by (a) HIGH PRESSURE HIGH TEMPERATURE (HPHT, mimics Earth, since 1955 GE); (b) CHEMICAL VAPOUR DEPOSITION (CVD, from methane gas on a seed crystal) — 2020s trend: lab-grown diamonds identical to natural; increasingly popular + cheaper. India is a major CVD diamond producer/exporter. USES of DIAMOND: (i) JEWELLERY (80% of natural, by value); (ii) ABRASIVE + CUTTING tools — drill bits, saw blades, surgical scalpels; (iii) HEAT SINKS in electronics; (iv) HIGH-PRESSURE ANVIL cells in research; (v) optical windows; (vi) quantum computing (NV centres). DIAMOND CARAT = 200 mg = 0.2 g.

cards.front:
Which of the following gases is used to extinguish fires in LARGE ELECTRICAL / COMPUTING EQUIPMENT (e.g., data centres)?

(A) Oxygen
(B) Chlorine
(C) CARBON DIOXIDE (CO₂) + INERT GASES
(D) Hydrogen
cards.back:
(C) CARBON DIOXIDE (CO₂) + INERT GASES

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — FIRE EXTINGUISHING — fire requires the ‘FIRE TRIANGLE’: FUEL + OXYGEN + HEAT (some add 4th element — CHEMICAL CHAIN REACTION — ‘fire tetrahedron’). REMOVE any one → fire goes out. For ELECTRICAL / ELECTRONIC equipment (servers, data centres, museum archives, aircraft), WATER + FOAM are UNSUITABLE: (a) water conducts electricity — shock risk + short circuits; (b) leaves residue damaging sensitive electronics + paper records; (c) can spread some burning liquids. PREFERRED EXTINGUISHING AGENTS for these environments: (1) CO₂ — CARBON DIOXIDE GAS: displaces oxygen below ~15%, suffocating the fire; colourless, odourless, non-conductive, leaves no residue; rapidly disperses. STANDARD CO₂ FIRE EXTINGUISHERS are black-banded in India (earlier entirely red, BIS IS 15683). Drawbacks: (a) lowers oxygen, dangerous for humans in enclosed spaces; (b) short-term cooling effect only. (2) DRY POWDER (Class A/B/C multi-purpose — sodium bicarbonate NaHCO₃, potassium bicarbonate KHCO₃, or monoammonium phosphate NH₄H₂PO₄). For class A (solid), B (liquid), C (gas) fires. Leaves residue. (3) CLEAN AGENTS — halocarbons + inert gas mixtures: (a) HALONS — Halon 1211 (BCF), Halon 1301 (BTM) — super-effective but BANNED under MONTREAL PROTOCOL as OZONE-DEPLETING; still used in critical aerospace + military till phase-out; replacements mandated since 1994. (b) HFC-227ea (HEPTAFLUOROPROPANE, FM-200) — widely used for data centre rooms; rapid discharge; no residue; breathable at design concentration. But is a GHG. (c) HFC-125, NOVEC 1230 (fluoroketone, 3M, low GWP, Tesla uses it for lithium battery fire). (d) INERGEN (IG-541) — mixture of 52% N₂ + 40% Ar + 8% CO₂; suppresses combustion while keeping air still breathable. (e) ARGONITE / IG-55 — 50% N₂ + 50% Ar. (f) IG-100 — pure N₂. (g) IG-01 — pure Ar. (4) WATER MIST — fine water droplets convert to steam, cool + displace oxygen; used on ships. FIRE CLASSES (most countries): CLASS A — solid materials (paper, wood, textiles) — water, foam; Class B — flammable liquids (petrol, oil) — foam, CO₂, dry powder; Class C — flammable gases — dry powder, water spray; Class D — combustible metals (Mg, Na, K, Al) — special dry powder (graphite, sodium chloride); Class E — electrical — CO₂, dry powder, clean agents; Class F/K — cooking oils/fats — wet chemical, foam. WATER vs GREASE FIRE: NEVER pour water on oil fires — causes massive flare-up (steam ejects hot oil). Smother with lid, use Class K extinguisher. COMMON EXTINGUISHER COLOUR (India, BIS): Red — Water / Class A; Cream — Foam / Class B; Black — CO₂ / electrical; Blue — dry powder; Yellow — wet chemical. (UK: red body, coloured band; USA: all red with label). displace oxygen without damaging equipment or leaving residue; safer than water/foam for live electronics; Argon, Nitrogen, mixtures like INERGEN.
cards.storedExplanation: FIRE EXTINGUISHING — fire requires the ‘FIRE TRIANGLE’: FUEL + OXYGEN + HEAT (some add 4th element — CHEMICAL CHAIN REACTION — ‘fire tetrahedron’). REMOVE any one → fire goes out. For ELECTRICAL / ELECTRONIC equipment (servers, data centres, museum archives, aircraft), WATER + FOAM are UNSUITABLE: (a) water conducts electricity — shock risk + short circuits; (b) leaves residue damaging sensitive electronics + paper records; (c) can spread some burning liquids. PREFERRED EXTINGUISHING AGENTS for these environments: (1) CO₂ — CARBON DIOXIDE GAS: displaces oxygen below ~15%, suffocating the fire; colourless, odourless, non-conductive, leaves no residue; rapidly disperses. STANDARD CO₂ FIRE EXTINGUISHERS are black-banded in India (earlier entirely red, BIS IS 15683). Drawbacks: (a) lowers oxygen, dangerous for humans in enclosed spaces; (b) short-term cooling effect only. (2) DRY POWDER (Class A/B/C multi-purpose — sodium bicarbonate NaHCO₃, potassium bicarbonate KHCO₃, or monoammonium phosphate NH₄H₂PO₄). For class A (solid), B (liquid), C (gas) fires. (c) HFC-125, NOVEC 1230 (fluoroketone, 3M, low GWP, Tesla uses it for lithium battery fire). (d) INERGEN (IG-541) — mixture of 52% N₂ + 40% Ar + 8% CO₂; suppresses combustion while keeping air still breathable. (e) ARGONITE / IG-55 — 50% N₂ + 50% Ar. (f) IG-100 — pure N₂. (g) IG-01 — pure Ar. (4) WATER MIST — fine water droplets convert to steam, cool + displace oxygen; used on ships. (UK: red body, coloured band; USA: all red with label). displace oxygen without damaging equipment or leaving residue; safer than water/foam for live electronics; Argon, Nitrogen, mixtures like INERGEN.

cards.front:
SULPHUR occurs commonly in nature in several ALLOTROPES. Its most stable allotrope at room temperature is:

(A) Monoclinic (β)
(B) Plastic (γ)
(C) RHOMBIC / α-SULPHUR
(D) Liquid
cards.back:
(C) RHOMBIC / α-SULPHUR

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — SULPHUR (S, atomic number 16, group 16 Chalcogens) — known to ancients as ‘BRIMSTONE’. YELLOW solid at room temp; insoluble in water; soluble in CS₂. Exists in many ALLOTROPES (structural variants): (1) RHOMBIC / α-SULPHUR — YELLOW, brittle, octahedral/rhombic crystals; density 2.06; m.p. 112.8°C; MOST STABLE below 96°C; composed of PUCKERED CROWN-SHAPED S₈ RINGS. (2) MONOCLINIC / β-SULPHUR — needle-like, pale-yellow crystals; formed when rhombic is heated above 96°C; m.p. 119°C; stable between 96 and 119°C; also S₈ rings but packed differently. (3) PLASTIC / γ-SULPHUR — amorphous, dark-amber, rubbery; formed by rapidly cooling boiling S (~444°C) in cold water; S atoms form LONG CHAIN polymers; unstable, reverts to rhombic over time. (4) MILK OF SULPHUR / colloidal — fine yellow powder. OCCURRENCE: free in NATURE as S₈ (volcanic regions — Sicily, Texas, USA; once mined near Mount Etna); as SULPHIDES (pyrite FeS₂ ‘fool's gold’, galena PbS, chalcopyrite CuFeS₂, cinnabar HgS, stibnite Sb₂S₃); as SULPHATES (gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O, barite BaSO₄, epsom salt MgSO₄·7H₂O); in organic matter (proteins — amino acids cysteine + methionine; coal, petroleum); in HUMAN BODY (~140 g in adult, 3rd most common element after Ca, P). FRASCH PROCESS (1891 by Herman Frasch) — earlier main method: superheated steam (165°C) pumped into underground sulphur deposits; sulphur melts + rises via air-lift; cooled on surface — 99.9% pure. Nowadays, ~90% of industrial S is RECOVERED as by-product from desulphurisation of oil+gas (CLAUS process). USES: (1) SULPHURIC ACID (H₂SO₄) — ‘KING OF CHEMICALS’; most produced industrial chemical; CONTACT PROCESS uses V₂O₅ catalyst: S + O₂ → SO₂ → SO₃ → H₂SO₄. Uses: fertilisers (SSP single superphosphate, DAP diammonium phosphate), lead-acid batteries, detergents, petroleum refining, explosives, dye/pigments. H₂SO₄ is 80% of sulphur's use. (2) GUNPOWDER — 75% KNO₃ + 15% charcoal + 10% SULPHUR (ancient Chinese, 9th c.); used in fireworks, pyrotechnics. (3) MATCHES — red P + KClO₃ + S for striking head. (4) RUBBER VULCANISATION — Charles Goodyear 1839; heating rubber + sulphur → strong cross-linked elastic rubber (essential for car tyres, industrial rubber). (5) FUNGICIDE + INSECTICIDE — lime-sulphur spray. (6) MEDICINE — Ayurvedic ‘gandhaka’; antibiotic sulfa drugs (sulphonamides) like sulphanilamide — first large class of antibiotics (1935, Prontosil, Domagk Nobel 1939); acne cream. (7) BLACK GUNPOWDER + FIREWORKS pyrotechnics. (8) HYDROGEN SULPHIDE H₂S — rotten-egg smell; volcanic vents; toxic (more lethal than HCN at higher conc). (9) SO₂ — used as PRESERVATIVE (E220) in wine, dried fruits; bleaching wool + silk; dressing of jute. SULPHUR-containing amino acids: CYSTEINE (forms disulphide bridges stabilising proteins like insulin, keratin in hair/nails — that is why burnt hair has characteristic S smell), METHIONINE (start codon translation). HAIR PERMS — reshape by breaking + reforming disulphide bonds. yellow, brittle crystals; puckered S₈ rings; m.p. 113°C; most stable below 96°C; transitions to monoclinic above that.

cards.front:
PHOSPHORUS in the form of WHITE PHOSPHORUS (P₄) is:

(A) Stable and inert
(B) Extremely REACTIVE + TOXIC + SELF-IGNITES in AIR above 34°C
(C) Soluble in water
(D) The most abundant form in nature
cards.back:
(B) Extremely REACTIVE + TOXIC + SELF-IGNITES in AIR above 34°C

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — PHOSPHORUS (P, Z=15, group 15 Pnictogens). DISCOVERED 1669 by HENNIG BRAND (German alchemist) while experimenting with URINE (boiled 50 buckets down to a paste, distilled → glowed in dark — white phosphorus); 1st element discovered since prehistoric times; name from Greek ‘phos’ = light + ‘phoros’ = bearing (‘light-bearer’). Several ALLOTROPES: (1) WHITE PHOSPHORUS (WP, α-P₄) — colourless/yellow waxy SOLID; highly REACTIVE + TOXIC; bursts into flame spontaneously above 34°C in AIR (pyrophoric); stored UNDER WATER; emits faint green glow in dark (PHOSPHORESCENCE from slow oxidation to P₂O₃); extremely poisonous (lethal dose ~50 mg); causes ‘PHOSSY JAW’ (necrosis of jaw bone) — historical occupational disease in match-factory workers (19th c.). Used in military as INCENDIARY WEAPON (WP shells, smoke screens) — controversial under international humanitarian law due to burning injuries. Historic use in matches (dangerous, banned for safety — now red P used). WP has a tetrahedral P₄ molecular structure. (2) RED PHOSPHORUS — polymeric (chains of P atoms); dark red powder; NON-TOXIC + STABLE; ignition point ~260°C. Used in: (a) SAFETY MATCHES (on the striking surface; head contains KClO₃ + S + glass powder + glue); rubbed on red P strip → friction ignites P → heat ignites match head — invented 1855. (b) fireworks, smoke bombs; flame retardants; methamphetamine precursor (regulated). (3) BLACK PHOSPHORUS — LAYERED structure similar to graphite; MOST STABLE allotrope but requires high pressure to form; similar to 2D material like graphene — new research interest for electronics + batteries. (4) VIOLET PHOSPHORUS — crystalline; another stable allotrope. USES OF PHOSPHORUS (element): (1) FERTILISERS — P is one of 3 main plant macronutrients (NPK); as PHOSPHATE ROCK (Ca₃(PO₄)₂, fluorapatite) → processed to SUPERPHOSPHATE (Ca(H₂PO₄)₂) + TRIPLE SUPERPHOSPHATE + DAP (diammonium phosphate, (NH₄)₂HPO₄). Largest P use. (2) DETERGENTS (earlier — STPP, sodium tripolyphosphate; now restricted due to eutrophication). (3) MATCHES (red P). (4) FIREWORKS. (5) MILITARY — WP incendiaries. (6) PHARMACEUTICALS — metabolism-related drugs. (7) SOFT DRINKS — H₃PO₄ (phosphoric acid) in cola for tartness. (8) PHOSPHATE BUFFERS in biological labs. BIOLOGICAL ROLES — phosphorus is ESSENTIAL for life: (a) DNA + RNA backbones (phosphodiester bonds between nucleotides); (b) ATP — adenosine triphosphate, the ENERGY CURRENCY of cells (3 phosphate groups; hydrolysis of one phosphate releases ~30 kJ/mol of energy for cellular work); (c) BONES + TEETH — 85% of body's P is in bones as hydroxyapatite Ca₅(PO₄)₃(OH); (d) PHOSPHOLIPIDS of CELL MEMBRANES (bilayer, phosphate head + lipid tail); (e) PHOSPHORYLATION (adding phosphate) is a key regulatory mechanism for enzymes + proteins. DEFICIENCY: weak bones, fatigue, muscle weakness. Mostly sufficient in normal diet (meat, dairy, fish, nuts, pulses). PHOSPHATE ROCK is a FINITE RESOURCE — the P nutrient cycle does not have atmospheric fixation like N; concerns about ‘PEAK PHOSPHORUS’ (may run out in 50-100 years based on current consumption). 85% of world's phosphate rock is in MOROCCO (incl. occupied Western Sahara); other top producers: China, USA (Florida), Russia, Jordan. stored UNDER WATER; used in matches + incendiary weapons; red allotrope is safer and is the match-striking powder.

cards.front:
Of the NOBLE GASES (group 18), which one is used to fill LIGHT BULBS (incandescent + fluorescent) and in WELDING to provide an inert atmosphere?

(A) Helium
(B) Neon
(C) ARGON (Ar)
(D) Xenon
cards.back:
(C) ARGON (Ar)

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — ARGON (Ar, Z=18, Group 18 Noble Gases) — Greek ‘argos’ = ‘inactive’. Discovered 1894 by LORD RAYLEIGH + WILLIAM RAMSAY (Nobel Chemistry 1904) by comparing air-derived N₂ with chemically-prepared N₂ and finding a density discrepancy → a new heavier inert gas. First noble gas discovered. ABUNDANCE: 3rd MOST ABUNDANT gas in Earth's atmosphere (~0.93% by volume); more abundant than CO₂. Produced mainly by RADIOACTIVE DECAY of ⁴⁰K (potassium-40) in Earth's crust → ⁴⁰Ar → atmosphere. Argon is 99.6% ⁴⁰Ar. PROPERTIES: colourless, odourless, tasteless, non-flammable, INERT (doesn't form stable compounds under normal conditions; only fragile HArF known, 2000 discovery). Boiling point -186°C. Density ~1.4× that of air. USES (why ARGON dominates industrial inert applications): (1) INCANDESCENT LIGHT BULBS — the glass envelope is filled with mixture of ARGON (93%) + a little NITROGEN; prevents the tungsten filament from OXIDISING + REDUCES EVAPORATION of W (high-T sublimation) → extends bulb life; ditto for FLUORESCENT + CFL bulbs (Ar + Hg vapour). (2) WELDING SHIELDING GAS — TIG (tungsten inert gas), MIG (metal inert gas) welding use pure Ar or Ar-CO₂ mix to protect the weld pool from oxygen + nitrogen of atmosphere; essential for stainless steel, aluminum, titanium welding. (3) METAL PROCESSING — Ar atmosphere for Ti + Zr + W production (these otherwise react with O₂ + N₂). (4) PRESERVATION — protective atmosphere for old/archival documents (National Archives, USA); wine preservation after opening; food packaging; pharmaceutical manufacture. (5) SEMICONDUCTOR industry — during silicon crystal growth, inert atmosphere. (6) CRYOGENIC coolant (though liquid N₂ cheaper). (7) SCUBA DIVING — argon in dry suits for insulation. (8) DOUBLE-PANE WINDOWS — Ar between glass panes improves thermal insulation (lower conduction than air). NOBLE GASES (Group 18) — HELIUM, NEON, ARGON, KRYPTON, XENON, RADON, + synthetic OGANESSON (2006, discovered in Dubna Russia, element 118 — completes period 7). WHY ‘NOBLE’? Full valence shell (ns²np⁶, 8 electrons; helium is 1s²), making them extremely UNREACTIVE. Some rare compounds formed with F, O under forcing conditions (XeF₂, XeF₄, XeO₃, KrF₂ — predicted impossible till 1962 by Neil Bartlett's Xe[PtF₆]). HELIUM (He, Z=2) — 2nd lightest element; UNIVERSE'S 2nd MOST ABUNDANT (24%, formed in Big Bang + stellar fusion); on Earth RARE (from radioactive α decay in crust, extracted from natural gas in Texas, USA + Qatar + Russia + Algeria); used in BALLOONS (non-flammable, unlike H₂ which caused Hindenburg 1937), MRI MAGNETS (liquid He coolant, -269°C, superconducting magnets), DEEP-SEA DIVING (mixed with O₂ as heliox to avoid nitrogen narcosis), ROCKETS (pressurising fuel tanks), WELDING of aluminium, leak detection, LAB cryogenics. Helium speaks ‘squeaky’ because sound travels faster in lighter gas. LIMITED SUPPLY concerns — cosmic helium lost to space, not renewable on Earth. NEON (Ne, Z=10) — ‘NEW’; in NEON SIGNS (red-orange glow); TV displays; cryogenics (-246°C). KRYPTON (Kr, 36) — flash lamps, some lasers. XENON (Xe, 54) — photography flash, high-intensity searchlights, car headlights (HID Xenon lamps), ION PROPULSION in spacecraft, general anaesthetic, excimer lasers (XeCl, XeF). RADON (Rn, 86) — radioactive; seeps into basements in some areas → LUNG CANCER risk; naturally from U decay. Ramsay won 1904 Chemistry Nobel for discovering several noble gases. 3rd most abundant gas in atmosphere (0.93%); inert; inexpensive; fills incandescent bulbs (prevents W filament oxidation + sublimation) + arc welding shield (TIG, MIG); cryogenic applications.

cards.front:
Which gas is used to fill WEATHER BALLOONS, and why is it preferred over hydrogen?

(A) Nitrogen — cheap and abundant
(B) HELIUM — because it is NON-FLAMMABLE (hydrogen is); lifting power ~92% of hydrogen's but safety-critical after accidents like HINDENBURG 1937
(C) Argon — heavier than air, floats better
(D) CO₂ — longer altitude hold
cards.back:
(B) HELIUM — because it is NON-FLAMMABLE (hydrogen is); lifting power ~92% of hydrogen's but safety-critical after accidents like HINDENBURG 1937

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — HELIUM (He, Z=2) — used to fill WEATHER BALLOONS, blimps, zeppelins, scientific balloons (NASA stratospheric balloons), party balloons. REASONS for preferring HELIUM over HYDROGEN (even though H₂ is cheaper + gives slightly better LIFT — 1 L of H₂ lifts 1.114 g in air vs He 1.024 g): (1) NON-FLAMMABLE / INERT — He cannot burn or explode; H₂ is highly flammable + explosive in air (4-74% by volume). (2) SAFER — HINDENBURG DISASTER (6 May 1937, Lakehurst, New Jersey, USA): the German zeppelin LZ 129 Hindenburg, filled with 200,000 m³ of H₂, caught fire + exploded during landing, killing 36 of 97 people on board. Broadcast live on radio (famous ‘OH, THE HUMANITY!’ reportage by Herbert Morrison). This ended the commercial airship era. After WWII, Helium (under USA near-monopoly at the time) was made accessible for non-military use. Modern airships (Goodyear Blimp, Zeppelin NT, Sergey Brin's Pathfinder 1) use HELIUM. (3) LIFTING POWER DIFFERENCE is marginal (~8%); safety premium is huge. (4) WEATHER BALLOONS — launched ~1,000+ times/day worldwide by meteorological agencies (India Meteorological Department, NOAA, etc.) for ATMOSPHERIC DATA (temperature, humidity, pressure, wind profile) up to 30+ km altitude; carry RADIOSONDES that transmit real-time data; balloon expands + BURSTS at ceiling; data ends, package parachutes down. Rubber/latex balloons, He-filled. (5) PARTY BALLOONS — though arguably wasteful since He is a FINITE RESOURCE on Earth. OTHER HE USES: (a) MRI machines — liquid He (-269°C, boiling point) cools superconducting magnets of MRI + NMR spectrometers + particle accelerators (LHC at CERN uses 120 tonnes of liquid He). MRI requires a STEADY SUPPLY of He (quench = loss is disaster). (b) SCUBA DIVING ‘HELIOX / TRIMIX’ — He replaces N₂ in breathing gas for deep diving to avoid nitrogen narcosis (‘rapture of the deep’) + decompression sickness (‘the bends’) at depths >50 m. (c) LEAK DETECTION — He atoms are small + inert + rare in atmosphere; He-leak detectors are sensitive. (d) WELDING of aluminium/Mg/refractories. (e) GROWING SILICON CRYSTALS (semiconductor industry). (f) ROCKETS — SpaceX Falcon 9 uses He to pressurise LOX + RP-1 tanks. (g) LABORATORY cryogenics. HELIUM SUPPLY CRISIS: He is extracted from NATURAL GAS wells (0.3-7% He content, formed by radioactive decay deep underground); richest wells in USA (Amarillo, TX), QATAR, ALGERIA, RUSSIA (Amur project, Gazprom). US FEDERAL HELIUM RESERVE in Cliffside TX (largest in world, 1925 established for military airships; sale mandated 1996; finally privatised 2023). Concerns: He released to atmosphere is LOST to space (too light to retain); not renewable at human timescales. SCIENTIFIC COMMUNITY calls for restrictions on balloon/wasteful uses. INDIAN He: India imports nearly all its He; some extracted from natural gas (ONGC), but mostly imported. ISRO uses He in rockets (PSLV + GSLV stages). 2023 — HELIUM India Pvt Ltd started domestic purification. Hydrogen may return: 2020s — hybrid airships (Hindenburg-plus-safety) proposed with inert He outer lift + hot-air core.

cards.front:
OZONE (O₃) in the STRATOSPHERE (~20-30 km altitude) is beneficial because it:

(A) Adds breathable oxygen to the atmosphere
(B) Absorbs most of the Sun's HARMFUL ULTRAVIOLET (UV-B, UV-C) RADIATION
(C) Regulates Earth's temperature via CO₂ buffering
(D) Creates rainfall
cards.back:
(B) Absorbs most of the Sun's HARMFUL ULTRAVIOLET (UV-B, UV-C) RADIATION

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — OZONE (O₃, ‘activated oxygen’) — an ALLOTROPE of OXYGEN consisting of 3 oxygen atoms in a bent triangular molecule (vs common O₂). TWO KEY atmospheric locations: (1) STRATOSPHERIC OZONE (the ‘OZONE LAYER’) at ~15-35 km altitude, concentrated around 20-30 km (Chapman cycle); BENEFICIAL — absorbs ~97-99% of the Sun's dangerous ULTRAVIOLET RADIATION (UV-B 280-315 nm + UV-C 100-280 nm); protects life from skin cancer, cataracts, immune suppression, DNA mutations, coral damage. (2) TROPOSPHERIC / GROUND-LEVEL OZONE (0-10 km, near surface) — HARMFUL pollutant; component of photochemical SMOG (formed by NOₓ + VOCs + sunlight); respiratory irritant, reduces lung function; damages plants + crops. Good ozone up high, bad ozone down low. OZONE LAYER DEGRADATION: discovered 1974 — MARIO MOLINA + F. SHERWOOD ROWLAND (both Nobel Chemistry 1995 with Paul Crutzen) showed that CHLOROFLUOROCARBONS (CFCs — Cl₃CF, Cl₂CF₂, used since 1930s as refrigerants, aerosol propellants, foaming agents, solvents) release Cl radicals in the stratosphere on UV exposure; each Cl can CATALYTICALLY destroy ~100,000 ozone molecules. The ANTARCTIC OZONE HOLE was confirmed in 1985 by BRITISH ANTARCTIC SURVEY (Farman, Gardiner, Shanklin in Nature) — a massive thinning of ozone over Antarctica each spring (September-October). MONTREAL PROTOCOL on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer, signed 16 September 1987, Montreal, Canada; entered force 1 Jan 1989; RATIFIED by 198 UN parties (the ONLY UN treaty ratified universally) → phased out CFCs, halons, methyl bromide, CCl₄, CH₃CCl₃. Developed nations banned by 1996; developing countries by 2010. Replacements: HCFCs (transitional, phasing out by 2030-2040); HFCs (no Cl, hence no ozone effect, but HIGH GWP greenhouse gases — being replaced under KIGALI AMENDMENT 2016 with HFOs + natural refrigerants like CO₂, NH₃, HCs). RESULT: ozone layer is RECOVERING — expected to fully heal by ~2040 (middle latitudes), 2045 (Arctic), 2066 (Antarctic per WMO 2022 assessment). The Montreal Protocol is the GREATEST ENVIRONMENTAL TREATY SUCCESS STORY — proof that collective global action works. 16 September = World Ozone Day. OTHER OZONE FACTS: (a) Pungent smell after thunderstorms (lightning creates O₃ from O₂); (b) USED in water + wastewater treatment as disinfectant (STRONGER oxidiser than Cl₂, no residue); (c) used to bleach paper, textiles; (d) industrial deodorisation; (e) atmospheric chemistry research; (f) MEDICINE — ozone therapy (controversial); (g) dangerous to humans at >0.1 ppm (lung irritant, edema). DOBSON UNIT (DU) — measurement of ozone column thickness; 1 DU = 0.01 mm of pure ozone at 0°C + 1 atm; normal ozone column ~300 DU; ozone hole when <220 DU; minimum over Antarctica reaches ~90 DU. OZONE + UV cycle: O₂ + UV (<242 nm) → 2O; O + O₂ → O₃; O₃ + UV (200-320 nm) → O₂ + O; continuous steady state. But Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂; ClO• + O → Cl• + O₂ — Cl catalyst not consumed, destroys ozone. protecting life from skin cancer, cataracts, DNA damage; measured in DOBSON UNITS.

cards.front:
CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) is a SILENT KILLER because it is:

(A) Coloured and foul-smelling but odour-blind
(B) COLOURLESS + ODOURLESS + TASTELESS
(C) Bright orange + pungent smelling
(D) Liquid at room temperature
cards.back:
(B) COLOURLESS + ODOURLESS + TASTELESS

Metals, Non-metals & Blocks — CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) — a COLOURLESS, ODOURLESS, TASTELESS, NON-IRRITATING, highly toxic gas. HIGHLY DANGEROUS because: (1) SENSORY EVASION — humans cannot detect it without instruments (no smell, no colour, no taste); VICTIMS often unaware until they collapse. (2) MECHANISM OF TOXICITY: CO binds to HAEMOGLOBIN (Hb) with an affinity 240× greater than O₂; forms CARBOXYHAEMOGLOBIN (COHb); red blood cells cannot release O₂ to tissues → HYPOXIA (oxygen starvation) → tissue damage → death. Even 0.04% CO in air can be lethal within hours. (3) ALSO inhibits cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondria; binds myoglobin in muscles. Brain + heart most affected (high O₂ demand). SYMPTOMS: mild — headache, dizziness, nausea, fatigue (often mistaken for flu); moderate — confusion, vomiting, chest pain, drowsiness; severe — unconsciousness, seizures, coma, death. TREATMENT: remove from source + 100% oxygen (in severe cases hyperbaric oxygen therapy). SOURCES of CO: (1) INCOMPLETE COMBUSTION of carbon-containing fuels: gas geysers in poorly-ventilated bathrooms (major cause of bathroom deaths in India); vehicle exhausts (catalytic converters reduce CO → CO₂); kerosene stoves, portable heaters, charcoal grills, improperly vented fireplaces; (2) HOUSE FIRES (smoke kills by CO poisoning before flames); (3) INDUSTRIAL processes (blast furnaces for steel use CO as reducing agent: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂); (4) Cigarette smoke (contains 3-6% CO — chronic smokers have 5-10% COHb). ATMOSPHERIC CO — not a major greenhouse gas but PRECURSOR of ground-level ozone + methane. PREVENTION: install CO detector (alarms at 50-70 ppm); ventilate all combustion appliances; never run generators in closed spaces; annual inspection of gas appliances. INDIAN BUREAU of STANDARDS recommends CO detectors in homes with gas appliances. Signs: ‘GEYSER IN BATHROOM’ deaths regularly reported (Kerala, Goa, Delhi, Mumbai in winter — monsoon months closed ventilation). NFPA (USA) recommends <9 ppm as safe; >100 ppm = dangerous. CO as USEFUL: (1) METALLURGY — reducing agent in blast furnaces (extracting Fe from Fe₂O₃ since ancient times); (2) WATER GAS (CO + H₂) — produced by passing steam over red-hot coke; (3) PRODUCER GAS (CO + N₂) — from burning coke in limited air; used as industrial fuel; (4) FISCHER-TROPSCH process — CO + H₂ over Fe/Co catalyst → synthetic hydrocarbons (used by Germany in WWII, South Africa during apartheid-era oil embargo); (5) CARBONYL process — purification of Ni (metal + CO → Ni(CO)₄ → decomposed back to pure Ni, Mond process); (6) CARBONYLS — organometallic compounds widely used in industrial + lab chemistry; (7) ORGANIC CHEMISTRY — carbonylation reactions (hydroformylation, Reppe chemistry). CARBON DIOXIDE (CO₂) vs CO — CO₂ is odourless + tasteless + colourless too BUT not toxic at normal levels (we exhale it); dangerous only at high concentrations (displaces O₂; >10% → unconsciousness; volcanic vents, LAKE NYOS 1986 disaster in Cameroon where 1,700 asphyxiated by CO₂ cloud from limnic eruption). CO₂ IS A GREENHOUSE GAS — primary driver of anthropogenic climate change. geysers, vehicles, heaters. binds HAEMOGLOBIN 240× STRONGER than O₂, forming CARBOXYHAEMOGLOBIN → oxygen starvation; victims die without realising; produced from INCOMPLETE combustion.

cards.front:
The functional group that defines an alcohol is:

(A) Aldehyde (−CHO)
(B) Hydroxyl (−OH) attached to a saturated carbon
(C) Carboxylic (−COOH)
(D) Amino (−NH₂)
cards.back:
(B) Hydroxyl (−OH) attached to a saturated carbon

Organic Chemistry — ALCOHOL — −OH attached to an sp³ (saturated) carbon. R−OH. Examples: methanol CH₃OH, ethanol C₂H₅OH, propan-2-ol (isopropyl alcohol). PHENOL — −OH attached to an aromatic ring (sp² carbon of benzene); chemically distinct from alcohols (more acidic). ENOL — −OH on a C=C carbon (usually unstable). Alcohols are classified by the carbon bearing OH — primary (R−CH₂OH), secondary (R₂CHOH), tertiary (R₃COH).

cards.front:
Methanol (CH₃OH) is also called wood spirit because:

(A) It is extracted from forest pine
(B) It was historically obtained by destructive distillation of wood
(C) It smells like wood
(D) It is used to polish wood
cards.back:
(B) It was historically obtained by destructive distillation of wood

Organic Chemistry — Methanol — historic name 'wood alcohol' / 'wood spirit' because it was obtained by the destructive distillation of wood (pyrolysis without air). Modern industrial production: catalytic synthesis from CO + 2H₂ (syngas) over a Cu/ZnO/Al₂O₃ catalyst. Highly toxic — small ingestion causes blindness (optic-nerve damage by formate, the toxic metabolite produced by alcohol dehydrogenase + aldehyde dehydrogenase) and death. Treatment: ethanol or fomepizole (competitive inhibitors of ADH) + dialysis. Used as solvent, antifreeze, fuel, and precursor for formaldehyde, acetic acid, MTBE.

cards.option3: It is used to polish wood

cards.front:
Ethanol used in industries is often 'denatured' by adding methanol or pyridine. The purpose is to:

(A) Increase its calorific value
(B) Make it unfit for human consumption (so excise duty for industrial alcohol need not be paid as for potable alcohol)
(C) Lower its boiling point
(D) Change its colour
cards.back:
(B) Make it unfit for human consumption (so excise duty for industrial alcohol need not be paid as for potable alcohol)

Organic Chemistry — Denatured (or 'methylated') spirit — ethanol with poisonous additives (methanol, pyridine, denatonium benzoate — the bitterest substance known) so it cannot be drunk. This avoids the high excise duty levied on potable alcohol while allowing industrial use as solvent, fuel, cleaner. India's blending programme E20 — petrol with 20% ethanol; achieved Apr 2025 (5 years ahead of the 2030 target). Ethanol obtained from sugarcane molasses, broken rice, maize. Power alcohol = anhydrous ethanol blended with petrol.

cards.front:
Glycerol (glycerine) is a tri-hydric alcohol with 3 −OH groups. Its IUPAC name is:

(A) Propan-1-ol
(B) Propane-1,2,3-triol
(C) Propan-2-ol
(D) Ethane-1,2-diol
cards.back:
(B) Propane-1,2,3-triol

Organic Chemistry — Glycerol — HOCH₂−CHOH−CH₂OH; IUPAC name propane-1,2,3-triol. Sweet, viscous, non-toxic; used in cosmetics, soaps (glycerol is a byproduct of soap-making by saponification of fats), pharmaceuticals (cough syrups, suppositories), foods (humectant E422), nitroglycerine (explosive — Alfred Nobel's dynamite, 1867). Propan-1-ol — CH₃CH₂CH₂OH (mono-hydric). Propan-2-ol — IPA, isopropyl alcohol, used in hand sanitiser. Ethane-1,2-diol — ethylene glycol (HOCH₂CH₂OH), antifreeze, polyester (PET) precursor.

cards.front:
Phenol (C₆H₅OH) is more acidic than ethanol primarily because:

(A) Phenol has more −OH groups
(B) The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance / delocalisation of the negative charge into the benzene ring
(C) Phenol has lower molecular weight
(D) Phenol forms hydrogen bonds with water
cards.back:
(B) The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance / delocalisation of the negative charge into the benzene ring

Organic Chemistry — Phenol pKa ≈ 10; ethanol pKa ≈ 16 — phenol is ~10⁶ times more acidic than ethanol. Reason: when phenol loses H⁺, the resulting phenoxide ion (C₆H₅O⁻) has the negative charge delocalised over the aromatic ring (resonance into ortho/para positions). Ethoxide (C₂H₅O⁻) has the negative charge localised on oxygen — less stable. EWGs (NO₂, CN, X) on the ring increase acidity of phenols (ortho/para positions especially); EDGs (CH₃, OCH₃, NH₂) decrease acidity. Used as an antiseptic (Joseph Lister, 1865) — though largely replaced; now used to make Bakelite, aspirin, paracetamol, dyes.
cards.option3: Phenol forms hydrogen bonds with water

cards.front:
Diethyl ether (C₂H₅−O−C₂H₅), an early surgical anaesthetic, has the general formula R−O−R′. Ethers are characterised by:

(A) An OH group
(B) An oxygen atom bonded to two carbon (alkyl/aryl) groups
(C) A C=O double bond
(D) A halogen atom
cards.back:
(B) An oxygen atom bonded to two carbon (alkyl/aryl) groups

Organic Chemistry — Ether — R−O−R′. The two R groups can be the same (symmetrical: dimethyl ether, diethyl ether) or different (asymmetrical: methyl ethyl ether). Diethyl ether — used as a surgical anaesthetic (William Morton, 1846) — replaced by safer agents (halothane, isoflurane). Highly volatile + flammable. Methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE) — petrol additive (octane booster, replaced tetraethyl lead). Cellosolve — ethylene glycol monoethyl ether, industrial solvent. Crown ethers — cyclic polyethers, complex with metal cations (used for selective ion extraction).

cards.front:
The 'absolute alcohol' used in laboratories refers to:

(A) Pure methanol
(B) Anhydrous ethanol — ethanol containing essentially no water (>99.5%)
(C) Ethanol-water 50:50 mixture
(D) Phenol
cards.back:
(B) Anhydrous ethanol — ethanol containing essentially no water (>99.5%)

Organic Chemistry — Ordinary distillation of fermented broth gives ~95.6% ethanol — an azeotrope with water (boils 78.2 °C). To get above 99.5% ('absolute alcohol'), one must break the azeotrope: (1) Drying agents like CaO (quicklime); (2) Azeotropic distillation with benzene (older industrial method); (3) Molecular sieves (zeolites) — modern + safer. Used in spectroscopy, in the lab as a non-aqueous solvent, in pharma, as fuel-grade ethanol. Rectified spirit ≈ 95% ethanol; methylated spirit ≈ 95% ethanol + 5% methanol; surgical spirit ≈ 70% ethanol with castor oil + methanol — the 70% concentration is most effective at killing microbes (water + ethanol both needed to disrupt cells).

cards.front:
Which functional group is present in alcohols?

(A) −COOH
(B) −OH (hydroxyl)
(C) −CHO
(D) −NH₂
cards.back:
(B) −OH (hydroxyl)

Organic Chemistry — Alcohols carry the hydroxyl (−OH) group attached to a saturated carbon. Examples: methanol CH₃OH, ethanol C₂H₅OH, propanol C₃H₇OH. Distinct from phenols where −OH is attached to an aromatic ring. Other groups: −COOH = carboxylic acid; −CHO = aldehyde; −NH₂ = amine; −CO− (between carbons) = ketone; −OR = ether; −COOR = ester.

cards.front:
Acetic acid (vinegar's main component) belongs to which class of organic compounds?

(A) Ester
(B) Carboxylic acid
(C) Aldehyde
(D) Ketone
cards.back:
(B) Carboxylic acid

Organic Chemistry — Acetic acid CH₃COOH — carries the −COOH (carboxyl) group → carboxylic acid. Vinegar is a 4-8% aqueous solution of acetic acid. IUPAC name: ethanoic acid. Carboxylic acids are weak acids (pKa ~4.76 for acetic) — partially dissociate to give H⁺ and acetate ion. Reactions: acid + alcohol → ester + water (Fischer esterification, a classic SSC question).

cards.front:
Formaldehyde (HCHO) — used in biological preservation and resin manufacture — is the simplest:

(A) Alcohol
(B) Aldehyde
(C) Ester
(D) Carboxylic acid
cards.back:
(B) Aldehyde

Organic Chemistry — Aldehydes have −CHO at the end of a carbon chain. HCHO (formaldehyde / methanal) — simplest aldehyde, only 1 C. Next: CH₃CHO (acetaldehyde / ethanal). Aldehydes give Tollens' (silver mirror) and Fehling's tests positive — distinguishes them from ketones. Formaldehyde is a 37% solution called formalin — used to preserve cadavers, biological specimens, and as a precursor to Bakelite plastic.

cards.front:
Methylamine (CH₃NH₂) belongs to the class of compounds called:

(A) Alcohols
(B) Primary amines
(C) Esters
(D) Nitriles
cards.back:
(B) Primary amines

Organic Chemistry — Amines — derivatives of NH₃ where 1, 2 or 3 hydrogens are replaced by alkyl/aryl groups → primary (RNH₂), secondary (R₂NH), tertiary (R₃N). CH₃NH₂ has just one alkyl on N → primary amine. Amines are basic (lone pair on N can accept H⁺); cause the 'fishy' smell. Examples: aniline (C₆H₅NH₂) — primary aromatic amine, used in dyes; trimethylamine (CH₃)₃N — tertiary, the smell of rotten fish.

cards.front:
The pleasant fruity smell in many ripe fruits and perfumes is mainly due to:

(A) Aldehydes
(B) Esters
(C) Ketones
(D) Phenols
cards.back:
(B) Esters

Organic Chemistry — Esters (−COOR) — formed by carboxylic acid + alcohol with H₂SO₄ catalyst (Fischer esterification). Common fruit-aroma esters: ethyl butanoate (pineapple), n-octyl acetate (orange), isoamyl acetate (banana), methyl salicylate (wintergreen). Industrial uses — solvents, perfumes, artificial flavours, plasticisers. Saponification = ester + NaOH → soap + alcohol (basis of soap-making).

cards.front:
Acetone (propan-2-one, CH₃COCH₃) — a common solvent in nail-polish remover — has which functional group?

(A) Aldehyde (−CHO)
(B) Ketone (>C=O between two carbons)
(C) Alcohol (−OH)
(D) Carboxylic acid (−COOH)
cards.back:
(B) Ketone (>C=O between two carbons)

Organic Chemistry — Acetone CH₃−CO−CH₃ — the carbonyl (C=O) sits BETWEEN two alkyl groups → ketone. Aldehydes have C=O at the END of the chain (−CHO). Acetone is the simplest ketone; produced industrially from cumene hydroperoxide alongside phenol. A natural product of fat metabolism — elevated in diabetic ketoacidosis (giving breath a 'fruity' smell). Boiling point 56 °C; miscible with water.

cards.front:
Match the functional group with its IUPAC suffix used in nomenclature — which pairing is INCORRECT?

(A) Alcohol — '-ol'
(B) Aldehyde — '-al'
(C) Ketone — '-one'
(D) Carboxylic acid — '-ene'
cards.back:
(D) Carboxylic acid — '-ene'

Organic Chemistry — IUPAC suffix for carboxylic acids is '-oic acid' (e.g., ethanoic acid for CH₃COOH), NOT '-ene' (which is the suffix for alkenes / double bond). Other key suffixes: alkanes '-ane', alkenes '-ene', alkynes '-yne', alcohols '-ol', aldehydes '-al', ketones '-one', amines '-amine', esters '-oate', amides '-amide'. Match the suffix carefully — exam papers love this trap.

cards.front:
HYDROCARBONS contain only:

(A) Carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen
(B) Carbon and hydrogen atoms only
(C) Carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen
(D) Hydrogen and oxygen atoms only
cards.back:
(B) Carbon and hydrogen atoms only

Organic Chemistry — HYDROCARBONS = compounds of ONLY C + H. Three families: ALKANES (C_nH_(2n+2); single bonds, saturated; methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀); ALKENES (C_nH_(2n); 1 double bond, unsaturated; ethene C₂H₄, propene C₃H₆); ALKYNES (C_nH_(2n−2); 1 triple bond; ethyne / acetylene C₂H₂). Plus AROMATICS (with benzene-ring; benzene C₆H₆, toluene). Sources: PETROLEUM (crude oil), NATURAL GAS, COAL.

cards.front:
METHANE (CH₄), the main component of NATURAL GAS, is also a:

(A) Halogen, like chlorine in air
(B) Greenhouse gas (~25× CO₂'s effect)
(C) Noble gas, inert + non-reactive
(D) Heavy gas, denser than air
cards.back:
(B) Greenhouse gas (~25× CO₂'s effect)

Organic Chemistry — METHANE (CH₄) — simplest hydrocarbon (1 C + 4 H). Major natural gas component (~80-95%). GREENHOUSE GAS — 25-86× more potent than CO₂ over 100/20 years. Sources of CH₄ emissions: cattle (enteric fermentation), rice paddies, landfills, oil + gas leaks, melting permafrost (a feedback risk). LIGHTER than air. Burns to give CO₂ + H₂O + heat. India's Bharat Stage VI norms address some hydrocarbon emissions. Distractor 4 — methane is LIGHTER than air (escapes upward; useful: gas leaks rise to ceiling).

cards.front:
ETHENE (ethylene) C₂H₄ has a:

(A) Single bond between two C atoms
(B) Double bond between two C atoms
(C) Triple bond between two C atoms
(D) No bond between the C atoms
cards.back:
(B) Double bond between two C atoms

Organic Chemistry — ETHENE (ethylene): CH₂=CH₂. C=C double bond + 4 C-H bonds. ALKENE family: CₙH₂ₙ. Used: (1) PLANT HORMONE — ripens fruit (Banana ripening, mango ripening with ethylene-releasing chemicals like ethrel — illegal in many places, calcium carbide also used illegally). (2) POLYMERIZATION → POLYTHENE / POLYETHYLENE (most common plastic — bags, bottles); (3) precursor in industrial chemistry. ETHYNE (ACETYLENE) C₂H₂ — TRIPLE bond; oxy-acetylene welding burns very hot.

cards.option2: Triple bond between two C atoms
cards.option3: No bond between the C atoms

cards.front:
BENZENE (C₆H₆), discovered by Faraday in 1825, is:

(A) Alicyclic, with single bonds in the ring
(B) Aromatic (delocalised π electrons in ring)
(C) Aliphatic chain compound, like alkanes
(D) Inorganic salt, with ionic bonding only
cards.back:
(B) Aromatic (delocalised π electrons in ring)

Organic Chemistry — BENZENE (C₆H₆) — prototypical AROMATIC compound: 6 carbons in planar HEXAGONAL ring; alternating single + double bonds (Kekulé structure 1865) — but actually 6 DELOCALISED π-electrons spread evenly over the ring (= AROMATICITY). Hückel's rule: aromatic if (4n+2) π electrons (n=1 for benzene → 6). Stable, distinctive 'aromatic' smell (originally named for fragrance). CARCINOGENIC. Found in petrol, cigarette smoke. Used in: making styrene, phenol, plastics, drugs, dyes. AROMATIC family includes: TOLUENE (methyl-benzene), XYLENE, NAPHTHALENE (mothballs).

cards.option3: Inorganic salt, with ionic bonding only

cards.front:
LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas, used as cooking fuel) is mainly a mixture of:

(A) Methane and ethane mainly
(B) Propane (C₃H₈) + butane (C₄H₁₀)
(C) Hydrogen and helium mainly
(D) Carbon monoxide and dioxide
cards.back:
(B) Propane (C₃H₈) + butane (C₄H₁₀)

Organic Chemistry — LPG = mostly PROPANE (C₃H₈) + BUTANE (C₄H₁₀); some ratio depends on country (India winter formulation different from summer). Distinctive smell = ETHYL MERCAPTAN (added as warning of leaks; LPG itself is odourless). Stored under PRESSURE as LIQUID in cylinder; vaporises when released. CNG (Compressed Natural Gas — used in CNG vehicles): mainly METHANE (~95%). PNG (Piped Natural Gas — household + commercial): same as CNG. India produces LPG from refineries + imports; PMUY (Ujjwala) gave free LPG connection to ~10 crore poor households.

cards.front:
PETROLEUM (crude oil) is separated into useful fractions by:

(A) Filtration through fine paper screen
(B) Fractional distillation by boiling pts
(C) Magnetic field separation tools used
(D) Electrolysis with metal electrode plates
cards.back:
(B) Fractional distillation by boiling pts

Organic Chemistry — FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION at petroleum refineries. Crude oil heated; vapour rises in tall fractionating column; different fractions condense at different heights based on BOILING POINT. From bottom (heaviest) to top (lightest): bitumen / asphalt → fuel oil → diesel → kerosene → naphtha → petrol/gasoline → LPG → refinery gas. Each fraction further refined. India's major refineries: Reliance Jamnagar (world's largest), IOC's Mathura + Panipat + Gujarat, BPCL Mumbai, HPCL Visakhapatnam.

cards.front:
POLYTHENE (plastic bags) is made by polymerising:

(A) Methane (CH₄) repeatedly
(B) Ethene/ethylene (CH₂=CH₂)
(C) Acetylene (HC≡CH)
(D) Benzene (C₆H₆) ring molecules
cards.back:
(B) Ethene/ethylene (CH₂=CH₂)

Organic Chemistry — POLYTHENE / POLYETHYLENE — long-chain polymer of ethene monomers: nCH₂=CH₂ → −(CH₂−CH₂)ₙ−. Two main types: LDPE (Low-Density PE — branched chains; soft, flexible — plastic bags, squeeze bottles); HDPE (High-Density PE — linear chains; harder — bottles, pipes, crates). World's most produced plastic. ENVIRONMENTAL ISSUE: doesn't biodegrade easily; plastic pollution. Many states banned single-use plastic bags. Other common plastics: PVC (polyvinyl chloride — pipes), PS (polystyrene — packaging), PP (polypropylene — bottle caps, ropes), PET (polyethylene terephthalate — water bottles), PTFE (Teflon — non-stick coating).

cards.front:
Which has the formula CnH2n+2?

(A) Alkanes (saturated hydrocarbons)
(B) Alkenes (with C=C bond)
(C) Alkynes (with C≡C bond)
(D) Aromatic compounds (benzene)
cards.back:
(A) Alkanes (saturated hydrocarbons)

Organic Chemistry — ALKANES — saturated hydrocarbons; only single C−C bonds; general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. EXAMPLES: methane CH₄ (n=1), ethane C₂H₆ (n=2), propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀, pentane C₅H₁₂, hexane C₆H₁₄, heptane C₇H₁₆, octane C₈H₁₈, nonane C₉H₂₀, decane C₁₀H₂₂. PROPERTIES: chemically INERT (saturated bonds), low reactivity except combustion + halogenation. STATES at room T: C₁-C₄ gas (methane, ethane, propane, butane); C₅-C₁₇ liquid (gasoline, kerosene, diesel range); C₁₈+ solid (waxes, asphalt). HYDROCARBON GENERAL FORMULAS: (1) ALKANES: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (saturated). (2) ALKENES: CₙH₂ₙ (one C=C double bond). (3) ALKYNES: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (one C≡C triple bond). (4) CYCLOALKANES: CₙH₂ₙ (ring, single bonds). (5) AROMATIC: typically based on benzene C₆H₆. INDIA INDUSTRIAL: NATURAL GAS (mostly CH₄) increasingly used for cooking (PNG/CNG); LPG = liquefied propane + butane (used in household cylinders). CALORIFIC VALUE — alkanes are excellent fuels: methane ~55 MJ/kg, octane ~47 MJ/kg, ethanol (not alkane but for comparison) ~30 MJ/kg. NOMENCLATURE: IUPAC system uses prefix-suffix to count carbons + indicate type. PYQ FREQUENCY: alkane formula in NEET, NCERT, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
BENZENE has the structure of a:

(A) Six-membered aromatic ring with delocalized π electrons
(B) Five-membered ring of carbons (option here)
(C) Linear chain of six carbons (option here) too
(D) Eight-membered cubical ring (option here) too
cards.back:
(A) Six-membered aromatic ring with delocalized π electrons

Organic Chemistry — BENZENE (C₆H₆) — flat, hexagonal ring of 6 carbon atoms; each C has 1 H attached. AROMATIC because: (1) Cyclic. (2) Planar. (3) All atoms in ring sp²-hybridized. (4) Has 6 π-electrons in delocalized π-orbitals (Hückel's 4n+2 rule, n=1). RESONANCE: alternating single-double bonds in two structures average to ALL EQUIVALENT bonds (~139 pm, between single 154 pm and double 134 pm). HISTORICAL: F.A. KEKULÉ (1865, Germany) proposed cyclic structure after a dream of a snake biting its own tail (legend). KEKULÉ STRUCTURES: alternating C=C bonds (Lewis structure approximation). MODERN: delocalized π electrons (more accurate). PROPERTIES: clear, COLORLESS LIQUID, BP 80°C; sweet aromatic smell; CARCINOGEN (causes leukemia); flammable. USES: solvent, raw material for plastics (polystyrene, polyester), nylon (caprolactam intermediate), drugs. AROMATIC COMPOUNDS: benzene + derivatives (toluene, xylene, naphthalene, anthracene). KEKULÉ-NAMED rings + 1,3,5-cyclohexatriene = benzene. POLYAROMATIC HYDROCARBONS (PAHs): naphthalene (mothballs), anthracene; in coal tar, vehicle exhaust — many carcinogenic. PYQ FREQUENCY: benzene structure in NEET, JEE-Main 1-2× per cycle.
cards.option2: Linear chain of six carbons (option here) too

(4) Has 6 π-electrons in delocalized π-orbitals (Hückel's 4n+2 rule, n=1). RESONANCE: alternating single-double bonds in two structures average to ALL EQUIVALENT bonds (~139 pm, between single 154 pm and double 134 pm). HISTORICAL: F.A. KEKULÉ (1865, Germany) proposed cyclic structure after a dream of a snake biting its own tail (legend). KEKULÉ STRUCTURES: alternating C=C bonds (Lewis structure approximation). MODERN: delocalized π electrons (more accurate). PROPERTIES: clear, COLORLESS LIQUID, BP 80°C; sweet aromatic smell; CARCINOGEN (causes leukemia); flammable. USES: solvent, raw material for plastics (polystyrene, polyester), nylon (caprolactam intermediate), drugs. AROMATIC COMPOUNDS: benzene + derivatives (toluene, xylene, naphthalene, anthracene). KEKULÉ-NAMED rings + 1,3,5-cyclohexatriene = benzene. POLYAROMATIC HYDROCARBONS (PAHs): naphthalene (mothballs), anthracene; in coal tar, vehicle exhaust — many carcinogenic. PYQ FREQUENCY: benzene structure in NEET, JEE-Main 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
ACETYLENE (used in welding torches) has the chemical formula:

(A) C₂H₂ (alkyne with C≡C bond)
(B) C₂H₄ (alkene with C=C bond)
(C) C₂H₆ (alkane with C-C bond)
(D) CH₄ (methane natural gas)
cards.back:
(A) C₂H₂ (alkyne with C≡C bond)

Organic Chemistry — ACETYLENE — IUPAC name ETHYNE — chemical formula C₂H₂; the SIMPLEST ALKYNE (contains C≡C TRIPLE BOND). STRUCTURE: H−C≡C−H (linear); strong triple bond stores high energy. PROPERTIES: colorless gas, distinctive garlic-like smell (impurity), explosive at high pressure (>2 atm), highly flammable. PRODUCTION: industrially from CALCIUM CARBIDE + WATER → CaC₂ + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + C₂H₂↑. COMMERCIAL: stored DISSOLVED in acetone in cylinders (avoids explosive pressure). USES: (1) OXY-ACETYLENE TORCH — welding/cutting metals (flame ~3000°C, hottest commercial flame). (2) Production of vinyl chloride (PVC plastic precursor), acrylonitrile (polymers). (3) FRUIT RIPENING — calcium carbide releases acetylene which mimics ethylene plant hormone (BANNED in India under FSSA — health hazard for fruit ripening; modern method uses ETHYLENE). (4) Old GAS LAMPS (carbide lamps) for caves, bicycles, miners. (5) Rocket propellant in some applications. RELATED: ETHYLENE C₂H₄ (ALKENE) — used to ripen fruits naturally; raw material for polyethylene plastic. METHANE CH₄ — natural gas, simplest alkane. PYQ FREQUENCY: acetylene formula and uses in NEET, JEE-Main, NCERT 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION is used to separate:

(A) Crude petroleum into useful fractions
(B) Salt from sea water (evaporation)
(C) Iron from its ore (smelting)
(D) Sugar from cane juice here
cards.back:
(A) Crude petroleum into useful fractions

Organic Chemistry — FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION — crude oil (PETROLEUM) is heated in REFINERY column; different hydrocarbon fractions VAPORIZE and CONDENSE at different heights based on their BOILING POINTS. KEY FRACTIONS (top to bottom of column, low to high BP): (1) PETROLEUM GAS (LPG) — methane, ethane, propane, butane (BP < 40°C). (2) PETROL/GASOLINE — C₅-C₁₂ (40-180°C). (3) NAPHTHA — C₆-C₁₀, raw material for petrochemicals. (4) KEROSENE — C₁₀-C₁₆ (180-260°C); aircraft fuel (jet fuel). (5) DIESEL — C₁₂-C₂₀ (~260-340°C); trucks, generators, ships. (6) FUEL OIL — heavy fraction, ships, industrial heating. (7) LUBRICATING OIL — engine oil, grease. (8) PARAFFIN WAX — candles, polishes. (9) BITUMEN/ASPHALT — road surfaces, roofing. INDIA REFINERY CAPACITY: ~5 million barrels/day (4th largest globally). KEY REFINERIES: Reliance Jamnagar (largest in world, 1.24 million b/d), IOC Mathura, BPCL Mumbai. CRACKING: heavier fractions broken down to lighter, more valuable ones using catalysts (FCC — Fluid Catalytic Cracking). REFORMING: low-octane to high-octane gasoline. INDIA crude imports: ~85% imported (from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, UAE, Russia). PYQ FREQUENCY: fractional distillation in NEET, NCERT 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
STRUCTURAL ISOMERS of butane (C₄H₁₀) are:

(A) n-butane and iso-butane (2 isomers)
(B) Three different isomers exist here
(C) Five isomers (over-counted)
(D) Only one form of butane only
cards.back:
(A) n-butane and iso-butane (2 isomers)

Organic Chemistry — BUTANE C₄H₁₀ has TWO STRUCTURAL ISOMERS: (1) n-BUTANE (normal butane) — straight chain: CH₃−CH₂−CH₂−CH₃. (2) ISO-BUTANE (or 2-methylpropane) — branched: (CH₃)₃CH = CH₃−CH(CH₃)−CH₃. BOTH have formula C₄H₁₀, same molecular weight, but DIFFERENT physical/chemical properties. KEY DIFFERENCES: (a) BP: n-butane −0.5°C; iso-butane −12°C (branched is slightly more compact, weaker van der Waals → lower BP). (b) Density, solubility differ slightly. NUMBER OF ALKANE ISOMERS by C count: 1 (CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈ all have only 1); 2 (butane); 3 (pentane); 5 (hexane); 9 (heptane); 18 (octane); 35 (nonane); 75 (decane). RAPID GROWTH: more carbons → exponentially more isomers. PROPANE C₃H₈: only ONE structure (CH₃−CH₂−CH₃; branching impossible). LPG: COMMERCIAL LPG = ~60% n-butane + ~40% propane (varies by season). 'I-BUTANE' / 'ISOBUTANE' is also a refrigerant (R-600a, used in modern eco-friendly fridges). USES of BUTANE: (1) LIGHTER fluid. (2) AEROSOL propellant. (3) Refrigerant. STRUCTURAL ISOMERISM: same formula, different connectivity. Other types: STEREOISOMERISM (same connectivity, different spatial arrangement). PYQ FREQUENCY: alkane isomers in NEET, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.
