cards.front:
ETHENE (ethylene) is used in industry as the basis for which polymer?

(A) Polyethylene (most-used plastic)
(B) Nylon (a polyamide rubber)
(C) Cotton (a natural fiber)
(D) Wool (an animal fiber)
cards.back:
(A) Polyethylene (most-used plastic)

Organic Chemistry — ETHENE / ETHYLENE C₂H₄ — simplest alkene; polymerizes to POLYETHYLENE (PE), the world's MOST PRODUCED PLASTIC (~100 million tonnes/year globally). REACTION: n × CH₂=CH₂ → −(CH₂−CH₂)−ₙ (polymerization with catalysts like Ziegler-Natta). TYPES OF POLYETHYLENE: (1) LDPE (Low-Density) — flexible, used for plastic bags, films, squeeze bottles. (2) HDPE (High-Density) — stiff, used for milk jugs, containers, water pipes. (3) LLDPE (Linear LDPE) — combines properties. USES: plastic bags, bottles, pipes, electrical insulation, packaging films, geomembranes. ETHYLENE — also used as: (1) PLANT HORMONE — naturally produced by ripening fruits; ripens others (banana with apple = banana ripens fast). (2) PRECURSOR for ETHYLENE GLYCOL (antifreeze, polyester PET fabric). (3) ETHANOL production. (4) Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) — via vinyl chloride. (5) Polystyrene — via styrene. INDIA: Reliance, IOC, GAIL, ONGC operate large ethylene crackers. PROBLEM — PLASTIC POLLUTION: PE is SLOWLY DEGRADING (centuries); ocean garbage patches; bans on single-use plastics. SOLUTIONS: recycling (limited), bioplastics (PLA), reduce-reuse-recycle. INDIA banned single-use plastic items (1 July 2022). PYQ FREQUENCY: PE-ethylene link in NEET, NCERT, JEE-Main 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
OCTANE NUMBER of a fuel measures:

(A) Resistance to engine knocking
(B) Number of carbon atoms here
(C) Energy content per litre fuel
(D) Density relative to water
cards.back:
(A) Resistance to engine knocking

Organic Chemistry — OCTANE NUMBER (or 'octane rating') — measures a fuel's ability to RESIST 'KNOCKING' (premature ignition) in spark-ignition engines. Higher octane = better resistance = smoother engine performance, especially in high-compression engines. SCALE: (1) ISO-OCTANE (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) = 100 (very resistant). (2) n-HEPTANE = 0 (highly knock-prone). FUEL OCTANE NUMBER = % of iso-octane in a hypothetical iso-octane/n-heptane blend with same knocking. INDIA PETROL OCTANE: regular petrol is 91 RON (Research Octane Number); premium 'Speed Plus' / 'XTRA Premium' is 95-99 RON. RACING fuels: 100+ RON. KNOCKING (PINGING): when fuel ignites BEFORE the spark reaches it (due to compression heat) → 'pinging' sound, engine damage. HIGH-COMPRESSION ENGINES (e.g., turbocharged) need HIGHER octane. ADDITIVES historically used: TETRAETHYL LEAD ((C₂H₅)₄Pb) — banned globally due to LEAD POISONING (health, environment). Replacement: ETHANOL (10-20% blend in petrol — also boosts octane); MTBE (in some countries, but contaminates groundwater). E20 INITIATIVE in INDIA (2025): 20% ethanol blend in petrol — reduces import + emissions. CETANE NUMBER — analogous for DIESEL fuels (measures ignition quality, not anti-knock). PYQ FREQUENCY: octane number in NEET, JEE-Main, GA 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
The general molecular formula for alkanes is:

(A) CₙH₂ₙ
(B) CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
(C) CₙH₂ₙ₋₂
(D) CₙH₂ₙ₋₁
cards.back:
(B) CₙH₂ₙ₊₂

Organic Chemistry — Alkanes — saturated (all single bonds) hydrocarbons — formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Methane (n=1, CH₄), ethane (n=2, C₂H₆), propane (n=3, C₃H₈). Alkenes (one C=C double bond) — CₙH₂ₙ. Alkynes (one C≡C triple bond) — CₙH₂ₙ₋₂. Cycloalkanes — CₙH₂ₙ (same as alkenes but saturated ring).

cards.front:
LPG (liquefied petroleum gas) sold in Indian cylinders is chiefly a mixture of:

(A) Methane and ethane
(B) Butane and propane
(C) Ethylene and acetylene
(D) Methane and hydrogen
cards.back:
(B) Butane and propane

Organic Chemistry — LPG — mostly butane (C₄H₁₀) and propane (C₃H₈), with a small amount of ethane. Both gases liquefy under moderate pressure, which is why they can be stored in cylinders. Ethyl mercaptan (a sulphur compound) is added as an odourant for leak detection. CNG used in vehicles and piped gas — mostly methane. Methane is the main constituent of natural gas.

cards.front:
The first member of the alkyne series — with a triple bond — is:

(A) Methyne
(B) Ethyne (acetylene)
(C) Propyne
(D) Butyne
cards.back:
(B) Ethyne (acetylene)

Organic Chemistry — The first alkyne is ethyne (C₂H₂, H-C≡C-H) — also called acetylene. Methane-based alkyne isn't possible (need ≥ 2 carbons to form a triple bond). Acetylene burned with oxygen gives a flame temperature of ~3,100 °C — used in oxy-acetylene welding / cutting of steel. It's also the starting material for making PVC (via vinyl chloride) and many other chemicals.

cards.front:
The gas that ripens fruits (commonly used artificially to ripen mangoes and bananas) is:

(A) Acetylene
(B) Ethylene (ethene)
(C) Methane
(D) Propane
cards.back:
(B) Ethylene (ethene)

Organic Chemistry — Ethylene (ethene, C₂H₄) — a plant hormone naturally produced by ripening fruit. Commercially used in ripening chambers. Calcium carbide (CaC₂) was widely (illegally) used in India — it reacts with moisture to release acetylene (a mimic hormone) + traces of arsenic / phosphorus (harmful); banned under the PFA / FSSAI Rules. Food-grade ethylene sachets or gas rooms are the safer legal alternative.

cards.front:
Two compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements are called:

(A) Isotopes
(B) Isomers
(C) Allotropes
(D) Homologues
cards.back:
(B) Isomers

Organic Chemistry — Isomers — same molecular formula, different structure. Example — butane (n-butane, straight chain) and isobutane (2-methylpropane, branched) are C₄H₁₀. Isotopes — same element, different neutrons. Allotropes — same element, different physical forms (diamond vs graphite). Homologues — members of a series differing by a -CH₂- unit (methane, ethane, propane …).

cards.front:
Petrol / diesel are obtained from crude oil by:

(A) Electrolysis
(B) Fractional distillation
(C) Sublimation
(D) Magnetic separation
cards.back:
(B) Fractional distillation

Organic Chemistry — Crude oil is a mixture of hundreds of hydrocarbons. In a refinery, it is vaporised and passed up a tall fractionating tower; different fractions condense at different levels by boiling point — petroleum gas (lowest) < petrol < naphtha < kerosene < diesel < lubricating oil < fuel oil < bitumen (residue at the bottom). India's major refineries — Jamnagar, Paradip, Vadinar, Kochi, Mathura, Panipat.

cards.front:
The 'octane number' of a petrol fuel is a measure of its:

(A) Calorific value
(B) Resistance to knocking (pre-ignition)
(C) Density
(D) Viscosity
cards.back:
(B) Resistance to knocking (pre-ignition)

Organic Chemistry — Octane number — how well a petrol resists 'knocking' (pre-ignition by compression, causing engine rattle). Higher number = higher resistance = suits higher-compression engines. Iso-octane is rated 100, heptane 0; a petrol rated 95 behaves like a 95:5 iso-octane:heptane blend under test. Tetraethyl lead was the original anti-knock additive; phased out for health / environmental reasons. Modern alternatives — ethanol, MTBE. India's petrol is mostly 91-95 RON; premium / 'power' grades go to 97-100.

cards.front:
The simplest hydrocarbon, found as the main component of natural gas, is:

(A) Ethane
(B) Methane
(C) Propane
(D) Butane
cards.back:
(B) Methane

Organic Chemistry — Methane (CH₄) is the first member of the alkane series and makes up 70-95 % of natural gas and biogas. It is also a potent greenhouse gas — about 25 times more effective per molecule than CO₂ over 100 years. Ethane (C₂H₆), propane (C₃H₈), butane (C₄H₁₀) are the next members; LPG is mainly a mix of propane and butane.

cards.front:
The functional group —OH is characteristic of which class of organic compounds?

(A) Aldehydes
(B) Alcohols
(C) Carboxylic acids
(D) Esters
cards.back:
(B) Alcohols

Organic Chemistry — Alcohols carry the hydroxyl (—OH) group attached to a saturated carbon. Examples: methanol CH₃OH, ethanol CH₃CH₂OH. Aldehydes have —CHO (e.g., formaldehyde HCHO); carboxylic acids have —COOH (acetic acid CH₃COOH); esters have —COO-R (ethyl ethanoate). Phenols also have —OH but attached to an aromatic ring.

cards.front:
The alcohol present in alcoholic beverages such as beer and wine is:

(A) Methanol
(B) Ethanol
(C) Propanol
(D) Glycerol
cards.back:
(B) Ethanol

Organic Chemistry — Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) — produced by the yeast fermentation of sugars (glucose, fructose) — is the drinkable alcohol in beer (4-8 %), wine (10-14 %) and spirits (40 %+). Methanol (CH₃OH) is highly toxic — causes blindness and death even in small doses; illicit 'hooch' poisoning cases are methanol contamination. Glycerol is a triol used as a sweetener and humectant.

cards.front:
Benzene, a common aromatic hydrocarbon, has the molecular formula:

(A) C₆H₁₂
(B) C₆H₆
(C) C₆H₁₄
(D) CH₄
cards.back:
(B) C₆H₆

It was first proposed in this structure by Kekulé. C₆H₁₂ is cyclohexane (saturated); C₆H₁₄ is hexane (straight-chain saturated); CH₄ is methane. Benzene is a known carcinogen; exposure from petrol fumes is tightly regulated.

Fatty acids build lipids; nucleotides build nucleic acids (DNA, RNA); monosaccharides like glucose and fructose build carbohydrates.

cards.front:
An ALKANE reacting with halogen in presence of UV light undergoes:

(A) Addition reaction
(B) Substitution reaction (free-radical mechanism)
(C) Polymerisation
(D) Reduction
cards.back:
(B) Substitution reaction (free-radical mechanism)

Organic Chemistry — Alkanes are saturated → cannot undergo addition. With X₂ + UV → SUBSTITUTION (free-radical, chain mechanism: initiation, propagation, termination). CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, then → CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄. Mixture of products. Addition reactions belong to alkenes/alkynes (e.g., CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br). Elimination — opposite of addition; commonly E1/E2 dehydrohalogenation.

cards.front:
Ethylene (CH₂=CH₂) reacts with Br₂ to form 1,2-dibromoethane. This is an example of:

(A) Substitution
(B) Electrophilic addition across the C=C double bond
(C) Free-radical halogenation
(D) Saponification
cards.back:
(B) Electrophilic addition across the C=C double bond

Organic Chemistry — Alkenes (C=C) — π bond — undergo ADDITION reactions. With Br₂: orange Br₂ → colourless. The 'bromine water test' decolourises with alkene. Markovnikov's rule (asymmetric reagents like HBr): H attaches to the C with more H's already (i.e., adds H to C with most H — 'rich gets richer'). Anti-Markovnikov with peroxides (radical mechanism). Other addition reactions: hydrogenation (H₂ + Ni catalyst), hydration (H₂O + acid → alcohol), HCl addition, hydroboration-oxidation.

cards.front:
When ethanol is heated with concentrated H₂SO₄ at 170 °C, the product is:

(A) Acetaldehyde
(B) Ethylene (ethene) — by acid-catalysed dehydration
(C) Acetic acid
(D) Diethyl ether
cards.back:
(B) Ethylene (ethene) — by acid-catalysed dehydration

Organic Chemistry — C₂H₅OH at 170 °C with conc H₂SO₄ → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O. Acid-catalysed DEHYDRATION (an elimination reaction; intramolecular). At 140 °C, two ethanol molecules can dehydrate INTER-molecularly to give diethyl ether: 2 C₂H₅OH → C₂H₅-O-C₂H₅ + H₂O. With acidified KMnO₄/K₂Cr₂O₇ → ethanol oxidises to acetaldehyde (mild) → acetic acid (strong). Distinct mechanisms based on conditions.

cards.front:
The reaction between an alcohol and a carboxylic acid (with acid catalyst) producing an ester + water is called:

(A) Hydrolysis
(B) Esterification (Fischer esterification)
(C) Saponification
(D) Halogenation
cards.back:
(B) Esterification (Fischer esterification)

Organic Chemistry — Fischer Esterification: R-COOH + R'-OH ⇌ R-COO-R' + H₂O (H₂SO₄ catalyst, heat). Reversible. Le Chatelier — shift right by removing water (Dean-Stark trap) or excess alcohol. Used industrially for fragrances, plasticisers (DEHP, DBP). Saponification — opposite-direction (with NaOH instead of acid): ester + NaOH → carboxylate salt (soap) + alcohol. Hydrolysis (acidic) — ester + water → acid + alcohol.

cards.front:
Vegetable oils (liquid at room temperature) are converted to vanaspati / dalda (semi-solid) by:

(A) Halogenation
(B) Hydrogenation — addition of H₂ across C=C double bonds with Ni catalyst
(C) Polymerisation
(D) Saponification
cards.back:
(B) Hydrogenation — addition of H₂ across C=C double bonds with Ni catalyst

Organic Chemistry — Vegetable oils — unsaturated triglycerides (multiple C=C). Hydrogenation: H₂ + Ni catalyst (~150 °C, 5 atm) → saturates double bonds → solidifies the fat. Industrial process used to make vanaspati ghee from groundnut/cottonseed/soybean oil. Concern: PARTIAL hydrogenation creates 'trans-fats' (cis isomer flips to trans during reaction), which raise LDL cholesterol, lower HDL → cardiovascular risk. FSSAI capped trans-fat in PHVOs (partially hydrogenated vegetable oils) to ≤ 2% by 1 January 2022.

cards.front:
Polythene (polyethene) is formed by:

(A) Condensation polymerisation
(B) Addition polymerisation of ethylene (CH₂=CH₂) units
(C) Substitution polymerisation
(D) Elimination polymerisation
cards.back:
(B) Addition polymerisation of ethylene (CH₂=CH₂) units

Organic Chemistry — Polyethene = (-CH₂-CH₂-)ₙ — repeated ethylene units join via ADDITION polymerisation; no byproduct (every atom of monomer ends up in polymer). Initiated by free radicals (peroxides), Ziegler-Natta catalyst (Ti/Al), or metallocene catalyst. CONDENSATION polymerisation — releases small byproducts (water, HCl) — e.g., nylon, polyester (PET), Bakelite, urea-formaldehyde. Other addition polymers — PVC (vinyl chloride), polypropylene, PTFE (Teflon), polystyrene, neoprene rubber, polyacrylonitrile.

cards.front:
When ethanol is OXIDISED with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (orange) or KMnO₄ (purple), the colour:

(A) Stays unchanged
(B) Changes (orange → green for K₂Cr₂O₇; purple → colourless for KMnO₄) as oxidation proceeds
(C) Becomes black
(D) Becomes blue
cards.back:
(B) Changes (orange → green for K₂Cr₂O₇; purple → colourless for KMnO₄) as oxidation proceeds

Organic Chemistry — K₂Cr₂O₇ — Cr(VI) orange → Cr(III) green during reduction. KMnO₄ — Mn(VII) purple → Mn(II) colourless. Ethanol gets oxidised: CH₃CH₂OH → CH₃CHO (acetaldehyde) → CH₃COOH (acetic acid). Useful tests in qualitative organic chemistry to detect oxidisable groups (alcohols, aldehydes). Excess strong oxidiser will go all the way to acid; mild conditions (PCC, DIBAL-H) stop at aldehyde. Industrial breath analysers historically used these colour changes (now electrochemical).

cards.front:
ORGANIC CHEMISTRY is the chemistry of which element's compounds (with hydrogen + some others)?

(A) Nitrogen
(B) Carbon
(C) Oxygen
(D) Sulphur
cards.back:
(B) Carbon

Organic Chemistry — ORGANIC CHEMISTRY = chemistry of CARBON compounds (except CO, CO₂, carbonates, cyanides, carbides — these are considered inorganic). Carbon is special because of CATENATION (ability to form long chains + rings — C-C bonds are very stable, ~347 kJ/mol), TETRAVALENCY (can form 4 bonds), and its ability to form SINGLE, DOUBLE, and TRIPLE bonds. Over 10 million known organic compounds vs ~300k inorganic. FRIEDRICH WÖHLER (1828) accidentally synthesised UREA (NH₂CONH₂) from ammonium cyanate — first organic compound made from inorganic starting materials → destroyed the 'VITAL FORCE THEORY' (that organic compounds required a living 'vital force'). Today all life is known to be carbon-based. Organic chem branches: hydrocarbons (alkanes/alkenes/alkynes), alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, acids, esters, amines, amides, ethers, aromatics.

cards.front:
The simplest HYDROCARBON and the main component of NATURAL GAS + biogas is:

(A) Ethane (C₂H₆)
(B) Methane (CH₄)
(C) Propane (C₃H₈)
(D) Butane (C₄H₁₀)
cards.back:

Main component (70-90%) of NATURAL GAS + BIOGAS (also CO₂, small amounts of other gases). Also present in MARSH GAS (decomposition of vegetation in water), FIREDAMP (coal mines — explosive), RICE PADDIES (bacterial methanogenesis), CATTLE BELCH (~4% of global methane). Alkane nomenclature (first 10): Meth-, Eth-, Prop-, But-, Pent-, Hex-, Hept-, Oct-, Non-, Dec-. CNG (Compressed Natural Gas): vehicle fuel, mostly methane. LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas): mostly propane + butane. Shale gas revolution in USA made natural gas cheap since 2010s.

ETHYL ALCOHOL (the drinkable alcohol) and METHYL ALCOHOL (the toxic wood alcohol) differ by:

(A) Number of carbon atoms
(B) Presence of oxygen
(C) Type of bond (single vs double)
(D) Nothing; they're identical
cards.back:
(A) Number of carbon atoms

Organic Chemistry — METHANOL (CH₃OH, 'methyl alcohol', 'wood alcohol' — originally distilled from wood): TOXIC (even small amounts cause blindness, death — metabolised to formaldehyde + formic acid in body). Industrial uses: solvent, fuel, formaldehyde production. ETHANOL (C₂H₅OH, 'ethyl alcohol', 'drinking alcohol'): the only alcohol safe for human consumption (still intoxicating + carcinogenic long-term, but not acutely fatal in small doses). Made by fermentation of sugars (yeasts) or industrially from ethylene. Uses: alcoholic beverages, solvent, fuel (E85 ethanol-gasoline), hand sanitisers (60-70%), antiseptic. Spurious liquor tragedies in India = methanol contamination (common illegal distilleries). HIGHER alcohols: Propanol (3C), Butanol (4C), etc. Isomers: n- (straight chain), iso- (branched). ethyl = 2C, methyl = 1C.

BENZENE (C₆H₆) is the simplest AROMATIC hydrocarbon. Its structure features:

(A) A linear chain of 6 carbons
(B) A hexagonal ring of 6 carbons with alternating single/double bonds
(C) A tetrahedral arrangement
(D) Two separate CH₃ groups
cards.back:
(B) A hexagonal ring of 6 carbons with alternating single/double bonds

Organic Chemistry — BENZENE — discovered 1825 by MICHAEL FARADAY. Structure elucidated 1865 by FRIEDRICH AUGUST KEKULÉ (claimed inspiration from a dream of a snake biting its tail — ouroboros). Hexagonal planar ring, 6 carbons with alternating C=C and C-C bonds — but in reality ALL bonds are EQUIVALENT due to DELOCALISED π electrons (resonance hybrid). Represented as hexagon with circle inside. 3 pairs of delocalised electrons (6 π electrons). AROMATICITY criteria (Hückel's rule): planar, cyclic, continuous conjugation, 4n+2 π electrons (n=0,1,2... — so 2, 6, 10, 14...). Benzene = n=1 (6 π electrons). Benzene + derivatives (toluene = methylbenzene, xylene, phenol, aniline, naphthalene) are called AROMATICS — many have distinctive aromas (from which the class gets its name). Today: 'aromatic' is a formal structural term; not all aromatics smell pleasant.

cards.front:
FORMALIN (used to preserve biological specimens) is an aqueous solution of:

(A) Formic acid
(B) Formaldehyde
(C) Ethyl alcohol
(D) Acetone
cards.back:
(B) Formaldehyde

Organic Chemistry — FORMALIN = 37-40% aqueous FORMALDEHYDE (HCHO, methanal) + typically 10-12% methanol to stabilise. Uses: preservation of biological specimens (fixes tissues by cross-linking proteins), embalming, disinfectant, germicide. Carcinogenic — restricted use. FORMALDEHYDE is the simplest ALDEHYDE. Aldehyde general formula: R-CHO. Common aldehydes: HCHO (formaldehyde/methanal), CH₃CHO (acetaldehyde/ethanal — oxidation of ethanol causes 'hangover'), CHO-CHO (glyoxal), Benzaldehyde (almond smell). KETONES have R-CO-R': ACETONE (propanone, CH₃COCH₃ — nail polish remover), METHYL ETHYL KETONE. Distinguishing ald vs ketone: Tollens' reagent (silver mirror test — aldehyde +, ketone −), Fehling's/Benedict's (aldehyde + for aliphatic, ketone −). Uses of formaldehyde: Bakelite, plywood, textiles. typically 37-40%; methanal, HCHO.

cards.front:
POLYTHENE (PE) — the most widely used plastic — is a polymer of:

(A) Propylene
(B) Ethylene
(C) Styrene
(D) Vinyl chloride
cards.back:
(B) Ethylene

Organic Chemistry — POLYTHENE / POLYETHYLENE (PE) = polymer of ETHYLENE (ethene, H₂C=CH₂): n(C₂H₄) → -(CH₂-CH₂)ₙ-. Most produced plastic globally (~100 million tonnes/year). Grades: LDPE (Low-Density — plastic bags, squeeze bottles, film), HDPE (High-Density — milk jugs, pipes, detergent bottles — stronger, opaque). Other major polymers: POLYPROPYLENE (PP — from propylene; yogurt cups, bottle caps); POLYSTYRENE (PS — thermocol, disposable cups, CD cases); PVC (polyvinyl chloride — pipes, flooring; from vinyl chloride which is a carcinogen); POLYESTER/PET (bottles, fabric — from terephthalic acid + ethylene glycol); TEFLON (PTFE — non-stick; from tetrafluoroethylene); NYLON (from diamines + dicarboxylic acids); BAKELITE (phenol + formaldehyde — FIRST synthetic plastic, 1907 by Leo Baekeland — thermosetting). Polymers: repeating MONOMER units via addition or condensation. ethene, C₂H₄.

cards.front:
The 4 major classes of BIOMOLECULES in living organisms are:

(A) Carbohydrates, Proteins, Lipids, Nucleic acids
(B) Vitamins, Minerals, Water, Enzymes
(C) Acids, Bases, Salts, Oxides
(D) Hormones, Neurotransmitters, Antibodies, Receptors
cards.back:
(A) Carbohydrates, Proteins, Lipids, Nucleic acids

Organic Chemistry — FOUR major biomolecules: (1) CARBOHYDRATES (sugars, starches — (CH₂O)ₙ; energy + structural). Monosaccharides (glucose, fructose) → Disaccharides (sucrose = glu+fru, lactose = glu+gal, maltose = glu+glu) → Polysaccharides (starch — plant storage, glycogen — animal storage, cellulose — plant cell wall, chitin — fungi/arthropods). (2) PROTEINS (chains of ~20 amino acids, folded 3D). Enzymes, hormones, structural (collagen, keratin), transport (hemoglobin), defence (antibodies). (3) LIPIDS (insoluble in water). Triglycerides, phospholipids, steroids, waxes. Energy storage, membranes, hormones. (4) NUCLEIC ACIDS (DNA, RNA — chains of nucleotides). Store + transmit genetic information. Also: VITAMINS + MINERALS are NOT biomolecules per the traditional classification — they're micronutrients (although vitamins are organic compounds). WATER is inorganic but essential (60% of body).

cards.front:
Functional group identification: -COOH (carboxylic acid), -OH (hydroxyl), -CHO (aldehyde), -NH₂ (amine). Which functional group is found in ACETONE?

(A) -COOH (carboxylic acid)
(B) -CO- (carbonyl, KETONE)
(C) -OH (alcohol)
(D) -O- (ether)
cards.back:
(B) -CO- (carbonyl, KETONE)

Organic Chemistry — ACETONE = PROPAN-2-ONE = (CH₃)₂CO. A KETONE — characterised by the CARBONYL group (C=O) in the MIDDLE of a carbon chain. General ketone: R-CO-R'. Aldehydes have C=O at the END (R-CHO, always with at least one H on the carbonyl carbon). KEY FUNCTIONAL GROUPS (memorise): -OH = alcohol/hydroxyl; -CHO = aldehyde; -CO- = ketone; -COOH = carboxylic acid; -COO- = ester/carboxylate; -NH₂ = amine (primary); -O- = ether; -CONH₂ = amide; C=C = alkene; C≡C = alkyne; -NO₂ = nitro; -X (F/Cl/Br/I) = halide; -SO₃H = sulphonic acid; C6H5- = phenyl (benzene ring). Suffixes: -ol (alcohol), -al (aldehyde), -one (ketone), -oic acid (carboxylic), -yl (radical).

cards.front:
Which of the following is used as a 'LAUGHING GAS' in anaesthesia (also a greenhouse gas)?

(A) Methane (CH₄)
(B) Nitrous Oxide (N₂O)
(C) Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
(D) Ozone (O₃)
cards.back:
(B) Nitrous Oxide (N₂O)

Organic Chemistry — NITROUS OXIDE (N₂O) — 'LAUGHING GAS'. Discovered 1772 by Joseph Priestley. Anaesthetic properties noted by Humphry Davy (1800), who coined the name due to giggling effects. First clinical use as dental anaesthetic: Horace Wells (1844, USA). Still used today in dental + obstetric anaesthesia (in 50:50 N₂O/O₂ mixture, 'Entonox'). Also used as an oxidiser in rockets + whipped-cream aerosol propellant. GREENHOUSE GAS: ~300× more warming than CO₂ per kg, ~114-year atmospheric lifetime. Main sources: agricultural N fertilisers, livestock, industrial emissions. DISCOVERED: Methane (Volta 1776), CO₂ (Joseph Black 1754), Hydrogen (Henry Cavendish 1766), Oxygen (Joseph Priestley 1774, also Carl Scheele 1772 independently). OTHER INHALATION ANAESTHETICS: Ether (1842 by Crawford Long), Chloroform (1847 James Young Simpson for childbirth), Halothane (1956), Isoflurane, Sevoflurane (modern).

cards.front:
Consider the following about HYDROCARBONS. 1. Alkanes are saturated and have the general formula CnH2n+2. 2. Alkenes contain at least one C=C double bond and exhibit geometric (cis-trans) isomerism. 3. Benzene is an aromatic hydrocarbon with the formula C6H6 and each C-C bond length is intermediate between a single and double bond. 4. Methane is the principal component of LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas). Which are correct?

(A) 1, 2 and 3 only
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(C) 2 and 3 only
(D) 1 and 4 only
cards.back:
(A) 1, 2 and 3 only

Organic Chemistry — Statement 4 is WRONG — LPG is mainly PROPANE (C3H8) and BUTANE (C4H10), not methane. Methane is the main component of CNG (Compressed Natural Gas) and of BIOGAS. Statements 1, 2, 3 are standard organic-chemistry facts.

cards.front:
Match the polymer with its monomer. A. Polythene. B. PVC. C. Teflon. D. Nylon-6,6. List-II: 1. Tetrafluoroethene. 2. Ethene. 3. Vinyl chloride. 4. Hexamethylenediamine + adipic acid.

(A) A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4
(B) A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4
(C) A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4

Which of the following is INCORRECTLY matched?

(A) Ethanol (C2H5OH) — common drinking alcohol
(B) Methanol (CH3OH) — highly toxic; 'wood spirit'
(C) Formaldehyde (HCHO) — used in preservation of biological specimens
(D) Acetic acid (CH3COOH) — used as a disinfectant and bleach
cards.back:

The 'greenhouse potential' of methane (CH4) over a 100-year period is ROUGHLY how many times that of CO2?

(A) ~5×
(B) ~28×
(C) ~200×
(D) ~1000×
cards.back:
(B) ~28×

cards.front:
Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is produced by reacting salicylic acid with:

(A) Methanol
(B) Acetic anhydride
(C) Sodium carbonate
(D) Ammonia
cards.back:
(B) Acetic anhydride

First synthesised by Bayer (Felix Hoffmann, 1897) as a safer alternative to salicylic acid itself, which was harsh on the stomach.

cards.front:
Consider the following about SOAPS and DETERGENTS. 1. Soaps are sodium/potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids. 2. Soaps do NOT work well in hard water because they form insoluble precipitates (scum) with Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ ions. 3. Detergents work in hard water because their sulfonate head does not precipitate with Ca/Mg. 4. Both soaps and detergents clean by having a hydrophilic head and a hydrophobic tail that solubilises oil/grease in water via micelles. Which are correct?

(A) 1, 2 and 4 only
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(C) 1 and 4 only
(D) 2 and 3 only
cards.back:
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4

Organic Chemistry — All four correct. Soap: R-COONa. Scum = Ca(RCOO)2. Detergent: R-SO3Na — the calcium sulfonate salt is soluble, so no scum. Cleaning mechanism identical — dual-character molecule forms micelles around grease droplets.

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT a greenhouse gas?

(A) Nitrous oxide (N2O)
(B) Ozone (O3)
(C) Nitrogen (N2)
(D) Methane (CH4)
cards.back:
(C) Nitrogen (N2)

Organic Chemistry — Molecular N2 does NOT absorb infrared radiation (its vibrational modes are IR-inactive because it is a homo-nuclear diatomic with no dipole moment). It is ~78 % of the atmosphere but not a greenhouse gas. CH4, N2O, O3, CO2, H2O, CFCs, HFCs, SF6 all ARE greenhouse gases.

Which of the following is the CORRECT IUPAC name of CH3-CH(OH)-CH2-CH3?

(A) Butan-1-ol
(B) Butan-2-ol
(C) Butan-3-ol
(D) Pentan-2-ol
cards.back:
(B) Butan-2-ol

Organic Chemistry — 4-carbon chain → 'butan-'. -OH is on C2 (numbering from the end that gives lowest locant to -OH). So butan-2-ol. 'Butan-3-ol' is the same molecule mis-numbered (numbering should always give the principal group the lowest locant — 2 not 3).

cards.front:
Approximately what percentage of dry air (by volume) is nitrogen?

(A) 21%
(B) 78%
(C) 1%
(D) 0.04%
cards.back:
(B) 78%

Applied Chemistry — Dry-air composition: N₂ ~78.09%, O₂ ~20.95%, Ar ~0.93%, CO₂ ~0.04% (~420 ppm in 2024, rising), Ne ~0.0018%, He ~0.0005%, CH₄ ~0.00019%. Water vapour varies 0-4% depending on humidity (excluded from 'dry' calculations). Composition is uniform up to ~80 km altitude — homosphere. Above 80 km, lighter gases (H, He) rise; heavier ones sink — heterosphere.

cards.front:
The MOST abundant noble gas in Earth's atmosphere is:

(A) Helium
(B) Argon (~0.93%)
(C) Neon
(D) Krypton
cards.back:
(B) Argon (~0.93%)

Applied Chemistry — Argon — 0.93% of atmosphere. Mostly Ar-40 produced by radioactive decay of K-40 over Earth's lifetime. Used in inert atmospheres (welding, incandescent bulbs to prevent filament oxidation), Geiger counters. Other noble gases: Ne ~18 ppm, He ~5 ppm (escapes Earth's gravity continuously — global helium reserves limited!), Kr ~1 ppm, Xe ~0.09 ppm, Rn (radioactive, trace, indoor air pollutant). Helium is more abundant in the universe (after H), but rare on Earth's atmosphere.

(A) Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
(B) Methane (CH₄)
(C) Oxygen (O₂)
(D) Nitrous oxide (N₂O)
cards.back:
(C) Oxygen (O₂)

The Paris Agreement covers CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, HFCs, PFCs, SF₆, NF₃ ('Kyoto basket').

cards.front:
Atmospheric CO₂ concentration in 2024 was approximately:

(A) ~280 ppm (pre-industrial)
(B) ~420 ppm — highest in 800,000 years
(C) ~600 ppm
(D) ~1000 ppm
cards.back:
(B) ~420 ppm — highest in 800,000 years

Applied Chemistry — Mauna Loa observatory measurements (Keeling curve): CO₂ = 280 ppm pre-industrial → 315 in 1958 → 421 ppm (May 2024 monthly average). Highest in 800,000 years per Antarctic ice cores. Increasing ~2.5 ppm/year. Methane similarly: pre-industrial ~720 ppb → ~1,920 ppb in 2024. India's CO₂ emissions per capita are still low (~2 tCO₂/yr) vs USA (15) or China (8) — but total emissions are 3rd largest globally (~7% of total).

cards.front:
The gas responsible for ACID RAIN (along with NOₓ) is primarily:

(A) Helium
(B) Sulphur dioxide (SO₂)
(C) Argon
(D) Methane
cards.back:
(B) Sulphur dioxide (SO₂)

Applied Chemistry — SO₂ — released by burning sulphur-rich coal, ore smelting, vehicle exhaust. In atmosphere SO₂ + O₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ → H₂SO₄. NOₓ → HNO₃. These dissolve in raindrops → 'acid rain' (pH < 5.6, sometimes <4). Damages forests, freshwater life (especially fish, amphibians), buildings (limestone CaCO₃ dissolves: Taj Mahal yellowing). Reduced sharply since 1990s in West with flue-gas desulphurisation in coal plants. Major SO₂ emitters today — India, China.

Carbon monoxide (CO) is highly toxic to humans because it:

(A) Is acidic in water
(B) Binds to haemoglobin ~250× more strongly than O₂, blocking oxygen transport
(C) Causes immediate dehydration
(D) Is radioactive
cards.back:
(B) Binds to haemoglobin ~250× more strongly than O₂, blocking oxygen transport

Applied Chemistry — CO + Hb → carboxyhaemoglobin (HbCO) — bond strength ~250× greater than HbO₂. Blocks the haemoglobin's oxygen-carrying capacity → cellular hypoxia → headache, dizziness, nausea, unconsciousness, death. Sources: incomplete combustion (vehicle exhaust without catalytic converter, faulty heaters, charcoal stoves indoors), forest fires, smoking. Antidote: 100% O₂ inhalation; hyperbaric O₂ in severe cases. CO is COLOURLESS, ODOURLESS, TASTELESS — silent killer. Domestic CO detectors save lives.

cards.front:
Among the noble gases, the one used in lasers and producing BRIGHT RED-ORANGE GLOW in 'neon signs' is:

(A) Argon
(B) Neon — gives the iconic red-orange light
(C) Krypton
(D) Helium
cards.back:
(B) Neon — gives the iconic red-orange light

Applied Chemistry — Each noble gas glows a characteristic colour when high voltage passed through low-pressure tube — Neon = bright red-orange (the only true 'neon' in 'neon signs'). Argon = pale lavender (with phosphor → bright white). Helium = orange-yellow. Krypton = dim greenish-white. Xenon = bright blue-white. Decorative 'neon signs' often use mixtures + coloured glass + phosphor coatings to produce other colours; only the genuine red-orange is from neon itself.

cards.front:
Building blocks of PROTEINS are:

(A) Glucose units (sugars chained)
(B) Amino acids (linked by peptide bonds)
(C) Fatty acids (long carbon chains)
(D) Nucleotides (DNA bases, sugar)
cards.back:
(B) Amino acids (linked by peptide bonds)

Applied Chemistry — PROTEINS are POLYMERS of AMINO ACIDS, joined by PEPTIDE BONDS (−CO−NH−). 20 standard amino acids; humans need 9 ESSENTIAL ones from diet (rest body can synthesise). Each amino acid: −NH₂ + −COOH + R-group (side chain) on a central carbon. PROTEIN STRUCTURE 4 levels: PRIMARY (amino acid sequence), SECONDARY (alpha-helix, beta-sheet — H-bonding patterns), TERTIARY (3D folding via various bonds), QUATERNARY (multiple sub-units, e.g., Hb has 4). INSIGHT — proteins do EVERYTHING: enzymes (catalysts), structural (collagen, keratin), transport (Hb), antibodies (immune), hormones (insulin), receptors. RELATED: carbs polymerise glucose; nucleic acids polymerise nucleotides; lipids aren't true polymers.

cards.front:
GLUCOSE has the molecular formula:

(A) C₆H₁₂O₆ (a hexose sugar)
(B) C₅H₁₀O₅ (a pentose sugar)
(C) C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ (a disaccharide)
(D) C₂H₅OH (an alcohol)
cards.back:
(A) C₆H₁₂O₆ (a hexose sugar)

Applied Chemistry — GLUCOSE: C₆H₁₂O₆ — HEXOSE (6-C) sugar; primary energy source for cells. Same formula as FRUCTOSE (fruit sugar) + GALACTOSE — these are STRUCTURAL ISOMERS (same molecular formula, different structures). DISACCHARIDES (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁): SUCROSE = glucose + fructose (table sugar); LACTOSE = glucose + galactose (milk sugar; some adults are lactose-intolerant — lack the enzyme lactase); MALTOSE = glucose + glucose. POLYSACCHARIDES: STARCH (plant storage), GLYCOGEN (animal storage in liver + muscles), CELLULOSE (plant cell walls — humans CAN'T digest because no enzyme cellulase; ruminants can via gut bacteria).

cards.front:
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is built from:

(A) Amino acid building blocks here
(B) Nucleotides (sugar + phosphate + base)
(C) Glucose + fructose units chained
(D) Fatty acids + glycerol esters
cards.back:
(B) Nucleotides (sugar + phosphate + base)

Applied Chemistry — NUCLEIC ACIDS (DNA + RNA) are POLYMERS of NUCLEOTIDES. Each nucleotide = (1) PENTOSE SUGAR (deoxyribose for DNA; ribose for RNA); (2) PHOSPHATE group; (3) NITROGENOUS BASE — A, T, G, C in DNA (T replaced by U in RNA). Nucleotides linked by PHOSPHODIESTER bonds → backbone. Two strands of DNA pair via H-bonds: A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds). 'CHARGAFF'S RULE': %A = %T, %G = %C in DNA. Watson + Crick (1953) discovered double-helix structure (with Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data — Photo 51). Nobel 1962. Human DNA: ~3 billion bp; 23 chromosome pairs.

cards.front:
FATS + OILS (triglycerides) are esters of:

(A) Glucose + fatty acids
(B) Glycerol + 3 fatty acids
(C) Amino acids + glycerol
(D) Cholesterol + carboxylic acids
cards.back:
(B) Glycerol + 3 fatty acids

Applied Chemistry — TRIGLYCERIDES = GLYCEROL (3-OH alcohol) + 3 FATTY ACIDS, linked by ester bonds. SATURATED fatty acids (no C=C) → solid at room temp (animal fats — butter, ghee). UNSATURATED (1+ C=C) → liquid (vegetable oils — olive, sunflower). HYDROGENATION turns oils into solid fats (vanaspati ghee) — but creates TRANS FATS (linked to heart disease). OMEGA-3 / 6 / 9 FATS = unsaturated, named by position of first double bond. CHOLESTEROL — different class (a STEROL, not glyceride; component of cell membranes; precursor of bile salts + sex hormones + Vit D). HDL = 'good' cholesterol; LDL = 'bad'.

cards.front:
Most ENZYMES (biological catalysts) are:

(A) Lipids (fat-based catalysts)
(B) Proteins (with specific 3D shapes)
(C) Carbohydrates (sugar polymers)
(D) Nucleic acids (DNA + RNA only)
cards.back:
(B) Proteins (with specific 3D shapes)

Applied Chemistry — ENZYMES — usually PROTEINS (some are RNA — ribozymes — discovered later; expanded definition). Function: speed up biochemical reactions by lowering activation energy. SPECIFIC: each enzyme acts on a specific SUBSTRATE (lock-and-key model; or induced-fit). Affected by: pH, temperature (DENATURATION at high temp); inhibitors. Examples: AMYLASE (saliva — breaks starch), PEPSIN (stomach acid — proteins), TRYPSIN (small intestine — proteins), LIPASE (fats), LACTASE (lactose). NAMES often end in '-ASE'. INSIGHT — without enzymes, life would be too slow; some reactions take seconds with enzymes vs years without.

cards.front:
Which biomolecule provides the MOST energy per gram (~9 kcal/g)?

(A) Carbohydrates (~4 kcal/g energy)
(B) Fats / lipids (~9 kcal/g energy)
(C) Proteins (~4 kcal/g energy)
(D) Vitamins (no energy supply)
cards.back:
(B) Fats / lipids (~9 kcal/g energy)

Applied Chemistry — ENERGY DENSITY: FATS ~9 kcal/g (highest); CARBS ~4 kcal/g; PROTEINS ~4 kcal/g; ALCOHOL ~7 kcal/g. WHY fats give more energy: more reduced (more C-H bonds, less oxidised) → more energy released on oxidation. EVOLUTIONARY: fats are concentrated energy storage — animals store excess as fat. WATER content also matters: fats anhydrous (no water) → very compact storage. Glycogen in muscles/liver is stored WITH water → less energy-dense in body. Vitamins + minerals: NO calories themselves, but ENABLE other reactions. INSIGHT — daily Indian dietary need ~2000-2500 kcal; obesity = excess fat storage from chronic surplus calories.

cards.front:
VITAMIN C (Ascorbic acid) is also a:

(A) Strong base (alkaline reaction)
(B) Water-soluble vitamin (antioxidant)
(C) Fat-soluble vitamin (stored in body)
(D) Mineral (iron in haemoglobin)
cards.back:
(B) Water-soluble vitamin (antioxidant)

Applied Chemistry — VITAMIN C = ASCORBIC ACID. WATER-SOLUBLE (along with B-complex). ANTIOXIDANT (neutralises free radicals). Helps: collagen synthesis (skin, blood vessels, bones), iron absorption, immunity, wound healing. DEFICIENCY → SCURVY (bleeding gums, weakness, joint pain — historically killed many sailors before fresh fruit/limes became standard). RDA ~75 mg/day (more for smokers). SOURCES: amla, citrus, guava, capsicum, kiwi, berries, leafy greens. Cooking destroys ~20-50% (heat-sensitive). VITAMINS classification: WATER-SOLUBLE (B + C, excreted excess in urine, daily need); FAT-SOLUBLE (A, D, E, K — stored in liver/fat, can accumulate to toxic levels).

cards.front:
Glucose and fructose have the same molecular formula (C₆H₁₂O₆) but differ in structure. They are called:

(A) Allotropes
(B) Isomers
(C) Isotopes
(D) Polymers
cards.back:
(B) Isomers

Applied Chemistry — Isomers — compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements and hence different properties. Glucose has an aldehyde group; fructose a ketone group — they taste differently (fructose is sweeter) and have different functions. Allotropes — different physical forms of the same element (diamond vs graphite for carbon). Isotopes — atoms of the same element with different neutron counts.

cards.front:
The sugar found in milk is:

(A) Sucrose
(B) Lactose
(C) Fructose
(D) Maltose
cards.back:
(B) Lactose

Applied Chemistry — Lactose — the disaccharide found in milk — breaks down by the enzyme lactase into glucose + galactose. 'Lactose intolerance' is a deficiency of lactase. Sucrose is table sugar (from sugarcane / beet); glucose + fructose. Fructose — fruit sugar (also in honey). Maltose — from grain germination (barley); glucose + glucose.

cards.front:
Proteins are polymers of:

(A) Fatty acids
(B) Amino acids
(C) Nucleotides
(D) Monosaccharides
cards.back:
(B) Amino acids

Applied Chemistry — Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. 20 standard amino acids build almost all proteins; 9 are 'essential' (must come from food). Fatty acids build lipids; nucleotides build DNA/RNA; monosaccharides build carbohydrates. Protein shape follows from sequence — a folding error can cause diseases (prion diseases, Alzheimer's).

cards.front:
The chemical messenger that carries information from DNA out of the nucleus to the ribosomes is:

(A) tRNA
(B) mRNA
(C) rRNA
(D) miRNA
cards.back:
(B) mRNA

Applied Chemistry — mRNA (messenger RNA) is transcribed from DNA in the nucleus and carries the genetic code to the ribosome, where it is translated into protein. tRNA (transfer RNA) brings amino acids to the ribosome and matches them to mRNA codons. rRNA (ribosomal RNA) is the structural RNA of the ribosome itself. miRNA (microRNA) is a short RNA that regulates gene expression.

cards.front:
Starch is stored in plants chiefly as a reserve of:

(A) Proteins
(B) Energy (polysaccharide)
(C) Structural support
(D) Genetic material
cards.back:
(B) Energy (polysaccharide)

Applied Chemistry — Starch is a polysaccharide of glucose — the main energy store in plants. Grain seeds (rice, wheat), tubers (potato) and roots (cassava) store starch. Iodine turns blue-black on contact with starch — the classic test. Animals store glucose as glycogen in liver / muscles. Cellulose (another glucose polymer) gives structural support to plant cell walls.

cards.front:
Which of the following is a water-soluble vitamin?

(A) Vitamin A
(B) Vitamin C
(C) Vitamin D
(D) Vitamin K
cards.back:
(B) Vitamin C

Applied Chemistry — Water-soluble vitamins — Vitamin C and the eight B-complex vitamins. Not stored in large amounts; excess excreted in urine; must be eaten regularly. Fat-soluble — A, D, E, K — stored in liver / adipose tissue; hypervitaminosis possible if over-supplemented. Vitamin C sources: amla, citrus, guava, chilli.

cards.front:
Fats and oils are chemically:

(A) Esters of glycerol and fatty acids
(B) Polymers of amino acids
(C) Complex sugars
(D) Compounds of iron and calcium
cards.back:
(A) Esters of glycerol and fatty acids

Applied Chemistry — Fats and oils are triglycerides — triesters of glycerol and three fatty acids. 'Fats' are solid at room temperature (animal fats, tropical oils); 'oils' are liquid (most vegetable oils). Saturated fats have no C=C double bonds; unsaturated fats have one (mono-) or more (poly-). Trans fats are partial hydrogenation products, considered unhealthy.

cards.front:
The chemical name of 'common salt' used in cooking is:

(A) Sodium bicarbonate
(B) Sodium chloride
(C) Sodium hydroxide
(D) Sodium carbonate
cards.back:
(B) Sodium chloride

Applied Chemistry — Common salt = sodium chloride (NaCl). Sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃) — baking soda; sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) — washing soda; sodium hydroxide (NaOH) — caustic soda. Indian table salt is fortified with potassium iodate to prevent goitre. Sea water is ~3.5 % NaCl by weight; Sambhar Lake and Rann of Kachchh are important sources of salt in India.

cards.front:
'Quicklime' — used in whitewashing — is chemically:

(A) Calcium hydroxide
(B) Calcium oxide
(C) Calcium carbonate
(D) Calcium chloride
cards.back:
(B) Calcium oxide

Applied Chemistry — Quicklime — CaO — made by heating limestone (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂). On adding water — exothermic slaking to give calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)₂), 'slaked lime', used in whitewashing. Lime water is a dilute solution of Ca(OH)₂; turns milky on passing CO₂ (that's the basic chemistry test for CO₂).

cards.front:
'Dry ice' — used in cold storage and stage smoke — is the solid form of:

(A) Ice (water)
(B) Carbon dioxide
(C) Liquid nitrogen
(D) Calcium carbide
cards.back:
(B) Carbon dioxide

Applied Chemistry — Dry ice — solid CO₂. Sublimes directly to gas at −78.5 °C at standard pressure (does not melt — hence 'dry'). Used to keep ice cream and frozen foods cold during transit, for rapid cooling in lab work, and for stage 'smoke' effects (fog comes from water condensing around the cold CO₂ vapour). Liquid nitrogen is colder (−196 °C) but is liquid, not solid, at its boiling point.

cards.front:
'Vinegar' is a dilute aqueous solution of:

(A) Hydrochloric acid
(B) Acetic acid
(C) Citric acid
(D) Oxalic acid
cards.back:
(B) Acetic acid

Applied Chemistry — Vinegar — 4-8 % acetic acid (CH₃COOH) in water. Made by the bacterial fermentation of ethanol. Citric acid is in lemons and limes (not vinegar); oxalic acid in spinach and some rust-removers; HCl in stomach acid (toxic at vinegar-level concentrations on skin). Acetic acid gives pickles and chutneys their sour taste and preserves food. ethanoic acid.

cards.front:
'Marble' — used in buildings like the Taj Mahal — is a rock form of:

(A) Silicon dioxide
(B) Calcium carbonate
(C) Iron oxide
(D) Aluminium silicate
cards.back:
(B) Calcium carbonate

Applied Chemistry — Marble — a metamorphic rock, chiefly calcium carbonate (CaCO₃), formed from limestone under heat and pressure. Because it is a carbonate, it reacts with acids — which is why acid rain (H₂SO₄, HNO₃) is eating into the Taj Mahal's white Makrana marble. Silicon dioxide — quartz / sand. Iron oxide — rust. Aluminium silicate — the mineral base of common clays.

cards.front:
'Bleaching powder' — widely used to disinfect water and to bleach cotton — has the chemical name:

(A) Calcium hydroxide
(B) Calcium hypochlorite
(C) Calcium carbonate
(D) Sodium hypochlorite
cards.back:
(B) Calcium hypochlorite

Applied Chemistry — Bleaching powder — CaOCl₂ / more precisely a mixture that contains calcium hypochlorite Ca(OCl)₂ — produced by passing chlorine gas over dry slaked lime. Releases Cl₂, which is the active bleaching / disinfecting agent. Used in paper and textile mills for bleaching, and in municipal water treatment and swimming pools. Liquid bleach (in laundries) is sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) solution.

cards.front:
'Gypsum' — used to make plaster of Paris — is chemically:

(A) Anhydrous calcium sulphate
(B) Calcium sulphate dihydrate
(C) Calcium chloride dihydrate
(D) Sodium sulphate dihydrate
cards.back:
(B) Calcium sulphate dihydrate

Applied Chemistry — Gypsum — CaSO₄·2H₂O. Heated to around 120 °C, it loses 1.5 water molecules to give plaster of Paris — CaSO₄·½H₂O. When PoP is mixed with water again, it sets within minutes as it re-crystallises into gypsum. Widely used in medical casts, decorative mouldings, blackboard chalk. Pure gypsum also occurs in nature as selenite crystals.

cards.front:
Atoms of the same element having different mass numbers (different number of neutrons) are called:

(A) Isobars
(B) Isotopes
(C) Isotones
(D) Isomers
cards.back:
(B) Isotopes

Applied Chemistry — Isotopes — same element (same atomic number Z, same chemical behaviour) but different mass numbers (different neutron counts). H has three: protium ¹H, deuterium ²H, tritium ³H. Common confusables: Isobars — different elements, same mass number (e.g. ⁴⁰Ar and ⁴⁰Ca). Isotones — same neutron count, different elements. Isomers (in chemistry) — same molecular formula, different structure. Mass number A = protons + neutrons.

Nuclear FISSION involves:

(A) Combining of light nuclei
(B) Splitting of a heavy nucleus into smaller nuclei
(C) Neutron absorption only
(D) Electron capture
cards.back:
(B) Splitting of a heavy nucleus into smaller nuclei

Applied Chemistry — Fission — heavy nucleus (e.g. ²³⁵U) absorbs a slow neutron and splits into two roughly equal smaller nuclei (e.g. Ba and Kr) + 2-3 free neutrons + ~200 MeV energy. Discovered 1938 by Otto Hahn, Fritz Strassmann, Lise Meitner. Free neutrons can trigger more fissions → chain reaction → atomic energy / atomic bomb. Fusion is the OPPOSITE — light nuclei combine. Sun's energy comes from p-p fusion of hydrogen → helium, releasing far more energy per kg than fission.

cards.front:
Which type of radiation has the highest penetrating power and the lowest ionising power?

(A) Alpha (α)
(B) Gamma (γ)
(C) Beta (β)
(D) Neutron
cards.back:
(B) Gamma (γ)

Applied Chemistry — Penetration: γ > β > α (gamma needs lead/concrete to stop). Ionisation: α > β > γ (heavy alphas pack the most charge but get absorbed quickly). Alpha — He nucleus (2p+2n); stopped by paper. Beta — fast electron; stopped by aluminium foil. Gamma — high-energy photon (electromagnetic); needs lead. Neutrons — uncharged, very penetrating, slowed by hydrogen-rich material (water, paraffin).

cards.front:
The 'half-life' of a radioactive isotope is the time required for:

(A) All atoms to decay
(B) Half of the original atoms to decay
(C) Half of the energy to be released
(D) Two new isotopes to form
cards.back:
(B) Half of the original atoms to decay

Applied Chemistry — Half-life (t½) — time taken for HALF of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay; constant for a given isotope, independent of temperature, pressure, or quantity. Examples: C-14 (5,730 years — used in archaeological dating up to ~50,000 years); U-238 (4.5 billion years — used to date the Earth); I-131 (8 days — medical thyroid imaging); Tc-99m (6 hours — medical imaging). After n half-lives, fraction remaining = (1/2)ⁿ.
cards.option2: Half of the energy to be released

cards.front:
India's first nuclear reactor, commissioned in 1956, was named:

(A) Cirus
(B) Apsara
(C) Dhruva
(D) Purnima
cards.back:
(B) Apsara

Applied Chemistry — Apsara — 1 MW research reactor at Trombay, commissioned 4 August 1956 by Homi Bhabha. Asia's first nuclear reactor. Used 80%-enriched uranium fuel supplied by UK. Decommissioned 2009; replaced by Apsara-U (2018) using Low-Enriched Uranium. Subsequent BARC research reactors — Cirus (1960), Zerlina (1961), Purnima (1972), Dhruva (1985, India's largest research reactor — 100 MW). Power reactors followed at Tarapur (1969 — first commercial), Kalpakkam, Kakrapar, Kudankulam.

cards.front:
Heavy water (D₂O), used as a moderator in CANDU-type reactors, has deuterium replacing hydrogen. Deuterium contains:

(A) 1 proton + 0 neutrons
(B) 1 proton + 1 neutron
(C) 2 protons + 1 neutron
(D) 1 proton + 2 neutrons
cards.back:
(B) 1 proton + 1 neutron

Applied Chemistry — Deuterium (²H or D) — isotope of hydrogen with 1 proton + 1 neutron. Discovered 1931 by Harold Urey (Nobel 1934). Heavy water (D₂O) is ~10% denser than ordinary H₂O; freezes at 3.8 °C, boils at 101.4 °C. Used as MODERATOR in PHWR (Pressurised Heavy Water Reactor) — slows neutrons without absorbing many of them, enabling natural uranium (cheaper, no enrichment) to sustain a chain reaction. India's PHWRs at Kakrapar, Kaiga, Narora, Tarapur are CANDU-style.

cards.front:
India's three-stage nuclear programme — drawn up by Homi Bhabha — culminates in stage 3 with:

(A) Pressurised water reactors using imported enriched uranium
(B) Thorium-based reactors using U-233 bred from thorium-232
(C) Coal-cycle integrated reactors
(D) Fusion reactors
cards.back:
(B) Thorium-based reactors using U-233 bred from thorium-232

Applied Chemistry — Bhabha's three-stage programme: (1) Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWR) — natural U-238 fuel, produces Pu-239 + electricity. (2) Fast Breeder Reactors (FBR) — burn the Pu-239 from stage 1 + breed U-233 from thorium blanket. India's PFBR at Kalpakkam (started low-power ops 2024). (3) Thorium reactors using bred U-233 — exploits India's vast Th-232 reserves (~25% of world). Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) being developed at BARC. India holds ~9.6 lakh tonnes of monazite (thorium-rich) along Kerala/TN/Odisha beaches.

cards.front:
A polymer is best described as:

(A) A small organic molecule
(B) A large molecule built from repeating subunits called monomers
(C) An ionic compound
(D) A type of metal alloy
cards.back:
(B) A large molecule built from repeating subunits called monomers

Applied Chemistry — Polymer (Greek 'poly' many + 'mer' parts) — long chains/networks of repeating monomer units. Natural polymers — cellulose (glucose monomers), starch, proteins (amino acid monomers), DNA (nucleotides), rubber (isoprene). Synthetic polymers — polyethylene (ethylene), PVC (vinyl chloride), nylon, Teflon, polyester, Bakelite. Two formation reactions — Addition polymerisation (monomers add directly, no byproduct) and Condensation polymerisation (loses small molecules like water).

cards.front:
Polythene is a polymer of:

(A) Vinyl chloride
(B) Ethylene (ethene)
(C) Acetylene
(D) Phenol
cards.back:
(B) Ethylene (ethene)

Applied Chemistry — Polythene / Polyethylene — repeating −CH₂−CH₂− units made from ethylene C₂H₄ via addition polymerisation. World's most widely produced plastic. Two main types: LDPE (Low Density, ~0.92 g/cm³, branched, used in plastic bags, films) and HDPE (High Density, ~0.96 g/cm³, linear, used in milk jugs, pipes, hard hats). PVC = polyvinyl chloride (from vinyl chloride CH₂=CHCl). PVA = polyvinyl acetate. PS = polystyrene (from styrene C₆H₅CH=CH₂).

cards.front:
Bakelite — the world's first synthetic plastic (1907) — is a:

(A) Thermoplastic
(B) Thermosetting plastic (cannot be remelted once cured)
(C) Elastomer
(D) Natural polymer
cards.back:
(B) Thermosetting plastic (cannot be remelted once cured)

Applied Chemistry — Bakelite — Leo Baekeland (1907) — phenol-formaldehyde resin. Thermoset: once cured, it cannot be remelted (cross-linked 3D network). Used in electrical switches, plug sockets, telephone handsets, kitchen utensils, billiard balls. Other thermosets: Melamine, Urea-formaldehyde, Epoxy, Polyurethane (some). Thermoplastics — soften on heating, can be remoulded (PE, PVC, PS, PP, nylon, acrylic). Elastomers — stretchy (rubber, silicone, neoprene).

cards.front:
Teflon — known for non-stick cookware coatings — is chemically:

(A) Polyethylene with chlorine
(B) Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) — repeating −CF₂−CF₂− units
(C) Polyvinyl chloride
(D) Polyester
cards.back:
(B) Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) — repeating −CF₂−CF₂− units

Applied Chemistry — Teflon — DuPont brand for PTFE, accidentally discovered 1938 by Roy Plunkett. C-F bond is one of the strongest in chemistry → PTFE is chemically inert, slippery, withstands −240 to +260 °C. Used in cookware (since 1960s), gaskets, plumbing tape, expedition clothing (Gore-Tex laminate), wire insulation. Concerns about PFOA/PFAS additives (forever chemicals); newer products are PFOA-free.

cards.front:
Nylon-6,6 is formed by condensation polymerisation of:

(A) Vinyl chloride and styrene
(B) Hexamethylenediamine + Adipic acid (each contributing 6 carbons → name nylon 6,6)
(C) Methyl methacrylate
(D) Acrylonitrile + butadiene
cards.back:
(B) Hexamethylenediamine + Adipic acid (each contributing 6 carbons → name nylon 6,6)

Applied Chemistry — Nylon-6,6 — Wallace Carothers (DuPont, 1935). Condensation polymerisation between hexamethylenediamine (H₂N-(CH₂)₆-NH₂, 6 carbons) and adipic acid (HOOC-(CH₂)₄-COOH, 6 carbons → 4 carbons + 2 COOH-C = 6) — hence '6,6'. Forms amide linkages (-CO-NH-) like proteins. Loses water as byproduct. Strong, lightweight, stockings, parachutes, ropes. Nylon-6 is from caprolactam (just one monomer, ring-opening polymerisation).

cards.front:
PET (Polyethylene Terephthalate), used in soft-drink bottles, has the recycling identifier number:

(A) 1 (♻ inside triangle)
(B) 2
(C) 5
(D) 7
cards.back:
(A) 1 (♻ inside triangle)

Applied Chemistry — Resin Identification Codes (1-7, used worldwide): 1 = PET / PETE (water bottles, soda bottles, polyester fibres); 2 = HDPE (milk jugs, shampoo); 3 = PVC (pipes, vinyl); 4 = LDPE (grocery bags); 5 = PP (yoghurt cups, bottle caps); 6 = PS (foam cups, packing peanuts); 7 = OTHER (bioplastics, polycarbonates, mixed). Lower numbers (1, 2, 5) generally most recyclable. PET is also used as polyester fibres in clothing.

cards.front:
Natural rubber is a polymer of which monomer?

(A) Ethylene
(B) Isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene)
(C) Vinyl chloride
(D) Styrene
cards.back:
(B) Isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene)

Applied Chemistry — Natural rubber — cis-1,4-polyisoprene, from the latex of Hevea brasiliensis tree (Pará rubber, Brazil origin). Vulcanisation (Charles Goodyear, 1839) — heat with sulphur → cross-links → improves elasticity, durability, heat resistance — basis of tyres. Synthetic rubbers — Styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR, in tyres), Polybutadiene, Neoprene (chloroprene), Buna-S, Buna-N. Largest natural-rubber producer — Thailand; India is one of the top 5 (Kerala accounts for 90% of India's production).

cards.front:
The chemical reaction by which soap is manufactured (alkali + fat → soap + glycerol) is called:

(A) Polymerisation
(B) Saponification
(C) Hydrogenation
(D) Esterification
cards.back:
(B) Saponification

Applied Chemistry — Saponification — alkaline hydrolysis of triglyceride (fat or oil) to give soap (sodium / potassium salt of fatty acid) + glycerol. Reagents: NaOH gives 'hard' soaps (bar soap); KOH gives 'soft' soaps (liquid hand soap, shaving soaps). Fats from oils — palm, coconut, olive, tallow. Industrial process: 'hot process' (heat + lye, faster) or 'cold process' (room temperature, slower 4-6 weeks for cure). Glycerol is a valuable byproduct (used in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals).

cards.front:
A soap molecule is described as 'amphiphilic' — meaning it has:

(A) Two acidic ends
(B) A hydrophobic (water-hating) hydrocarbon tail AND a hydrophilic (water-loving) ionic head
(C) Only hydrophilic groups
(D) No charged groups
cards.back:
(B) A hydrophobic (water-hating) hydrocarbon tail AND a hydrophilic (water-loving) ionic head

Applied Chemistry — Soap = sodium salt of long-chain fatty acid, e.g., sodium stearate CH₃(CH₂)₁₆COO⁻Na⁺. Long hydrocarbon tail (~12-18 C) is hydrophobic / lipophilic; ionic carboxylate head is hydrophilic. In water, molecules form MICELLES — spherical clusters with tails pointing inward (trapping oil/dirt) and heads facing outward (water-soluble). This is how soap removes greasy dirt — the dirt gets emulsified inside micelles and washes away.

cards.front:
Soap does NOT lather well with HARD water because:

(A) Hard water dissolves the soap completely
(B) Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions react with soap to form an insoluble scum
(C) Hard water increases pH
(D) Hard water destroys the hydrocarbon tail
cards.back:
(B) Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions react with soap to form an insoluble scum

Applied Chemistry — Hard water contains Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ from dissolved CaCO₃ / MgCO₃ / sulphates / chlorides. These react with soap (RCOO⁻Na⁺) to form Ca(RCOO)₂ / Mg(RCOO)₂ — INSOLUBLE 'scum' (curdy white precipitate). So most soap is wasted before any lather forms. Detergents (synthetic surfactants) overcome this — their Ca/Mg salts are soluble. Also softening hard water (adding Na₂CO₃ — washing soda; or ion-exchange resins) is a fix.

cards.option3: Hard water destroys the hydrocarbon tail

cards.front:
Synthetic detergents are advantageous over soaps mainly because:

(A) They are cheaper to make
(B) They work even in hard water and acidic conditions
(C) They are 100% biodegradable
(D) They contain no surfactant
cards.back:
(B) They work even in hard water and acidic conditions

Applied Chemistry — Detergents contain sulphonate (-SO₃⁻) or sulphate (-OSO₃⁻) hydrophilic heads instead of carboxylate. Their Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ salts are SOLUBLE — no scum in hard water. Also work in acidic conditions (where soap precipitates out as the free fatty acid). Drawback — many older 'branched-chain' detergents (alkyl benzene sulphonates) are non-biodegradable, polluting waterways. Modern 'linear' alkyl sulphonates + biological enzyme additives are biodegradable + greener. Look for 'eco-friendly' label.

cards.front:
The pH of normal household soap solution is typically:

(A) Strongly acidic (pH 2-3)
(B) Mildly alkaline (pH 9-10)
(C) Neutral (pH 7)
(D) Strongly alkaline (pH 13)
cards.back:
(B) Mildly alkaline (pH 9-10)

Applied Chemistry — Soap is a salt of a strong base (NaOH/KOH) + weak acid (long-chain fatty acid). Hydrolyses in water to give a slightly alkaline solution (pH ~9-10) — explains the slippery feel. Strongly alkaline soap (>pH 11) can be irritating to skin. Some skin-friendly soaps (Dove, Pears) are formulated to be 'mild' (pH ~7). Detergents are usually pH 7-10. Indicator like phenolphthalein turns pink in soap solution (pH > 8.3 trigger).

cards.front:
What component is mainly added to make soaps appear opaque + 'milky'?

(A) Sodium silicate
(B) Titanium dioxide (TiO₂) — opacifier and whitener
(C) Sucrose
(D) Ethanol
cards.back:
(B) Titanium dioxide (TiO₂) — opacifier and whitener

Applied Chemistry — TiO₂ — high refractive index → scatters light → opaque white appearance. Used in toothpastes, paints, sunscreens, foods (E171, though now banned in EU since 2022 over health concerns) for the same reason. Other soap additives: sodium silicate (water glass — makes the bar harder), glycerine (humectant for skin softness), perfumes, antibacterials (triclosan was banned by US FDA in 2016 for OTC washes), pumice/oat for exfoliating soaps, dyes for colour. Transparent soaps use sugar/alcohol to dissolve crystallisation.

cards.front:
Cleansing action of soap relies on the formation of:

(A) Crystals
(B) Micelles trapping oil/dirt in their hydrophobic core
(C) Free radicals
(D) Polymers
cards.back:
(B) Micelles trapping oil/dirt in their hydrophobic core

Applied Chemistry — Above the Critical Micelle Concentration (CMC), surfactant molecules cluster into spherical structures called micelles. Hydrophobic tails point inward, trapping oily dirt; hydrophilic heads face outward into water. The micelle (with its dirt cargo) is washable. Without surfactants, oil + water don't mix. CMC for SDS (sodium dodecyl sulphate, common detergent) ≈ 8 mM. Below CMC — soap behaves as individual molecules, no cleaning action.

cards.front:
Common SALT — sodium chloride — has the chemical formula:

(A) NaCl
(B) NaHCO₃
(C) Na₂CO₃
(D) NaOH
cards.back:
(A) NaCl

Applied Chemistry — SODIUM CHLORIDE (NaCl) — common table salt. Ionic compound. Essential for animal life (Na+ and Cl- ions key for nerve/muscle function, osmotic balance). cards.front:
SOAP and DETERGENTS both clean, but differ in:

(A) Chemical nature: SOAP is sodium/potassium salt of long-chain fatty acids; DETERGENT is a synthetic salt of sulphonic acid
(B) Temperature of use
(C) Colour
(D) Nothing — they're identical
cards.back:
(A) Chemical nature: SOAP is sodium/potassium salt of long-chain fatty acids; DETERGENT is a synthetic salt of sulphonic acid

Applied Chemistry — SOAPS vs DETERGENTS: SOAPS = sodium (or potassium) salts of long-chain FATTY ACIDS (e.g., sodium stearate, palmitate, oleate). Made by SAPONIFICATION — fat/oil + NaOH → soap + glycerol. POTASSIUM soaps are softer (shaving creams). Sodium soaps are harder (bar soaps). PROBLEMS with soap: forms INSOLUBLE 'SCUM' with hard water (Ca²+/Mg²+ ions) → wastes soap + doesn't clean well. DETERGENTS = SYNTHETIC surfactants, typically sodium salts of SULPHONIC acids (alkylbenzene sulphonates — ABS/LAS). ADVANTAGES: work in hard water (Ca/Mg sulphonate salts are soluble), cold water, more lathering. Both have HYDROPHOBIC TAIL (long hydrocarbon chain — dissolves in grease) + HYDROPHILIC HEAD (-COO⁻ or -SO₃⁻ — dissolves in water) → form MICELLES that trap dirt/grease and wash it away. Early detergents had BRANCHED chains (non-biodegradable, polluted water); modern detergents are LINEAR (LAS — biodegradable). First synthetic detergent: BASF Germany 1907. Persil 1907, commercial household products by 1950s in India (Surf 1959 by Hindustan Lever). alkylbenzenesulphonates.

cards.front:
The chemical used to DISINFECT DRINKING WATER + KILL BACTERIA in municipal water supplies is:

(A) Sodium chloride
(B) CHLORINE (Cl₂) or bleaching powder
(C) Ammonia
(D) Sulphuric acid
cards.back:
(B) CHLORINE (Cl₂) or bleaching powder

Applied Chemistry — CHLORINATION — adding chlorine gas (Cl₂) or chlorine compounds (bleaching powder = CaOCl₂, calcium hypochlorite, sodium hypochlorite NaOCl) to drinking water to kill pathogens. Chlorine reacts with water to form hypochlorous acid (HOCl) which is a powerful oxidiser. DOSE: ~0.2-1 mg/L residual chlorine. Introduced in the West around 1900s; in India early 20th c. + mass implementation post-1950s — eliminated waterborne epidemics (cholera, typhoid). Drawback: can form TRIHALOMETHANES (THMs) — potential carcinogens at high levels. ALTERNATIVES: OZONE (O₃ — powerful, no aftertaste, but no residual protection); UV LIGHT (kills microbes, no chemicals); IODINE tablets (backpacking); BOILING; FILTRATION (activated carbon, RO). OTHER chemical uses in daily life: BLEACH — sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) for laundry + cleaning, calcium hypochlorite for pools. ANTACIDS — magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia), aluminium hydroxide, calcium carbonate; neutralise stomach acid. FIRE EXTINGUISHERS — CO₂, foam, powder. BAKING POWDER — NaHCO₃ + acid (cream of tartar) + starch — releases CO₂ to raise dough. VINEGAR — 5-8% acetic acid. calcium oxychloride.

cards.front:
Which gas is used to RIPEN green fruits artificially (e.g. green bananas turning yellow)?

(A) Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
(B) Ethylene (ethene, C₂H₄) — plant hormone
(C) Nitrogen (N₂)
(D) Ozone (O₃)
cards.back:
(B) Ethylene (ethene, C₂H₄) — plant hormone

Applied Chemistry — ETHYLENE (C₂H₄) — a natural PLANT HORMONE that triggers FRUIT RIPENING. Released naturally by fruits as they ripen ('climacteric' fruits — banana, apple, mango, tomato, avocado, pear). Used commercially to trigger uniform ripening: (a) ETHYLENE GAS in sealed chambers — safe, preferred method. (b) CALCIUM CARBIDE (CaC₂) — BANNED in India for fruit ripening since 2011 (Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954, Section 44-AA). Calcium carbide reacts with moisture to release ACETYLENE + also contains traces of ARSENIC + PHOSPHORUS — toxic. Common in India despite ban. Also unsafe: burning newspaper / kerosene fumes in closed banana warehouses. Another ripening agent: ETHEPHON (2-chloroethylphosphonic acid — releases ethylene slowly; used as a plant growth regulator). OTHER HORMONES: (1) AUXINS (growth, root development — IAA indole acetic acid); (2) GIBBERELLINS (stem elongation, seed germination); (3) CYTOKININS (cell division); (4) ABSCISIC ACID (stress response, bud dormancy); (5) ETHYLENE (fruit ripening + flower senescence).

cards.front:
PEARLS are primarily made of:

(A) Silicates
(B) Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃ in the form of aragonite) + conchiolin
(C) Iron oxides
(D) Pure crystalline silicon dioxide
cards.back:
(B) Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃ in the form of aragonite) + conchiolin

Applied Chemistry — PEARLS = predominantly CALCIUM CARBONATE (CaCO₃) in the form of ARAGONITE crystals (a specific crystal form of CaCO₃), held together by CONCHIOLIN (a protein). Same material as MOTHER-OF-PEARL (nacre) that lines the inside of oyster shells. Formation: when an irritant (sand grain, parasite) gets into an OYSTER or mussel, the animal secretes concentric layers of nacre around it → pearl. NATURAL pearls are rare; 99% of jewelry pearls today are CULTURED (a tiny bead is inserted into the oyster, which then coats it). Pearl qualities: size, shape (round best), lustre, surface, colour (white/pink/black/gold depending on oyster species + water conditions). India's Southern pearl fisheries: Gulf of Mannar (TN), earlier Gulf of Kutch. Famous pearls: LA PEREGRINA (Elizabeth Taylor), PEARL OF LAO TZU (largest ~6.4 kg), TAJ MAHAL PEARL. OTHER 'GEMS/STONES' by chemistry: DIAMOND = pure CARBON in tetrahedral lattice; RUBY + SAPPHIRE = aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) with Cr/Fe/Ti impurities; EMERALD = beryllium aluminium silicate (Be₃Al₂Si₆O₁₈); QUARTZ = SiO₂; TURQUOISE = hydrated copper aluminium phosphate; MARBLE = metamorphosed CaCO₃; GRANITE = igneous rock (quartz + feldspar + mica); CORAL = CaCO₃ with organic matter. organic matrix.

cards.front:
Which chemical is called the 'KING OF CHEMICALS' due to its industrial importance?

(A) Hydrochloric acid (HCl)
(B) SULPHURIC ACID (H₂SO₄)
(C) Nitric acid
(D) Methanol
cards.back:
(B) SULPHURIC ACID (H₂SO₄)

Applied Chemistry — SULPHURIC ACID (H₂SO₄) — called the 'KING OF CHEMICALS' because of its vast industrial usage. World production: ~300 million tonnes/year (> any other manufactured chemical). INDUSTRIAL USES: (1) FERTILISER production (super-phosphate, ammonium sulphate — ~50% of global H₂SO₄ goes here); (2) Lead-acid BATTERIES (car batteries use dilute H₂SO₄ as electrolyte); (3) Petroleum refining (catalyst, cleaning); (4) Detergent manufacture (sulphonation); (5) Dye + pigment industry; (6) Steel pickling (to remove oxide layers); (7) Lab uses (as a drying agent — hygroscopic + oxidising); (8) Chemical synthesis. Industrial production: CONTACT PROCESS (S → SO₂ → SO₃ → H₂SO₄) using V₂O₅ catalyst. Discovered by alchemist Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721-815 AD) + Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (c. 865-925). Historical name: 'OIL OF VITRIOL' (thick oil-like appearance). Very corrosive — causes severe burns. India is the 5th-largest producer globally. OTHER IMPORTANT INDUSTRIAL CHEMICALS: AMMONIA (NH₃, Haber-Bosch process, for fertilisers + explosives), CHLORINE (Cl₂, chlor-alkali process, for PVC + disinfection), ETHYLENE (basis of polyethylene, PVC, ethanol), METHANOL (fuel, formaldehyde production).

cards.front:
'STAINLESS STEEL' is resistant to corrosion because of a thin protective layer of which oxide on its surface?

(A) Iron oxide (Fe₂O₃)
(B) Chromium(III) oxide (Cr₂O₃)
(C) Nickel oxide
(D) Copper oxide
cards.back:
(B) Chromium(III) oxide (Cr₂O₃)

Applied Chemistry — STAINLESS STEEL corrosion resistance: due to a thin (<10 nm), invisible, impermeable layer of CHROMIUM(III) OXIDE (Cr₂O₃) that forms spontaneously on the surface. It's PASSIVE + SELF-HEALING — if scratched, re-forms immediately in the presence of oxygen. Hence 'stainless' / 'rustless'. Minimum chromium content for stainless steel: 10.5% (by weight). Invented 1913 by HARRY BREARLEY (Sheffield, UK). GRADES of stainless steel: (1) 18/8 or 304 — 18% Cr + 8% Ni — most common (kitchenware, utensils); (2) 316 — adds 2-3% Mo — better corrosion resistance (marine, chemical plants, surgical); (3) 410, 420, 440 — martensitic, heat-treatable — knives, cutlery. Rust on normal iron: Fe → Fe₂O₃·xH₂O (red-brown, flaky, NOT protective — falls off, exposing fresh iron). Corrosion rate depends on Cr content + environment. Other passivating oxides: ALUMINIUM → Al₂O₃ layer (why aluminium looks dull grey, not shiny); TITANIUM → TiO₂; COPPER → Cu₂O (reddish patina → green basic carbonate 'verdigris' over time — Statue of Liberty is copper patinated green). HOT DIP GALVANISATION (Zn coating on iron) — Zn preferentially corrodes, protecting iron even if scratched (SACRIFICIAL protection). forms a passive self-healing layer.

cards.front:
Which METAL is liquid at room temperature?

(A) Sodium
(B) Mercury
(C) Gallium
(D) Aluminium
cards.back:
(B) Mercury

Elements & Mixed — Mercury (Hg) is the only metal liquid at ordinary room temperature (melting point −39 °C). Gallium melts in the hand (~30 °C) but is solid at typical room temperature of 20-25 °C. Bromine is the only liquid non-metal at room temperature.

cards.front:
Consider the following about CORROSION OF IRON. 1. It requires both oxygen AND water. 2. It is an electrochemical (galvanic) process. 3. Galvanisation (zinc coating) protects iron by acting as a sacrificial anode. 4. Painting works purely as a physical barrier. Which are correct?

(A) 1, 2 and 3 only
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(C) 1 and 4 only
(D) 2 and 3 only
cards.back:
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4

Elements & Mixed — All four correct. Rusting = electrochemical, needs O2 + H2O. Zn is more reactive than Fe, so in galvanising it corrodes preferentially, saving the iron. Paint provides a physical barrier that keeps water + O2 from reaching the iron surface (not sacrificial).

cards.front:
The HARDEST natural substance known is:

(A) Iron
(B) Diamond
(C) Graphite
(D) Quartz
cards.back:
(B) Diamond

Elements & Mixed — Diamond = tetrahedral network of sp³ C-C bonds → hardest natural substance. Mohs 10. Graphite (hexagonal layers) is SOFT despite being the same element. (Synthetic materials harder than diamond exist — e.g., wurtzite boron nitride under specific conditions.)

cards.front:
A MOLE of any substance contains:

(A) 6.022 × 10²³ particles
(B) 6.022 × 10²⁴ particles
(C) 1 kg of mass
(D) 22.4 litres of volume at STP
cards.back:
(A) 6.022 × 10²³ particles

Elements & Mixed — Avogadro's number NA = 6.022 × 10²³ per mole (exact since 2019 SI redefinition). Distractor D is a partial truth — 22.4 L is the molar volume of IDEAL GAS at OLD-STP only (1 atm, 0 °C), not a definition of the mole. atoms/molecules/ions.

cards.front:
Which of the following is INCORRECTLY paired?

(A) Bleaching powder — Ca(OCl)Cl
(B) Plaster of Paris — CaSO4·½H2O
(C) Gypsum — CaSO4·2H2O
(D) Washing soda — NaHCO3
cards.back:
(D) Washing soda — NaHCO3

Elements & Mixed — Washing soda is Na2CO3·10H2O (sodium carbonate decahydrate). NaHCO3 is baking soda. Other three pairings are correct. Trap: both have 'soda' in the name.
